#3580. Dolly Parton Is Gone, But Dollywood Will Always Love Her

“RIP Dolly Smoky Mountain Angel” was one of the first signs we saw as we pulled up on the side of a motel in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee. Just down the same road was another memorial to her on a Burger King sign. This was in early October. Dolly Parton, the country singer and actor, widely considered a Great American Who Everyone Loves, had died, at the age of 80, in late August. I am not the kind of person who cries over celebrity deaths, but after I heard that she died, I went to my closet to find a Dolly Parton T-shirt I had bought the one time I saw her live, at a concert of mostly acoustic songs in Queens in 2016. I couldn’t find it. I blamed my brief flirtation with the Marie Kondo method, but there was no way that T-shirt hadn’t sparked joy.

Early October in Sevier County, in far eastern Tennessee, where Parton was born, is full of cabins on some parcels of land that dot the ancient Appalachians. But among the rolling green expanses are Mexican supermarkets, coffee shops, apple orchards, and pumpkin patches. This is where she opened the amusement park Dollywood in 1986. The Great Smoky Mountains National Park draws masses about 13 miles from Dollywood. The fancier of my friends identified the area as where the Blackberry Farm resort is. But Pigeon Forge has a feeling of a Jersey Shore boardwalk in Appalachia, with a strip of businesses that sell vapes and ATV rides and Moon Pies a block from a Margaritaville hotel.

Parton opened Dollywood in 1986 at the foothills of the Great Smoky Mountains. Today, it draws in millions of people annually—loving fans who don her iconic pink cowboy hat or accessories honoring the park's famous Grist Mill Cinnamon Bread (a cult favorite).

Locals heap the kind of praise on Parton that we’ve come to expect knowing her reputation as a goddess among mortals. “People don’t understand what she did for this place and meant to this place. She threw lots of money at it and went out of her way to take care of this place,” an Uber driver named Eric told me as we exited the highway into Dollywood, with its script logo and “love every moment” greeting signs. “I got to meet her three times at the park because she would just show up and stand there with a crowd of people. For someone who’s been famous as long as she’s been famous you’d expect a certain air of haughtiness,” he says. “But I was stunned at how kind she was.”

Parton’s job title at the park was dreamer-in-chief, and part of Dollywood’s allure is that it’s a shrine to her life and career. There’s a replica of the two-room wood cabin where she grew up a sharecropper’s daughter, in close quarters alongside her parents and 10 siblings. Her home, not even 500 square feet, had no electricity nor running water. (The original home still stands about 10 miles away but isn’t open to the public.)

Parton wrote the country ballad “I Will Always Love You” in 1973 as a heartfelt farewell to her longtime business partner Porter Wagoner. Now, fans honoring Dolly's memory have used the slogan for the park's new annual festival, which opens in March 2027.

That modest beginning is plenty known, but Dollywood also celebrates Parton as she became a household name and wildly rich. The Dolly Parton Experience is a museum devoted to her trajectory, from Nashville ingenue to a celebrity among celebrities (photos show her with Mick Jagger in the ’60s and Whitney Houston in the ’90s). It has a gallery devoted to her Imagination Library, which has donated more than 300 million books to children around the world. Another building across a landscaped path celebrates her role in the workplace revenge comedy 9 to 5 (September 25 has now been christened a holiday in Sevier County) and houses a half dozen of her wigs, sorted by decade, all platinum, all voluminous. A plaque commemorates her wig stylists, starting with her Aunt Colleen. Parton’s costumes are scattered around the tributes, including a black flared jumpsuit with a hot pink shirt and neck ruffle so intense it looks Elizabethan. One wall features one of Parton’s famously self-effacing quotes: “It costs a lot of money to look this cheap.”

In her mobile home, which guests line up around to take a tour, she has a closet with a hanging yellow diamanté dress, a full-size bathtub because she preferred baths to showers, mirrored ceilings because she was claustrophobic, and cheeky digital clocks that display her most hallowed time zones: Dollywood (5:53 p.m. ET) and Nashville (4:53 p.m. CT). I ask our tour guide, a woman in a sparkly vest, how she and the park employees have fared without Parton. “Today is the first day I haven’t cried,” she admits.

Dollywood is more than a museum—it's an amusement park. The 165-acre Pigeon Forge carnival features over 50 rides and Dollywood's Splash Country, a 35-acre water park.

But more than a museum, Dollywood is an amusement park, and a much bigger one than I had realized. It’s a place where you can stand in line for 45 minutes to buy a corn dog while listening to a four-person singing-and-dancing group in the vein of the Mickey Mouse Club does peppy but half-assed covers of Fleetwood Mac and Van Halen. Looping rollercoasters and water tube rides leave families soaking wet in matching T-shirts commemorating their vacations. Dondre, my colleague and our photographer for this journey, waits probably a full hour to squeeze into a vintage muscle car with me so I can simulate steering around a track. It wasn’t until deep into our wait time that we realize this is a children’s ride. At this point, the two of us notice that, in the sea of people, we are the only ones who are childless, wearing dark colors, and audibly bemoaning that Dollywood is dry. (Parton was not a strict teetotaler, but the park bills itself as assertively family-friendly. “Weapons and alcoholic beverages are not permitted on Dollywood Property” is the only explanation given on its website.) No one else seems to care. The ride is quick, but we are ecstatic, high on refillable Diet Cokes, kettle corn, and driving a car, which neither one of us knows how to do in real life.

Some park employees have not fared well without Parton. One tour guide admits: “Today is the first day I haven’t cried." Parton passed away on August 25 at the age of 80 after a battle with cancer.

We don’t want real life at Dollywood. We want the dreamer-in-chief’s dreams. For dinner, we hit the 8:30 show of Dolly Parton’s Stampede in Pigeon Forge, an equestrian version of dinner theater where guests are served a whole chicken, pulled pork, corn, greens, a biscuit, pie, and unlimited soda, all to be eaten by hand while the not so vague perfume of manure wafts through the air. Horses with cowboys and cowgirls astride them jump through rings of fire, someone does wire work while dangling from the ceiling, and American flags fly in abundance. We catch a pig race. Sooo-ey! At another point, a volunteer from the audience disappears from a barrel before our eyes. The whole thing feels psychedelic, and we peak when performers in butterfly wings ride around to Parton’s song “Love Is Like a Butterfly.” I squeal as a few actual buffalo take the arena. After the show, I ask a cowboy how the majestic creatures are as animal coworkers, and he shakes his head. “There’s a reason I stick to horses.”

Even in the perfect bubble of Dollywood, in the wake of her death, Parton’s spirit has already faded into the nostalgia.

There isn’t enough acknowledgement of Parton’s death at the park for my taste; no candlelit vigil or impersonators we can hug. By the second day, my mania has subsided, giving way to contemplation. I ask fellow parkgoers if they have come to pay respects. Every single one replies that their trip has been planned long before. My attempts to make small talk with strangers doesn’t result in the fantasy of one collective mourning. Families in seasonal T-shirts seem shy and uninterested in chatting with me, a strangely inquisitive middle-aged woman who wants to ask them if they’ve heard the rumor that Dolly Parton was secretly covered in tattoos. (They haven’t.) A friend group of two lesbian couples from Pennsylvania brushes off my line of questioning around whether Parton might have been more than just queer-friendly (rainbow Dollywood shirts and backpacks and trucker caps are for sale). Too soon, they say, and shake their heads—too salacious to be airing gossip. I ask other strangers if they have heard the family drama over Parton’s estate. Most dismiss me, but another Uber driver, this one named Austin, says, “She has a huge estate and a big family, and it was always going to happen. We’ll see how it plays out.” (In November, the lawsuit was dropped, and Parton’s nephew said he was happy to put the issue behind him.)

The butterfly is a key part of Dollywood's logo, representing Parton's personal emblem. As a little girl growing up in the Smoky Mountains, she was fascinated by butterflies and related to their gentle grace. She cemented the motif into her career in 1974 with the hit song, “Love is Like a Butterfly.”

Maybe, I say to Dondre, no one will talk to me because I, unlike about 50% of the people there, am not wearing a T-shirt emblazoned with a Bible verse, a military slogan, or a celebration of America’s 250 years. I keep pointing out paintings of crosses and eagles and American flags—often all combined on one canvas together—for sale. Dondre says, in a kind way, that nothing is more cliché than hearing someone from New York talk about other parts of the country. Maybe what made Dolly Parton so winning—her apparent lack of judgment—is not something I inherently have. It can’t hurt to try to be a little more like Parton in our own daily lives.

Maybe she had an optimism no one can ever replace. And that’s ultimately okay because you can try to channel that anywhere. Even in the perfect bubble of Dollywood, in the wake of her death, Parton’s spirit has already faded into the nostalgia, a curio like Graceland, but with a vintage steam train ride.

I succumb and buy a Christmas ornament with Parton dressed as Santa and eat a chicken salad sandwich served on a butterfly-logo-shaped pretzel. I guess I enjoy Dollywood the way I enjoy going dancing in Berlin gay clubs or karaoke birthday parties: It is an experience, and a fun one, but not what I would choose. I will never, in the vein of a Disney Adult, be a Dolly Adult. More power to those who cherish their season passes. But Parton doesn’t even have to be core to your identity for you to enjoy an intricately branded amusement park. Its unchanging presence is a comfort. If you need to commune with her earthly treasures, there is always Dollywood. May her costumes and wigs remain.

Dollywood will always be a place for fans and dreamers alike to marvel in the wonder of the country icon’s extraordinary career and charming home.

It appears the Barefoot Contessa knew a thing or two about Batman's travel plans.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I spend a lot of time keeping up with the 2026 movie schedule and all the upcoming superhero movies, but Jennifer Garner left me thinking about a Batman production from a decade ago. The actress recently shared a fond memory involving Ben Affleck, Ina Garten and an unforgettable family trip to Paris. I love that the Caped Crusader barely scratches the surface of what made it so special.

During a conversation on Happy Hour with Ina Garten, the 13 Going on 30 actress recalled taking her children overseas while Affleck was filming in London. Apparently, the comic book movie production provided the perfect excuse to get out of town for a while. Garner explained:

When my kids were little, I went to Paris. Ben was shooting some Batman-ish movie in London, and we went for six weeks. I took them out of school. It was the last time I really took kids out of school, but it was wonderful. It was incredible. It was so fun.

I recently revisited Affleck and Garner's time making Daredevil together, so hearing her describe his later superhero blockbuster as some "Batman-ish movie" is especially funny. I imagine Affleck had a few more specific words for the project, but I appreciate Garner remembers the family adventure rather than whatever Bruce Wayne was getting up to at the time.

Her timing also helps identify the film. While Justice League arrived in theaters in 2017, Affleck and the production spent months filming in London the previous year. Reports from that April confirmed that Garner and their three children planned to stay in the U.K. during production. By May, the family had also been spotted vacationing in Paris. So, despite the wonderfully vague description, Justice League appears to be our Batman-ish culprit.

There's a bittersweet wrinkle to the timeline. Garner and Affleck announced their separation in 2015, before the trip, and officially filed for divorce in 2017. Their divorce was finalized the following year. That makes this a particularly sweet memory of their family life during a complicated period. The two have maintained a close co-parenting relationship since, with Garner recently praising Affleck for helping care for their children while she works.

Apparently, we have Ina Garten to thank for one of Garner's favorite memories from the trip. With her youngest son, Samuel, only 4 at the time, Garner shared photos of the kids with Garten, who suggested they take a boat ride along the Seine. Really, who am I to argue with the Barefoot Contessa about how to spend an afternoon in Paris?

Garner recalled cruising down the river as the city began lighting up around them, and the experience stuck with her. She's since made a point of doing it whenever she returns to Paris, and looking back at those original photos still reminds her of how happy the kids were. She told Garten that her suggestion made the whole thing "such an adventure." I love that something as simple as taking a boat ride became one of those family memories she keeps coming back to.

Garten's Paris recommendations didn't stop there. Years later, when Garner returned with her eldest daughter Violet, she texted her friend for another round of suggestions. This time Garten sent them to a handbag boutique, a cheese shop, a specialty food market and a restaurant specializing in soufflés. Violet apparently enjoyed the itinerary so much that she retraced their steps while studying abroad. Now I'm wondering how I get Ina Garten's number before my next vacation.

I like hearing Garner speak so fondly about those days, especially knowing what was happening in her personal life at the time. It also makes me wonder how many wonderful family memories get made while Hollywood's biggest productions happen in the background.

Affleck might have been busy bringing his take on The Dark Knight to life; his wife and kids were apparently having an adventure all their own. Something tells me those Paris photographs mean a whole lot more to her than another superhero movie ever could.

#3578. If You Loved 'Below,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Foggy, cold, and hardscrabble, the community of Snook’s Arm, Newfoundland, is the perfect spot for ocean-borne horror in Netflix's Below. This sense of place sets the series apart, though the characters who inhabit it are equally fascinating. Led by Josh Hartnett’s grounded performance as Calvin, the show has atmosphere for days, and a creepy and compelling story that effortlessly balances chills and deep emotional beats.

If you ate this show up like a voracious sea creature and you’re craving more slow-burn, deeply human horror (and you’ve already explored all the similar streaming series out there), it’s time to move on to feature-length terror, and there's one classic movie that fits the bill.

When it comes to kindred sea monster stories, Jaws is the obvious choice. Seaside setting? Check—a pre-glam Martha’s Vineyard stands in for Amity Island, with beautiful beaches and crashing waves to spare. A tight community under threat? Check—Amity Island feels like a very real place, and its citizens have concerns and grudges as legitimate as Calvin’s in Below. Shocks and frights? This is Jaws, a film that transformed the entire business of blockbuster movies, renowned to this day for its masterful depiction of a relentless natural force threatening an entire town.

The basic story also echoes Below's: When a young woman is killed by a shark during a night swim, Amity Island Police Chief Martin Brody (Roy Scheider) tries to close the beaches to protect the public, but Mayor Vaughn (Murray Hamilton) refuses, as Amity Island depends on the tourist trade for its survival. After a young boy is killed, Brody teams up with shark hunter Quint (Robert Shaw) and oceanographer Hooper (Richard Dreyfuss) to hunt the beast, and the three soon find themselves in over their heads as they discover how big and relentless the shark really is. Both stories share themes of economic necessity trumping safety in a changing world and concepts of a small group of people fighting a terrifying natural threat.

Like almost every horror film or series since 1975, Below owes a debt to Jaws in terms of storytelling and technique. From the isolated, ocean-centric setting (and monster) to the way Below shows you only flashes of its central terror, if you enjoyed the series, you will absolutely love the classic that influenced it. Stream Jaws on Netflix, or rent it on Prime Video.

Already seen Jaws, or rewatched it, and still in need of more terrifying movies in the same vein as Below? Here are a few more movies that you’ll love.

The Bay takes a different approach to its scares than Below—it’s a found-footage horror film. But it shares the remote, water-centric setting, the focus on a small community, and a story that pulls from the terror of a fundamental element—water—being polluted and corrupted. In the coastal community of Claridge, Maryland, citizens fall severely ill and begin dying in large numbers, sparking chaos. As investigators race to discover the source of the affliction, the carnage gets seriously gnarly. Just like in Below, the ultimate threat stems from the way people recklessly abuse the world we depend on for survival, and the local residents are center stage in the fight. Stream The Bay on Tubi or rent it on Prime Video.

One aspect of Below that resonates strongly with viewers is the human element; the Penney family’s internal tensions feel earned and real, and the way the larger community struggles with several existential crises is messy in a gloriously human way. The Host is also about a family struggling against a horrific, waterborne monster—when a mutant creature attacks a crowd near the Han River, Park Gang-du loses his grip on his young daughter, and she’s snatched up by the monster. But when Gang-du receives a phone call from his daughter telling him she’s still alive but trapped with the creature in the sewers, his family escapes quarantine, gears up, and goes after her, no matter the odds (or the corrupt government agencies standing in the way). Stream The Host on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

Based on H.P. Lovecraft’s The Shadow Over Innsmouth, Dagon begins with four friends on a boat off the coast of Spain. When a storm wrecks the boat and injures one of them, a couple—Paul and Barbara—travel on foot to a nearby village to seek help. What they find instead is a terrifying place paying the price for worshiping a demon named Dagon in exchange for wealth and safety—but at a price that slowly rose, eventually transforming the villagers into something inhuman. Just like Below, the movie explores the choices communities make to survive, and the personal costs that aren’t always clearly understood. Stream Dagon on The Roku Channel or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you loved Below’s foggy, liminal feel and the constant dread of what might be lurking in the mist or under the waves, unseen until it’s too late, John Carpenter’s classic is a must-watch. As the small coastal town of Antonio Bay approaches the centennial of its founding, a strange fog rolls in from the sea and envelopes the town. As the body count rises, the true story of the town’s founding and subsequent prosperity is revealed—and the long-deferred price for the crimes of the town’s ancestors is in the fog, determined to find some element of justice. Stream The Fog on Kanopy or Plex, or rent it on Prime Video.

If remote communities like Snook’s Arm are inherently creepy to you, check out Offseason. When Marie (Jocelin Donahue) learns that her mother has passed away and has been buried in Lone Palm, the isolated beach town where she grew up, she’s outraged—her mother was very clear that she didn’t want to be buried there. Marie travels to Lone Palm as tourist season ends, just a day before the bridge to the mainland closes for the year, which gives the town a liminal, nightmarish aspect familiar to anyone who’s lived in a tourist town during the offseason. As a storm moves in, Marie and her boyfriend find the townsfolk behaving quite strangely—and soon, it all whips up into a maelstrom of terror that fans of Below will appreciate. Stream Offseason on Hoopla or rent it on Prime Video.

#3577. Colin Farrell's Remake Of A '90s Sci-Fi Movie Is One Of Prime Video's Biggest Streaming Hits

"Total Recall" (2012) is directed by Len Wiseman, who most recently oversaw the 2025 "John Wick" offshoot "Ballerina" and previously helmed the "Underworld" films between 2003 and 2016. He is, unfortunately, also responsible for 2007's "Live Free or Die Hard," which, despite making the third spot on /Film's "Die Hard" movie ranking, we simply could have done without.

Unlike the 1990 original, "Total Recall" is set entirely on an Earth ravaged by chemical war, leaving only the United Federation of Britain (UFB) and the Colony (Australia) habitable. Whereas Arnold Schwarzenegger's Douglas Quaid had dreams of Mars, which turn out to be long-buried memories, Colin Farrell's counterpart finds himself experiencing nocturnal visions of being a secret agent. Bored of his factory job on The Colony, he enlists the company Rekall to implant artificial memories to match his dreams, which he soon learns are, in fact, memories of having worked as a UFB agent. Hunted by his former employers, he teams up with Jessica Biel's Melina, a member of a rebel group known as The Resistance. But as the pair try to outrun the UFB and their Chancellor Vilos Cohaagen (Bryan Cranston), the line between fantasy and reality becomes increasingly blurred.

Ahead of the film's debut, /Film asked: "Is 'Total Recall' the least essential film of the summer?" The answer, according to most critics, was yes. But it seems the Prime Video crowds are willing to give it another shot. Per streaming viewership tracker FlixPatrol, "Total Recall" is the No. 3 most-watched movie on Prime Video in the United States as of November 9, 2026. What's more, based on the film's trajectory thus far, it could be set for a chart-topping run. "Total Recall" debuted on the charts at No. 9 on November 7, 2026, before jumping to fourth the following day and hitting No. 3 the day after. By the end of the week, Farrell's forgotten remake might just hit No. 1 — not bad for a film with a 30% critic score on Rotten Tomatoes.

Both Philip K. Dick's story and the 1990 "Total Recall" film feature Mars. But the 2012 remake actually has more in common with Paul Verhoeven's rendition than the novel, using characters that only appear in the movie and adhering more closely to the big-screen storyline. That might have seemed like a reasonable approach, given how the first film was so successful. Unfortunately, Len Wiseman's effort didn't emulate the offbeat comedy of the original, which was so sharply rendered by Arnold Schwarzenegger and gave the film such a unique tone. Despite featuring some impressive action scenes, Wiseman's version also managed to feel like a generic sci-fi actioner, all of which combined to yield a less-than-impressive critical response.

That said, Roger Ebert was impressed enough to bestow three stars on the film — just half a star less than the 1990 version — and called it a "well-crafted, high-energy sci-fi." Still, even he had to admit that the film was one of several sci-fi movie remakes that should have never happened, ending his review by writing, "It never touched me emotionally, though, the way the 1990 film did, and strictly speaking, isn't necessary." Others were much more condemnatory, with David Sexton of the London Evening Standard giving the film one star and writing, "We used to do the future so much better. Let's not forget that. Let's forget this instead."

Normally, that should deter you from joining the "Total Recall" renaissance on Prime Video. But considering that, since the movie's debut, we've been subjected to an onslaught of streaming movie shabbiness, it might be worth a go to see if the remake really is bad or whether that's merely a memory implanted by the critics.

#3576. Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries Face Democratic Leadership Revolt After Midterms

The latest conflict brewing in the Democratic Party’s cold war between the blue dogs and the insurgent progressive wing is the fight over its next congressional leaders. But with no alternate candidates stepping up to run, it’s hard to determine how real the threats to replace Senator Chuck Schumer and Representative Hakeem Jeffries actually are.

At least six incoming Democratic senators—including Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed, South Carolina’s Annie Andrews, Minnesota’s Peggy Flanagan, Illinois’s Juliana Stratton, Kansas’s Adam Hamilton, and Maine’s Troy Jackson—have said they won’t support Schumer for majority leader. Michigan senator Elissa Slotkin has called for a “a new generation of leadership.” Even Cory Booker, who praised Schumer for helping engineer last week’s blue wave, stopped short of saying whether he would support him. On Monday, Richard Blumenthal did the same, but walked by his comments later in day, saying he would support Schumer. And Jon Stewart said that the senator “does not understand the urgency of the moment and what the future demands.” Regardless, Schumer is confident. His aides say he has enough votes to become the next majority leader.

In the House, several incoming Democrats—including Claire Valdez, Angela Gonzalez-Torres, Darializa Avila Chevalier, Melat Kiros, Adam Hamawy, Chris Rabb, and Donavan McKinney—have been noncommittal with their support for Jeffries, while Ohio democrat Don Leonard has threatened to seek alternative leadership unless Jeffries changes his position on Israel.

There’s an online effort to prevent Jeffries from becoming Speaker of the House. A change.org petition demanding that House Democrats reject Jeffries as their next Speaker has attracted more than 1 million signatures as of Sunday, with actor Mark Ruffalo among those encouraging people to sign. But scroll to the bottom of the petition, and you’ll find a disclosure: Its creator, Nicole Whitted, is a paid “Change Ambassador” who receives compensation from change.org in connection with the signatures. “Thousands of organizations and brands worldwide run similar programs and in the social-cause space specifically, it’s a way to encourage people with reach and influence to use their voice for causes they care about,” Whitted told Vanity Fair in a statement.

Whitted also said she was traveling to Washington, DC next week to urge congresspeople to vote against Jeffries, and to meet with Representative Ayanna Pressley, whom Whitted told VF she’ll be supporting for Speaker. Pressley’s team did not respond to Vanity Fair’s request for comment sent on Sunday. Neither did her closest congressional allies, Rashida Tlaib, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, or Ilhan Omar.

Reports indicate that some congresspeople have been flooded with calls from constituents urging them to find new party leadership. But one Democratic aide told Vanity Fair that they’ve noticed what they claim is a coordinated effort to undermine Jeffries on social media, including AI-generated videos attacking Jeffries that have gotten tens of thousands of engagements.

The Brooklyn congressman does have good relationships with members of both the moderate “blue dogs” and the party’s progressive flank. Ocasio-Cortez has already backed him, and last month, Representative Ro Khanna declared that “Hakeem Jeffries is going to be Speaker.” “Don’t believe what you’re seeing on the internet,” the aide said. “It’s not reality.”

Schumer’s allies, meanwhile, have been reminding skeptics of the work he did to deliver the Democratic majority. The New York senator helped recruit candidates including Roy Cooper and Sherrod Brown, while the Democratic political operation supporting Senate candidates spent lavishly on competitive races. According to final figures provided to Vanity Fair, Senate Majority PAC and its affiliates spent nearly $407 million across races in eight states, including $150 million in Ohio, $67 million apiece in Iowa and Michigan, $65 million in Maine, and $40 million in Texas, all of which flipped. Another $14 million went toward Kansas, with smaller investments in Mississippi and South Carolina—$2.2 million and $750,000 respectively. Some of that money helped elect candidates who are now skeptical about whether Schumer should stay in charge.

In the House, each party will choose its leadership this month, but in order to become Speaker, a candidate still needs to get a majority of the entire chamber, usually 218 members, to vote for them when the new Congress convenes in January. It’s a little easier in the Senate, where the Democrat will only need to win a simple majority of their own caucus in an anonymous early December vote to become majority leader.

El-Sayed has suggested Maryland senator Chris Van Hollen, although a source close to Van Hollen told Vanity Fair that he isn’t planning to run, instead setting his sights on a potential presidential campaign in 2028. “Prior to selecting a majority leader, Senator Van Hollen believes the caucus needs to have an honest and open conversation about how we move an agenda forward that reflects the will of the American people,” says a Democratic aide familiar with the senator’s thinking. “He’s made clear that Democrats need to use their power to immediately end the illegal war with Iran, advance a robust pro-worker kitchen table agenda, and fight political corruption.”

Another name circulating among Democratic aides is Hawaii senator Brian Schatz, a relatively young progressive who has developed relationships across the party’s ideological factions and is already pursuing the number-two leadership position being vacated by retiring senator Dick Durbin.

“He’s the heir apparent,” one Democratic aide told Vanity Fair, describing Schatz as someone who could appeal to both progressives and moderates. Asked about speculation surrounding his leadership ambitions, Schatz’s spokesperson offered a noncommittal response: “I don’t have anything new to share on this but will keep you posted if that changes.”

Some Democrats are also hesitant to replace their experienced leaders after they’ve been given this narrow opportunity to get stuff done with control of both chambers of Congress. “I don’t think you’d want somebody new who’s, like, learning the ropes while we have the opportunity to really get meaningful legislation passed for the American people,” another Democratic aide said.

Still, the fighting online and on cable news exposes a tension within the Democratic Party. Moderates see the blue wave as vindication of the party’s disciplined, affordability-focused strategy. Progressives see it as a mandate for a more ambitious agenda—and a rejection of the establishment’s familiar faces.

Both factions are claiming the election as their own victory. But before they can fight over what to do with their new power, they’ll have to decide who’s going to lead them.

#3575. I Tested Strava's New Integration With Gemini, and I Have Thoughts

Once connected, you can ask questions like:

"Am I getting faster at the same heart rate?"

"Can you give me a detailed analysis of how I performed in my last race?"

"How is my strength training impacting my running?"

Some important context here: Strava's AI "insights" have sort of sucked, and annoyed me, in the past. Athlete Intelligence (conveniently abbreviated as AI) is the Strava feature that writes text responses to your workouts. Strava calls these "insights," but as far as I can tell they mostly regurgitate the information from the workout description, sometimes with added errors. I've found AI fitness summaries largely useless, and Strava's version checks every box: It doesn't use enough context to understand what's going on, it presents generic advice as if it were personal, and it's overconfident in incomplete data. So, skeptical as I am, I gave Strava's latest Google Gemini integration a whirl. Here's what it does, how to set it up, and whether it's worth it.

The first question I asked was one of Strava’s examples, "Am I getting faster at the same heart rate?" Gemini said yes, I was seeing solid efficiency gains. Like many AI tools, it told me what I wanted to hear. I had to point out that heat and temperature are huge variables. When I steered the chat in that direction, Gemini, of course, agreed immediately ("you hit the nail on the head") and explained that my mid-September long runs happened in 75–84°F weather with higher humidity, which inflates heart rate, while October's cooler temperatures made the same effort look better. That's an important caveat the first answer left out entirely.

I then asked it to compare my past marathons, and in many ways, I had fun here. For instance, the suggested follow-ups prompted me to think of questions I hadn't put on my list, like comparing my weekly running volume and long-run frequency leading into different races in different years.

Unfortunately, the results weren't reliable at first. When I asked for a detailed analysis of every marathon-distance effort since 2019, Gemini said I had exactly one, the Marine Corps Marathon on October 25, 2026. In reality, I've logged at least eight. When I asked why it couldn't see them, it explained that its access is limited to my recent history, roughly summer 2026 onward, because of how pagination limits the number of past activities returned at once. It also offered a workaround: Give it specific dates and locations.

That workaround works, but it means you have to already know what you're looking for. And still, it wasn't consistent. In other answers, Gemini referenced my 2025 NYC Marathon and 2024 Philadelphia race, so the data's reach seems uneven. You need to be able to query older date ranges as directly and specifically as possible, and even still, double-check any numbers that matter to you.

I then asked "What am I doing right and what am I doing wrong as a runner?" After knowing the queries need to be so specific, I intentionally wanted to test a vague, simplistic question. The answer was, true to form, overly flattering—though I didn't disagree with the guidance itself. I need more speed workouts! I know this! I didn't need a chatbot to tell me, though maybe some other Strava user does. Gemini's suggestions (polarize training, add one dedicated threshold day) are sound, yes, but they’re also generic. Most recreational runners could glance at my Strava and spot the same strengths and weaknesses. Similarly, Gemini then set itself up for a slam dunk by prompting me to ask whether my easy runs were too fast. The answer: My easy days were happening at nearly my marathon pace (about 9:43/mi), and I should slow down by 45–90 seconds per mile, to roughly 10:30–11:15/mi. I completely agree. That being said, my big takeaway here remains the same: Don't confuse AI-generated advice as some newfound, personalized insight. It’s often the same conventional wisdom you already know, or could figure out with a tiny bit of research from a real, human source.

If you ask me—a human!—this is a classic case of using AI for rote tasks, but then saving critical thinking for your own human brain. Gemini didn't surface anything wildly insightful, and it skipped important considerations like the effect of heat on heart rate, until I raised them myself. But it pulled data faster than I could have by hand, and its follow-up prompts nudged me toward comparisons I might not have thought of.

For many users, the smartest approach may be to skip AI summaries and focus on raw data. After all, your training load, sleep duration, and heart rate trends are already perfectly actionable.

As with all things AI, it’s important to mind the gap between data and wisdom. So much wisdom gets lost—forfeited, even—when you blindly trust an AI coach. Make sure you aren’t offloading all the other skills you need as a runner and as a human, like your ability to listen to your body and maybe run a little slower in the heat, even when it makes your data look “worse.”

If you do use Google Gemini to analyze your Strava data:

Be specific about dates and locations when asking about older activities.

Push back. Ask about weather, terrain, and fatigue before accepting a flattering conclusion.

Treat the output as a fast data pull, not a personal coach.

#3574. Robert Pattinson's James Bond Comments Resurface 14 Years Later Amid Casting Rumors

Fresh off his electric performance in the dark, unsettling media satire "Primetime," Robert Pattinson is said to be in contention for the role of James Bond. According to The Hollywood Reporter, Pattinson screen tested for the part in Denis Villeneuve's upcoming Bond reboot movie for Amazon MGM Studios, which puts him in the running alongside several other well-known contenders. For the actor, it has been a long time coming. It seems that, 14 years ago, Pattinson envisioned stepping into the 007 role at a later point in his career.

In a 2012 interview with The Sun (via NDTV), the British star said he'd "definitely like to go for Bond" but wanted to wait another 20 years. "There'd be nothing worse than, like, 'Let's get a fresh-faced Bond!'" he added. "That would be the worst idea in the world. It would be ridiculous to reinvent it as some young posh kid." At the time, he was just starting to make his transition from teen heartthrob to chameleonic leading man, and was promoting what has since become known as one of Pattinson's best movies, David Cronenberg's "Cosmopolis." Since then, much has changed, and while it hasn't quite been two decades, it seems the actor wasn't kidding when he said he'd one day like to play 007.

Back in October 2026, it was reported that Josh O'Connor was one of the Bond finalists, alongside "Fantastic Beasts" actor Callum Turner, and "Slow Horses" star Jack Lowden. Since then, reports have claimed that Nicholas Hoult and Pattinson are also in the final group, which means five actors are now vying for the role of England's greatest spy. If Pattinson does land the role, it will be yet another major success for the actor and, given his prior comments, a particularly satisfying one.

In his interview with The Sun, Robert Pattinson seemed entirely opposed to the idea of a young James Bond. "After Daniel Craig you have to have some baggage," he said of the erstwhile Bond actor, who reinvented the spy for a new generation with the unbeatable "Casino Royale" in 2006. "I'd have to be tortured in the first few scenes. I'd have to do the first film with one arm or something." It's unclear just how serious Pattinson was at the time, but he seemed to have an awareness of just how tortured a version of Bond Craig portrayed during his tenure in the tux.

With that in mind, it will be interesting to see, if Pattinson does land the part, whether he doubles down on the haunted loner version of 007 he mentioned in his 2012 comments. The best Bonds have all had an edge to them, but it might be that Denis Villeneuve and Amazon MGM want to go in a different direction after the diminishing returns of the Craig era Bond films.

As it stands, nobody knows for sure who will play the lead role in Villeneuve's upcoming film. Based on the finalists, one thing we do know is that Amazon won't be going the "young posh kid" route, to use Pattinson's phrasing. All the contenders are 36 years old, except for Pattinson who at 40 is the oldest of the bunch. With final screen tests said to have already taken place, it won't be long before we get an official announcement, and if Pattinson does land the role we at least know he's been mentally preparing for 14 years.

#3572. Why Those Flashy Halloween Contacts Are a Bad Idea

Contacts with cat pupils or neon colors can be fun, but are you sure you want to put a piece of plastic from a costume store into your eye? Experts, like those at the American Academy of Ophthalmology, warn against it. These non-prescription contacts are technically illegal in the U.S. (even though plenty of companies sell them anyway). The CDC warns that the risks include "eye sores and vision loss."

Cheap Halloween contacts tend to be one-size-fits-all, but the AAO points out that contacts should never be one-size-fits-all. A contact that is too large or too small for your eye can cause corneal abrasions, corneal ulcers, and can result in infections like keratitis. Infections can, in severe cases, lead to blindness. A 2017 report from the FDA found bacterial contamination in 27% of costume contacts.

If you do wear contacts (Halloween or otherwise), the AAO recommends keeping an eye out for symptoms like redness, swelling, pain, or excessive discharge. Seek care as soon as you suspect an infection. Your eyes are more sensitive to infections than other parts of the body, so be cautious.

Legally, contacts require a prescription, so if those colored contacts you're eyeing can be bought without showing a doctor’s prescription, they’re not legit. The real thing can be expensive, though: I found prices of $40 and up from lens.com, Discount Contacts, and Wicked Eyez.

These websites all let you order online, but you’ll have to provide your prescription information before you can check out. Fortunately, the Federal Trade Commission has ruled that providers must give you your contact prescription after a fitting so that you can take the prescription elsewhere. And they cannot charge you extra for this.

Once you’ve got the lenses, you have to know how to take care of them. If you wear contacts every day, you already know the drill. But if you’re just picking up a pair to use with a costume, here are the basics:

Wash your hands before handling the lenses.

Store them in contact lens solution, and keep the lenses and their case clean.

And for Pete’s sake, don’t share them with your friends!

Just remember, the bloodshot look stops being cool after you take your zombie costume off.

#3571. 22 Years Later, The Polar Express' Best Line Is Still One Of The Best Christmas Movie Quotes

Published in 1985, Chris Van Allsburg's picture book "The Polar Express" is a staple of children's Christmas literature. Filmmaker Robert Zemeckis brought its yuletide magic to the silver screen in 2004 with an animated film. Zemeckis had once blended live-action and animation in "Who Framed Roger Rabbit" by sticking Bob Hoskins next to cartoon characters, and with "Polar Express," he aimed to achieve an even deeper fusing of mediums with motion capture.

"Polar Express" didn't open to the smoothest ride. With an exorbitant $170 million budget, the movie was greeted by some as a failure for grossing only $286 million. The use of motion capture animation made the whole thing look uncanny (and became a "30 Rock" punchline), which is the last thing you want for what's meant to be a heartwarming family movie. Not that this stopped Zemeckis from using the same "Polar Express" style in 2007's "Beowulf" and 2009's "A Christmas Carol" (featuring Jim Carrey as Scrooge). "The Polar Express" divided critics in its day, as seen by its 55% Rotten Tomatoes score. Roger Ebert gave it a perfect four stars rating, but others couldn't get over the creepy animation.

But any kids movie seen by enough kids of its generation usually transforms into a classic with time. The movie is also often re-released in theaters during the holiday season. There have been events like branded Polar Express train trips or "Polar Express in Concert," too. Many see "The Polar Express" as a ride they like to take again and again, and, as of 2024, a sequel was in very early development. Let's take a look at one of the film's most memorable quotes.

"One thing about trains: it doesn't matter where they're going. What matters is deciding to get on."

The Conductor (Tom Hanks) tells this to the Hero Boy (Daryl Sabara, with some motion capture work from Josh Hutcherson) at the end of the latter's adventure. The boy is departing the Polar Express and returning home, never to doubt the existence of Santa Claus again. It's a clear rewording of the "it's the journey, not the destination, that matters" aphorism, but tweaked in a way to fit the story's themes of faith and belief.

Note that, in the film, we see the Conductor makes the kids choose to get onboard. The train shows up in front of their house, he tells them they're going to the North Pole, and if they refuse, he shrugs and says "suit yourself." The Hero Boy only jumps on when the train starts pulling out of his yard, seizing his moment and making his leap of faith at the last chance.

Faith is only faith if you believe without having true proof that the object of your belief is real. Even for something as harmless as choosing to believe in Santa Claus, making a choice of what to do with your life requires faith. Note also the other name for a train: a locomotive, a name all about movement. What matters is deciding to get on the train, the Conductor says, because choosing to not get on means standing in place and surrendering to fear of change. It's a good message to have in mind during Christmas, as one year closes out and a fresh one is about to blow in like a winter storm — or, indeed, a train arriving at a station.

#3570. Elon Musk’s Cybertruck Is Dumb, Ugly, and Mercifully Dead

In March 2024, a Tesla Cybertruck speeding down Sunset Boulevard slammed head-on into the Beverly Hills Hotel’s iconic entrance sign just before midnight. Passersby winding through the Flats slowed down to watch as Elon Musk’s statue to his own insecurities—the stainless steel embodiment of nuance-free American ego—demolished in front of Hollywood’s unofficial canteen.

Every decade gets the iconography it deserves. At just about the midpoint of the 2020s, ours had arrived, fully formed.

And now the Cybertruck is dead, which is wonderful news. Musk, who’s having a historically bad November, announced late last week that Tesla will be “winding down” production of the Cybertruck around mid-2027, putting an end to the most hated car in America. I was going to call it the most polarizing car in America, but honestly, no one likes this thing. And it’s not entirely due to anti-Elon sentiment: Tesla’s general sales have been relatively steady, going down a bit as Musk went full DOGE mode in 2025 before rebounding in 2026. People like Elon’s cars. They just do not like the Cybertruck.

True, its death has been mourned by some—especially the self-selecting devotees who installed bulletproof glass in their Cybertrucks before shooting them with rifles. These people exist. But mostly, the news has been greeted with a rush of enthusiasm, relief, and, more than anything else, blue-pilled schadenfreude.

Now would be the right moment in the news cycle for an art writer such as myself to make a contrarian argument: that the Cybertruck was secretly a design masterpiece—some kind of neo-Donald Judd breakthrough unleashed ahead of its time.

I am not going to make that argument, because that is not true. Not even close. No one in the future will look back on the Cybertruck as an unheralded art object. It’s The Jetsons for meatheads, a Batmobile for people who secretly root for the Joker. It looks like a birdhouse designed by Zaha Hadid, which I would love to have as a vessel for feeding hungry birds at my (sadly hypothetical) Zaha Hadid house. But I would not want it as a vehicle to park in a driveway. It is a bad car.

And yet, that crashed Cybertruck in front of the Beverly Hills Hotel is seared into my brain, playing on repeat like the most un-subtle Lana Del Rey song ever written. Even beyond that crash, the Cybertruck is the ultimate symbol of this surreal and cruel decade, one that started with a global pandemic and a government suggesting the possibility of a bleach injection as treatment. It’s a decade that wound through four years of a former president denying the lawful election of a current president, only to see that former president return to power. Through it all, we’ve sunk deeper into our collective psychosis—one that’s forced us into rooms with our devices, addicted to social media and artificial intelligence, consuming half-real information and spewing it back out into the world.

It’s a perfect world for the Tesla Cybertruck to define.

The Cybertruck arrived right at the dawn of the decade, in what we can now see as a completely different timeline.

Musk unveiled the car in November 2019 at Tesla’s design studio. Head designer Franz von Holzhausen attempted to demonstrate the vehicle’s shatterproof glass by hurtling a metal ball at a window at full speed. The window shattered. Great omen! It was also pretty weird that Musk was introduced by a hologram of someone called “Cybergirl,” who people speculated was actually a hologram of Grimes, the pop star Musk was dating at the time.

Plenty of design press fawned over the shiny new thing—“Long live the Cybertruck. See you in the Thunderdome,” wrote Dwell. But Wired wisely asked the opinion of an actual expert: Raphael Zammit, who chairs automobile design at Motor City’s own College for Creative Studies.

“I was like, ‘Oh my goodness! What did Tesla do? What did they do?” he said. “It literally breaks every rule we tell to our students. It’s what we tell them not to do.”

Regardless, the Cybertruck started to infiltrate the cultural atmosphere. It was lampooned on The Simpsons. There were countless memes. It was embraced, very early, by rappers. Weeks after the unveiling, Travis Scott used his personal connections to the Tesla CEO (they did Christmas together with the Kardashian-Jenners) to snag a Cybertruck for his video for “Gang Gang,” a posse cut with the Cactus Jack crew.

Three years later, Pharrell Williams, 21 Savage, and Tyler, the Creator featured the Cybertruck in their video for “Cash In, Cash Out”—rendered in Claymation. Offset’s video for “Swing My Way” has Anok Yai sitting atop a Cybertruck. Bad Bunny said, “Me monté en la Cybertruck y me acordé de la Montero de los viejos tiempo.” Meek Mill said, “They was doing cyber attacks, so I bought a Cybertruck.”

The cars fascinated artists too. Julia Wachtel’s CyberChrist, on view at Todd Von Ammon’s DC gallery, von ammon co, earlier this year, pictures Jesus Christ pulling an elongated Cybertruck behind him. I recall with great happiness the perverse thrill of Frieda Toranzo Jaeger’s Cybertruck, a painting in her 2022 show at MoMA PS1. These artists were certainly taking a critical eye toward the Cybertruck, but for some art collectors, there was nothing ironic about it. At least, a specific kind of collector. When I arrived at the convention center for Art Basel Miami Beach in 2024, the first full year of Cybertruck distribution, there was a line of Cybertrucks wrapped around the block.

But that’s the thing about the Cybertruck: There was always more supply than demand. Musk initially hoped to sell 250,000 units per year. According to automotive data platform Kelley Blue Book, Tesla moved nearly 39,000 of them in 2024, a decent start. In 2025, sales dropped, then dropped again in 2026.

Perhaps the Cybertruck could have endured the ridicule of design experts, car enthusiasts, and aesthetes with even just a whiff of good taste if it weren’t for the massive backlash that accompanied Musk’s move into radical right-wing politics, and his full-throated support of Donald Trump. After his efforts at DOGE resulted in the gutting of USAID and other agencies, along with unprecedented and remorseless mass firings, Cybertrucks started getting vandalized around the country. Some owners tried to protect their weird boxy investments with mea culpa stickers—“I bought this before Elon went crazy,” etc.—but no one believed that, or really cared. The cars got defaced. No one stepped in to intervene. The Cybertrucks deserved it.

There was also a bleaker incident that parallels the Cybertruck at the Beverly Hills Hotel: the dystopian hellscape of the Cybertruck that exploded on the Las Vegas Strip, in front of the Trump International Hotel & Casino. The man responsible for that explosion served in the US Army, and authorities believe he suffered a self-inflicted gunshot wound just before the vehicle detonated. The Beverly Hills crash was an accident in which no one was harmed—but the charred, deadly remains of the truck in Las Vegas seemed downright terrifying, a vision of American capitalism and greed that had met its grisly moment.

Perhaps now, with a new era of Washington poised to define the final years of this most delirious of decades, we’ll eventually look back at the Cybertruck with at least some nostalgia for its silliness, its boxy stupidity, its pop culture ubiquity. If it does linger in the annals of history, maybe we’ll think of the Cybertruck as a roadbound folly of the world’s first trillionaire, and a footnote in Musk’s legacy, for better or for worse.

Put it this way: By the time Hollywood studio heads arrived at the Polo Lounge for their Monday power lunches, the mess of the Cybertruck that had crashed at the Beverly Hills Hotel the night before was gone. Almost as if it never happened at all.

It's been a wild week for fans of the superhero genre. Yesterday the internet exploded when it was revealed that James Gunn and Peter Safran were stepping down as co-CEOS of DC Studios, and there are countless questions about how upcoming DC movies and shows will be affected. Some fan reacts are making me especially concerned about Lanterns (which is streaming with a HBO Max subscription) and more.

Gunn's tenure as DC's head has been cut short, and it's unclear if the first slate of projects called Gods and Monsters will still move forward. The director/writer/producer took to social media with a statement about his departure, and some of the responses on Threads are cutting me to the core. Case in point: the following response which has a whopping 1.8k likes.

Goddammit, we're never getting another Lanterns season are we?

Well, now I'm depressed. Ever since its first season ended, fans have been wondering if Lanterns would get a second season on HBO. After all, there's plenty more Green Lantern lore to explore, with the writer Venessa Baden Kelly interested in bringing in Kilowog to the series. Unfortunately, Gunn's departure might put the show's second season in jeopardy, especially after Lanterns was the subject of fan backlash.

This isn't the only depressing fan response to James Gunn's threads post. Another one that's hitting hard and has over 900 likes reads:

We're never getting a full DC run ever. 😭

Ouch. While the Marvel Cinematic Universe has become a well-oiled machine over its nearly two decades in theaters, the same can't be said for things at DC. The former DCEU began with Zack Snyder's movies, which quickly put the Justice League together rather than methodically giving them solo movies. Unfortunately that shared universe started becoming less and less interconnected over the years, eventually ending with Aquaman 2.

James Gunn and Peter Safran were hoping to make a more cohesive franchise with the DCU, and there were a number of thrilling crossovers in the first few titles. While we'll still get to see a number of characters collide when Man of Tomorrow hits theaters next summer, it's unclear exactly how the burgeoning shared universe will continue afterward. For hardcore superhero fans, it feels like we'll never get a DC counterpart to the MCU, which is super depressing.

Right now there are more questions about the DCU than answers. Gunn and Safran were replaced by former Marvel executive and producer Jeremy Latcham, who obviously has experience in the genre. We'll just have to wait and see what comes next.

The next DC movie hitting theaters is Man of Tomorrow on July 9, 2027. For now fans can see Clayface in theaters as part of the 2026 movie release list.

#3568. One of the Best QLED TVs of 2026 Is Over $1,300 Off Right Now

TCL has been pushing the boundaries of QLED TVs, making some of the best in the market at very competitive prices. This year, the company released its QM8L model, introducing a new design and impressive features and specs to a series that isn't even their flagship. Right now, the 65-inch QM8L is $1,197.99 (originally $2,499.99), $100 cheaper than it was just earlier this month, reaching its lowest price since it launched in April, according to price-tracking tools. Larger sizes are also seeing substantial discounts.

One of the first things you'll notice about the QM8L is the “Zero Border” bezel design, which gives it a modern, minimalistic look. When you turn it on, you'll likely note how bright this TV gets, which is a huge advantage QLEDs have over OLEDs. TCL claims it reaches 6,000 nits—seeing as the brightest OLED TV on the market only reaches 700 nits, no OLED can come close to this unit's brightness. Another important spec to note here is the local dimming zones: TCL claims this TV has up to 4,000, which means it gets top-tier backlight control, limited light blooming (thanks in part to TCL's "Halo Control"), and incredible contrast levels that some might not be able to distinguish from an OLED.

As many of us won't manually calibrate our TVs, the picture modes you can switch to in the settings will be most people's go-to. This TV's "Filmmaker mode" provides accurate color and picture, and if you're a gamer, you can use the native 144Hz high-refresh rate. If you don't already have a surround sound system at home and want to keep a minimalist setup, the QM8L comes with Dolby Atmos-ready Bang & Olufsen speakers, which offer above-average audio output compared to most TVs. You can read more about these features in CNET's 8.8/10 review. If 65 inches isn't quite right for your home theater setup, take a look at the QM8L's other sizes, which are also discounted right now.

#3567. How Nicolas Cage Really Feels About Ryan Gosling Playing Ghost Rider

In September 2026, Nicholas Cage slammed the Marvel Cinematic Universe for becoming a "glorified WWE." But that doesn't mean he's displeased about Ryan Gosling preparing to take on a role that he previously played — Johnny Blaze, aka Ghost Rider — in Marvel Studios' upcoming movie "Ghost Rider."

Cage's "Ghost Rider" ended up flopping its way to a franchise back in 2007, with the actor returning for the 2012 sequel "Ghost Rider: Spirit of Vengeance." Despite seeing sort of okay returns at the box office, neither film was a hit with critics, and after "Spirit of Vengeance," Johnny Blaze was relegated to cinematic history as Marvel Studios pushed ahead with the MCU. But at San Diego Comic-Con 2026, the studio announced that Gosling is set to star in a new Ghost Rider film, with "Deadpool & Wolverine" director Shawn Levy overseeing the project. Meanwhile, Cage has nothing but nice things to say about that.

The actor spoke to The Hollywood Reporter at the premiere of his new sports biopic "Madden" (the trailer for which left us wondering how David O. Russell is still making movies). "Ryan's going to do his thing with it, and I'm looking forward to seeing it," Cage told the outlet. "Ryan knows how I feel about him as an actor. We've had nice conversations, and we stay in touch. I was happy for him and wished him best of luck on his adventures, and I look forward to seeing the movie."

2007's "Ghost Rider" was written and directed by Mark Steven Johnson and saw Nicholas Cage in the title role, a motorcycle stuntman who sells his soul and transforms into a flaming emissary of Hell. Peter Fonda played the villain Mephistopheles, Ryan Gosling's wife Eva Mendes was Cage's love interest Roxanne Simpson, and Sam Elliot played mentor Carter Slade/The Caretaker. Sadly, despite a decent cast, the film received pretty terrible reviews. It did, however, make $228.7 million at the box office on a $110 million budget, which was evidently enough for Sony Pictures to make a sequel. But 2012's "Ghost Rider: Spirit of Vengeance" was met with even more scathing reviews, and despite bringing in a reasonable $132.5 million in theaters on a $57 million budget, the film marked the end of Cage's run as the hero.

Now, Gosling is set to take on Ghost Rider for the character's MCU debut, and it remains to be seen what direction the movie will take. Cage previously told JoBlo that Johnson's film "should've been an R-rated movie," adding that David S. Goyer's original script was "still a movie that should be made." Obviously, Marvel Studios won't be using Goyer's screenplay, but fans have yet to get a truly dark Ghost Rider film, and Gosling's outing as the character could — and, if you ask Cage, should — be it.

For now, THR claims "Heated Rivalry" star Connor Storrie is in talks to play the film's villain. Rosamund Pike was also previously reported to be a top pick for the love interest in Gosling's "Ghost Rider," but for now, we'll have to wait for official news.

Marvel Studios' "Ghost Rider" hits theaters on July 28, 2028.

#3566. Avedon Director Ron Howard On Richard Avedon’s “Creative Courage,” and His Favorite Images From 'In the American West'

In his new documentary Avedon, director Ron Howard traces the vivid legacy of the influential photographer Richard Avedon, which premieres November 11 on Netflix. “The subjects he worked with on the commercial side of his career were dazzling and beautiful, and he was so entertaining and expressive in the way that he would shoot them. But I really had no idea how he applied his status, his influence, his access to tell this other kind of story about human beings that was honest, insightful, and more journalistic,” Howard tells Vanity Fair.

The glamorous heights of Avedon’s career were what first caught Howard’s attention. “I became aware of him really in the ’80s. Then it was even his TV commercials, like Brooke Shields [in Calvin Klein ads],” Howard said. Later, he realized a few of his favorite portraits were taken by Avedon. One of these was a portrait of a young Kareem Abdul-Jabbar at a playground in New York holding a basketball “and kind of casually standing there looking straight into the camera. It’s not against a white background…” notes Howard. “I know Kareem a little bit. It so captured the foundational strength of character and intelligence that Kareem carried with him along with his basketball talent.”

Initially, Howard, who spent three years making the film, thought it was going to be more focused on the fashion and celebrity worlds that Avedon inhabited. However, his fascination with photographs like “sad Marilyn” (Avedon’s 1957 portrait of Marilyn Monroe) grew into a respect for the full breadth of Avedon’s career, and his “creative courage as an artist.”

In the film, footage of Avedon and new interviews with Lauren Hutton, Tina Brown, Adam Gopnik, Hilton Als, Joel Meyerowitz, Larry Gagosian, and Avedon’s son John, among others, paint a picture of a driven, curious, and sometimes mercurial artist. In the 1950s, Avedon’s career took off when he began shooting for Harper’s Bazaar, Vogue, and Vanity Fair. He injected a sense of play and prewar European glamour into his images by drawing inspiration from the films of Fred Astaire and Ginger Rogers. Eventually, he ventured into documentary assignments and more political subjects, including Nothing Personal (1964), a photobook with text by James Baldwin that captured the tensions of the Civil Rights era alongside a broader look at American life, a three panel portrait of anti-war protesters the Chicago Seven, and members of America’s political and financial elite at the time of the country’s bicentennial (“The Family”) for Rolling Stone. At the height of his career, he seemingly shifted quite easily from photographing celebrities to documenting anti-war protests and the counterculture of the 1960s, even when his work was met with mixed reactions.

Dovima with elephants, evening dress by Dior, Cirque d’Hiver, Paris, August 1955.

James Baldwin, New York, January 9, 1963.

Avedon (left) with Gloria Vanderbilt and Sidney Lumet at a party for the movie premiere of East of Eden (dir. Elia Kazan), 1955.

“We tried to reflect the risks he took and the transitions he made with his art and his career,” Howard shares. Had Howard made the documentary in Avedon’s lifetime, he would have liked to have asked him directly about the turning points in his career. “In all the interviews, he just kind of made it seem like it was a natural step. But to me, it's not a natural step to stop getting thousands and thousands of dollars an hour to shoot commercials and shoot for the world's most read magazines, and go to Vietnam where no one was really. He wasn’t on assignment initially… he just committed.”

In 1979, the Amon Carter Museum of American Art in Fort Worth, Texas, commissioned Avedon to capture a portrait of the West. He worked on this ambitious portfolio periodically through 1984, traveling across 17 states like California, Colorado, Iowa, North Dakota, Texas, and Wyoming, with assistants and a researcher, Laura Wilson, who helped Avedon arrange 752 portrait sittings. (Wilson also documented the making of the project in her own remarkable photographs and writing.) In total, Avedon printed 124 photographs (some as large as four feet tall) and exhibited them at the museum in 1985. The result was In the American West—a turning point in Avedon’s career. Prior to the project’s completion, in 1983, Vanity Fair ran five photographs from the eventual series, showing coal miners covered in dust and one lone oil worker alongside a feature on Wagner’s operas and an excerpt of Gabriel García Márquez’s Chronicle of a Death Foretold.

“One of the reasons I was drawn to [In the American West] is because my family roots are in the Midwest,” Howard says. “I see a lot of truth in these images.”

Avedon conducting a portrait session for In the American West beside his 8x10 camera.

In a similar fashion to August Sander’s massive undertaking People of the 20th Century, Avedon went looking for “men and women who work at hard, uncelebrated jobs, the people who are often ignored or overlooked,” Wilson wrote. In doing so he joined a whole legion of photographers whose images have come to define broad swaths of middle and western America. But unlike common readings of Sander’s project at the time, Avedon was clear that his version of the West was totally subjective, more of a cinematic panorama than an objective record. He was emphatic that all photographs are filtered through the photographer’s eye, and become their interpretation. Through Wilson, he declared, “This is a fictional West. I don’t think the West of these portraits is any more conclusive than the West of John Wayne.”

Below, Howard reflects on five of his favorite photographs from Avedon’s In the American West.

“I asked if that was makeup, and I was assured that none of it was. [Avedon] set up, and just as workers were coming off their shift, he was getting them in front of the camera. I mean, wow, this is what these workers look like. This is what was in their lungs and their pores. I have cousins and uncles who worked in the oil fields. I never had any idea that they had their days looking like they’d been through what this guy has been through on his shift.”

“The boy with the rattlesnake was the first photo that [Avedon] took where he knew he was going to get at something deeper... He felt like this was almost religious iconography in a way, or mythic. [The subject] was a teenager. As Avedon says, he's a boy turning into a man, and here he's doing this kind of work, so it speaks to a transformation. It also speaks of that region as a very pragmatic region. My own dad, to try to get some spending money [in the ’30s], was hunting and trapping raccoons to sell skins to the junk dealer or possums they could eat. Absolutely just a pragmatic way of life there. So that image always resonated with me. It is also featured in the documentary because it was the proof in [Avedon’s] mind that he was going to be able to identify moments and individuals that would be arresting and mean a lot on an artistic level.”

“The beekeeper is, of course, a stunning image–one that doesn't have that much to do with the American West. I think [Avedon] could have found somebody like that in almost any corner of the planet, but it certainly is fascinating and a tribute to the research team that was working with him to help find him.”

“The maintenance worker who’s dressed up in a really flashy suit, suit jacket, tie and hat, that just looks very familiar to me. I mean, the jacket and all the embroidery on it, the flowers, I never saw anything like that with my family. They didn’t have that kind of flourish. This guy looks like he could be a country western singer or could be trying to be a country western star. But the hat, the tie, the gaze, the posture looks very, very familiar to me. That looks like a hardworking guy getting dressed up on the weekend.”

#3565. These Sony ANC Headphones Are on Sale for $128 Right Now

It's hard to convince yourself to spend nearly half a grand on premium headphones, like the Sony WH-1000XM6, even if you consider yourself an audiophile. Not everyone can afford those prices, which is why the budget, mid-tier, and premium tiers exist. While the premium 1000XM6 headphones are over three times the price of the mid-tier Sony WH-CH730N, they're not three times as good. The Sony WH-CH730N are $128 (originally $179) right now, the lowest price they've ever been according to price-tracking tools, and they offer an amazing value for your money.

It's pretty impressive what $128 in headphones gets you in 2026. The CH730N uses the same Sony Connect app as the premium headphones; as a result, you get a 10-band slider on the EQ menu, a battery care feature that extends the longevity of your battery life, 50 hours of juice, ANC, Ambient Sound (transparency mode), Multipoint to connect to two devices at once, and Bluetooth 6.0. The Adaptive Sound Control feature can detect your activity (walking, sitting down, loud environment, etc.) and automatically switch the level of ANC and transparency to make your experience as comfortable and seamless as possible.

The microphones are decent and use a feature to isolate your voice in noisy environments. I love that there's an AUX connection to give you the option, which seems to be coming back with newer headphones. The design is light and will feel like plastic, but they are comfortable to wear for long sessions. If you're looking to maximize the quality of headphones you can get for your money, the Sony WH-CH730N offer a pretty compelling option at $128.

#3563. A Star Trek Moment Involving Tribbles And Klingons Was Cut For Being Too Disgusting

In 60 years of the "Star Trek" franchise, the Klingon Empire has faced countless foes across the galaxy. They've taken on the Federation, the Romulans, and the Dominion, but true "Trek" fans know that there is one enemy above all other that spurred the Klingons to their greatest battle, in which many warriors died with honor for the fate not just of the Empire, but the universe itself: Tribbles. Remember Tribbles, the little fuzzy puffballs that make adorable little cooing noises and don't do anything but make more Tribbles? Yeah, those things are one of the greatest threats to the entire "Star Trek" universe, and Klingons hate them even more than they hate most other creatures. Unless, that is, they're served up for lunch.

As unlikely as it might seem, the mutual enmity between the Klingon Empire and the troublesome Tribbles is long-established "Trek" canon , and even inspired a moment in "Star Trek VI: The Undiscovered Country" that would've included a tasty nod to their hateful history. The only problem was that once the props were made, the scene was deemed to be simply too gross for audiences and wound up on the cutting room floor.

According to the 1995 book "The Making of the Trek Films," "Star Trek VI" was slated to include a moment in which a Klingon prison guard took a break from enforcing Captain Kirk and Dr. McCoy's prison sentence to tear open a Tribble and devour its guts raw as a snack. In reality, the "guts" in question were actually just gummy worms and tapioca, a combination that we can only assume pairs well with Klingon bloodwine and prune juice. The effect, however, was so disgusting that the bit was cut from the film, presumably because tearing open a cute little ball of fluff and sucking out its innards is a bit off-putting for the average theatergoer.

The edible Tribble — which could have been a pretty amazing marketing opportunity for hungry "Trek" fans who really wanted to commit to their Klingon cosplay — was designed by model builder Greg Jein, a multi-time Academy Award nominee with a long history with the franchise. In addition to creating several props for "Star Trek VI," including Chancellor Gorkon's animal-horn chalice, he worked on "Star Trek: The Motion Picture," "Star Trek V," and was part of the team that built the original model of the Enterprise-D used in "Star Trek: The Next Generation."

As for the Tribbles, which were almost named Fuzzies, they first appeared in one of the most well-remembered episodes of the original "Star Trek," "The Trouble With Tribbles." That episode established that they consume and reproduce at a phenomenal rate, able to explode, according to Mr. Spock, from a single Tribble to a population of 1,771,561 in a mere three days. As McCoy pointed out, they are essentially "born pregnant," a very efficient system that winds up presenting a lot of problems when it comes to resources. That episode also established that while most space-faring species find them docile and cuddly, Tribbles have a natural aversion to Klingons.

In the "Star Trek: Deep Space Nine" episode "Trials and Tribble-ations," the Klingon Worf revealed that in the century since the original "Star Trek," the sheer reproductive frequency of Tribbles presented "an ecological menace" to the Empire. As billions of Tribbles tore through resources eating everything in their path and exponentially breeding, much like the real-life invasive rabbits that inspired their creation, Klingon warriors hunted them to extinction ... mostly. Time travel shenanigans returned them to the galaxy after that episode, and the third season of "Picard" included a cameo from a "genetically altered Tribble" that looked more like the face-hugging baby Xenomorphs from "Alien" than the classic fuzzballs.

With Tribbles back in the galaxy, it remains to be seen whether they'll become a problem for the Federation and the Klingons again. Now that we know that they can make a tasty snack, though, the solution to that issue seems to be solved in a manner both honorable and delicious. Then again, if those gummy worm guts become a delicacy, the Klingon Empire may have met its match in the greatest foe of all: high blood sugar.
