#3548. Yellowstone's Downfall Can Be Traced Back To One Moment

There was a time when "Yellowstone" was on top of the world, so far as mainstream television was concerned. What started as a somewhat unassuming Western TV show on an upper-tier cable channel became a breakout hit, in no small part thanks to the participation of Oscar-winner Kevin Costner in the lead role as John Dutton. "Yellowstone" set a huge record as the most-watched show of 2022. It was massive. Then, it all came crashing down.

"Yellowstone" Season 5 became its last, with a massive gap between "Part 1" and "Part 2" of that season. Series creator Taylor Sheridan decided to focus more on the show's spin-offs, as well as his other projects, with the series finale airing in December 2024. That was that. But where, exactly, did it all go wrong? When was the downfall of this once mighty TV titan? Frankly, it's not that hard to figure out.

To put my cards on the table, I've not seen a single episode of the show. I'm merely someone who writes about this stuff professionally and pays attention to the business. Anyone who does that can tell you with confidence that the behind-the-scenes drama between Sheridan and Costner is without a doubt what doomed "Yellowstone." Once Costner checked out, however that actually went down, the writing was on the wall.

Indeed, it was reported in May 2023 that Costner was leaving "Yellowstone" after Season 5. That raised eyebrows and sounded alarms. Any time a lead actor leaves a show, that's to be expected. But as the headlines continued to swirl, it became clear that this wasn't just a guy stepping away from a series. There was much more to the story.

To this day, it's still not entirely clear how everything went down. What we know for sure is that Taylor Sheridan became the busiest man in showbusiness, with a ton of series on the air, all of which he was chiefly responsible for. Kevin Costner, meanwhile, had other projects he wanted to do while also fronting "Yellowstone." Tension mounted. It even came to light that Costner was "very upset" with "Yellowstone" Season 2, long before his departure.

The gap between the end of "Part 1" of "Yellowstone" Season 5 and "Part 2" is where things really started to go south. Costner wanted to go make his long-planned Western movie saga "Horizon," which he did. But that conflicted with the planned schedule for the show, which caused issues. Not for nothing, we still don't know what's going on with "Horizon: An American Saga — Chapter 2" after the first movie bombed in theaters. But that's another story.

Sheridan has explained Costner's surprising "Yellowstone" exit, suggesting that the actor stayed on the show even longer than he wanted to in the first place:

"Even though Kevin was ready to go —he had other things he wanted to do — he stayed on for another two seasons, and that was just because the show was such a behemoth and such a huge hit that the notion of giving up a hit before it had run of juice to squeeze is very foreign to a network."

But it's not that simple. Costner explained his "Yellowstone" exit and said he'd "probably go to court" over it in 2023. It wasn't an amicable parting of ways. The main point is that Costner leaving and the feud that went on undoubtedly derailed the show. It's that simple.

It's also worth pointing out that even when Kevin Costner was still on the show, things were far from rosey. Costner's clash with a co-star reportedly left "Yellowstone" lead Kelly Reilly in tears, and while Costner has a bit of a reputation for being difficult to work with in general, reports like this are still a bad look. At a certain point, even wildly popular TV shows are forced to buckle to external pressures, particularly when they involve their leading men.

Be that as it may, Taylor Sheridan and Paramount have made the most out of the situation. It's a real lemons/lemonade deal they've got going on. Spoilers, but "Yellowstone" Season 5 dealt with John Dutton by revealing he's dead. The show moved on and got to its finale without him. More than that, Sheridan has made the most of the greater "Yellowstone" universe he established by not only developing prequels such as "1883" and "1923" but spin-offs as well.

First and foremost is "Dutton Ranch," which is getting a Season 2. What happens beyond that remains to be seen, but its protagonists Beth Dutton (Reilly) and Rip Wheeler (Cole Hauser) have effectively picked up where John Dutton left off. There's also "Marshals," which has brought Luke Grimes' Kayce Dutton to network TV, resulting in a big hit on CBS. So, even without Costner, the "Yellowstone" franchise has thrived. It wasn't a happy marriage or a happy divorce, but the dust settled, and everyone figured out a path forward.

JBL’s Live 780NC over-ear headphones are down to $139.95 from $249.95, a $110 discount that brings them to their lowest price ever, according to price trackers. #3546. How to unlock Fire Arrows in Zelda Ocarina of Time

Unlocking Fire Arrows is a great way to expand Link's arsenal in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake. By hitting targets with these special arrows, Link can set them on fire, which is fairly useful in different scenarios, from fighting certain enemies to lighting totems to open doors. Before you can get your hands on them, you will need to progress through the story and solve a riddle.

If you need help figuring out all the steps, don't fret. Here's how to unlock Fire Arrows in Zelda Ocarina of Time.

Before you start shooting Fire Arrows around Hyrule, you need to meet two prerequisites: get the Fairy Bow from the Forest Temple and complete the Water Temple in Lake Hylia.

If you have already finished the Water Temple, head to the largest island in the middle of the lake (the one with the large tree) and read the tablet located on the its southeast side. The message says, "When the lake is full and dawn breaks, release an arrow toward the halo of light," which basically means that you need to shoot an arrow at the sun.

Wait until daytime and aim your bow at the rising sun. If you're visiting the lake during the night, you can use the Sun's Song to speed the process up. As you aim your bow at the sun, an orange-reddish circle will appear around it, indicating that you should fire the arrow. A short cutscene will play, showing the arrow landing on the island in front of you. Head there and pick up the Fire Arrow.

When it comes to using Fire Arrows, it's important to keep in mind that they aren't a separate type of arrow. What you unlock is the ability to magically imbue your arrows with fire. While this means you won't have to carry a stock of each type, it also means that you have only one set of arrows to use, whether you're shooting regular or Fire Arrows. Additionally, Fire Arrows cost one magic power per shot, considerably limiting the number of times you can use them.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is a little bit different than the original game, so if you need guides to help you through, we don’t blame you. We have walkthroughs for all the dungeons, from the Deku Tree to Ganondorf's Castle. We also have guides for the sillier, in-between parts of the game, like when you have to find Richard (the dog) or Cuccos.

For those going for 100% completion, we also have guides on where to find every Piece of Heart, every Gold Skulltula token, and where to plant every Magic Bean.

#3545. Paapa Essiedu, Harry Potter’s New Snape, Is Ready for Questions

When Paapa Essiedu was just 25 years old, he was cast as Hamlet by the Royal Shakespeare Company. In an instant, he joined the ranks of all-time greats like Ben Kingsley, Kenneth Branagh, and Mark Rylance. “I still remember the day that my agent rang me up and told me I’d got that job,” he says 11 years later. “I was gassed about it for about three seconds. And then I was like, ‘Fuck, what have I done?’”

Critics loved Essiedu as the Danish prince. “It was good,” he says casually of his star-making performance. Yet his casting provoked headlines for another reason: He was the first Black actor to play Hamlet at the RSC. “There was this—not even fascination—this obsession with the fact that I was a Black person who was doing it,” he recalls.

The Olivier-winning, Emmy-nominated performer now views that stint as a dry run for the most high-profile role of his career: potions professor Severus Snape in HBO’s highly anticipated and deeply polarizing Harry Potter television series. “I kind of draw a small pathway in comparison to the freeway that I’m on now,” he says.

There is likely not a soul alive who isn’t familiar with J.K. Rowling’s multibillion-dollar franchise about a boy wizard. After seven primary books, a variety of secondary volumes, eight feature films, multiple spin-offs, a Broadway play, and rides and shops at six Universal theme parks worldwide, Harry Potter arguably has name recognition rivaling that of Hamlet, or Jesus. Though “don’t let my auntie hear you comparing Harry Potter to the Bible,” says Essiedu. “Trust me, she can shut down the whole of Vanity Fair like that.” He flicks his wrist. “On the record, I’m not agreeing with this here, just in case.”

Essiedu was raised in the east London neighborhood of Walthamstow by his mother, who never imagined her son might have a career as a professional actor. “Single Ghanaian woman parent?” he says. “It was not on the top-five list of jobs that were made available.” His father, who lived back in Ghana with Essiedu’s half-siblings, died when Essiedu was 14. “He was there, but he wasn’t there,” Essiedu says.

The 36-year-old describes his childhood as “fully millennial”: “Slap-bang in the middle, pre-internet, pre-fucking-Netflix, on-demand television, just barely dealing with Game Boy Colors. Life was analog,” he says. But while many his age are predisposed to wax poetic about life in the ’90s, Essiedu doesn’t see it with entirely rose-colored glasses. “In many ways, it was fucking boring,” he says with a laugh. “There was a lot of just staring out the window and hoping some shit was going to happen.”

Reading became “something that was quite crucial to stop me from eating my own hands,” he says—including the Harry Potter books, which “were coming out regularly at the precise time that I was starting to develop my taste for literature…. The world that was created was so full. Can you imagine, like, 12-year-old boys, 13-year-old boys reading 600-page books, 700-page books about wizards? We’re meant to be out here in the streets playing football, basketball, whatever. I’m like, ‘I’m going home. I’m reading the book. I’m inside.’”

ALL GROWN UP “They’re considering me for a teacher. That means I’m fucking old now," says Essiedu. "When you’re a kid, teachers don’t even have ages. They’re just old."

When he was 18, Essiedu joined the National Youth Theatre—a selective performing arts training center in London where actors like Daniel Day-Lewis, Helen Mirren, and Daniel Craig honed their craft. Essiedu auditioned for a distinctly teenage reason: “Let’s just say there was someone that I wanted to be around who was also going to National Youth Theatre,” he says cheekily. After getting accepted, Essiedu raised the money he needed to attend, going around his school asking friends and acquaintances for donations. The crush might not have lasted—“let’s say the person who I was supposedly following disappeared”—but a lifelong passion for performing developed.

“I found myself just in this room surrounded by people who were talking about Shakespeare and talking about Harold Pinter and Jez Butterworth,” he says. “By luck, really, I found myself in a room that gave me the idea to basically burn down all of my mother’s ambitions for myself and go in a different direction. Arguably, it turned out okay.”

After his star turn as Hamlet, Essiedu got an Emmy nomination for his supporting role in Michaela Coel’s I May Destroy You. He wasn’t surprised when the show made a recent New York Times list of 100 best TV shows of the 21st century: “Of course it was on that list,” he says. “I think it was a phenomenally singular and confident and brave and unprecedented piece of work.”

Then Francesca Gardiner and Mark Mylod—a pair of Emmy-winning Succession alums—reached out to let him know they were interested in him for the new Harry Potter. Snape was the only part he wanted, though the role was a bit of a reality check: “They’re considering me for a teacher. That means I’m fucking old now. When you’re a kid, teachers don’t even have ages. They’re just old.”

GOOD NEWS “I got a lot of love as well," he says. "That really fuels me as much as the hate.”

Essiedu put his pride aside and met with Gardiner and Mylod. Much to his surprise, after a two-hour chat about the show, Essiedu found out he had the part. “Professor Snape requires an extraordinary actor,” Gardiner tells VF via email. “He has to be intimidating, dangerous, sometimes very funny, but there’s also an enormous amount that he’s concealing. You need someone who can make you feel that there’s a whole other story unfolding beneath the one you’re watching. Someone who can convey depth and complexity without necessarily saying a word. Someone with real intensity. Paapa is one of those rare actors who can do all of that.”

Acting stalwart John Lithgow stars opposite Essiedu as Hogwarts headmaster Albus Dumbledore. Over the phone, the veteran says he’s never acted with anyone quite like Essiedu. “He is so focused and intense, and yet there’s an ease to his acting,” says Lithgow. “He just has a great sense of how mysterious he is, which is what makes him so compelling as Snape in Harry Potter.”

“We simply needed one of the greatest actors in Britain to do it justice,” agrees Mylod, also via email. Essiedu “has extraordinary range, and I always, always believe him.”

In April 2025, HBO announced that Essiedu had won the role of Snape—played with an inimitable snarl in the film franchise by the late great Alan Rickman. Essiedu read the books to prepare, but opted not to watch the movies. “To be honest, I never watched the movies when I was younger,” he says. “I still don’t think I really know what happens in Deathly Hallows because I read it so quickly that it didn’t really seep in. I was like, ‘This shit is complicated as hell, man. Dumbledore’s dead? What the fuck?’”

But even if he only has passing familiarity with Rickman’s take on the character, Essiedu says he’s not focused on trying to reinvent Snape or make people forget about his predecessor’s work. “The guy is an icon. He’s a legend,” Essiedu says of Rickman. “Anyone who’s ever met Alan or spoken to him or been friends with him have all reached out to me and spoken about what Alan would’ve thought about my casting. There’s so much goodwill, and I really feel him with me.”

The public’s reaction was decidedly more complex. After Essiedu’s casting was announced, the internet erupted, with certain corners deeply upset that a Black man was stepping into the role. In March, Essiedu told The Times of London that he’d received death threats from so-called Harry Potter fans: “Quit or I’ll murder you,” one said.

Essiedu doesn’t have a problem with good-faith criticism. “There’s some people who are just like, ‘I’ve done my research, and I know what kind of actor you are, and you suck.’ And they’re totally entitled to their opinion,” he says. “Then there are the people who are like, ‘You are bad because you are Black’—which, to me, is racist.” He stops to reconsider his words for a moment. “Well, actually not ‘You’re bad because you are Black.’ But there is a racially driven animosity.”

In the final weeks before the series premiere, though, Essiedu is most concerned with a third group, one he has real empathy for. “There are people who have got such a tight and deeply felt connection to something that they believe is theirs, and it feels like somebody is trying to take their thing and break their thing,” he says. Essiedu has a message for that cohort: “I know that’s not what I’m trying to do. I’m not trying to break anybody’s nothing. After this, we’re not going to burn the books. We’re not going to remove the DVDs of the films. It’s not the end of that. That all still exists.”

And Essiedu is quick to point out that the vitriol hasn’t been universal: “I got a lot of love as well,” he says. “That really fuels me as much as the hate.”

He’s also aware that he could avoid much of the bad stuff by staying offline—if only it were that easy. “You’ve got your DMs, and then there’s the bit where it says ‘request’ or ‘hidden,’” he says. “You know you shouldn’t go in there. You know you don’t need to scratch that itch. But you can’t stop yourself from doing it. You want to know what the face of the monster looks like.”

Essiedu’s showrunner, at least, has his back. “It’s appalling that anyone should be subjected to that kind of abuse in any circumstances,” writes Gardiner. “He has handled it with incredible grace, and I have nothing but the greatest respect for him…. Paapa has absolutely nailed the role, and it is that performance that deserves our attention.”

Having seen the first two episodes of the series—which feature about 30 seconds of Essiedu’s Professor Snape—I can say that the only major difference between the Harry Potter from yore and the new series is Essiedu’s casting, at least so far. Though the plot unfolds more slowly—the show has eight hours to fill, after all, rather than two—the world of the series looks more or less the same as the one in the original films, from Hogwarts to Diagon Alley to the Dursleys’ house. Dominic McLaughlin, Arabella Stanton, and Alastair Stout, who play Harry, Hermione, and Ron, respectively, bear a striking resemblance to their forebears, Daniel Radcliffe, Emma Watson, and Rupert Grint—particularly McLaughlin. In this milieu, Essiedu’s dreadlocked Snape stands out—which has potentially given the trolls more ammo.

Essiedu as Professor Snape in Harry Potter on HBO.

Essiedu says he’s “very clear-minded in my head about what I want to do and what I’m trying to achieve, and the potential of it.” Having more time to tell the story means “hopefully I get the opportunity to pull the contradictions and the unexpected masks of Severus so that eventually we get a human being that is fully fleshed [out] and living and breathing. That was my ambition, and is my ambition. And you can judge me sometime—in 2039 or whatever it is—as to whether it’s been successful or not.”

There’s another reason one might have some trepidation about joining the staff of Hogwarts at this particular moment. In the past decade, J.K. Rowling—the mastermind behind Harry Potter—has descended into what her critics characterize as anti-transgender activism, using her apparently endless supply of cash to support gender-essentialist policies in the UK. While Rowling is adamant that she is not anti-trans, some, like The Matrix director Lilly Wachowski, have said that anyone who supports the Harry Potter franchise is “supporting trans genocide.”

Shortly after he was cast in the series, Essiedu signed an open letter in support of the transgender, nonbinary, and intersex community. Rowling then made a post on X saying that she does not have the power to fire him from the show—but wouldn’t even if she could.

“I have been super clear about my position on this topic, and that is the reason why she spoke out about me,” says Essiedu. “I’m really keen not to make a kind of ‘them and us’ dynamic here. I’m not really here to speak about Jo’s politics or to be a mouthpiece for her. I can only be really, really clear about what I believe and be consistent with that.”

So, what does he believe? After a bit of equivocating (“I don’t want to talk about Jo at all,” he repeats), Essiedu says the following with his chest: “I believe, in my bones, that trans people, queer people, people of all creeds and color have got the right to be treated with respect and dignity and safety at all times—whether they’re in the workplace, whether they’re at home or in the street, whatever. That’s what I believe, and that’s the way that I choose to live my life. That’s the creed by which I live.”

Perhaps that statement presents an inherent contradiction. Rowling is actively involved with the new series and will generate income from it that she could then use to fund her pet causes. But Essiedu believes Rowling’s books—rather than her politics—prove why it’s important to tell Harry’s story again for a new generation.

“When I come back to this story—this actual story—I’m thinking about the themes that it explores,” he says. “Themes of forgiveness, and good triumphing over evil, and of accepting people for who they are and allowing people to really be themselves within a world where anything is possible. I feel like there is something at the center of the story that we own, at least as much as anybody else, that still has the potential to do really, really, really beautiful things.”

#3544. The Bose Premium Smart Ultra Soundbar Is Now Cheaper Than It Was During Prime Day

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Amazon has dropped the Bose Smart Ultra Soundbar to $649 from its usual $999, taking $350 off and bringing it to the lowest price we've seen so far, according to price trackers. PCMag rated the Smart Ultra "outstanding," highlighting its ability to deliver surprisingly immersive Dolby Atmos audio without requiring a room full of additional speakers. If you don't need Bose's top-tier model, there's a less expensive option as well: the Bose Smart Dolby Atmos Soundbar ($399, down from $429), which sits below the Smart Ultra in the lineup.

The Smart Ultra uses a 5.1.2-channel design with nine drivers, including two upward-firing drivers that bounce sound off the ceiling to create height effects. In practice, that means movies, TV shows, and games feel larger and more spacious than they do through most single-bar setups. Bose also includes its AdaptiQ room-calibration system, which measures your room's acoustics and adjusts the sound accordingly. The process takes a few minutes, but it helps the soundbar perform better across different spaces rather than relying on a one-size-fits-all tuning profile. The soundbar also works as a smart speaker, with Amazon Alexa built in and support for Apple AirPlay 2, Google Cast, Spotify Connect, Bluetooth, and multi-room audio through the Bose app.

Its biggest compromise is bass—for a single soundbar, its low end is respectable, but it can't fully replace what a dedicated subwoofer brings to action movies, concerts, or bass-heavy music. The good news is that Bose allows you to expand the system later with compatible wireless subwoofers and surround speakers if you decide you want more impact. For anyone looking for a premium one-piece soundbar that delivers convincing Dolby Atmos effects, clear dialogue, built-in smart features, and a much larger soundstage than TV speakers can provide, the Smart Ultra remains one of the strongest standalone options available, especially at this price.

#3543. The Crow Star Bill Skarsgård Knows Exactly What Went Wrong With The Remake

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

The world waited 30 years for a remake of "The Crow," and to say it wasn't worth the wait would be an understatement. Now, that movie's star, Bill Skarsgard, has opened up about the experience. When it comes to what went wrong, Skarsgard has a pretty good idea.

A lot of actors almost played the Crow before Skarsgard got stuck with it, but the movie focuses on soulmates Eric and Shelly who are brutally murdered. Eric is given a chance to save the love of his life and has to traverse the worlds of the living and the dead in search of revenge. Rupert Sanders ("Snow White and the Huntsman") wound up in the director's chair.

That partnership wasn't fruitful. "The Crow" was dubbed a "dull, lifeless, meaningless remake" by /Film at the time. It also wasn't a success commercially. On a recent episode of the "Happy Sad Confused" podcast, Skarsgard reflected on the 2024 movie's failure. What it really comes down to is a rush job that went into production without a finished script:

"I think the lesson was that I'm not signing on to anything without a finished script. But it's surprising how common it is that something gets green-lit and then you're struggling with finishing the script because the dates are already set and the studio's already locked everything in motion. And it's like, 'Oh, the script needed...'"

There is a long dark history behind "The Crow" franchise, most notably the death of the original movie's star Brandon Lee towards the end of production. To state the obvious, making a bad movie isn't anywhere near on that level, but there is something to be said for this seeming doomed from the outset.

"That was something that Rupert [Sanders] and I just struggled with," Bill Skarsgard added. "We were like, 'Okay, the first script came in two months before we started to shoot.' It was an insanely rushed process in that regard. But I don't regret any of the roles that I've done. And I think they could be good experiences; they could be bad experiences. But how you learn from them is really what it's about."

Hollywood had been attempting to remake "The Crow" for years before it finally happened. Many actors and directors came and went over the years. Nothing materialized. "Aquaman" himself Jason Momoa got very, very close to making it back in 2018. But days before filming was set to begin, it all fell apart. "The Crow" remake was dead again as both Momoa and director Corin Hardy exited.

It never totally died though and, eventually, it came around to Bill Skarsgard. On paper, he was a good fit for the role. But you can only polish a turd so well and, if the script is a turd, he can only do so much.

"The Crow" remake bombed at the box office, pulling in just $24 million worldwide against terrible reviews. At the very least, Skarsgard walked away with an important lesson and doesn't have any regrets. He's just very unlikely to sign on for a potential franchise role again if the script isn't airtight.

You can grab "The Crow" on Blu-ray or DVD from Amazon.

In just a few years, The Traitors has become an Emmy-winning sensation for those with a Peacock subscription. Luckily for fans, the studio behind the show has given us another campy reality competition series with The Mob. I'm mad that basically all my favorite contestants have been whacked, especially my number one. Still, there is one way this new show is beating The Traitors IMO.

Two episodes of The Mob have been airing weekly for those with a Hulu subscription, and I've been loving how silly the show is. While RuPaul's Drag Race alum Willam Belli is a top tier reality TV star, that unfortunately didn't stop Maria from whacking her in the the last episode. I'm officially in mourning after seeing my favorite Ru Girl eliminated, but I still have to give The Mob its flowers for one way that I think it's superior to The Traitors.

Considering what a soundbite machine Willam was throughout her six-episode arc on The Mob, the rest of the season will presumably be way less entertaining. Still, I have to say that I much prefer the Hulu show's "jobs" over the missions that we're shown during The Traitors.

For both of these shows, contestants must complete tasks in order to bank money for their respective prize pots. While The Traitors is a wildly popular show, there are plenty of fans who are simply disinterested in the missions, with some even fast forwarding through them altogether. Sure, the inclusion of shields could affect the game as a whole, but for the most part the missions don't feel super important to the show. Namely because the time limits on them seemingly aren't accurate, and the contestants appear to have plenty of time to complete them.

This isn't the case for The Mob. It appears that the time limits are legit for the jobs, as we've seen the cast run out of time and lose money in basically every single episode. This gives those jobs a real sense of stakes, something that is arguably the biggest criticism about The Traitors. The latter series could learn a few things from the Hulu show regarding missions, but we'll have to wait and see if the next celebrity season follows time limits more closely. That doesn't appear to be happening in Traitors: New Blood.

New episodes of The Mob air Mondays on Hulu as part of the 2026 TV schedule. Additionally, The Traitors: New Blood puts out new installments Thursdays on NBC, before streaming the next day on Peacock. We'll just have to see if the new competition show ends up having a long life on Hulu.

Turns out, sharing headspace with Gollum is murder on your sleep schedule.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I've been quoting Gollum's "my precious" voice for more than two decades, usually to annoy someone within earshot. Andy Serkis has spent considerably more time inside the character's head, and apparently, Middle-earth's most obsessive resident has started interfering with his sleep. Considering he is returning to play Gollum while also directing The Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum, I suppose there's no escaping him now.

The actor opened up to The Times about revisiting the role he first took on 26 years ago. The new film is headed for the 2027 movie schedule, and while fans have plenty of reasons to be excited to see him back in a motion-capture suit, Serkis admitted the reunion has been doing a number on his already restless mind. Here's how he described it:

I’ve just lived with Gollum for such a long period. I’m a terrible sleeper. My mind is pretty active, and it has been insane going back to the character I started playing 26 years ago, and so I’m waking up at night. Actually, I don’t know if I’m asleep or awake, but I think, Am I directing you, Gollum? Or you me? Are we arguing?’ My mind is…busy.

I'm sorry, but imagining Serkis getting into a middle-of-the-night argument with Gollum is kind of hilarious. It gets even funnier when you remember that Peter Jackson compared the movie's psychological approach to Joaquin Phoenix's Joker. Apparently, getting inside Gollum's head is proving a little more complicated than anyone anticipated. This is a character who famously argues with himself, after all. Now he's apparently taking that talent into his actor's sleep schedule. I'd have enough trouble directing a movie without one of its stars trying to conduct a meeting inside my skull at 3 a.m.

Of course, a lot is riding on this particular trip back to Middle-earth. The Star Wars veteran actor first appeared as Gollum in 2001's The Fellowship of the Ring, and his performance-capture work helped change what audiences expected from digital characters, although Peter Jackson and the crew weren't entirely sure what to make of him at first. He returned in The Hobbit movies, but The Hunt for Gollum gives him a bigger responsibility than ever. He's stepping behind the camera for a film centered on the very character he helped make famous.

That means revisiting the voice, movements and personality that have become second nature over the years. We previously covered how writer Philippa Boyens was impressed by Serkis' physical commitment when she saw him back in his motion-capture suit. He's 62 now, and getting down on all fours to play that creature sounds exhausting enough before you factor in the sleepless nights.

I actually wrote last year about Serkis admitting he "cannot escape" Gollum. At the time, I took that as a career observation. Apparently, it also applies at bedtime. While promoting his new memoir, My Pressures, he discussed how playing a role can change an actor and how hard it can be to leave a character behind. Gollum has occupied a corner of his professional life for over a quarter-century. No wonder returning to that mindset is taking some adjustment.

At least he'll have some familiar faces around. Peter Jackson is producing alongside Fran Walsh and Boyens, while Ian McKellen and Elijah Wood are returning as Gandalf and Frodo. Wood has even said he thinks Serkis is the perfect person to direct a movie about Gollum.”

I'm excited to see what the mo-cap pioneer does with Gollum now that he's calling the shots, but I hope he gets a decent night's sleep before opening weekend. After 26 years, the poor man deserves a few hours without hearing "precious" in his head.

#3540. The Top 10 Movies Right Now, According to Streaming Data

The most streamed movie in October was Steven Spielberg's Disclosure Day, but half of the month's top ten is made up of season-appropriate horror movies. This year's two most successful horror movies, Backrooms and Obsession, made the list; so did a classic (Halloween from 1978) and an art movie about the genre that Halloween created,Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma. Perfect double feature. Rounding out the list is the all-around-excellent Hokum. If you're not into horror, you might like Golden Arm, a comedy that refused to die, star-studded comedy The Invite, or ultimate crowd-pleaser Project Hail Mary.

Legendary director Steven Spielberg returns to the extraterrestrials he loves so much with a thriller that's a spiritual sequel to Close Encounters of the Third Kind. Disclosure Day details the events that lead up to the revelation that aliens are among us. Josh O’Connor plays Dr. Daniel Kellner, a cybersecurity expert for a government contractor who uncovers explosive evidence that his employers would kill to keep secret. Meanwhile, a TV meteorologist (Emily Blunt) begins speaking in an alien language. It all sets the stage for a series of set pieces and chases leading to the biggest revelation in human history. Stream Disclosure Day on Peacock.

Director Kane Parsons' analog horror breakthrough is proof that atmosphere, mood, and a fascinating story is scarier than CGI monsters every time. Based on the viral YouTube series of the same name, Backrooms tells the story of Clark (Chiwetel Ejiofor), a store owner who discovers a labyrinthian liminal space in his furniture shop's basement. Renate Reinsve plays his therapist, who goes downstairs for a visit and does not find it easy to return. A hit with critics—Backrooms is sitting at 86% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes—and audiences, Backrooms is a delicious Halloween treat for horror fans. Stream Backrooms on HBO Max.

Director Curry Barker is still in his 20s, but his debut theatrical feature is the kind of horror film that changes the entire genre. Obsession is a classic "be careful what you wish for" story that feels fresh thanks to its talented young cast, unpredictable plot, and careful pace. Michael Johnston plays a young man too scared to tell his crush how he feels, so he wishes she'd fall in love with him instead. The result is a nightmare embodied by Inde Navarrette, whose portrayal of the villain/victim is at once harrowing, terrifying, and heartbreaking. Obsession is the best horror movie I've seen in years. Stream Obsession on Peacock.

This comedy-drama from A24 is packed with heavy-hitting actors. Olivia Wilde, who also directed the film, plays Angela, and Seth Rogen plays her husband, Joe. With the straight-laced couple's marriage on thin ice, Angela and Joe invite their more, uh, open-minded neighbors Piña, played by Penélope Cruz, and Hawk, played by Edward Norton, over for dinner. The evening unravels in hilarious ways, changing everyone's life. If you're a fan of smart, honest comedy, you will really like The Invite. Stream The Invite on HBO Max.

With Hokum, Director Damian McCarthy (Oddity, Caveat) carefully builds a suffocatingly creepy story around Adam Scott's portrayal of Ohm Bauman, a celebrity novelist and unmitigated jerk who travels to the isolated Bilberry Woods Hotel in Ireland to scatter the ashes of his parents and finish his book. Bauman soon learns that the lore of the hotel includes an ancient witch who feeds her victims to the creatures of hell, and she might be more than just a local legend. Hokum is a horror movie for fans of dreadful atmosphere and careful pacing instead of gore or jump-scares. Stream Hokum on Hulu.

With a title like this, it's not going to be a normal movie. Director Jane Schoenbrun’s I Saw the TV Glow and We're All Going to the World's Fair are two of the most fascinating, fiercely original horror movies of the last decade, and their third film follows in those strange footfalls. While it's technically a meta re-imagining of the slasher genre, Miasma goes way deeper than Scream ever could. It's a postmodern exploration of why the slasher genre's cocktail of sex, death, and subversion casts such a strong spell on interesting, weird people. Definitely see this movie. Stream Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma on Mubi.

When Golden Arm was released in 2021, not many people paid attention—with the pandemic in full swing, people didn't seem to have room for a quirky, indie comedy about a woman's quest to win the ladies' arm-wrestling championship—but it's a new age, and you should stream Golden Arm. It's sitting on a perfect score at Rotten Tomatoes, the movie's stars, Mary Holland and Betsy Sodaro, are charming and hilarious, and you can catch Golden Arm on Fandango, a free streaming service. What's not to love? Stream Golden Arm on Fandango or Prime Video.

In this crowd-pleasing sci-fi flick, Ryan Gosling stars as Ryland Grace, a middle school science teacher who is blasted into the firmament in a last-ditch effort to save the world. Grace is the only person on Earth who might know how to protect the sun from a cosmic infection that threatens all life, but he's definitely not an astronaut and doesn't see himself as a hero either. Will he rise to the occasion and learn something about his inner strength and resilience while saving us all from death? My money is on, "yeah, probably." Stream Project Hail Mary on MGM+, Prime Video, and Philo.

Hundreds of slasher movies have been released since Halloween came out in 1978, but none have surpassed the original. Michael Myers' expressionless visage and the synthesizer theme have become universally recognized cultural signifiers for "horror movie," and every shot in Halloween has been stolen countless times, but the movie is so good, it's still scary. Watch or re-watch Halloween now! Stream Halloween on Philo, AMC+, and Prime Video.

Directed by and starring Ben Affleck, Animals is a thriller that tells the story of Mark Kimball, a Los Angeles mayoral candidate whose son is kidnapped and held for ransom. Having spent every dime on his outsider campaign, Kimball is forced to turn to extreme methods to guarantee his son's safe return, even if it conflicts with his public persona as a man of the people. Animals is a taut, expertly directed movie that should more than satisfy fans of political thrillers. Stream Animals on Netflix.

#3539. Sydney Sweeney Delivered One Of Her Best Performances In A Beloved HBO Miniseries

Most will know Sydney Sweeney for her performance as Cassandra "Cassie" Howard in "Euphoria" and for starring in Paul Feig's excellent wicked thriller "The Housemaid." Many will likely also be aware of her box office smash hit rom-com "Anyone But You" co-starring Glen Powell. But Sweeney is a deceptively diverse actor who has delivered some excellent performances over the last decade, as evidenced by her role in the HBO miniseries "Sharp Objects."

This eight-episode psychological thriller series is based on a novel by Gillian Flynn, who's best-known for having written "Gone Girl" (the 2014 David Fincher-helmed film adaptation of which saw the true crime trend coming well in advance). But four years after the "Seven" director put his spin on Flynn's material, "Buffy the Vampire Slayer" alum Marti Noxon took a shot at it with "Sharp Objects."

Noxon's adaptation of Flynn's 2006 novel took the form of a 2018 HBO miniseries starring Amy Adams as an alcoholic crime reporter who returns to her hometown to look into the murders of two young girls. There, she's forced to reckon with her past trauma. Sweeney appears in the show as a similarly troubled teen who meets Adams' character during her stay in a psychiatric hospital. It's one of the actor's best yet most overlooked performances.

Sydney Sweeney has had her share of hits, but she must also be used to some of her best work going overlooked. Indeed, Sweeney's 2025 film "Americana" was completely ignored at the box office and her psychological drama "Clementine" came and went without much fanfare amidst the 2020 COVID-19 lockdowns. But while it was nowhere near the cultural phenomenon that "Euphoria" was at the height of its success, "Sharp Objects" did receive widespread praise upon its debut in 2018, earning eight Emmy award nominations and garnering Sweeney significant attention for her portrayal of psychiatric patient Alice.

Alice shares a self-harm problem with Amy Adams' Camille Preaker — who, after returning to her hometown of Wind Gap, Missouri, finds herself reflecting on her time in treatment. In these flashbacks, we see her meeting Alice, who handles her own issues by retreating into her iPod. The pair formed a bond during their time in the facility, and it seems Sweeney managed to impress "Sharp Objects" director Jean-Marc Vallée while filming her scenes as well.

As the actor once told Harper's Bazaar, "[Vallée] kept bringing me back more and more for different scenes, and he'd add me in here and there, so really, he and I were able to build my character together." It seems that was a result of Sweeney's dedication to the role, which, as she told the outlet, involved going to hospitals "where there were patients that self-harmed" and spending time with them. Equally impressive was the fact that, as she previously told Nylon, she would film her "Sharp Objects" scenes on weekends before getting on a red-eye flight to Portland to film her scenes for Netflix's "Everything Sucks!" Both ended up being two of Sydney Sweeney's best projects.

"Sharp Objects" was met with critical praise upon its 2018 debut, earning an impressive 92% "certified fresh" rating on Rotten Tomatoes and garnering Sydney Sweeney attention for her portrayal of Alice. 2018 was, of course, the year before "Euphoria" began airing on HBO. As such, Sweeney had yet to break through with her portrayal of Cassie Howard. But with "Everything Sucks!," a role on Season 2 of "The Handmaid's Tale," and her appearance in "Sharp Objects," she had managed to build some serious momentum going into the show, ultimately paving the way to her becoming a household name.

"Sharp Objects," in particular, garnered praise from critics. Writing for Rolling Stone, Alan Sepinwall highlighted Sweeney's performance in what he referred to as a "versatile, era-spanning year" for the actor. Sepinwall added that both she and fellow "Sharp Objects" actor Eliza Scanlen were "names to watch," which turned out to be a particularly prescient observation. Years later, in 2023, Frank Bruni looked back on Sweeney's ascension in a piece for The New York Times, mentioning her appearance in "Sharp Objects" and noting how it had helped her become "prestige TV royalty."

Sadly, Alice isn't typically mentioned as one of Sweeney's best roles, but her quietly powerful performance was proof, even before she debuted as Cassie, that she was a versatile actor capable of nuanced portrayals. She'd prove as much once again in 2019 when she played the title role in the nerve-wracking dramatic thriller "Reality," which is well worth a watch in its own right. But if you missed "Sharp Objects" back in 2018, give it a go on HBO Max.

#3538. Why Princess Diana Dressed William and Harry Identically, Even Though They Didn’t Like It

Princess Diana had a keen sense of style. It was a talent the late princess (who arrived at court at a very young age and was therefore still unfamiliar with the ins and outs of high fashion) developed over the years with the help of experts in the field—and which has repeatedly earned her the title of style icon.

It comes as no surprise, then, that her keen eye for new trends and her passion for the most sought-after pieces were also reflected in the fashion choices she made for her two children, Prince William and Prince Harry, whom she loved to dress alike from a very young age, no matter the occasion.

Prince Charles and Princess Diana with their sons, William and Harry. July 1986.

Princess Diana, it must be said, was neither the first nor the last mother to choose identical outfits for her children, but it seems this habit was not merely a fashion game. According to a report by Marie Claire, the princess’s former butler, Paul Burrell, reportedly said that Diana’s choice to dress William and Harry identically was a way to reinforce the idea that, in her eyes, there was no difference between the two—even though everyone around her showed preferential treatment toward the eldest son, the future heir to the throne.

Princess Diana with her sons, William and Harry. August 1986.

That’s why the princess waged her own battle, even choosing to dress her two sons in matching outfits, almost as if to convey a sense of unity and equality in their appearance. If these were indeed some of the reasons behind the brothers’ identical looks, it certainly wouldn’t be surprising. We know full well how Diana insisted on equal treatment for her two sons, who, for their part, apparently didn’t much care for their mother’s tendency to choose identical outfits. “The boys hated that, by the way; they didn’t want to be dressed the same,” Burrell added.

Princess Diana with her sons, William and Harry. July 1988.

This statement has also been confirmed by Prince Harry himself. In the 2017 television documentary, Diana, Our Mother: Her Life and Legacy, which aired on the 20th anniversary of Princess Diana’s death, her two sons spoke openly about their mother. The younger son said with a smile: “I genuinely think she got satisfaction out of dressing myself and William up in the most bizarre outfits—normally matching. It was weird shorts and little shiny shoes with the old clip-on.”

Princess Diana with her sons, William and Harry. August 1989.

Bermuda shorts and patent leather shoes with straps—all the rage in the ’80s and ’90s—were, in fact, two of the key elements of the outfits Diana put together for her boys. The lineup also included matching shirts, polos, and sweaters. “Looking back at the photos, it just makes me laugh, and I think, ‘How could you do that to us?’” Harry added with a touch of irony.

As they grew up, the two, of course, began to rebel against this tradition—particularly William, who, according to Harry’s account, at one point refused to have anything to do with being his brother’s twin. “Funnily enough, we got to the age when William would turn round and go: ‘Oh, this is ridiculous. You know, I’m the older brother. Why do I have to be dressed the same as him?’” he recalled. “Hang on a second. If you’re going to dress differently, I’m not going to be the only person dressed like this. This is just ridiculous!” Harry replied.

As with any growing boy, things gradually began to change, and the two brothers started to develop their own independent style. But one can’t help but pause to consider how every choice—even the most trivial, like picking out an outfit—was a statement of intent for the beloved princess. Always in the name of love.

Prince Charles and Princess Diana with their sons, William and Harry. December 1986.

Princess Diana with her sons, William and Harry. July 1988.

Princess Diana with her sons, William and Harry. June 1987.

Princess Diana with her sons, William and Harry. October 1990.

Princess Diana with her sons, William and Harry. May 1992.

Princess Diana with her sons, William and Harry. August 1995.

#3537. The Top 10 TV Series Right Now, According to Streaming Data

October's ten most-streamed series are packed with your future favorite shows. There's a couple of modernizations of horror franchises for Halloween (Carrie and Crystal Lake), as well as new horror series Below and Phony. There's an excellent new superhero series Lanterns, sprawling family drama East of Eden, and new seasons of favorites Ted Lasso, Slow Horses, The Diplomat, and Mobland. So don't even try to tell anyone there's nothing on.

Horror master Mike Flanagan (Haunting of Hill House, Midnight Mass) re-imagines Stephen King's tale of teenage telekinesis, taking the story from the 1970s to now, complete with cyber bullying, smart phones, and a modern sensibility. The core of the tale, though, remains the same, as does the titular character's bloody coming-of-age. Powered by a talented young cast that includes Siena Agudong as Susan and Summer H. Howell as the title character, Carrie is a trick-or-treat for horror fans. Stream Carrie on Prime.

Based on John Steinbeck's pillar of Western literature, East of Eden follows three generations of the hardscrabble Hamilton family and the upscale Trask family, farming and ranching clans in California's Salinas Valley. The show's production is a multigenerational story too: It was written and created by Zoe Kazan, whose grandpa Elia directed the 1955 film version of East of Eden. All respect to Elia Kazan, but Steinbeck's story is so massive, it needs a seven-part mini-series. East of Eden is the kind of sprawling, melodramatic story that episodic television was made for. Stream East of Eden on Netflix.

Like Carrie, Crystal Lake reimagines a horror classic—in this case, Friday the 13th—and expands the lore even beyond the 12 films in the franchise. If you've ever wondered how Pamela Voorhees, played here by Linda Cardellini, became a serial murderer, and how her son Jason ended up a relentless, camp-counselor-killing-machine who lives at the bottom of a lake, Crystal Lake has all the answers. In a lot of ways, this show is better than all of the movies. Stream Crystal Lake on Peacock.

Apple TV's Slow Horses delivers a realistic, nuanced take on espionage by detailing the lives of the losers of British Intelligence. Instead of chiseled good guys and gals saving the world, the agents of Slough House are a team of dysfunctional, troubled souls trying to do the right thing (usually) in a morally gray world, just like real agents. Their leader, gruff, obnoxious Jackson Lamb, is played to perfection by Gary Oldman. Slow Horses has an almost perfect Rotten Tomatoes score over its first five seasons, and season 6 is setting new records. Stream Slow Horses on Apple TV+.

DC's TV revamp of Green Lantern details what happens when experienced Lantern Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) trains the new guy, John Stewart (Aaron Pierre), on how to wield the mysterious and powerful Green Lantern Ring. It's a reserved, neo-noir style take on the comic mythos, as the heroes investigate a series of murders tied to an extraterrestrial threat. Lanterns is pulling in a better than 90% fresh ratings from Rotten Tomatoes, so it's definitely worth a stream. Stream Lanterns on HBO Max.

Created by Jesse McKeown and starring Josh Hartnett, Charlie Heaton, and Mackenzie Davis, Below is set in a Newfoundland fishing village beset with aquatic horror. When the Canadian government offers the residents of Snooks Arm a ton of money to relocate, no one really knows why, but ice fisherman Calvin Penney (Hartnett) suspects it has something to do with the monster he saw under the ice when he was a child. If you like taut creature feature style horror, check out Below. Stream Below on Netflix.

Season four of Ted Lasso sees the title character, played by Jason Sudeikis, returning to the UK to take on a new challenge: coaching the Lady Greyhounds, AFC Richmond's second-division women's football team. This multiple Emmy Award-winning series still has all the heart, humor, and positivity of the original run. Stream Ted Lasso on Apple TV+.

The mystery that drives creepy coming-of-age drama Phony is killer: Sonny Cooke, played by Sam Nivola, is a teenager with a very close relationship to his devoted single mother Ellen, played by Connie Britton. After a freak car accident, he wakes up convinced that his mom is an impostor. She looks the same, but there's something off about her in a way that Sonny can't describe, so he sets out to solve the mystery. Phony is rated over 90% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes. Stream Phony on Hulu.

In season four of political thriller series The Diplomat, the Kate Wyler, played by Keri Russell, finds that diplomatic relations between the U.S. and the UK are starting to crumble, and so is her marriage. Meanwhile, U.S. president Grace Penn, played by Allison Janney, and VP Hal Wyler, played by Rufus Sewell, continue their conspiracy to steal a Russian super-weapon, nudging the nation toward war with our longtime adversary. In other words, it's an international mess, with a few powerful people keeping the world from descending into chaos. If you like political intrigue, this is the series for you. Stream The Diplomat on Netflix.

Who doesn't love a sprawling organized crime drama? In Mobland, the crime is being organized in Great Britain, where two warring London crime families, the Harrigans and Stevensons, are locked in a battle for underworld power. In the middle of the crossfire is Harry Da Souza, a gritty fixer played to gruff perfection by Tom Hardy. Season 2 finds Da Souza in the unenviable position of holding together the Harrigan family on the verge of civil war. If you like backstabbing, scheming, murder, and other tropes of high-stakes crime thrillers, you'll like Mobland. Stream Mobland on Paramount+.

#3536. James Gunn's DC Universe Is Being 'Dismantled' As DC Studios Prepares Another Reset (Report)

These DC reboots are starting to become a bit of a tradition. In the wake of James Gunn and Peter Safran "stepping down" as DC Studios co-heads, it seems the new guard is ready to tear down almost their entire cinematic project. At least, according to a new report.

Puck's Matthew Belloni claims to have heard that "plans are already afoot" for new DC Studios head Jeremy Latcham — who steps into the role of president and chief creative officer of DC Studios as of December 1, 2026 — to scrap almost everything Gunn and Safran had planned post-"Man of Tomorrow," "The Batman: Part II," and an unnamed HBO series. As Belloni put it, "So DC goes back into reboot mode ... again."

This is the second major reset for DC's cinematic enterprise (third if you count the pre and post-Walter Hamada era), and it frankly seems like a dire state of affairs. When Gunn and Safran were brought in to head up the newly-christened DC Studios back in 2022, they had grand plans to revive the franchise following a disappointing end to the DC Extended Universe or "Snyderverse." This was supposed to be the moment DC turned things around and finally matched Marvel's cinematic success with an ambitious shared universe. Now, it's all come to a premature end as Skydance CEO David Ellison (who now oversees the newly merged Paramount and Warner Bros.) seemingly prepares to take a wrecking ball to Gunn and Safran's still fledgling DC Universe.

In his article, Matthew Belloni noted how James Gunn and Peter Safran reported to the Warner Bros. Discovery CEO, a post previously held by David Zaslav. The erstwhile head of Warners seemed perfectly happy to let his newly appointed DC Studios co-heads take full creative control. But, as Belloni noted, "Maybe it was too much freedom... hence 'Supergirl.'"

This is, of course, a reference to the box office flop that was this year's "Supergirl," a solo outing for Milly Alcock's Kara Zor-El that brought in just $126.5 million at the box office against a $170 million budget. And while /Film's own "Supergirl" review argued the movie has an aspirational and uplifting message and is nowhere near as bad as its box office returns may suggest, Belloni opined that David Ellison no doubt viewed the failure of "Supergirl" as a result of Gunn and Safran being given too much creative power. Hence, that simply won't be the case with Ellison now in charge.

This also means that while Jeremy Latcham is replacing the former DC Studios co-bosses, he will have nowhere near as much freedom and instead report only to Skydance studio heads Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein. Depending on how you felt about Gunn's creative decisions, then, this is either a good or disappointing development. But even if you like the idea of Ellison and his studio heads calling the shots and keeping DC on a tight leash, none of this bodes well for the brand's cinematic fortunes moving forward — especially if Ellison and co. really do intend to discard Gunn's entire DC roadmap and start from scratch.

When James Gunn and Peter Safran were appointed co-heads of DC Studios, the franchise desperately needed a hard reset. A string of flops in 2023, which included the box office bomb of superheroic proportions that was "The Flash" (a movie which, as it happens, Gunn once called "probably one of the greatest superhero movies ever made"), marked an ignoble end for the DC Extended Universe, and it was Gunn's job to reset, regroup, and revitalize the entire thing. Instead, he opted for a soft reboot that retained several elements of the DCEU. Even at the time, it seemed misguided, and it feels like all the more of a misstep in hindsight.

Now, David Ellison and his executives are, according to Puck, rebooting the entire thing. But it seems like it's all too late. Audiences were never going to be won over by animated "Creature Commandos" series or a potential Mister Miracle animated show. By all means, take a few risks, but maybe save them for after DC has regained some respect among mainstream viewers. Instead, we're at a point where the whole thing is being scrapped yet again, and most people simply do not care about these behind the scenes developments. They just want good movies (which, at this point, have been in short supply).

As Matthew Belloni observed in his report, the last decade has really "only solidified Kevin Feige's run at Marvel [Studios] as all the more remarkable" when compared to DC's struggles. Of course, with Jeremy Latcham having spent many years as a Marvel Studios producer, there's a chance he might turn things around. But by now, audiences are surely tired of having to keep up with these reboots, soft or otherwise.

#3535. Batman Just Officially Saved DC Comics From a Terrible Fate

Reports also indicated DC Comics boss Jim Lee has ‘welcomed’ the news of James Gunn and Peter Safran’s ousting

Business mergers always come with shake-ups, and Skydance's recent acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery was inevitably going to be messy in some way. What was unexpected, however, was this week's announcement that James Gunn and Peter Safran would be stepping down as co-heads of DC Studios. At the same time, Skydance has initiated layoffs in other divisions such as Skydance Games. One area that seems to have escaped the chopping block for now, though, is DC Comics.

Bleeding Cool reports that, according to multiple sources, no one at DC Comics has been offered voluntary buyouts like other divisions were this October. The surprising reason for this comes down to performance. Apparently, DC Comics is outperforming a number of other Warner Bros. departments and is actively turning a profit. Much of that success is directly laid at the feet of Absolute Batman, Scott Snyder and Nick Dragotta's tent-pole series for the publisher's phenomenal Absolute line. Absolute Batman has been both a critical and commercial success, helping DC surpass Marvel in sales. As Bleeding Cool puts it, "no one wants to kill that golden batgoose." There is also an animated adaptation of the comic currently in the works.

There may be another wrinkle to the story, however. The report also states that the company's organizational structure makes roles and responsibilities unclear, meaning that Skydance does not want to risk accidently firing someone integral to the success of books like Absolute Batman. Due to this nebulous organization, Batman seems to have saved DC Comics from going through a major shake-up.

A shocking part of Bleeding Cool's report also revealed that DC Comics publisher, president, and CCO Jim Lee has "welcomed the news of Jeremy Latcham's appointment." Latcham is replacing Gunn and Safran. According to Bleeding Cool's sources, Lee has felt like he has been frozen out at DC Studios by the outgoing pair. This has instigated Lee's decision to work more publicly on projects outside of DC, perhaps preparing to exit his role. That may change with Gunn and Safran gone.

At the same time, rumors are swirling that DC scribe Tom King may be ousted as well, or perhaps just be looking to jump ship. The writer has penned a number of well-received runs at DC, such as Supergirl: Woman of Tomorrow, Mister Miracle, Omega Men, and more. He was also tapped by Gunn to be an architect of the new DC Universe, with several projects being based on his comic work. King also helped create HBO's Lanterns. Now, it seems like King could be leaving DC for a possible return to Marvel. With his divisive Wonder Woman run about to end and Gunn and Safran out, it might be the best opportunity for King to go on to other things.

Spoiler alert! This story discusses the Live Shows Y2K Week on The Voice Season 30, which aired November 9. Episodes are available to stream the day after they air with a Peacock subscription.

The Voice has been airing on the 2026 TV schedule for a hot minute, but Live Shows are finally underway in Season 30 of NBC’s long-running singing competition. This week they were paying tribute to the hits of the late ‘90s and early 2000s. Yes, it was Y2K week, and veteran coach Adam Levine, who I should note won Season 29 with Alexia Jayy, and The Voice newbie Queen Latifah saw their combined six singers take on songs by Aerosmith, Britney Spears, *NSYNC, Bon Jovi, Avril Lavigne, and even fellow coach Kelly Clarkson, each demonstrating the talent that has kept them in the competition until now.

The Top 13 of the season – the coaches’ picks plus fan-voted Kyle Davis, Team Kelly’s 61-year-old singer – kicked of the night by performing a version of “Everybody (Backstreet’s Back”) by the Backstreet Boys that made me want to get up and dance.

It wasn’t until everyone had sung their hearts out that I got mad about the fact that being on the West Coast (in Los Angeles) means that voting is already closed by the time the live shows air. Seriously, I watch this show religiously, and I'm not able to keep a deserving singer from going home? Bummer. People actively not voting for the contestant I think should go through? Yeah, I can get big mad.

One of the most noticeable aspects of the Live Shows is just how fast the episodes can breeze by. While showcasing six singers in rehearsal before their performances, which now includes band members and back-up singers, it only left room for their coach and one other to give feedback while the East Coast viewers were voting.

A fun fact about me is that I love a great Britney Spears cover that puts a spin on her songs that we all know so well. One of my favorites is the slowed down, deeply pained version of “Baby One More Time” from the Scottish rock band Travis. So, when Team Queen’s Lillie Kolich took on the Crossroads star’s 1999 hit “(You Drive Me) Crazy,” I got excited to hear what she was going to do with it. Her sultry take on the otherwise upbeat dance track felt interesting and new and full of swag, and really made Lillie stand out for me.

That’s why I was really surprised, and definitely unnerved, when she was eliminated from the reality competition. She delivered a performance that stood out for being something different that could showcase her artistry. As someone unafraid of putting her own stamp on a classic, I was excited to see what choices she would make moving forward and am now disappointed that I won’t get that chance. What happened with the votes y'all?

Look, I don’t want to take anything away from Queen Latifah’s two remaining singers. It took a lot of guts for Mia Knight to take on the Kelly Clarkson song “Miss Independent” in front of the O.G. American Idol winner herself. It’s not an easy song, but she handled the pressure to deliver with ease. Then, there was BigCountry, who had the liveliest performance of the night, rocking out to Bon Jovi’s “It’s My Life” with his big voice and big personality never letting the stage effects overpower him.

We have one more round of Y2K Week, as we get to hear Team Kelly and Team Riley duke it out before one of those singers is cut. Once the Season 30 winner is crowned in December, Keke Palmer will be taking on hosting duties for Season 31’s The Voice: Celebrity. Until then, keep tuning in to NBC on Mondays (and if you're like me not voting) to see how this all plays out.

#3533. No Reservations: Jessica Craig-Martin Serves Up a Rowdy, Inside Account of ’80s Indochine

No one is famous when they are at home. In New York in 1984, all it took to be famous was to leave the house with intent to commit fame. Beautiful youths were shot through the fame cannon at a rate that made Warhol’s fifteen minutes seem like a century. A cloud of new money hovered over the city, ominously gathering dollars, dropping sudden fortunes on those who knew how to make it rain. No veneer of philanthropy was needed to whitewash the excesses of the wealthy. Conspicuous consumption was the new normal. The new designer clothes all had giant shoulder pads. So did the buildings. The thick-walleted and soft-bellied moved around the city at night in chauffeur-driven carapaces. Eurotrash was the latest import. Fast-talking cocaine replaced nodding-out heroin. The words supermodel and art star fell from heavily glossed lips. Everyone wanted to see and be seen. But where? Studio 54 was closed, disco was dead. Brian McNally’s new restaurant, Indochine, was poised to become the epicenter of ’80s decadence.

Jessica and another waitress with Rupert E at Indochine, 1986.

Waitressing seemed like the best way to make money. I’d met Brian while traveling with the Mardens in France, and he’d mentioned he was opening a restaurant. I had left New York as a hip urban waif with short dark hair and pale skin. I returned curvy and brown-skinned, with long hair that had turned blond in the sun. I wore no makeup and had no interest in fashion, feeling I’d done all that as a teen. I wore vintage ’40s dresses from flea markets, and plastic jelly sandals. When I dropped by 420 Lafayette to ask for a job, Brian looked me up and down and gave me a sly wink. “Yeah, you’ll do.” The question of waitressing experience did not come up.

On opening day, I arrived to find the staff running around frantically with hammers and paintbrushes; stenciling palm leaves on the walls; putting up wallpaper; accepting deliveries of banana trees, ducks, orchids, MSG, and Champagne. There was no way in hell we were going to be ready. I grabbed a brush.

Indochine opened that night, walls still wet, with a private party for Julian Schnabel’s opening at the Mary Boone Gallery. Art dealer Pat Hearn sang Patsy Cline songs wearing a tight 1950s gold brocade dress. Warhol superstar, writer, and genius-about-town Taylor Mead got up on a table to give a hilarious impromptu speech. The crowd danced all night. With one private event after another, opening night lasted a month.

Brian was truly brilliant with people. He made everyone feel like they were in the right place at the right time, and that they were clever, sexy, witty, charming, or all of the above. He was just as comfortable with Henry Geldzahler as he was with Madonna. He could converse on any topic and did so with an easy British charm and lack of pretension that disarmed even the worst snobs.

Moira Hodgson gave us two stars, but other critics found the food “rather ordinary” or “unspectacular,” and everyone agreed that the service was appalling. Ironically, as Brian pointed out later, this became part of the charm of the place. Brian had a strict policy of never refusing a reservation, no matter how overbooked we were. He knew the frenzy at the bar and long waits for booked tables only increased our status as the most sought-after restaurant in town.

When Brian told me my shirt was wrinkled, I said, “Brian, chill out. This is linen. It’s supposed to be wrinkled.” In fact, the shirt could have done with a quick press, but I had only one white shirt and no intention of buying an iron or paying for dry cleaning. Fortunately the waitstaff started to add increased personal touches to the black-and-white dress code until it disappeared. Brian stopped objecting when he saw that the stylish staff was becoming one of the draws of the place. Soon most of us were unrecognizable as waitstaff, leading to many a black-suited banker being called upon for drinks or the check while navigating his way to the bathroom.

Taylor Mead became a nightly fixture at the bar, offering brilliant quips while dining on Dewar’s. Larissa slept on her barstool, her lit cigarette in an elegantly raised hand until someone said, “Larissa!” causing her to reanimate and flick her ash while shouting: “Dahhhh-ling!” She was a movie star who didn’t need movies. If Larissa came to Indochine to sleep, John F. Kennedy Jr. and Daryl Hannah came to break up and reunite, using the vestibule to break up and the bathroom for make-up sex. Carol Channing brought her own silver. Dolly Parton brought her own food. She was on a raw-vegetable and booze diet: “Just gimme the most expensive bottle in the house, honey.” Bianca Jagger ordered her meals in one low, unsmiling breath: “Steamed vegetables no soy sauce no hot sauce no sugar no salt no MSG.” What she didn’t know was that in the kitchen there were three tubs of white powder that went into every single dish: salt, sugar, and MSG.

Dead-eyed debutantes danced in their Manolo’s on tables strewn with platters of spicy beef salad, celebrating an addition to the Guinness dynasty. I wouldn't start using a camera for another eight years, but my mother says Indochine is where I became a photographer.

One night Lena Horne spat her gum directly into my hand. “Gum,” she’d said, after beckoning me over, after which I’d instinctively put my hand out. I gave it to my boyfriend Nick for his birthday. A strand of Cindy Crawford’s hair was the following year’s gift. (We never did get around to cloning her.) Saturday nights were Bridge and Tunnel. I opened the bathroom door to find a woman in high-heeled white boots giving a blowjob to some guy, his soft leather pants around his ankles. Laurie Anderson and I waited to pee while they finished. After that we referred to Saturdays as “White Boot Nights.” Warren Beatty leaned casually against a column, asking a waitress, “You’re a dancer, right? I can see the dance in your body.” A few months later, there he was, leaning against the column again. He asked the same waitress, Robin, “You’re a dancer, right?” Robert De Niro would sit at the end of the bar checking out the scene. Then he’d leave and call the restaurant from his idling limo. He’d ask the maître d’ to tell a woman he found attractive that he was on the phone. Sometimes women simply left their dates mid-meal to join him. One night the Beastie Boys brought a homeless man to dinner who’d asked them if they could spare some change. Even the odd exiled dictator made an appearance. The shah of Iran booked one table for himself and his wife, and three for his bodyguards. I noted their ankle holsters.

The waitstaff was made up of ambitious, creative young New Yorkers. Among them were Fidel Márquez, a painter; Masha Calloway, a fashion designer; and Darrell Maupin, who would open his own successful restaurant, Flamingo East. They and Robin Renzi, the dancer, became my close friends. Robin would later launch the jewelry line Me&Ro with Michelle Quan, who left Indochine for a modeling career. All I had going on outside of work were drawing classes at the New York Academy of Art a few days a week. I had not yet located any particular ambition. I went for dinner with friends, danced all night, and had sex all day. I remember being furious with Brian for a remark he made when I arrived at work: “You look like you just got fucked all day.” I was outraged, but it occurred to me later that he was absolutely right.

There was an ecstasy dealer who took to dropping by the restaurant around midnight. We’d take the pills toward the end of our shifts, hoping no customers would linger too long. After work we’d head to the clubs, needing catharsis and easily spending the money we had just spent hours earning. The Sisyphean irony of this went unnoticed. I was amused to discover that working at Indochine had a certain cachet. Waiters and waitresses were swept past the velvet ropes into all the clubs. I was initially surprised by the mini celebrity status conferred by waiting tables, but it says a lot about the era, which was all about tipping status on its head. Julian Schnabel was flipping burgers ten minutes before he became famous overnight with his broken-plate paintings. With his sensational-looking wife, Jacqueline, on his arm and New York at his feet, he seemed to be starring in his own biopic as he swept into Indochine night after night. “Jessica, get yourself a glass—have some of this Cristal,” he would say with a beneficent wave of his arm. It was the only restaurant in town where you could see Madonna, Sean Penn, Chris Walken, and Andy Warhol in one booth, John Waters and Divine in the next, and Henry Kissinger and his wife having a quiet dinner in another.

A certain high-powered lawyer was easily the restaurant’s most repugnant client, a considerable achievement. On one occasion he was approached by his waitress, Demetrious, a Black, bald, and beautiful torch singer who always wore huge brass earrings in the shape of Africa.

“Can I offer you something from the bar?” she asked him.

“Yes. I would like a different waitress,” he told her without looking up. She ignored him, went away, and returned calmly.

“I already told you, I want another fucking waitress,” he spat.

She shrugged. “I’m your waitress. I guess you’ll just have to deal with it.”

“GET THE FUCK AWAY FROM ME YOU UGLY BLACK BALD BITCH!”

She leaned in. “Sitthefuckdownandshutthefuckupyoudumbwhite-muthafucka,” she said in one breath. Beaten, he sat. I begged Brian to ban him, but Demetrious just shrugged it off. She was used to fighting her own battles and had already moved on.

At first, I was shocked by the overtly sexist behavior and banter at the restaurant. In the art world men did not compare the sex appeal of women in the presence of other women—or to their faces. There was rampant sexism and misogyny in the art world, of course, but it was generally more institutional and less visible to the naked eye. Men in the art world were less likely to openly grab one’s ass, or to make saliva-drenched comments about the run in your stockings inspiring in them an urge to bend you over a table. The art world had its share of knuckle-draggers—but the likelihood of being kneed in the balls by the objects of their desire kept them somewhat held in check. The women who raised me considered that feminism had “worked.” Their very existence was proof. No one thought the work was over—the ERA had failed to pass, after all—but the essential equality of women was beyond question, and the idea of acting coyly around men was considered absurd. However, the liberation train I’d been raised on had not reached restaurant culture. I was shocked to see so many women pushing out their tits, wiggling and giggling for their power-suited dates. Ironically, I’d been sheltered by my avant-garde upbringing.

I met Huy Chi Le on my first shift at Indochine. He was my age and had just arrived in New York from Vietnam. He spoke almost no English. Huy worked six nights a week at Indochine and seven days at another restaurant, working twice the number of hours to make the same amount of money as a waiter. When Huy was promoted at both venues to waiter, he kept both jobs, still taking just a half day off a week. He sent funds to his family and saved the rest. He established credit, obtaining an Amex gold card while we waiters were living out of tip envelopes and dancing all night. He bought a house in Brooklyn and sponsored his family to come over one by one. By the time Brian was ready to sell, Huy was poised to buy. He is now the owner of several businesses, a multimillionaire, and—with former manager Michael Callahan and former waiter Jean-Marc Houmard—co-owner of the still incredibly popular, and now legendary Indochine.

#3532. This New Chrome AI Feature Reads Your Gmail to Make Filling Out Web Forms Easier

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Google Chrome is making it easier to autofill online forms with more than just contact information and credit card numbers. For users with Personal Intelligence enabled, Gemini will now suggest items like order numbers, tracking information, membership IDs, and booking confirmations from Gmail messages when completing forms in Chrome.

Chrome's expanded autofill capabilities use Gemini to read your emails and surface suggestions, meaning you don't have to click back and forth between tabs or manually search for codes or confirmations in your inbox. When you click a form field that has a corresponding piece of data, a pop-up menu appears and indicates that an item is "Suggested by Gemini." You can click this to autofill the suggestion as well as open an additional menu to see the specific source (the original email) or remove the suggestion. The latter doesn't delete anything from Gmail; it simply dismisses the suggestion in Chrome.

As Android Police reports, Google started testing enhanced autofill in Chrome this summer using data from other connected apps like Google Photos. The feature currently rolling out is specific to Gmail and is coming first to U.S. users who have Personal Intelligence enabled on desktop as well as in the Android and iOS apps when using Gemini in Chrome.

In the blog post announcing the enhanced autofill feature, Google states that "sensitive data is encrypted" and that users can manage autofill, including enabling or disabling enhanced suggestions, via Chrome's settings.
