#3510. Big Walk AI Controversy Is a GOTY Awards Twist Sparking a Bigger Debate

An IGF voter stance marks a new hardline for the industry

Big Walk, one of the best-reviewed games of 2026 and by all measures a Game of the Year darling, faces a crossroads on the eve of awards season. Following a recent disclosure of AI use from its developer, Big Walk’s chances at one awards show seem fraught. And its shot at the big one (December’s Game Awards) might be impacted. But it’s not just a chapter in 2026’s awards show saga. In many ways, it’s a boiling over of a debate that’s been bubbling in the games industry for several years now.

On Monday, a group of 19 Independent Game Festival (IGF) jurors, including Immortality director Sam Barlow and Friends at the Table host Austin Walker, shared a statement saying they would not vote for any game that used generative AI tools in any capacity — including for code.

On Bluesky, Barlow said that this discussion among IGF jurors is always lively, but that this year’s “conversation was even more intense.”

Why? It did not take long for at least part of the reason to become clear: Big Walk used generative AI tools in development, developer House House revealed in its voluntary disclosure to the IGF. (In a follow-up statement, Barlow noted that the impetus for the conversation was more broadly about the volume of games that make use of generative AI, and that Big Walk was the "tricky edge case.")

In a statement to Aftermath (also cross-posted on the developer’s website), House House said that “well under 0.1% of Big Walk’s code” had anything to do with generative AI tools, and those tools were used solely to “help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs.” House House also noted that the studio used large language models (LLMs) to generate a baseline, which the team then “modified into game code.” House House’s statement gets into it in full, but the studio pointed to a lighting issue as an example of how LLMs helped with the final phase of Big Walk’s development, amounting to “about 10 lines of code.”

That might seem small in the grand scheme of things, but a hard line is only a hard line if you don’t cross it. And for 19 members of the IGF jury, that’s the line.

The group of jurors cite several reasons for its stance against generative AI, including the technology’s widely documented negative impacts on the economy, the labor market, the environment, and the global informational pipeline. They also say that AI use is “not a foregone conclusion” in the games industry, and, as independent developers, see this as an opportunity to take a stance that many people working at larger companies might not have the leeway to take.

Critically, the inclusion of code as part of the hardline is not something you see every day. Generally, the colloquial argument against generative AI use is reserved for disciplines that are considered more “creative” in nature: art, writing, composition, voice acting, and so forth. You often see people make exceptions for technical work, like programming. This stance from part of the IGF jury marks a clear public expansion of the tent among an influential games industry group, and it’s not lost among a subset of the community that isn’t always public-facing. Responses to Walker’s Bluesky post of the statement are full of programmers thanking the jurors for considering coding an art form.

The debate isn’t merely broken down among clean lines of “AI good” vs. “AI bad.” Some see it as a betrayal not just that House House used these tools but that it didn’t disclose that use upon release. If the use of an LLM was no big deal, the argument goes, why hide it? And if the company hid this instance, what else was hidden? (Though Steam requires a disclosure for generative AI use, it does not require that disclosure for the use of code or chatbots.)

For others, it’s just about the best case scenario for a worst-case situation. It’s a fairly minimal use, they say, and if strict delineations are made for the public disclosure of 10 lines of AI-generated code, wouldn’t that disqualify many video games? Plus, they say, House House seems reflective and open to change, pointing to the studio’s philanthropic efforts in the past as a sign of good will. (In 2020, following the release of Untitled Goose Game, House House pledged to donate 1% of its profits to organizations that help members of indigenous communities make rent.)

Will this ultimately affect Big Walk’s chances during awards season? Maybe! Though the statement was issued by fewer than 20 IGF jury members, it’s gained traction across both social and traditional media. And now that it’s become a matter of public interest and widespread discussion, there’s always the chance other voters are swayed by their arguments or otherwise hesitate to vote for Big Walk.

How this affects the Game Awards horse race is a cloudier issue. On Monday, Big Walk was all but a lock for a Game of the Year nomination, according to Polygon’s ongoing analysis of the race. But an indie game securing a GOTY nomination is always an uphill race — even without the albatross of controversy.

Yes, the technically indie game Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 smashed records and swept the 2025 Game Awards, but it also broke into the mainstream in an undeniable way. Big Walk, despite its impressive critical reception, has not. To secure the nomination, it needs every vote it can get from nominating jurors who are part of the indie gaming community, which largely rejects generative AI. To wit: Clair Obscur may have run the tale during the 2025 awards circuit, but ultimately had its Game of the Year award from the Indie Game Awards (note: not the same thing as the IGF) stripped over inclusion of AI.

Beyond awards, the entire saga seems an inflection point for an industry that has struggled to grapple with the encroachment of generative AI. Developers of all strata — from the creator of The Last of Us to the studio behind the Wendy’s JRPG — have taken public stances against the technology, refusing to use AI whatsoever in any part of development. They stand in contrast to prominent firms like Embark Studios, which caught heat for using AI in its 2023 shooter The Finals and then immediately used the same tools for its 2025 shooter Arc Raiders, or Epic Games, which is run by a CEO whose stance on LLMs could fairly be summarized as “Claude = Jesus 2.0.”

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

All the while, AI tools have proven a third rail for large portions of the gaming audience, often prompting public apologies from developers that disclose their use. House House joins that club.

“Big Walk was developed without an internal AI usage policy in place, and we consider that lack of policy a failure,” House House said in its statement. “We will work to have a more comprehensive policy going forwards.”

That’s good on House House. Stating some clearly defined rules for this sort of thing helps settle internal debate, and provides a north star for anyone working at the studio. It could even serve as a model for others in the industry to adopt. But the lack of policy shouldn’t land entirely on the shoulders of a small outfit in Melbourne — or any developer of any size, for that matter. At this point, generative AI tools have been publicly available for nearly half a decade. Until governments start taking the technology seriously and passing real regulations around what counts as acceptable use, this will keep happening.

Bruce Straley isn't all too fond of generative AI art

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

Every task you give to a genAI is one you are not paying a human for.

And it's not like game devs of any kind below the exec levels have a great work-life balance or obscene incomes.

Add to that the fact that current genAIs are trained on stolen data and I'm out.

Before you get mad at me, remember!: Awards are silly. The stakes here could not be lower.

I don't personally understand hard-line positions against using AI in *any* capacity. LLMs are extremely useful in helping break through a difficult coding problem. I consider myself the author of all of my code, even though I will use LLMs to troubleshoot issues, the same way I considered myself the author of my code when I would reference books, guides, and stackoverflow threads to help with tough problems.

Using AI output as very flexible reference material is meaningfully different (to me!) than using it to generate final products that you do not touch.

The use of AI for Big Walk strikes me as an appropriate application of the technology.

Keep it out of creative work but to me coding is fine. 99% of coding for games today is not creative, it's piecing together tools and frameworks that other people already made within an existing engine ecosystem. It's a mature technical field. I don't see why a developer should spend weeks or months pulling their hair out over a bug or performance issue, pulling overtime, suffering mentally and physically, when the tools exist to resolve the problem. And before anyone says that's overly dramatic try being a programmer with a hard deadline. It sucks!

I say this as someone who really does not like AI and won't support studios that use it, but I really don't think this is as simple as "they used it and they should be disqualified and boycotted". I do think there's room for nuance here, unfortunately people are going to be louder about this than they are about like, Disney and Adobe effectively killing off the entertainment industry as a viable career.

#3509. Why Prince William Is Reluctant to Become Head of the Commonwealth

Following King Charles’s successful nine-day tour to the Caribbean, the future of the Commonwealth has become a much debated subject. At last week’s Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Antigua and Barbuda, Charles, who was designated Head of the Commonwealth, a role he assumed after his late mother Queen Elizabeth, told assembled leaders he found the voluntary union of 56 nations to be a “source of enormous encouragement and pride.”

However, Buckingham Palace has made it clear this weekend that Charles will only serve as monarch in the Caribbean realms “for as long as they wish” and that the monarch is open to change. According to The Times, Charles is “fully open” to those realms removing him as head of state.

While Charles was in the Caribbean, there was ongoing debate about slave trade reparations, which the monarch addressed in his speech to CHOGM. Describing it as a “monstrous injustice” he expressed his “profound personal sorrow” but fell short of making a formal apology for Britain’s role in the slave trade. (Since King Charles is a ceremonial head of state, he is unable to apologize on behalf of Britain unless the government sanctions it.)

Amid calls for reparations, there are questions about the future of the Commonwealth and who its next head should be. In conversation with Vanity Fair, constitutional expert Ed Owens, author of After Elizabeth: Can the Monarchy Save Itself?, discusses what’s in store for the future.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

King Charles reacts near Antigua and Barbuda flags during a visit to Nelson's Dockyard, a historic naval base established in 1725, during his visit to Antigua and Barbuda on November 2, 2026 in St John's, Antigua and Barbuda.

Vanity Fair: Prince William has made it clear that he does not necessarily expect to follow his father as head of the Commonwealth, saying that the decision belongs to the Commonwealth itself.

Ed Owens: Prince William hinted after his difficult 2022 tour of Belize, the Bahamas, and Jamaica that he wasn’t focused on following his father as head of the Commonwealth. A couple of weeks ago The Times of London confirmed that the prince’s position was unchanged on this issue. Crucially, the position of head of the Commonwealth is not hereditary. King Charles got the role because his mother and predecessor, Queen Elizabeth II, actively lobbied Commonwealth heads of state to ensure that the role would pass to him when he became monarch, following her death. But it will not automatically transfer to William when Charles dies.

What is the Commonwealth and how significant is that statement?

The Commonwealth of Nations (as it’s officially known) is a voluntary association of 56 independent member states. Most of these member states were once colonies in the British empire. Decolonization began after World War II and most newly independent states—though no longer part of the empire—became part of the new Commonwealth. This new international body represented change but also continuity, enabling Britain to maintain a global (but mostly symbolic) presence at a time when its real geopolitical power was rapidly in retreat. The Commonwealth also provided a stage for the monarchy to continue to exercise an important international role. George VI was the last emperor and first Head of the Commonwealth. The latter role was invented by the British government to replace the former and allowed the monarch to maintain a semblance of global prestige while helping to facilitate the process of decolonization.

Although most member states have historical ties to Britain, any country can apply to join the Commonwealth—exemplified by recent members like Rwanda, Mozambique, Gabon, and Togo. Members commit to shared principles outlined in the Commonwealth charter, including democracy, human rights, the rule of law, and sustainable development. In reality, though, many member states have failed to live up to these principles, and the Commonwealth has, in recent years, felt morally directionless.

William’s reluctance to take on the mantle of Head of the Commonwealth isn’t that surprising: He and his advisers want to future-proof his reign. One way to do this is to identify potential problems in order to avoid them. The Commonwealth is one such potential problem, and William seems to have calculated that the headship of this organization likely represents more trouble than it is worth.

Does it represent a fundamental shift in the monarchy’s attitude toward the organization, or simply an acknowledgement that the old imperial relationship is no longer sustainable?

We have to remember that 15 members of the Commonwealth (including the UK) are also “realms”—i.e. their head of state is King Charles. I think it’s clear even to the current king that his position as monarch of the 14 realms beyond Britain is unsustainable. Eventually all 14 nations, and perhaps the UK too, will opt to become republics, cutting their ties with the crown. Those nations most likely to become republics soonest—owing to the fact that they have surging republican movements—are the Caribbean realms, two of which (the Bahamas and Antigua and Barbuda) King Charles visited during his recent tour to the Caribbean. Indeed, we can even interpret the tour as the king and his courtiers preparing the ground for this transition to republics. This is because, though former realms will no longer have as their head of state the incumbent monarch, they will almost certainly remain members of the wider Commonwealth.

What King Charles was trying to do with his latest tour was to inject energy and meaning into the idea of the Commonwealth, more than attempt to reinvigorate the personal bonds that connect him to his peoples in the Caribbean. In loudly acknowledging the injustices of the slave trade in which Britain was, for a long time, complicit, while also reminding his hosts that Britain was one of the first major powers to abolish and oppose slavery—the king has sought to address and ease concerns in ways that might enable the Commonwealth to function more cohesively in the future, irrespective of whether the UK’s monarch remains in post as head of the Commonwealth.

When Charles eventually leaves the throne, could the Commonwealth decide that it no longer needs a British monarch as its figurehead? What might replace that role? Will the Commonwealth continue?

I absolutely think [the] Commonwealth nations will look to replace the British monarch with a new figurehead. My sense is that many nations would already prefer to have a different kind of figurehead, for example a head who belongs to one of the 56 member states and is elected by member states for a set term. Alternatively, there could be some kind of “rolling” headship, whereby every member nation is invited to elect an official who will take a 12-month turn as head of the Commonwealth.

Whether or not the Commonwealth will continue is more difficult to say. Certainly one of the reasons it has survived until now is because of the energy and engagement of two British monarchs—Charles and Elizabeth II—who have viewed it as a potential force for good in the world. Without its connection to the British monarchy, it may lose what is left of its momentum. However, its survival also depends on wider geopolitical shifts: If individual governments within the Commonwealth view it as [a] useful arena for bringing together states who could benefit from closer association—be that economic, political, or military association—then it may continue long into the future.

There is an increasingly difficult conversation about Britain’s colonial past, slavery, and reparations. Charles has expressed personal sorrow over the slave trade, but the question of a formal apology remains politically and constitutionally complicated. How much freedom does the king actually have to address these issues, and could William take a different approach?

The king has very little freedom to apologize unless his government specifically sanctions and encourages such an apology. As the recent Caribbean tour made clear, I think Charles would prefer to strike a more nuanced line, reminding audiences that, despite the UK’s colonial past and its involvement in the horrors of slavery, Britain was one of the first major powers to abolish slavery and that it played an important role in bringing to an end the maritime trade in human chattel. Whether William takes a different approach will depend entirely on the UK government’s approach to formal apologies and reparations. My sense is that no government—at least not now or in the near-to-medium-term future—will agree to financial reparations, because historians, philosophers, and politicians are increasingly pushing back on such a solution, questioning why UK taxpayers (already under huge strain) should fork out huge sums for the wrongs committed by some of their ancestors more than two centuries ago.

What would Queen Elizabeth II make of this? She saw the Commonwealth as her father’s legacy and her second family.

I think she would probably be relatively relaxed, recognizing that times change and institutions have to evolve. Let’s not forget that as queen she oversaw many key alterations in the way both the monarchy and Commonwealth functioned through her long reign, as was required by shifts in politics, economics, culture, and social norms. While the Commonwealth was of emotional importance to her—not least for the way it connected her back to her father and predecessors—by the end of her reign it was already a shadow of what it once had been and she would have known that it was likely to continue on a trajectory of decline. William has decided that given the challenges and changes of the mid-20th century the monarchy and royal family’s future is likely to be stronger without the post-imperial baggage of the Commonwealth. I think his grandmother would have respected the way he is putting the family firm first in this instance.

#3508. The Cat In The Hat Is Another Box Office Flop Warner Bros. Can't Afford

Another weekend, another bad result for Warner Bros. "The Cat in the Hat" looked like it could help get Warner Bros. back on track at the box office. Instead? It became the latest in a string of flops that has defined the studio's year. Family-friendly movies have been very safe bets in recent years, and on paper, Dr. Seuss is very good intellectual property to exploit for a PG animated movie. But this didn't pan out as anyone had hoped.

Director Erica Rivinoja's "The Cat in the Hat" opened to a very disappointing $20 million domestically. It also pulled in just $10 million internationally, giving it a soft $30 million global start. That was only good enough for the number two spot, since "Godzilla Minus Zero" ruled the box office with a $30.5 million opening. Normally, it would be much safer to bet on the PG family movie over the R-rated Japanese monster movie. But this wasn't a normal situation, and instead, the animated movie was left fighting for scraps, relatively speaking.

The new movie sees the title character (voiced by "SNL" alum Bill Hader) take on his toughest assignment yet for the I.I.I.I. (Institute for the Institution of Imagination and Inspiration, LLC): to cheer up Gabby and Sebastian, a pair of siblings struggling with their move to a new town. It carries a reported budget in the $90 million range.

This major disappointment comes mere weeks after the Warner Bros. Discovery and Paramount merger was made official, with the mega-corporation Skydance now ruling over both studios. That corporation is lousy with debt and it needs Warner Bros. to deliver. Unfortunately for CEO David Ellison and his new film chiefs, they're walking into a messy situation. They've got a ship to right.

The storied movie studio had a stellar year in 2025, with massive hits like "Sinners" and "F1" to its name. Warner Bros. set a huge record that year with six movies in a row opening to at least $40 million, but 2026 has not been nearly as kind.

Skydance inherited a string of massive flops from the Warner Bros. deal, with its 2027 slate also looking a bit uneven. Things could get worse before they get better, as evidenced by the performance of "The Cat in the Hat." Granted, the year should end on a high note as "Dune: Part 3" is just around the corner, but even that can't make up for everything that preceded it.

A very rough rule of thumb for theatrical success has always been a movie making 2.5 times its budget, given that theaters keep around half of all money from ticket sales. So just how bad has the year been for Warner Bros? The studio's bombs/disappointments include "The Bride!" ($90 million budget / $24 million worldwide haul), "They Will Kill You" ($10 million budget / $19 million worldwide), "Mortal Kombat II" ($80 million budget / $129 million worldwide), "Supergirl" ($170 million budget / $126 million worldwide), "The End of Oak Street" ($90 million budget / $121 million worldwide), "Practical Magic 2" ($75 million budget / $106 million worldwide), and "Digger" ($180 million budget / $50 million worldwide).

Yikes. Tom Cruise's "Digger" alone will lose as much as $250 million. Hits like "Wuthering Heights" and "Clayface," encouraging though they may be, can't come close to making up for losses that pile up for would-be blockbusters like "Supergirl." Unfortunately, this Dr. Seuss adaptation now joins this ever-growing list of crushing disappointments. Skydance and the new team has their work cut out for them.

#3507. Apple Is About to Release a Touchscreen MacBook Pro (Plus Four More Devices)

Apple has had a busy fall. Head to the company's website, and you'll immediately be greeted by a sea of new products: the foldable iPhone Duo; the iPhone 18 Pro; HomePod mini 2; Apple Watch Series 12; the list goes on. It seems, under new Apple CEO Jon Ternus, the company is ready for a refresh of just about every product it sells. To that point, the company seems far from finished. Just this week, Apple is planning to release five brand new products, each launching on Friday. While four of these are Macs, Apple does have a new iPad in the works, as well. Here's everything new Apple is releasing this week.

Finally. For the first time, the iPad mini is about to ship with an OLED display. Apple's smallest tablet has always come with a standard screen. Despite its price tag, the iPad mini has never come with an OLED display, or even a mini-LED screen, until now. With this new model, there is no backlight. As such, each individual pixel on the iPad's display will be able to shut itself off when displaying dark content. That will benefit the content you watch on this device, as well as the overall contrast of the screen.

Beyond the new OLED panel, the new iPad mini is thinner and lighter than the previous model. It also comes with Apple's newest A20 Pro chip, the same processor the company put in its iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo smartphones. The new device starts at $699 for 128GB of storage, though there are various upgrades, including nano-texture glass (add $100) and cellular (add $150).

Good news: There's a new iMac. Bad news: Not much is different here from the previous model. The biggest change here is the new M6 chip, which Apple says is up to five times faster than the iMac with M4 and up to 12 times faster than the iMac with M1. With that M6 chip, the iMac now supports Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. Other than that, this is the same iMac you may already know: It comes with a 24-inch LED display (no OLED, unfortunately), two or four USB-C ports (depending on the configuration), and a built-in 12MP webcam. If you're looking for a new all-in-one computer, or you've been considering upgrading your older iMac, this is likely a great choice. But if you already have an M-series iMac, it's not such an obvious upgrade. (My M1 iMac may be up to 12 times slower, but it's still plenty fast for me.) Apple didn't change the price here: The M6 iMac still starts at $1,499 for two ports, 16GB of RAM, and 256GB of storage.

Similarly, Apple's newest 14-inch MacBook Pro isn't much different from the previous model—save for the new processor. This model also comes with Apple's M6 chip, which Apple says is up to 13 times faster for AI processing than the M1 MacBook Pro. (Apple seems keen on convincing stubborn M1 users to upgrade this cycle.) Now, the company is offering this model of MacBook Pro in three chipsets, depending on use case: M6 for "entry-level" pro work; M5 Pro for mid-tier pro work; and M5 Max for the most demanding situations.

But, like the M6 iMac, this is the same MacBook Pro Apple sold before. It has a 14-inch mini-LED display with a refresh rate up to 120Hz. It comes with three Thunderbolt 4 (USB-C) ports, an HDMI port, and an SDXC card slot. It, too, has a 12MP webcam for video calls. Apple's newest MacBook Pro starts at $1,999, but you can quickly ramp up that price tag with screen, chip, memory, or storage upgrades.

Apple's most exciting product launch this week is undoubtedly the new touchscreen MacBook Pros. Unlike the M6 MacBook Pro, which only comes in the 14-inch variant, Apple's first touchscreen laptop comes in both 14- and 16-inch options. Apple says this touchscreen lets you scroll, zoom, or draw on the display. That works with basic functions, like web browsing or selecting files, but also with specific workflows, like playing virtual instruments in Logic Pro, or manipulating an object in a 3D modeling app. Like the iPad mini, this laptop comes with an OLED display (Apple calls it PROLED XDR), with up to 1,000 nits of typical brightness and 2,000 nits of HDR brightness. It also brings back the backlit Apple logo, something I've missed on my last two MacBooks.

This MacBook Pro also comes with the iPhone's Dynamic Island for the first time. This replaces the "notch" that other MacBook Pros and MacBook Airs currently ship with. It can function as a basic webcam, but also as a dedicated zone for Spotlight, Live Activities, and Siri AI. This machine comes in either M5 Pro or M5 Max variants—no M6 for this model—as Apple seems to be positioning it exclusively for the most taxing situations (particularly AI). The company says the new MacBook Pro has up to 13 more hours of battery life than Intel-based MacBook Pros, and can fast charge up to 50% in 30 minutes. It's essentially a supercharged version of the existing MacBook Pro.

As such, this is Apple's most expensive laptop. The 14-inch M5 Pro version starts at $2,899, while the 16-inch starts at $3,399. However, you can configure these machines to have outrageous price tags. The maxed-out 16-inch MacBook Pro is $14,549, roughly half of which is the 16TB of RAM.

#3506. Six Fitness 'Rules' That Don't Actually Matter

I’ve learned a lot in my many years in the gym, and beginner-me would be shocked and appalled by the things present-me does during workouts. With the benefit of experience, I now do exercises I used to think one should “never” do, and I’ve broken pretty much every other rule besides.

I've already explained a bunch of things you can stop worrying about as a beginner, but I’d like to expand on that list with a few more rules that even intermediate-level exercisers can ditch without consequence.

If you can theoretically do 13 bicep curls with a certain weight, how many curls should you actually do? One common misconception is that if you don’t do all 13, you’re leaving gains on the table. The rule kind of makes sense if you have truly no clue where to start; if you go until you can’t do a single rep more, then at least you know you’re not slacking off.

But the downside is that going to failure for every set of every lift is just going to make you exhausted. On bicep curls, maybe not so much, but once you’re squatting pretty heavy weights, you’re going to feel spent if you do every single set to failure, and that fatigue will get in the way of getting a good workout in consistently. What’s better is to follow a program that advises you on when to hold back and when it’s a good time to really push your limits. You’ll find that most of the time, you stop a set at least 2-3 reps shy of failure, and sometimes even more.

Rest days are a convenient tool for making sure you’re not overworking yourself, but that’s all. Organizations like the American College of Sports Medicine recommend leaving 48 hours between intense strength-training sessions for a given muscle, but if you look at where they get that number, it’s meant to be a general recommendation for beginners and for people who are exercising just to stay healthy. Once you’re talking about athletes or enthusiasts, the ACSM acknowledges that training most days of the week is fine if your program manages fatigue effectively. That may mean alternating between heavier and lighter days, rather than taking complete rest days.

The “10% rule” is a not-terrible guideline for figuring out how quickly to ramp up your training. But like many of these other myths, it’s a suggestion, not a commandment to be strictly obeyed.

As running coach Jason Fitzgerald told Lifehacker, “While the adage is to only increase weekly mileage by 10%, this may be either too conservative or even too aggressive depending on where you start from.” When you’re coming back from a short layoff, you can probably increase mileage a lot faster. Same goes if you’re a beginner and your mileage is overall very low; if you took the rule literally, you wouldn’t be able to increase from zero to any other number.

Meanwhile, serious running programs—once again, a program is a wonderful thing—may give you a bigger increase for a few weeks in a row, then cut back and decrease your mileage temporarily before ramping up again. Or they may keep you at the same mileage for weeks at a time before venturing a larger increase. If you were to stick to the 10% rule, you would miss out on the advantages of programs that work this way.

There are pros and cons to lifting before cardio, and to doing cardio before lifting. It’s more of an “it depends” than a rule. So here are some of the ways to decide which makes sense.

Your lifts tend to suffer when you’re fatigued, and doing them fresh is important to you

Cardio is your top priority, and you want to have more energy for it

Your lifts are the kind of thing that can get done even when you’re fatigued

Or you only intend to do a small amount of cardio before lifting

So a cyclist may prefer to do a strength workout after hopping off the bike, but a powerlifter would probably rather get their conditioning in after finishing squats for the day. Either is fine if you don’t care, or if you prefer to mix it up.

There are a few supplements that can help you in your fitness journey, but none of them are necessary. Creatine is one of the best-known muscle-building supplements. It’s understood to be effective, but here’s the thing: Just because it does something for most people doesn’t mean it does very much. If you decide it’s too expensive or just that you would rather not have another thing to remember to take every day, you’re not missing out on any substantial amount of gains.

Likewise, protein powder is a helpful way to get more protein in your diet, but you don’t need to use a supplement; you can just eat more protein-containing foods.

And finally, pre-workout drinks can give you more energy in the gym (it’s mostly caffeine), but the idea that you need it is a very recent development. Even ten years ago, it wasn’t really a thing. People showed up to the gym with a coffee or a coke or with no caffeine at all in their stomach, and worked out just fine.

Look, people have been exercising successfully for millennia, but all of our apps and devices weren't even a thing until the 2000s. Tracking every minute, every step, or every mile of your routine is not actually necessary. You’re still a runner even if you don’t have an app that knows how many miles you ran. You don’t even have to track your sets and reps in your lifting journal if you don’t want to. Your body is what knows how much work you put in, even if your phone were to get wiped overnight.

#3505. Jennifer Lawrence's R-Rated Spy Movie Is One Of HBO Max's Biggest Streaming Hits

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

An R-rated spy thriller starring Jennifer Lawrence is finding new life on HBO Max. The Oscar-winner's 2018 movie "Red Sparrow" has become one of the streamer's biggest hit movies, nearly a decade after its original release.

Directed by Francis Lawrence, who had previously worked with Jennifer Lawrence on "The Hunger Games" movies, "Red Sparrow" is currently the eighth-biggest movie on HBO Max right now, per FlixPatrol. It sits just above "The Wolverine" and just below "The First Purge." Olivia Wilde's comedy "The Invite" is still HBO Max's biggest streaming hit, but the fact that an eight-year-old thriller is right up there with the streamer's current biggest movies is meaningful.

"Red Sparrow" sees Lawrence play a deadly Russian spy. The film centers on Dominika (Lawrence), a former ballerina forced to enter Sparrow School, a government program that thrusts her into a treacherous espionage game. She emerges as a lethal agent, but is trapped in a world she desperately wants to escape. Joel Edgerton ("Warrior"), Matthias Schoenaerts ("Rust and Bone"), Charlotte Rampling ("Broadchurch"), Mary-Louise Parker ("Weeds"), and Ciarán Hinds ("Rome") also star.

The movie is based on the novel of the same name by Jason Matthews. Before it turned into a Lawrence and Lawrence "Hunger Games" reunion, "The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo" director David Fincher and Rooney Mara were poised to reunite for "Red Sparrow." Darren Aronofsky ("Black Swan") was also set to direct at one point. But after much back and forth with a revolving door of A-list talent coming and going, it became a Lawrence starring vehicle. The results were viewed as underwhelming at the time.

Critics weren't terribly kind to the thriller upon its initial release. It currently holds a not-so-great 45% approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes. /Film called "Red Sparrow" an "overlong waste of Jennifer Lawrence's talent" in our review from 2018. It also didn't resonate as well as Fox had hoped it would at the box office at the time.

Against a relatively steep $69 million budget, the movie pulled in $151 million worldwide. It was by no means a hit, especially relative to expectations. Keep in mind that Francis Lawrence and Jennifer Lawrence had a great track record together. "The Hunger Games: Mockingjay — Part 2" ruled the box office just a few years earlier, capping off a multi-billion-dollar run for that franchise. Not to mention that Lawrence was just a handful of years removed from her Oscar win for "Silver Linings Playbook."

Maybe it's because Lawrence remains a big star, with viewers seeking out stuff they haven't seen of hers before. Maybe it's because this sort of action/thriller is the perfect kind of "watch it on the couch" movie. Either way, what was once a disappointment is finding new life all these years later.

You can also grab "Red Sparrow" on 4K, Blu-ray, or DVD from Amazon.

#3504. How to get the Sinking Lure in Zelda Ocarina of Time

The Sinking Lure is an optional item you can find in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake, but the conditions for finding it are a little confusing. The lure itself isn't necessary for beating the game, and you can't even leave the fishing pond with it, so don't fret if this is something you're stuck on.

Below, we explain where to find the Sinking Lure in the Ocarina of Time remake, as well as what you can use the lure on.

Being honest, the conditions for getting the Sinking Lure to show up are a little confusing. We've explained our experiences across three different save files below.

For one, you may need to win the big prize in at least one time period. As young Link, you'll need to catch a that is at least 50 cm long to win the Piece of Heart, or as adult Link, you'll need to catch a fish that is at least 60 cm long to win the Golden Scale. We had a save file that had the Golden Scale but no Piece of Heart, and were able to find the Sinking Lure as young Link. Similarly, we have a save file where we have the Piece of Heart, but no Golden Scale, and we were able to find the lure as adult Link.

Additionally, the lure will actually only show up after you pay the Fishing-Pond Man the rupees and rent the rod. In our tests, he says something about the lure (either being against the rules or that it keeps showing up in his pond), whenever the lure does appear.

There are a few places it can spawn: by the smaller waterfall pouring into a stone fountain on the north side of the lake, at the larger waterfall on the south side of the lake, or by debris inside the pond.

We also noticed that when testing things out for this guide, if you leave the area and then immediately come back, the Sinking Lure will not show up again until you fully leave the map and come back. For example, we ran in and out of the shop a few times to try to find the various spawn locations, but the Sinking Lure never showed up again until we warped to the Temple of Time and hoofed it back to the fishing pond. When we returned, we found the Sinking Lure again right away.

Well, as the Fishing-Pond Man warns you, if you use the Sinking Lure on any of the regular bass in the pond, he will not give you a reward, with one exception. If you manage to actually catch the Hylian loach at the bottom of the pond, he'll give you 50 rupees.

The Sinking Lure makes catching fish much easier, except for the loach. However, the Sinking Lure does make it a bit easier to hook the loach, because they spend a majority of their time underwater. The Hylian loach will require a lot of patience to catch, as it jumps out of the water and changes directions a lot, and it just takes longer to reel in. That being said, catching the Hylian loach is mainly for clout, as you don't earn anything outside the purple rupee for nabbing it.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is a little bit different than the original game, so if you need guides to help you through, we don’t blame you. We have walkthroughs for all the dungeons, from the Deku Tree to Ganondorf's Castle. We also have guides for the sillier, in-between parts of the game, like when you have to find Richard (the dog) or Cuccos.

For those going for 100% completion, we also have guides on where to find every Piece of Heart, every Gold Skulltula token, and where to plant every Magic Bean.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3503. The Newest 4K Amazon Fire TV Stick Is Nearly 60% Off Right Now

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Amazon has cut the price of its latest Fire TV Stick 4K, dropping it to $24.99 from $59.99 and bringing it to its lowest price ever, according to price trackers. At this price, it's an affordable way to bring 4K streaming to an older television or give a sluggish smart TV a performance upgrade. And because this streaming stick measures just 3.6 inches and draws power directly from your TV's USB port using the included cable, it can sit out of sight behind your screen without taking up another wall outlet.

Despite its small size, it supports 4K streaming over Wi-Fi 6, along with HDR10, HDR10+, and HLG for improved contrast and color on compatible televisions. What you don't get is Dolby Vision or Dolby Atmos audio. If either is important to your home theater setup, the Fire TV Stick 4K Plus, currently $39.99, is worth considering for the extra $15. Otherwise, there's little to complain about when it comes to performance, with PCMag reporting that apps respond almost instantly and 4K streams load quickly with almost no blurry, low-resolution moments.

The redesigned Alexa voice remote is another improvement, with a more comfortable shape, an easier-to-find home button, and dedicated shortcuts for major streaming services. You can also use Alexa to search for shows, launch apps, or control compatible smart home devices. The software experience is less impressive, with advertisements and recommendations dominating the home screen, leaving relatively little room for your actual apps. There's also no support for Apple AirPlay or Google Cast, so sharing content directly from your phone isn't particularly convenient. Still, if you're comfortable with Amazon's interface and don't need the missing Dolby formats, the Fire TV Stick 4K delivers responsive streaming and a useful remote for just $25.

#3502. Avengers: Doomsday Billboard May Have Spoiled Thor's Biggest Power Upgrade Yet

Doomsday is almost upon us, and no, I'm not talking about Joe Russo's wretched vision of an AI garbage future. I am, of course, talking about he and his brother's latest Marvel team-up movie "Avengers: Doomsday" which may have just been partially spoiled by, of all thing, a billboard.

Per a Twitter/X post from Marvel Updates, new "Doomsday" billboards have gone up in Shanghai, one of which depicts Robert Downey Jr.'s Victor Von Doom summoning an energy blast. The other, however, is a bit more interesting. It shows Florence Pugh's Yelena Belova/Black Widow, Chris Evans' Steve Rogers/ ex-Captain America, Chris Hemsworth's Thor, and James Marsden's Scott Summers/Cyclops similarly wielding their various powers. But some fans have pointed out that the lightning surrounding Thor — who's seen holding his battle axe, Stormbreaker — appears yellow as opposed to the usual blue hue used in previous films and the "Doomsday" trailers themselves.

New banners for 'AVENGERS: DOOMSDAY' have been spotted in Shanghai. pic.twitter.com/iCOsrgdumJ

— Marvel Updates (@marvel_updat3s) November 10, 2026

This is notable, because it suggests Thor could be using a hugely powerful force known as the Odinforce in "Doomsday." This power, previously unused by the character in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, was created by the Kings of Asgard, and it could prove pretty handy in the Avengers' upcoming clash with Doctor Doom. For now, it remains unclear whether this billboard actually does spoil the inclusion of Odinforce in "Doomsday," but it would make a lot of sense for Thor to power up ahead of his battle with RDJ's villain. The only thing is, there's a major trade-off that comes with using this particular power, which could mean Hemsworth's hero is about to take a long nap.

The Odinforce comes with a big caveat. Those who use it must enter what's known as Odinsleep, whereby they become unconscious while recharging. If the Shanghai billboard does, in fact, show Thor using the Odinforce, that could spark a dramatic storyline for the character.

For some reason, Chris Hemsworth's hero has been given the character arc of Ross from "Friends." He started out as a fearless and formidable leader before demonstrating a more humorous side and eventually becoming a bit of a joke himself. 2019's "Avengers: Endgame" in particular was accused of fat-shaming the grief-stricken Thor, concluding the God of Thunder's journey from serious warrior to silly superhero. Even Hemsworth told GQ that 2022's "Thor: Love and Thunder" was "too silly," adding, "I think we just had too much fun."

When the remarkably dull "Avengers: Doomsday" teaser trailers debuted in early 2026, we did at least get our first look at a much more serious Thor, who will clearly be a lot less "silly" in the upcoming team-up movie than he has in other recent MCU projects. All of which is to say that allowing him to wield the Odinforce in "Doomsday," which could involve a major sacrifice, would be a nice way to treat the character more seriously, providing a dramatic storyline that perhaps sees him willingly embrace Odinsleep in his attempt to overpower Doctor Doom and save his friends.

As unimportant as it may seem to the uninitiated, the appearance of heroes' powers in "Avengers: Doomsday" is clearly something to which Marvel Studios pays close attention. We've already seen the studio upgrade the look of Doctor Doom's power energy to more closely resemble the famous Kirby Krackle of the comic books. As such, the color of Thor's lightning isn't as trivial at it may seem.

This isn't technically the first time fans have spotted hints of the Odinforce in "Avengers: Doomsday" promotional material either. Back in July 2026, Earth 616 posted on Twitter/X highlighting promotional art in which Thor is shown holding Stormbreaker with orange/yellow lightning surrounding the weapon.

Thor's lightning in the MCU has always been blue-white pure electrical power channeled through Mjolnir or Stormbreaker.

The yellow-gold lightning in this promotional poster is completely different from anything we have seen before.

In the comics the Odinforce manifests as... pic.twitter.com/4JQKlPte14

— Earth 616 (@MarvelExrth616) July 12, 2026

The post also points out that Thor prays to Odin in his "Doomsday" teaser trailer, saying, "Lend to me the strength of the All-Fathers, so that I might fight once more." All of this combined with the latest billboard revelation suggests we'll be seeing some sort of upgraded Thor in "Doomsday," though at this point, none of the speculation has been confirmed by Marvel.

Whatever happens, it seems the Russo Brothers have a much more serious story planned for Thor in "Doomsday," which is good news. Trailers have shown the character trying and failing to attack Doctor Doom and delivering solemn speeches to the various heroes who gather together to take on this latest threat to the MCU. Gaining the power of the Odinforce would be an exciting development that allows Hemsworth's character to finally regain his standing as one of Marvel's most formidable heroes.

"Avengers: Doomsday" hits theaters on December 18, 2026.

#3501. Best Actress Frontrunner Julianne Moore Nailed ‘The Debut’ by Singing, Styling Her Hair Like Liza Minnelli, and Avoiding Playing ‘Some Suffering Mom’

“Hello, I’m Julie,” said a radiant Julianne Moore, holding out her hand as she popped out of the elevator at Middleburg, Virginia’s Salamander Resort. Her hair was red, her skin was white, her dress as yellow as gold. A few hours later after a rapturous Middleburg Film Festival reaction to “The Debut,” we talked in a hotel meeting room. The A24 crowdpleaser has been wowing audiences and critics since Telluride.

Jesse Eisenberg has done it again. His follow-up to “A Real Pain,” which won Kieran Culkin the Supporting Actor Oscar, could score Best Actress for Moore. The musical comedy has earned Moore raves on the festival circuit for her role as a sad suburban homemaker turned anxious aspiring actress in a New Jersey community theater. Related Stories ‘The Debut’ Trailer: Julianne Moore Goes Full Julianne Moore in Jesse Eisenberg’s Riotously Funny Musical Theater Comedy Rejected Twice by Sundance, ‘Mouse’ Is One of the Year’s Best Movies. Why Aren’t More People Talking About It?

A sixth Oscar nomination is inevitable, and possibly a second Oscar win after “Still Alice” in 2015. It’s hard to believe she launched her career in 1988 as a regular on soap opera “As the World Turns.”

Moore is the current Best Actress frontrunner, even though she has won before. Sometimes nabbing an Oscar is a disadvantage in the Oscar race. But not if the performance is undeniable: Katharine Hepburn holds the record with four, while nipping at her heels are three-time winners Meryl Streep, Frances McDormand, Jack Nicholson, and Sean Penn.

Eisenberg wrote a rich character for Moore, knowing what the veteran actress could do with the childlike housewife Mona who, in order to learn how to act, must find herself. The director and actress had worked together on “When You Finish Saving the World” (2022). “[‘The Debut‘] is about this woman who has been chewed up but not spit out,” said Eisenberg, quoting Mona’s signature song. “It’s my point of view through somebody I consider a muse. I was writing something about myself as a seven-year-old in 1990, but I couldn’t picture anybody else except her doing it.”

It helped that Moore had told Eisenberg exactly what she was looking for. “I said I had just done ‘Dear Evan Hansen,’ and I loved singing, and I would love to have another opportunity,” she said. “I told him that I would love to do more comedy, and I didn’t want to play some suffering mom.”

Eisenberg put all of this in the screenplay, “but in the most surprising and inventive way,” she said. “He’s such a specific writer. He’s so incredibly empathetic. He has a compassionate worldview. He understands creativity. All of that stuff went into this wonderful and delightful story. It’s joyful and life-affirming too.”

Moore didn’t know she was playing a seven-year-old version of Eisenberg until he started telling that to the press. “Then he was like, ‘This is my experience of being a kid and going to community theater.’ But I could sense that there was a personal point of view in it. I very much felt with Mona that she was on a subjective journey, and that he was inside of that. With Mona, I always knew he was looking through her.”

“The Debut” is told from her point of view, as she tries to talk the overbearing local community theater director Jerry (Paul Giamatti) into hiring her, an untrained actress. He does it because he has no one else. But first, he must teach her how to act.

Mona dresses like a schoolgirl, with skirts, blouses, cardigan sweaters. “She’s so contained, and the way she learns is so literal,” said Moore, “the way a baby learns, like, you make a face at a baby, the baby makes a face back, but they don’t have intention behind it. But they’re learning things in an exterior way, and then they match it with feeling later on. So everything she’s doing is a childlike way of learning.”

Mona goes from an invisible nonentity in her own home to someone who demands attention. “She’s a kid who has found friends for the first time,” said Eisenberg. “She’s the girl who transferred to the right school at seven years old, and then the first rehearsal happens, and she is told she is terrible, and she has no idea why. And it’s the girl who transferred to the right school and gets an F on the very first test, and then the rest of the semester is panicking, and all she’s seeing is everybody else get A’s, and she still has the F, and she doesn’t know what to do. And then the teacher pulls her aside and says, ‘You either show up, or you are out on your ass.’ And something switches in her, and she makes the decision: ‘I am going to show up.’ And she begins to turn into a monster.”

The theater troupe embraces Mona as she unfolds like a flower. “We’ve been like those theater kids cracking corny jokes and finding community,” said Moore. “It’s all done with so much affection. Jesse looks at that world with not a hint of malice.”

Giamatti’s director relentlessly pushes the newbie through her paces until they have a powerful confrontation on the empty stage where he forces her to break down. Eisenberg reduced the actors’ anxiety by placing the eight-page showstopper in the middle of the shoot: not the beginning, and not the end. On the first day he went over to Moore’s apartment to talk about the movie. He said, “I really don’t want you to worry about that scene. I don’t want you to worry about memorizing that because I know that as an actor, I would I lose my mind. I would just be drilling it all the time, and I wouldn’t be able to concentrate. We’re going to have a teleprompter on that day. So don’t worry about it.”

So Moore worked on it normally, she said, “like I worked on everything else in the movie. So when we got to it, I knew it. I didn’t need a teleprompter. He knew instinctively as a director and an actor that what scares us sometimes is just a volume of language. He didn’t want to freeze me up. And having a partner like Paul who was so awake and aware and generous made it a pleasure. We were enjoying it when we did shoot it.”

Moore and Giamatti had never worked together before. She once introduced herself to him in a bookstore in Montauk. “He was very shy,” she said. “He is the greatest scene partner. I didn’t expect him to be so generous. He’s so funny, and he’s so dear. He’s present, incredibly modest, and as a partner, so available. Paul and I would work on it occasionally. When we were doing that scene, the rhythm was so important in it. You throw something, he hits it right back. It was our sense together of keeping it aloft, keeping it moving, keeping the river flowing. It felt electric with the two of us.”

The big blowout happens early in the story. “In a lot of movies, that kind of set piece would happen later,” said Moore. “Instead, it’s like a discovery place. It’s where she starts to begin to unlock herself emotionally, but she doesn’t learn from it. She comes in the next day, and starts to rehearse. And her belief is that acting is size, that it’s just huge, right? That’s when she starts yelling. She thinks it’s about being loud, which then allows her to go on the next journey with Jerry, where he says, ‘Let’s talk about feeling and reality and intention.’ So she’s slowly putting these pieces together. But that’s the first moment where she attaches something outside of herself to her own emotion.”

The whole shoot was fast, as Eisenberg didn’t have time to muck about and often shot just one take of a scene. “She and Paul Giamatti are so good on take one,” said Eisenberg. “It’s embarrassing. This is a small budget movie. The first two days of our schedule, we filmed in one day. The first two days, which were big ensemble musical numbers, we filmed in one day because we were prepared as a crew, but the actors were perfect on take one.”

Moore didn’t feel rushed. “It doesn’t feel, working with Jesse, like you’re moving too fast,” she said. “Working in independent film, you’re always moving quickly because you need to. You don’t have the time. You don’t have the money. So you want to move through things quickly. But I never felt rushed with him. I never I never felt like I was leaving something, that I didn’t get to complete something.”

The challenge for Moore, as it is for every actor shooting out of order, was making her character changes seamless. Eisenberg started with the theater scenes, then shot her family, and then jumped into Mona’s increasing weirdness. “The hardest thing always is making sure that you’ve pitched things correctly,” Moore said. “You want to make sure that you’ve managed to match it to another scene. So it was always hard to figure out. That’s our job.”

Eisenberg wanted Mona to move from looking quite childlike in the beginning, and swiftly move through her evolving transformations. Moore had fun with the costumes, figuring out the crazy wigs, makeup, and outfits in the second half. “Jesse had written that Mona electrocutes herself and destroys her hair, and that she was going to get her hair cut,” said Moore, “but he hadn’t written in a color change. We were messing around with it and trying to figure out what to do with hair and makeup and wardrobe and we had this idea that by having her dye her hair dark and chop it off, I wanted to homage the great ladies of musical theater, Liza Minnelli and Chita Rivera and Patti LuPone. It’s a wonderful Easter egg for that character.”

Making everything easier for Moore was actor-turned-director Eisenberg, who’d tell her when to ‘raise the stakes’ or ‘go hotter.’ “He’s maybe the most collaborative person I’ve ever worked with my entire life,” said Moore. “He listens to everyone. He asks people for opinions. He’ll ask people for notes, in a way that I would be like, ‘you don’t have to do that. This is your movie. It’s your creation.’ But he does collate opinion in a way. He’s fascinating in his generosity.”

Needless to say, singing her centerpiece song (“This City May Have Chewed Me Up (But It Hasn’t Spit Me Out”) was nervous-making, given that Moore was surrounded by Broadway super-belters like Tony winners Danny Burstein and Bonnie Tillman. “These people have the voices of angels,” said Moore. “When I did sing that song for the first time, and they’re all sitting there watching me, I think they did feel worried for me because they have so much ease. The song that she sings is so beautiful. In the singing of the song, she’s attaching her own emotional experience suddenly to the song. She understands the song in the moment she’s singing that. Somehow she wants more, and she knows that this is an avenue for her to find that. And so it’s a journey back to herself: finding that creativity and connection and community brings her to an essential sense of self.”

If degree of difficulty counts with Oscar voters, Moore may have that advantage.

A24 will release “The Debut” in theaters on Friday, December 11.

#3500. BritBox’s 4-Part Miniseries Is a Masterpiece You Can Binge in One Sitting

BritBox offers many period dramas and love stories, ranging from the unconventional romance The Other Bennet Sister to the chaotic family drama The Hardacres. While these recent releases have been gaining attention, they are far from the only shows worth watching on the streamer. BritBox has older series, and some are criminally underrated, but among the many options, one standout was released 22 years ago. BBC's North & South masterfully adapts Elizabeth Gaskell's 1855 novel with the same name, delivering a beautiful story that remains a favorite even after so many years.

North & South tells an endearing love story while also providing an in-depth look at the struggles of the lower class during the Industrial Revolution. It may not be the most classic combination, yet the series balances these two subjects beautifully. In fact, the biggest downside to the miniseries is that it has only four episodes for fans to enjoy, yet this makes it an ideal length to binge in a single sitting. For any period drama fans looking for weekend plans, North & South is the perfect option.

The central story of North & South is the slow-burn romance between Margaret Hale (Daniela Denby-Ashe) and John Thornton (Richard Armitage). The story begins when Margaret's family moves from a town in Hampshire to a more industrial environment in the north of England to avoid a scandal involving her clergyman father's (Tim Pigott-Smith) religious beliefs. It's a culture shock for Margaret, who must adjust to her new way of life and get to know the community. As these stories often go, Margaret meets Thornton, the local mill owner, but they don't get along. They quickly make assumptions about each other, with Margaret seeing Thornton as cruel and him considering her judgmental. Yet, as they get to know each other better, the romantic tension grows, giving fans something to root for.

Britain makes more detective television than any country has any business making, and somehow almost all of it is good. Here is the one you belong in, what it says about you, and the case for it being the best of the four.

You want the tea, the gossip and the vicar behaving oddly. Midsomer is a county where the scenery is beautiful, the fete is on Saturday and the murder rate is roughly that of a small war, and absolutely nobody involved thinks this is strange.

You feel other people's grief as if it were handed to you personally. Broadchurch is less a whodunnit than a study of what a small town does to itself when it finds out that the answer was always going to be somebody everybody already knew.

You go through things rather than around them. John Luther is the best detective in London and a liability to everybody who works with him, and the show is completely honest that those two facts are the same fact.

You say the thing and you do not dress it up. Vera Stanhope turns up in a hat and a mac, is rude to almost everybody, and is the only person in the room prepared to ask the question that the family has been waiting years for somebody to ask.

With this story at the center, North & South thrives on its characters. Both Armitage and Denby-Ashe deliver compelling performances as the leads, portraying characters that are simultaneously complex and understandable. This emphasizes Margaret and Thornton's animosity toward each other in the beginning. For example, their first encounter, where Thornton loses his temper at a mill worker, gives Margaret reason to doubt him, but Thornton's reaction comes from concern for his employees' safety. The layers to the characters make North & South a more interesting story, adding conflict without becoming too contrived. Ultimately, the story greatly benefits from Gaskell's writing, though North & South makes a few notable changes in adapting the original into this enduring series.

A richly textured saga charts one woman's rise from hardship to success.

While the love story is a significant part of the series, it is only a portion of what's going on in North & South. The miniseries also dedicates time to exploring the class divisions in 1850s England. By exposing the tension between mill workers and their employers, the series highlights social issues like workers' rights and the dark reality behind strikes at the time. Margaret's friendship with Nicholas Higgins (Brendan Coyle) and his ailing daughter Bessy (Anna Maxwell Martin) is as significant as the romance, as it places her in the midst of the conflict. Yet, the series explores both sides of the conflict, including Thornton's attempts to improve working conditions, though his mills aren't flawless.

North & South doesn't get an unlimited amount of time, yet it features a complex, layered story about the social issues of the 1850s. Yet the series doesn't just highlight labor issues. It explores regional divisions and the realities of industrialization. Ultimately, these grounded storylines create a more realistic tone than other series in the genre, which sets North & South apart. After two decades, the series may be slightly dated, but it remains a perfect binge-watch that period drama fans shouldn't miss.

North & South is streaming on BritBox in the U.S.

Amazon has knocked $100 off the latest Google Pixel Watch 5 (45mm, LTE), bringing it down to $429.99 from $529.99, its lowest price yet, according to price trackers. PCMag calls the Pixel Watch 5 the best smartwatch for Android users, largely because Gemini is built in so deeply—the assistant works proactively, so it can surface your flight details on the way to the airport or suggest a contact's number while you text about dinner plans, and a new AI-powered Health Coach reviews your workouts with tailored feedback, though some of its fitness advice sits behind a paid subscription.

Helping all of those AI features along is a faster Qualcomm processor that Google says improves the overall performance of this smartwatch by 20%, while RAM increases from 2GB to 3GB and storage doubles to 64GB compared with the Pixel Watch 4. And charging shouldn’t necessarily be a nightly routine, either, with the watch lasting up to 56.5 hours in testing. Heavier use will cut into that figure, but you should still have a good chance of making it through two full days with enough power left to track your sleep overnight.

#3498. King Ghidorah Is Ready for Its Close-Up: How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Cracked the Legendary Monster’s Next Evolution

“Godzilla Minus Zero” builds on the strong visual foundation — and/or the rubble of Tokyo’s Ginza district — that director Takashi Yamazaki pounded into his previous film, “Godzilla Minus One.” Like that first film, “Minus Zero” is in conversation with the big ideas and cultural/emotional resonances behind Toho’s giant monsters, and it’s attuned to the beloved visual details of the franchise, going all the way back to the original “Godzilla” and the Shōwa era.

But historically, for all kinds of budgetary and technological reasons, King Ghidorah is usually not ready for his close-up.

The amount of time that “Godzilla Minus Zero” spends with its three-headed mutant space dragon on the ground is a notable departure from how Ghidorah is most often depicted: in flight, or towering far above Godzilla. Even in closer shots in a CGI-rich film like “Godzilla: King of the Monsters,” when all three heads get ready to chomp up a puny human or 10, the emphasis is on Ghidorah’s scale. Three heads are more terrifying than one. Related Stories ‘Victorian Psycho’ Review: Maika Monroe Scares Up a Very Different Kind of Final Girl ‘Steps’ Review: A Disposable Fairy Tale Reminds Us That Cinderella Is Someone’s Hated Stepsister Too

But “Godzilla Minus Zero” spends a lot of time with just one head, or focused on just one head, and its Ghidorah is as scary on the ground as it is in the air, and this is in part due to the particular design experience that director Yamazaki and his team brought to the world’s deadliest gold dragon. Yamazaki was tapped to design “Godzilla the Ride” at Seibuen Amusement Park (its full name is Godzilla the Ride: Giant Monsters Ultimate Battle) in 2021 and therefore had to figure out a version of Ghidorah that would work from the other side of a safety rail.

Yamazaki and animation studio Shirogumi worked on a monster concept that would feel, according to “Minus One” and “Minus Zero” producer Kazuaki Kishida, “as though the audience was under attack by Ghidorah itself. So it had to be very scary and very close-up,” Kishida told IndieWire. “[In the ride,] we see Ghidorah basically crawling on the ground with its neck, because it has a very long neck, and then really going after the audience. To bring King Ghidorah very close to humans and bring the eyeline closer was a huge core concept for this. So there was a lot of research that had gone into the ride that we were able to apply to ‘Godzilla Minus Zero.'”

The film uses Ghidorah’s eyeline to great effect. One of the most unnerving moments in its initial attack on Matsumoto City, as scientists Kanji Murakami (Min Tanaka) and Akira Hagiwara (Ko Maehara) scramble to both document the new monster on the block and survive the utter destruction of whole city blocks, is a moment of getting really, uncomfortably close to Ghidorah’s eye.

That forced proximity to Ghidorah makes all the spectacular space-dragon stuff it can do even more effective, though these effects are also as grounded in the natural and the tangible as much as possible. For Ghidorah’s destructive beam, for instance, visual effects artist Tatsuji Nojima did more research than even he thought he could do on how lightning visualizes itself.

“Everyone sort of recognized the string of light, that line of light. But if you look at lightning in slow motion, it leaves a line of something that lingers — this is apparently just water vaporizing instantly and turning into plasma,” Nojima told IndieWire. “I don’t fully know the science behind it, but there’s a visual effect that lightning leaves behind. So for Ghidorah’s destruction beam, I wanted to emphasize that element of it. I scatter particles around, kind of blur the imagery, and then let it linger longer than it normally would.”

Of course, whenever the destruction beam hits something, Nojima and the VFX team got to build the explosion. But it’s that visual sense of Ghidorah’s power lingering, and of getting too close to where Ghidorah can see you, that makes this version of the monster feel so dangerous.

“Godzilla Minus Zero” is now playing in theaters.

#3497. The Out of Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: What Does 'Code Rot' Mean?

A weekly deep dive into the current trends, slang, and viral videos of youth culture in terms that even the squarest can understand.

This week's Out-of-Touch guide takes a look at a phenomena that's probably going to define the lives of generations of young people: Code rot—both actual computer-style code rot, and the more elusive cultural kind. I'm also taking a look at the fake controversy over the "cancellation" of Freddy Krueger, and finally, bringing things home with viral videos of boyfriends dancing.

Expect to hear young people talking about code rot for awhile, maybe for the rest of their lives. It's a concept that's going to affect them more than any previous generation. Code rot, or software rot, describes what happens to a computer program when the hardware and operating system it runs on advance. If older programs aren't updated, they become less stable and glitchy until they eventually become unusable.

The idea of code rot has really caught on in the young people's popular imagination, probably because they're going to spend a lot of their lives dealing with it. They've even taken the idea of code rot into life, and use the phrase to describe anything that is worn out or malfunctioning. If the ice cream machine isn't working at McDonald's, it's code rotted. Bad grades on a report card? Code rot.

Kids are making videos where they demonstrate actual code rot:

or point out physical things that are code rotted, like a cat:

Interestingly, a lot of the online discourse around code rotting concerns the massive video game platform Roblox. Because Roblox games there are made by users, there's often not a lot of incentive for the creators to keep the games current with the platform's changes, so a lot of Gen Z's childhood memories of playing games are sinking into code rot. Here's a video about it:

Another interesting wrinkle is the tone these videos take. Code rot is seen as apocalyptic. While it's mostly hyperbole, I think part of it is the realization that the entire world is code rotted. The old programs that used to run within the "Western Culture" operating system no longer apply and everything is starting to glitch out.

The meaning of "PDF file" depends on the context. If you're at work, it refers to a Portable Document Format file, a format created by Adobe that is famously hard for older people to open. In slang, though, PDF file is algo speak for "pedophile." Because that word is flagged by moderation software online, people say "PDF File" to skirt the censorship.

The run-up to Halloween brought a lot of online discourse about Nightmare on Elm Street villain Freddy Krueger. The supernatural serial murder/PDF File was supposedly cancelled online by overly woke, Gen-Z Tiktokers outraged that he is a child predator. The controversy started with a post from Entertainment Industry Reporter that points out how strange it is that in the '80s and '90s, Freddy Krueger, depicted in 1984's A Nightmare on Elm Street as a child murderer so driven by bloodlust he transcended death, was featured on dolls, board games, and lunchboxes aimed at children. It's a good point, but not a call for "cancellation."

Although the article does say that "Freddy Krueger lunchboxes shouldn’t exist," and that parents "shouldn’t have been buying their kids action figures of a child murderer," this is not a call to action. It's not suggesting cancellation of any kind, and it's hard to even conceive of what cancellation of a fictional character in an old horror franchise would even mean. The article is actually an observation about how merchandising (and low-quality sequels) change the meaning of art. But people online missed the point entirely and invented a scenario where "woke" young people are calling for the cancellations of a fictional villain for doing bad things.

I've been scouring TikTok, looking for even one video where someone is calling for "canceling" Freddy Krueger, and I can't find any, but there are hundreds, maybe thousands of videos like this:

In these videos, people point out how enraging it is that the woke people are calling for Krueger's cancellation and vowing that they won't let it happen. Even though it is not happening. There are even levels to the myths about woke mobs canceling Freddy. Supposedly, younger users were unaware that Krueger is depicted as a "PDF file" as well as a murderer in the 2010 reboot of the franchise, so there are online arguments about whether that's the reason he's being canceled. Even though no one is canceling anything. These anti-woke folks are, ironically, defending a fictional villain from cancellation by creating another fictional villain, the shadowy woke mob that's ruining horror movies. Meanwhile, the real villain is a lack of media literacy. Saying "wow, it's crazy that previous generations made a comedy mascot of such a terrible character and marketed him to children" is not the same as cancellation.

This week's viral videos are of boyfriends dancing. The newest thing on the TikTok is young women sharing video of their boyfriends getting down accompanied by a clip from the song "gay alligations fr. my girlfriend" by TikToker OH MICKEY. Like this:

It's a simple, silly template that maybe doesn't mean a whole lot, but this generation of young men are so messed up when it comes to relationships and masculinity, I'm always happy when a meme becomes popular that indicates that young women want goofy dudes, dudes who know how to dance, and dudes who act silly as boyfriends more than they want red-pilled, manosphere, looksmaxxing types. I don't know if these kinds of messages ever really "break through" to the underground of internet incels, but I like to hope they do, because a lot of young men are not OK.
