#3496. 4 Upcoming Fantasy RPGs Better Than Waiting for a New Dragon Age

The fire’s burning low. The road ahead looks grim. The companion who has spent half your journey needling you clearly has something on their mind, and you’re one or two correct dialogue choices away from getting them to spill. You pick a reply. You feel it land. Then somebody makes a joke about cheese, and the tension breaks.

This is one of the many things the Dragon Age franchise does well. In this series, from Origins to Veilguard, you gather a party of real-feeling companions and grapple with party management. These are also tactical games — games where you need to pause your combat encounters, point at the biggest threat, and hope against hope that your mage remembers she’s standing in a pool of fire. They’re political games, full of nobles and templars quibbling about the fates of their respective territories and teams. And they’re games where consequences stick. A choice you made in a prologue will come back to bite you hours (or entire games) later, usually while you’re just minding your own business collecting elfroot for a salve.

It may be unlikely that we’ll see a new Dragon Age title anytime soon. (Earlier this month, former Dragon Age writer David Gaider said that “the golden days are over.”) Yet there are still campfires worth stopping at. If you miss that feeling of saving Thedas by day and hanging out with your party of oddball companions by night, check out these four upcoming RPGs. Consider this your recruitment screen.

You can never keep every companion happy in Dragon Age. Solasta 2 eases you into this never-ending quest for balance by starting you off with your family. You lead the Colwall siblings, orphans from a household tied to a religious order sworn against an evil called Shadwyn. Soon, the siblings travel to a new continent, where the opening city, Caer Mar, comes with rebels, factions, and plenty of trouble.

If you liked pausing Dragon Age to plan every fight, this turn-based tactical RPG (which has been in Steam Early Access since March 2026) offers plenty of occasions to plan. Positioning, line of sight, and high ground decide most battles, and D&D fans will appreciate the chance to use spells like Magic Missile and Shatter to deal damage. Between fights, as you trek your way across Neokos, your role-playing choices will influence your standing with the world’s factions — which, in turn, changes how the world responds to you. Cross the wrong faction, and the merchants may stop selling you the good stuff.

Solasta 2’s Early Access only covers part of Act 1 and comes with a low level cap — you can only get to level 4 at this time. Developer Tactical Adventures says it intends to stay in Early Access for about a year, and 1.0 will raise the cap to 10 and finish the main questline. While you wait, you can play the first game, Solasta: Crown of the Magister. It’s a crunchier D&D experience, so brush up on your spell strategy before you boot it up.

What if the Dragon Age: Origins prologue cast you as a vagrant with a bad attitude and no plan? In Outward 2, you play an ordinary person in Aurai, a dangerous world where most people never leave their hometown walls. You’ll choose one of three starting scenarios — a miner in the northern mountains of Tramontane, a homeowner in the underground city of Haboob, or a vagrant in Simeon’s Bastion. Then, you’ll get a background and personality traits like Hoarder, Gourmet, or Lone Wolf that change your dialogue, starting gear, and aptitudes.

Surviving Aurai will take more than a sword. Hunger, thirst, exhaustion, and weather threaten you as much as the world’s creatures do…and you don’t get mounts or fast travel to give you a quick way out of a tight bind. This game is more committed to realism (read: suffering) than your usual RPG. Armor weight will change how fast you move. If you want to stay mobile during a fight, you’ll need to drop your backpack. You can wield a different weapon in each hand, like a sword and shield, dual axes, or a mace and pistol, and trainers teach skills for a fee. But you can’t just be focused on survival: Your choices will pull you toward a faction that will shape your story. Will you join a budding mercenary company, a society of historians, or a humanitarian mission? What’ll happen after you do?

Outward 2 will support online and split-screen co-op, which means your companions can also be your IRL friends. While you wait for this title, play the first Outward if you like your fantasy with a side of hypothermia. Regardless, bring a friend. And a warm cloak, because the seasons in Aurai show no mercy.

Release date: Feb. 23, 2027 (Feb. 18 with the Premium Edition)

Where to play: PS5, Windows PC, Xbox Series X

This game’s not out yet, but Albion already has opinions about you. Here, you play as the hero of Briar Hill, “an ordinary person made extraordinary by fate.” From there, it’s up to you to decide what kind of hero you’ll be. Your built-in rival is Isabel, played by Hayley Atwell, a driven, powerful hero on a quest to right a tragic injustice. She opposes you and Humphry, her former guardian. With interpersonal conflict this charged, who needs a world to save?

Dragon Age taught us that the world should remember what you did, and Albion takes the lesson seriously. Your reputation affects how the world’s 1,000+ handcrafted NPCs treat you. That reputation can reshape the world around you and grow your power. Beyond reputation, you can romance villagers, have children with them, and start your own cozy life while chaos reigns above you.

Dragon Age blends dark subject matter with humor very well. Fable seems ready to carry on that particular mission. One of its spells, “Befowl,” turns enemies into chickens (and undead enemies into undead chickens, naturally). Isabel has an injustice to right and you’re standing in her way, so keep that chicken spell handy.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

If you ever wished you could replay your first Dragon Age campaign and fix just one decision, Clockwork Revolution might be your invitation to do just that. Dragon Age gave us choices that follow you from game to game. InXile’s first-person RPG explicitly lets you rewrite your own decisions to answer the question: Would anything change if you could reverse something from your past?

You play Morgan Vanette, a customizable member of the Rotten Row Hooligans gang in Avalon, a steampunk city whose factions run from the slums to the golden mansions. The villain, Lady Ironwood, already rules Avalon, and she’s been using time travel to keep it that way. Vanette and a band of allies set out to turn back the clock and right her wrongs.

Sounds standard, right? The twist, here, is how you go about doing that. You’ll use a device called the Chronometer to change key moments in the past. This sounds excellent in terms of instant gratification, but the effects of those changes threaten to ripple outward. The people closest to you feel it first, and the crew you return to after time shenanigans may differ from the one you left. Your allies, Ulysses, Nazim, Erasmus, Hazel, and Anne, have lives of their own, with stories that don’t revolve around you. If you enjoy political chess, Lady Ironwood gives you a rival to follow. A flying automaton named Prentice will guide you through the branching realities. You’ll build a character with attributes, skills, and gear, hack hostile automatons, and use an ability called Displace to toss an explosive barrel at enemies. Whatever you do, just change the past carefully, because your crew will remember.

#3495. The Body: Netflix’s New 8-Part Psychological Thriller Is The Perfect Binge This Week

Netflix’s new 8-part psychological thriller follows a school dance initiation gone wrong, chilling visions, and a town gripped by hysteria. Arriving this Wednesday, November 11, this new thriller series is one of ScreenRant's top new shows to binge-watch on Netflix this week, due to its intriguing premise that blends mind-bending supernatural horror and classic coming-of-age drama. The series is created by Quinn Shephard, best known for Hulu's gripping crime mystery series Under the Bridge, which earned an 87% Rotten Tomatoes score.

All eight episodes of The Body premiere on Netflix this Wednesday, and it is the perfect new psychological thriller series to binge-watch this week. Shephard has described the series as being heavily inspired by 2000s classic movies such as Jennifer's Body and Mean Girls, which makes it the perfect follow-up series to watch after Prime Video's hit Mike Flanagan series, Carrie. Rooted in Catholic-based horror reminiscent of quintessential movies like The Exorcist and The Omen, The Body also leans into the dark history of the Salem witch trials.

The Body may arrive nearly two weeks after Halloween, but it may just be the spookiest release on Netflix's Fall 2026 streaming slate. Set in a small town in the United States, the series follows a group of students in the Lions, an exclusive dance team at their Catholic high school. Grace Franklin, played by Sofia Wylie, is the newest recruit to the elite club and must go through a drug-fueled initiation process spearheaded by the dance team captains, Anya Butler (Kristina Bogic) and Elise Zakaria​​​​​​ (Sara Boustany). The Lions perform a ritual to help their team win their regional championship competition but end up evoking something much more sinister on their entire community.

Following the ritual gone wrong, various members of the Lions begin to have prophetic visions, the first sign that their school and town are falling into a bout of mass hysteria. The story centers on Grace and the aftermath of her initiation process, which sparks the initial mystery that provides the backbone of the psychological thriller series. It also follows the Anderson family, with Lisbeth (Geena Meszaros) being a central figure in the supernatural mystery along with her brother, Leo (Jackson Kelly). The Body begins on Halloween night in 2004, making it a period piece that delivers plenty of millennial nostalgia, Y2K fashion, and early 2000s tech such as flip phones and CD players.

Netflix adds all 63 episodes of a gripping gangster drama, bringing 6 seasons of crime, betrayal, and high-stakes suspense to one unforgettable binge.

Reviews for The Body have yet to be released and could be a crucial factor in how the new Netflix thriller series will fare on its competitive viewership charts. Given the acclaim of Hulu's Under the Bridge, which earned Lily Gladstone (Killers of the Flower Moon) her first Emmy nomination, The Body is expected to be well-crafted and have great performances from its ensemble cast. The Body will have to beat out some of Netflix's top streaming hits right now, including Lupin, Black Doves season 2, and Taken: Natalee Holloway, if it wants to claim the platform's #1 viewership spot this week. As far as new releases go on Netflix in the coming days, The Body is the best to binge-watch.

#3492. The 10 Greatest Soft Magic Systems in Books, Ranked

It was Brandon Sanderson, far and away one of the most prolific and downright legendary fantasy authors currently working, who coined the terms "hard magic system" and "soft magic system" back in 2007 with his essay Sanderson's First Law. Whereas hard magic systems have very clear rules and boundaries, making it abundantly clear to readers how they work, soft magic systems have far more vague and undefined limitations, prioritizing wonder and awe over strict mechanics.

When well-crafted, soft magic systems can be among the very best in the entire history of fantasy literature. Their nebulous, mysterious nature can imbue any given novel with an unparalleled sense of breathtaking mystique, upping the stakes and adding to the scale and scope of the story. From classics like The Lord of the Rings to modern masterpieces like The Poppy War, there are many incredible books with some incredible soft magic systems.

R. F. Kuang's debut novel was The Poppy War, the first installment in the trilogy of the same name and undeniable proof of Kuang's tremendous quality as a fantasy author. Inspired by the Second Sino-Japanese War, it's about an impoverished orphan who enters an elite military academy, only to discover that she has a lethal aptitude for shamanism right as a devastating war breaks out with a rival empire.

Saying that Kuang, who holds a degree in Chinese history from Georgetown University, put an awful lot of research into The Poppy War would be a massive understatement. But it's not just the historical realism that makes this one of the best grimdark books of all time, but also the engrossing magic system. Where many soft magic systems end up feeling like deus ex machina, Kuang manages to keep hers mysterious while still filling it with psychological, narrative, and thematic layers.

The Black Company series of dark fantasy novels is almost undeniably Glen Cook's magnum opus, composed of some of the most influential fantasy books of all time. The series follows an elite band of cynical mercenaries and sorcerers, chronicling their exploits over four decades from the perspective of their doctor-historian. The series definitely peaks with its first installment, The Black Company, but is worth reading in its entirety for those who love dark fantasy.

The whole saga was one of the first true modern grimdark fantasy book entries, and its soft magic system remains one of the most fascinating that the subgenre has ever delivered. Magic here is an ability so intrinsic to certain gifted individuals that there's no need for hard rules here. Since the series is narrated by a character who's not a wizard, it's naturally imbued with even more powerful ambiguity and uncertainty.

People who love cozy fantasy and are looking for a great new book to read without committing to an entire series ought to consider Sangu Mandanna's The Very Secret Society of Irregular Witches. It's one of the most delightful cozy fantasy novels of the last six years, following a lonely witch who breaks the rules of her society by posting online magic videos. So, she's summoned to a remote English house to tutor three young orphan witches, finding romance and a new family.

It may not have the highest stakes or the most complex narrative, but that's what cozy fantasy is all about — it's also what makes this one of the best fantasy books of the 2020s so far. Its magic system is just as cozy as the story itself, with magic being a powerful force tied to witches' emotions and intuition. This angle helps the whole book feel all the more intimate, and makes it even easier to relate to the characters' feelings and mood.

Will George R. R. Martin ever actually deliver the conclusion of A Song of Ice and Fire? Fans have grown doubtful that he ever will, but even if The Winds of Winter never actually sees the light of day, this landmark saga would remain a must-read of the high fantasy genre. Starting with A Game of Thrones, the saga chronicles a brutal civil war between several noble houses for control of the Iron Throne, all while an ancient horror awakens beyond the edge of the world.

Virtually every exceptional installment of A Song of Ice and Fire is one of those books that belong on every fantasy lover's bucket list, and even though the series is not fundamentally about magic, it certainly contains plenty. Here, however, magic is an ancient, unknowable force operating well beyond the boundaries of human comprehension. Martin deliberately keeps things elusive and shrouded in mystery, which makes it feel dangerous, eerie, and distant.

Everyone loves a great fantasy drama that takes magic with full seriousness, but comedic fantasy is every bit as essential. And as far as comedic fantasy goes, it doesn't get much better than the work of Terry Pratchett. His Discworld series follows dozens of vastly different stories set on a flat planet balanced on the backs of four elephants who are themselves standing on the back of a giant turtle. Written by one of modern times' master satirists, it's a 41-novel series unlike any other.

From Night Watch to Small Gods to Guards! Guards!, Discworld is one of the fantasy book series with the best worldbuilding, which certainly includes a phenomenal magic system. Magic in Discworld is a brilliant subversion of the very idea of magic systems, used to interrogate human nature, characters' psyches, and the nature of fantasy storytelling itself. Though complex, it also provides the comedic fuel of many of the series' best outings.

Before one of the most perfect movies based on books, there was the book itself: Diana Wynne Jones' Howl's Moving Castle, the first installment in the Howl series. Highly influential and thoroughly delightful, this children's novel is the story of Sophie, who seeks refuge in a vain wizard's walking castle after a witch turns her into an old lady. There, she makes a pact with a fire demon to break both her curse and the wizard's.

Here, magic can be wielded simply by speaking life into inanimate objects, a system that operates on the same kind of soft rules that define the magic systems in oh so many of history's greatest classic folk tales. This approach makes it so that magic in Howl's Moving Castle is a response to the characters' emotions and thoughts, a simplicity which lets Jones embed that same magic in domestic activities with the utmost naturalism.

An orphaned boy discovers that he's a wizard on his eleventh birthday, going on to attend a magical boarding school and growing up to defeat the Dark Lord who murdered his parents. From such a seemingly simple, traditional Hero's Journey premise, the saga became the best-selling fiction book series of all time, all starting with the revolutionary Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (published in the United States as Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone).

Since these are all among the best-selling fantasy books of all time, this is also perhaps the most widely experienced soft magic system in the history of fantasy literature. Whimsical, intuitive, and often far more rooted in emotions than in particularly strict rules or limitations, Harry Potter's magic system sometimes flirts with elements that are on the harder side, but is ultimately the most culturally impactful soft magic system literature has ever seen.

Written by Robin Hobb, the sprawling Realm of the Elderlings series consists of several subseries (perhaps most notably the legendary Farseer trilogy). In it, an illegitimate royal prince's son, trained as an assassin and bound by forbidden magic, navigates a fractured world over the course of a massive 16-book epic. These are some of the fantasy books with the most interesting characters, the tightest plotting, and—of course—the best worldbuilding and magic-system writing.

Hobb's world features two primary magical forces: The Skill, a mental magic that connects minds over vast distances, and The Wit, a sensory magic that binds humans to animal companions. It seems simple on the surface, but Hobb constantly adds fascinating new layers to the system across those 16 novels, keeping the series' magic fresh, exciting, and thematically weighty throughout.

Almost universally recognized as the greatest and most influential fantasy novel of the entire 20th century, J. R. R. Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings was published in three separate volumes, but is technically all one single epic novel. For that matter, it's probably the best piece of epic fantasy ever written, and easily one of the best fantasy books of the 20th century. It follows Frodo, a hobbit who allies himself with a varied Fellowship to take a powerful, ancient ring and destroy it before it helps the Dark Lord Sauron regain his old power.

It's the gold standard of classic soft magic systems, and even though said system was technically introduced in The Hobbit and greatly expanded in The Silmarillion, it's The Lord of the Rings that sees the peak of its quality and entertainment value. Since the book is meant to operate so much like a modern myth, its magic feels like the magic of any other foundational mythology: deeply awe-inspiring, inherently tied to nature and the spiritual world, and impossible to fully pin down.

Ursula K. Le Guin was undeniably one of the most important authors in the whole history of speculative fiction, and the Earthsea Cycle is almost universally recognized as her magnum opus. This high fantasy book series consists of masterpiece after masterpiece, with some absolutely gorgeous prose and a clever subversion of traditional high fantasy tropes that has aged like fine wine.

But as great as virtually all aspects of the Earthsea Cycle, one of the most perfect fantasy book series ever, may be, many fans would agree that the magic system is the real star of the show. Rooted in disciplines like linguistics and Taoist philosophy, Earthsea's soft magic system is based on names, balance, and nature. It's deeply philosophical, elegantly constructed, and nothing short of gorgeous.

#3489. PlayStation Officially Cancels Live-service Shooter Fairgames

Sony's latest game cancellation adds to a long list of failed GaaS projects

Sony has canceled Fairgames (aka Fairgame$) three years after the live-service shooter was announced, Bloomberg reported on Tuesday. No one at its developer, Haven Studios, is getting laid off, and instead Haven will support other Sony Interactive Entertainment-owned studios, according to that report.

Farigames recently held a playtest and, according to an internal email reviewed by Bloomberg, feedback from that playtest didn't live up to PlayStation's expectations. "While the test demonstrated strong operational excellence, live ops readiness and community engagement, player feedback and retention results were mixed and fell short of the goals we had set," executives Sean Decker and John Doyle said in the email. With "challenging market conditions in the PVP shooter genre," Sony decided to cancel the game.

Fairgames reportedly had been reworked multiple times since its 2023 reveal. It would have been the debut game from Haven, which was founded in 2021 by former Assassin's Creed producer and Google Stadia Games and Entertainment head Jade Raymond, who has since left the studio. Haven was acquired by Sony in 2022.

Back in 2022, Sony announced a huge push for live-service games, aiming to release at least 10 by 2026. While games like Helldivers 2 and Gran Turismo 7 have been steady live-service hits, Sony's push has largely failed. Concord is the most notable misfire, as it was actually released before Sony reversed course and shut it down shortly after launch in embarrassing fashion.

A live-service God of War game, a multiplayer The Last of Us game, and many others were canceled before they could see the light of day. PlayStation studios working on live-service games, including London Studios, Firewalk Studios, and Bluepoint Games, were all shut down in recent years. In June, Sony laid off most of the Destiny team at Bungie, as "Destiny 2 fell short of expectations" with players. Recently, Horizon Hunters Gathering was reportedly delayed so it can be rebooted in response to negative player feedback (which sounds not too dissimilar to the Fairgames situation).

#3487. ‘Steps’ Review: A Disposable Fairy Tale Reminds Us That Cinderella Is Someone’s Hated Stepsister Too

The so-called villains of our childhood stories aren’t so bad when you look at things from their points of view. It’s a lesson that 21st century pop culture has taught us on a constant loop ever since “Wicked” kicked off an Oppenheimer-esque chain of tragedy that has seen everyone from Maleficent to Cruella de Vil humanized with their own origin story. It was inevitable that Cinderella’s allegedly wicked stepsisters would get their own mainstream version of the formula at some point (the Norwegian body horror movie exists in a separate, more ambitious category). If Hollywood can try to make us emphasize with someone who lives to kill puppies, anyone could have guessed that someone would slap a generational trauma label on literal children who grew up under the same evil matriarch as Cinderella. Related Stories ‘The Debut’ Trailer: Julianne Moore Goes Full Julianne Moore in Jesse Eisenberg’s Riotously Funny Musical Theater Comedy ‘Ink’ Trailer: Guy Pearce’s Rupert Murdoch Builds His Tabloid Empire in Danny Boyle’s Fleet Street Thriller

We’re long past the point where reimagining the classics from other characters’ perspectives earns you any credit for originality. If anything, those of us who have lived through the past two decades of pop culture might feel like stories where fairy tale side characters get to reclaim their agency are more omnipresent than actual fairy tales. But those original stories have endured in part because there’s always a new generation arriving to be wowed by them, and there’s no reason that the same principle can’t apply to the reimaginings, too.

Nobody whose age contains multiple digits needs to seek out “Steps” for any reason other than potentially entertaining their own children. But those young enough to be unfamiliar with the tropes it employs might be entertained or even moved by the material. “Cinderella” was an appropriate story to use for the purpose, as the beloved story of wish fulfillment doesn’t contain nearly as much emotional depth as better fairy tales like “Beauty and the Beast” or “The Little Mermaid.” Maybe it’s all part of a healthy cycle in which young kids can watch “Cinderella” and slightly older ones can watch “Steps” before graduating to stories and re-imaginings that have more to say. But on its own terms, the animated film comes across as little more than disposable corporate entertainment.

Directed by Alyce Tzue & John Ripa from a script by six credited writers (Ava Tramer, James Madejski, Jen Chuck, Dana Schwartz, and Felicia Ho wrote the screenplay and Kate Micucci also has a story credit), “Steps” is a well-meaning entry into the subgenre that follows the blueprint competently enough to avoid being offensive or memorable. It literally opens on an old storybook with a stereotypical voiceover narrator reading the text about Cinderella being mistreated by her wicked stepsisters — before Lilith (Ali Wong) slides into the frame yelling “Whoa whoa whoa” and declares that the fairy tale is “character assassination.” From there, it’s only a matter of time before the contemporary pop needle drops start.

“Steps” has no choice but to expand the thin mythology of “Cinderella” before it has a chance to tell the other side of the story. In this version, the stepmother isn’t wicked at all — she’s just an Asian dressmaker who constantly moves her two daughters Lilith and Margot (Stephanie Tsu) wherever the work takes her. When her marriage takes them to the kingdom of Alouette, all three of them see it as a chance for some much-needed stability. More than anything, the girls are excited to hang out with their new stepsister, Cinderella (Amanda Seyfried).

Yes, they started out as friends! (Where have you heard that one before?) The initial villain in “Steps” isn’t Cinderella, but the all-Caucasian kingdom where she lives. The newly blended family has fun sharing their cultural traditions, but Lilith and Margot quickly learn that everyone else sees them as outsiders. And when mean girls at school like Nikki Glazer’s Priscilla start freezing them out, Cinderella doesn’t do enough to stand up for them. Thus a sibling rivalry is born — turns out that Cinderella is also the mean stepsister that somebody else hates.

Lilith decides that if she’s not going to be accepted, she might as well rebel. Like a lot of pre-teens, she’s torn between an impulse to reject the social hierarchy around her and the unavoidable fact that she still defines herself by it. She’s more interested in destroying what she hates than figuring out what she likes, so she steals a magic wand from the Fairy Godmother (Bette Midler) and sabotages the royal ball, significantly complicating things for the Prince (Daniel Radcliffe) and sending the kingdom into free-fall. It isn’t long before she and her loathed step-sister have to take a journey through the forest to set things right.

From its unpleasantly slick animation to its picture-perfect storytelling — Cinderella thinks Lilith is mean and Lilith thinks Cinderella is dumb and ditzy, but they both learn there’s more to the other than meets the eye — “Steps” is an example of how you can do everything “correctly” and be left with a film that’s too smooth around the edges to resonate. There’s enough for kids to enjoy, but this won’t be one that parents find themselves unexpectedly invested in.

For all its modern cliches, “Steps” still contains a few moments of genuine pathos that tug at the heartstrings. We can all relate to being bullied as kids and the cosmic importance that our young brains assign to being left out, and the film handles those early scenes admirably well. But nothing in the movie is strong enough to transcend the fact that it’s packaged in a tired formula that has lost any subversiveness it once had. These villain-led reimagnings were introduced as a way to counteract the two-dimensional nature of fairy tales, but it’s starting to feel like we replaced those Happily Ever After endings with something equally superficial.

“Steps” streams on Netflix beginning on Friday, November 20.

#3486. How to Try 'Audio Intelligence' on Your Apple Watch Early

It has been a big year for Apple. There's a new CEO, prices have increased across the board, and there's been a seemingly endless rollout of new devices, including two new Apple Watches: the Series 12 and the Ultra 4. All things considered, these watches offer only minor upgrades over the previous models, shipping with new heart rate monitors and the latest S11 processor. But one of the biggest new watch features, "Audio Intelligence," is also the most controversial—and it's rolling out in beta today.

Audio Intelligence is Apple's branding for a new set of features exclusive to the Series 12 and Ultra 4. These features use the new Apple Watches' hardware, along with on-device and cloud-based AI, for tasks like sound and music identification as well as dictation. "Sound Recognition" can alert you to important sounds, like alarms and doorbells, while "Music Recognition" can automatically display songs playing around you—but these aren't the features you'll hear talked about in discussions of Audio Intelligence.

Rather, everyone is up in arms about "Live Rewind" and "Siri Recap." These Audio Intelligence features passively "listen" to your conversations throughout the day, and, using AI, deliver summaries of what was said. When you double-click your Apple Watch's crown to use Live Rewind, you'll get a loose transcript of the last 15 seconds of conversation it overheard, while Siri Recap can show summaries of all your in-person chats throughout the day. You can even configure a schedule for when your watch is "listening" for recaps—e.g., only run during work hours. Apple suggests each is intended to help jog your memory; maybe you use Siri Recap to remember important discussions you had that morning, while Live Rewind is meant for moments where you forget what someone just said. (As opposed to asking them to repeat themselves, I suppose.)

Apple's claims may or may not assuage your fears, but it seems the company is pushing on ahead regardless. Apple is releasing Audio Intelligence as part of iOS 27.3, which launches in beta on Tuesday. If you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4, you can try it out today, assuming you enroll in Apple's latest beta version.

To do so, you'll need to sign up for the Apple Developer program, since iOS 27.3 is rolling out first for devs. This program used to require a $99 fee, but you can skip it now if you opt for the free account. Once you enroll your Apple Account in this program, you can open your iPhone, head to Settings > General > Software Update > Beta Updates, and choose "iOS 27 Developer Beta." Go back one page, then follow the on-screen instructions to download and install iOS 27.3 when it's available.

#3485. 8 Upcoming Sci-Fi Movies, Ranked by Hype

2026 has been a strong and packed year for sci-fi cinema, anchored by both major box office sensations and indie hits. And now, the last stretch of the year is set to get bigger and bolder with some massive blockbusters that are arriving just before the year ends. From blockbuster cosmic spectacles to thought-provoking, human stories, and a brand-new Star Wars film starring Ryan Gosling, there are several highly anticipated sci-fi films to look forward to in the coming months.

2026 has seen several sci-fi hits so far, and the last weeks of the year will see the genre gearing up for an explosive finish with Denis Villeneuve’s Dune: Part Three, arriving just in time for the holidays. Also arriving at the same time is Marvel’s mammoth cinematic event Avengers: Doomsday, bringing the entire MCU together (one last time?). But this streak does not end here and will continue in the coming year. 2027 will also be the year when centenarian Mel Brooks returns with a Spaceballs sequel after four decades. So without further ado, here’s your guide to the most notable upcoming sci-fi movies, ranked by hype.

Directed by Brad Bird and written by Bird and Matthew Robbins, Ray Gunn is an animated sci-fi mystery set in a gigantic city called Metropia, in a retro-futuristic universe where humans and various interplanetary species coexist. The story follows the titular human private detective who takes up a murder case involving a famous multimedia star named Venus Nova, whose stardom is threatened by a scandal. The film stars the voices of Sam Rockwell as Ray and Scarlett Johansson as Venus, with Tom Waits, Matt Berry, Bobby Cannavale, Michelle Rodriguez, Alan Tudyk, and Patton Oswalt as notable characters.

Ray Gunn premiered at the 2026 BFI London Film Festival, where it received strong praise for its animation, action scenes, and voice acting, particularly from Rockwell, Johansson, and Waits. As is evident from its trailer, the film is a high-octane stunner, passionately inspired by Hollywood noir classics, joining the ranks of Brad Bird’s other acclaimed animated films like The Incredibles and Ratatouille. Following its theatrical release, Ray Gunn will also make its streaming debut on Netflix on December 18, 2026.

Mel Brooks’ classic satirical space opera film series returns after four decades with a brand-new sequel, Spaceballs: The New One, which picks up forty years after the events of the original 1987 film. In the upcoming film, villain Dark Helmet has returned, while Lone Starr is in hiding and Queen Vespa attends to her royal duties, so Prince Starburst, Vespa's son, and Destiny, a royal advisor, are tasked with finding Lone Starr and other allies to defeat the new threat. Brooks, Rick Moranis, Bill Pullman, George Wyner, and Daphne Zuniga reprise their roles from the previous film, with Lewis Pullman, Keke Palmer, Josh Gad, and Anthony Carrigan as new characters.

The new Spaceballs comes from director Josh Greenbaum, whom fans might know from films like Strays and The Dink, and is written by Josh Gad, Dan Hernandez, and Benji Samit. An '80s cult classic comedy, Spaceballs is among the best sci-fi parody films ever made and a major highlight of Mel Brooks’ career and legacy. Much like the first film, Spaceballs: The New One will mainly spoof the Star Wars franchise but is also expected to be a meta comedy about the modern nostalgia-obsessed culture, massive cinematic universes, and the rising trend of reboot films.

Directed by Eric Guillon, Claire Dodgson, and Jonathan del Val, Not Alone is an animated sci-fi rom-com centering on two scientists and clueless romantics, Joe and Fran, who are devising the world’s first plant-fueled rocket. When Joe finds himself harboring three alien fugitives stranded on Earth, he must figure out a way to send them home while also winning Fran’s love before it is too late. Timothée Chalamet and Selena Gomez voice Joe and Fran, respectively, with Brett Goldstein, Rob Brydon, Jamie Demetriou, and Diane Morgan voicing other key characters.

Not Alone marks Illumination’s first original feature since 2023’s Migration and the studio’s first romantic comedy, as well as its first feature film of 2027. As seen in the trailer, the film promises a wild, intergalactic adventure with adorable aliens and a charming love story at its heart that would appeal to everyone. While the film bears Illumination’s signature visual tone and style that has become synonymous with blockbuster animated franchises, Not Alone marks a shift from the studio’s traditional storytelling style, which is generally targeted towards a younger audience.

Directed by Grant Sputore, Godzilla x Kong: Supernova is a sequel to Godzilla x Kong: The New Empire and serves as the sixth film in Legendary Pictures’ Monsterverse franchise. In the film, Godzilla and Kong must team up once again, this time against a cosmic threat in the form of SpaceGodzilla. Dan Stevens reprises his role as Trapper from The New Empire, with Kaitlyn Dever, Jack O'Connell, Alycia Debnam-Carey, Matthew Modine, and Delroy Lindo as new characters, as well as Sam Neill in one of his final film roles.

Godzilla x Kong: Supernova marks the 40th film in the Godzilla franchise and the 14th film in the King Kong franchise, shifting the franchise into cosmic sci-fi territory. SpaceGodzilla first appeared in the 1994 film Godzilla vs. SpaceGodzilla as the main antagonist and is depicted as a crystalline, mutated clone of Godzilla. While the reappearance of two prehistoric behemoths in another earth-shattering monster war is what makes the upcoming film most hyped, Godzilla x Kong: Supernova is expected to dive deeper into the human-monster coexistence dynamic as well.

Directed by Francis Lawrence, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is the sixth film in the Hunger Games film series and an adaptation of Suzanne Collins' dystopian novel of the same name. Set 24 years before the events of The Hunger Games, Sunrise on the Reaping revolves around a young Haymitch Abernathy, who is selected to compete in the 50th Hunger Games and fight to the death in a televised spectacle. The film stars Joseph Zada, McKenna Grace, Jesse Plemons, Ralph Fiennes, Kieran Culkin, and Elle Fanning as key characters.

Sunrise on the Reaping serves as a sequel to The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes and a prequel to the 2012 film The Hunger Games, with Jennifer Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson reprising their roles from the films. The film premiered in London in October 2026, where it had an overwhelmingly positive reception, with critics praising Zada’s breakout performance and hailing the movie as the best installment in the Hunger Games film series so far. Franchise fans are sure to love the film’s mature and politically charged narrative of cruelty, grief, and rebellion.

Among the most anticipated films in the Star Wars franchise is the upcoming Star Wars: Starfighter, starring Ryan Gosling. Directed by Shawn Levy and written by Jonathan Tropper, the film is set five years after the events of 2019’s The Rise of Skywalker and follows Gosling’s cynical rogue pilot Kade Auberon, who is hired to escort a mysterious, Force-sensitive boy across a dangerous, lawless galaxy. The film also stars Amy Adams, Matt Smith, Mia Goth, Flynn Gray, Aaron Pierre, and Daniel Ings.

Star Wars: Starfighter is a standalone Star Wars film with no ties to the Skywalker Saga or legacy characters from the previous films. Produced by Levy and Lucasfilm, the adventure film does not require any prior knowledge of the franchise and its decades-spanning lore, making it accessible to general audiences while keeping the classic Star Wars magic intact. Starfighter is scheduled to release in May 2027, coinciding with the 50th anniversary of the first Star Wars film, which was released in May 1977.

Denis Villeneuve’s epic space opera franchise returns this December with its final chapter, Dune: Part Three, based on Frank Herbert’s 1969 novel Dune Messiah. Set nearly two decades after Timothée Chalamet’s Paul Atreides seized control of the Imperium, the film sees the emperor forced to face the true cost of power and the fate of those he loves as old allies and a long-lost love return and new enemies emerge. Most of the stars from the previous films reprise their roles, including Zendaya, Florence Pugh, Jason Momoa, Josh Brolin, Rebecca Ferguson, and Javier Bardem, with Robert Pattinson, Anya Taylor-Joy, and Isaach de Bankolé as new characters.

Dune: Part Three is one of the most anticipated sci-fi films of 2026 and marks the final installment in Villeneuve’s Dune film trilogy that began in 2021. Before its premiere, the film won the Golden Trailer Award for the original score by Hans Zimmer, who also composed the music for the previous two films. Alongside high-stakes battles and visceral action pieces, Dune: Part Three is expected to be much darker and more intimate than the previous Dune films, serving as a deconstruction of the classic tragic hero’s journey.

A much-awaited cinematic phenomenon, Anthony and Joe Russo’s Avengers: Doomsday is the 39th MCU film featuring the titular characters from Marvel Comics and a kind of sequel to 2019’s Avengers: Endgame. Intended to be a super-superhero film like never before, the new film brings together the Avengers, New Avengers, Fantastic Four, X-Men, and Wakandans, as well as other iconic characters to stop Doctor Doom and the collapse of the multiverse. Pretty much every MCU star is expected to appear in the film, including Chris Evans’ Steve Rogers / Captain America. Robert Downey Jr.’s return to the MCU in the new role of Victor von Doom is something to look forward to as well.

Arguably the most hyped film of 2026, Avengers: Doomsday is set up to be a massive showcase of the MCU’s legendary characters from all the previous films in an action-packed, CGI spectacle. For fans who might need a refresher on the characters, the multiverse mechanics, and how their arcs come together, Marvel Studios and Disney+ have curated an official "Countdown to Avengers: Doomsday" watch guide featuring a much smaller, streamlined list of essential titles. Releasing in the US following its UK premiere in December 2026, Doomsday will be followed by Avengers: Secret Wars, arriving in 2027.

#3483. ‘Victorian Psycho’ Review: Maika Monroe Scares Up a Very Different Kind of Final Girl

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on May 21, 2026 during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. Bleecker Street will release the film in theaters Friday, November 13.]

Winifred Notty is the sanest person she knows, or so the heroine (or anti-heroine, depending on how you might see it) of Zachary Wigon’s “Victorian Psycho” is quick to tell anyone who will listen. Or not, as star Maika Monroe delivers that damning and darkly funny insight into Winifred’s soul via a prim voiceover that seems to exist for her own benefit as much as the audience she seems to imagine.

That’s tangled enough, but there’s also this: Winifred doesn’t really know that many people, mostly because just about everyone she’s come across in her life is dead. Still, sane! Ish. Well, it’s not called “Victorian Psycho” for nothing. Related Stories ‘Steps’ Review: A Disposable Fairy Tale Reminds Us That Cinderella Is Someone’s Hated Stepsister Too ‘The Debut’ Trailer: Julianne Moore Goes Full Julianne Moore in Jesse Eisenberg’s Riotously Funny Musical Theater Comedy

Adapted for the screen by novelist Virginia Feito from her own work, the book comes recommended alongside its predecessor, “Mrs. March,” for anyone drawn to entertainment with “psycho” in the title.Beloved scream queen Maika Monroe (“It Follows,” “The Guest,” “Longlegs”) may be switching sides here, offering a twist on who horror fans root for once the blood starts flowing. (Hint: it’s the psycho.)

When we first meet Winifred, the Victorian-era governess is bound for her next assignment to teach the children of Mr. and Mrs. Pounds (Jason Isaacs and a sneaky-great Ruth Wilson, respectively) at their sprawling Yorkshire estate. “This won’t be like the other times,” she tells herself, winking mightily at how all those other times turned out. Our Winifred sports dead eyes and a rictus grin she works so very hard to fix in place. It’s even better when she attempts to imitate those around her, all the better to approximate “being human.”

No question, there’s something very wrong with Winifred. But what? You’ll find out soon enough. Possessed of “a darkness” she cannot shake, Monroe’s Winifred practically vibrates with the need to hold things together. It does not always work for her, but it is nearly always funny, deliciously and dementedly so.

Wigon and Freito don’t balk at the “psycho” promise of their story, as Winifred happily whacks away (often literally) at everyone icky, from gardeners to nurses (Thomasin McKenzie) and, yes, at least one baby. Killing scenes are elegantly, amusingly cut by editors Dustin Chow and Lance Edmands and designed for maximum gasps. Blood flows, then spurts, then pools. Sometimes it gets on Winifred’s face or her collar. She moves on, grimly and happily.

Cinematographer Nico Aguilar brings a similar energy to his work, shooting in and through keyholes, swinging his camera like a clock pendulum, even briefly adapting the perspective of a swallowed (redacted, for spoilers) as it travels into Winifred’s belly. It’s playful and gross, wholly fitting the material. Mostly, it’s so dark and fucked up you can’t help but laugh. OH! Did they do that? Yes, yes they did.

Possessed by the notion that she’s meant to be a part of the Pounds family (who would want to be? these aristocrats are monstrous), Winifred continues to fray. Bloodlusty audiences will be charmed by her go-for-broke attitude (more like go-for-the-throat), plus a steady stream of visual cues as to her current state. Dreams and nightmares merge, she’s haunted by the Pounds’ family mascot of a wild boar (particularly in an ever-morphing tapestry), and she simply can’t stop sneaking into places to stare at people while they sleep.

Clocking in at a tight 90 minutes, some changes to the also-slim book are smart, while others dilute its darkest impulses. Gone is the countdown to a Christmas massacre, which frames the novel; hell, gone is the whole Christmas massacre. Freito’s script leads up to a different sort of celebration, doing away with many of the most colorful supporting characters in the process (Mrs. Fancey, we hardly knew ye!).

That choice isn’t disastrous, although the execution of the big! final! event! is oddly watered down. Here it’s imagined as a battle of Winifred’s wills… but, erm, what wills? The book and the film each offer enough reasons for why our heroine is the way she is, Wigon’s film oddly bisects her spirit by implying she’s not fully on board with all the evil she commits.

For fans of the novel and its wonderfully unrepentant star, this choice might rankle; it’s also odd that Freito would go this route with her own adaptation. “Well, that’s not my ‘Victorian Psycho’ — and she’s not. That’s such a shame because for much of the film, she’s even better. By tempering her impulses and inner monologue, the film ends with less of the giddy gore that makes the rest of it such a dark treat. Dare we say it? We would have loved for this one to go full, ahem, boar.

“Victorian Psycho” premiered at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. Bleecker Street will release it in theaters on Friday, September 25.

#3482. Henry Cavill's The Witcher Replacement Has One Major Advantage Over Geralt Of Rivia

After starring on Netflix's The Witcher for three seasons, Henry Cavill's big role in an upcoming movie is the perfect next step in the actor's career, with one major advantage over his previous fantasy part. Before Liam Hemsworth took over the role of Geralt in season 4, Cavill had become synonymous with the character, making his exit so upsetting.

The world of The Witcher is bigger than any one cast member. The Witcher: Sirens of the Deep had a different Geralt, voiced by Doug Cockle, and built on a legacy that lasted even longer than Cavill had in the part. Cockle previously voiced Geralt of Rivia in all three The Witcher video games, helping to craft the character onscreen.

Considering that the games themselves informed much of the look and feel of the series, and were themselves drawn from The Witcher novels, that world is actually large enough to last without Henry Cavill. And the actor's talents have now been pointed toward a perfect role, with a character who has one major advantage over Geralt of Rivia.

Cavill's career in Hollywood is sure to be long and full of fantastic roles, but this upcoming project could become a defining film for the star.

After having played such iconic roles as Superman and Sherlock Holmes, his new take on another popular and beloved part could be the perfect chance for Cavill to do something truly unique, thanks to an incredible ability.

Henry Cavill will star in the upcoming remake of Highlander, where his lead character, Connor MacLeod, will have a power that no other characters in Cavill's past have. Connor MacLeod is an Immortal and serves as the center of the story as the titular Highlander, who is set to one day fight for The Prize.

While there is an inherent tension to Connor's existence, as captured by the original 1986 Highlander film's popular quote, "There can be only one", this is still an incredible power.

Born in the 16th century in Scotland, Connor has spent centuries exploring the Earth and training as a swordsman in order to one day be able to fight to become the last of his kind.

Connor has possessed some powers in addition to his immortality. During the Quickening, when an Immortal is killed, generally by another Immortal, a surge of energy escapes their body, allowing the victor to absorb the strength and memories of their fallen foe. This adds to a powerset that also includes enhanced regeneration.

Still, even with all of Connor's fantastic abilities, the character is important to compare against the roles that Cavill has played in the past. And while Geralt of Rivia might not be immortal, he does possess some fantastic skills that might make him even stronger than Connor could ever hope to be.

Geralt of Rivia actually shares some similarities in his powers with Connor MacLeod. While not hampered by a connection to a race of Immortals, which is itself an asset to Geralt's mortality, The Witcher's protagonist also has the benefit of slow aging, as well as tremendous skills in regeneration and healing.

Geralt, another trained swordsman, has greater speed, skill, and reflexes than Connor has generally been depicted as having. A fantastic tracker with elevated senses, Geralt has also been mutated in several ways that contribute to his incredibly enhanced physical powers of movement, fighting, and more.

If Geralt of Rivia and Connor MacLeod ever met in battle, it is hard to say exactly who would emerge triumphant, and much of that will depend on how the upcoming film depicts Connor. However, the more battle-hardened and practiced Geralt of Rivia would likely have at least a small advantage over his Highlander foe.

Regardless, both characters are excellent parts for Henry Cavill. And while The Witcher will continue to live on without him in some form, even after the Netflix series ends, this new and thrilling story of a rebooted Highlander is only about to get started.

#3481. 10 Best Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave Replacements

It's been several weeks now since Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave was released for Nintendo Switch 2, and fans around the world are still exploring this massive game. While you could easily sink hundreds of hours into playing through every Flame Lord's story, you may be wondering what to play after your adventures in Dagda are through. Worry not: we've compiled a list of games like Fortune's Weave to keep your strategic skills sharp while you wait for the story expansion DLC that's slated to be released sometime in 2027. While many of the games on this list are strategy RPGs, some incorporate other standout elements of Fortune's Weave, like its tournament-focused story or the opportunity to recruit dozens of allies.

If you enjoy negotiating tricky terrain and periodically swapping your character classes in Fortune's Weave, the 2025 remake of Final Fantasy Tactics will be right up your alley. While it's not quite as difficult as the 1998 PlayStation original, FF Tactics demands that you engage deeply with its job system and figure out which team compositions are necessary for a specific battle. You are very much expected to grind via "optional" skirmishes, even on normal difficulty, and that challenge leads to a satisfying sense of mastery. A surprisingly grim yet moving story about the exploitation of common people by the nobility makes this one worth revisiting again and again.

2023's Engage didn't manage to inspire a thousand ships like Three Houses, mostly because the story is pretty flat and forgettable. But it's still well worth playing, because the combat and maps are extremely fun. The central gimmick, Emblem Rings, allow you to equip anyone in your squad with the skills of a past Fire Emblem hero, allowing for some truly bonkers synergies and limitless possibilities for customization. Build a strong enough bond between a character and an Emblem, and they'll be able to inherit some of that Emblem's skills permanently. Engage has plenty of social-sim elements and overworld exploration, but for some reason I feel far less remorse about ignoring them here than I do in Fortune's Weave.

Are you the type of Fire Emblem player for whom permadeath is the only option? Then you'll vibe with the tough battles in this 2019 strategy game from indie developer Chucklefish. Wargroove features 12+ unique Commanders, each with a special ultimate ability called a "Groove" that charges during combat, like healing powers or building walls. My favorite commander is Caesar, a golden retriever in stately silver armor that's festooned with a plume of red feathers. In one mission, he and his troops enter an abandoned stronghold, only to find that it’s been overrun by rogues. These ruffians soon learn a harsh lesson: underestimate the dog general at your own peril. He's a beautiful boy and I will murder anyone who lays a finger on him.

This tactical RPG from Sega does away with grid-based maps, though it's similar to Fire Emblem in that you'll control an assortment of class types in turn-based combat. The watercolor aesthetics are unique and charming, but don't expect a ton of narrative depth from the game's anime riff on the Second World War. Thankfully, the combat is a far richer and deeper experience, thanks to elements like tanks, ordinance, snipers. The maps offer plenty of variety in terms of terrain, obstacles, and weather, and there are around 50 characters to recruit, each with their own unique abilities and perks. But don't get too attached; they can die permanently if they're wounded in battle.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

Sega's '90s entry into the strategy RPG genre hasn't enjoyed the decades-long success of Fire Emblem, but it still has plenty of memorable maps to enjoy, including a giant chessboard and a series of floating rafts. The story is bare-minimum hokum, even by '90s RPG standards: think "the magical seal has broken on ancient evil." But an assortment of truly unique characters — including a werewolf, a phoenix, and checks notes a flying jellyfish with ice magic make Shining Force 2 well worth checking out for retro game fans. If all the social sim elements and calendar management in Fortune's Weave stress you out, you'll find none of that here: just sweet, sweet grids punctuated by the occasional town. If you have Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack, you can find it in the Sega Genesis library.

If you enjoyed gradually unlocking the world map in Fortune's Weave, Vanillaware's 2024 tactical RPG takes a similar approach to exploration as you liberate towns and gather resources. The main story is pretty standard — you're tasked with assembling an army to overthrow the evil empire — but the optional adventures and character-driven missions have more meat on the bone. Like Fortune's Weave, Unicorn Overlord features more than 60 characters to recruit across a variety of classes. In a fun riff on the typical tactics formula, you'll combine those characters in squads of up to five for turn-based combat. You can even customize the order in which your skills and passive abilities trigger to maximize their damage-dealing potential. Vanillaware's painterly environments and character designs help make the experience easy on the eyes, too.

The Hundred Line is a choose-your-own adventure story first and a tactical RPG second. Even so, there's plenty for Fire Emblem fans to sink their teeth into. While your characters can't die permanently for plot reasons, their best attacks only unlock when they're close to death. Limited turns and massive waves of enemies encourage a high-risk, high-reward approach. You can use all your action points in a given turn, or save up a bunch to unleash hell all at once. While there are plenty of intricate, grid-based battles to chew on, its greatest similarity to Fortune's Weave is getting to see a variety of perspectives on crucial events. The Hundred Line features more than 20 distinct story routes and 100 unique endings. (And it was one of our favorite games of 2025!)

Did you spend countless hours befriending the various warriors scattered around Dagsion in Fortune's Weave, even if some of those recruits never even made it to the front line? If so, you should check out Konami's Suikoden series, especially the first two games, which got a lovely remaster back in 2025. These turn-based RPGs allow you to recruit 108 characters to join your fledgling army, though not all of them are playable. Some will perform vital functions around your castle, like running various shops, manning the storeroom, and even enabling fast travel. If you only play one game in this series, make it Suikoden 2. It chronicles a continent engulfed by war due to the bloodthirsty ambitions of Luca Blight, one of the most loathsome video-game villains of all time. In terms of sheer brutality and love-to-hate factor, Luca gives Fortune's Weave's Divine Emperor Dagda a serious run for his money.

First things first: Atlus's 2024 RPG features turn-based combat, rather than the map-based battles in Fortune's Weave. Beyond that, though, there are a ton of similarities between the two. Metaphor also blends a massively consequential fighting tournament with a popularity contest, as your group of heroes must gain renown across the land by accomplishing daring feats of bravery. While the game features eight playable characters, you can befriend dozens more through the Persona-like Follower Bonds system, which opens up new job classes as well as combat and exploration perks. And speaking of exploration, like Fortune's Weave, there's an extensive overworld map to explore during your free time, which allows you to unlock side quests, take on optional battles, and complete bounties.

Square Enix hasn't made a ton of strategy RPGs, and honestly, we're not sure why. Every time the company dips a toe in this pond, the results are usually something pretty special. That's the case for this 2022 tactical RPG co-developed with Japan-based studio Artdink. There are some overlong cutscenes you'll want to button-mash through, but the maps here are unique and well-designed. If you're a clever tactician, elevation, bodies of water, and even environmental obstacles like mine carts can all be used to turn the tide of battle in your favor.

#3480. Why I'd Choose the Oura Ring 5 Over the Cheaper Ultrahuman Pro

Ultrahuman’s Ring Pro is now officially on sale in the U.S., which makes this the perfect time to consider how this new device compares to the reigning champ in the smart ring market, the Oura Ring 5. Here's the short answer: While there’s a lot to like in the Ultrahuman Ring Pro, ultimately I think the Oura Ring 5 is just better at doing its job.

I’ve spent plenty of time with both rings, and admittedly, many of the differences between the two will come down to personal preference—for example, do you like the biohacking concept and the “next best actions” suggestions in the Ultrahuman app, or do you favor the soothing vibes of the Oura app? But when it comes to the devices themselves, there are big differences between them in terms of size, cost, and overall ease of use. Here’s my take on each, and why Oura is still my top choice.

The Oura Ring 5 is impressively small, and when you have to wear something on your finger, size matters a lot—and generally, smaller is better. The Oura Ring 5 is the smallest and most comfortable smart ring I’ve ever worn. I have a ton of photos here comparing it in size to other smart rings (including RingConn, older Oura rings, and an older Ultrahuman); suffice it to say, the Oura Ring 5 wins this category easily.

When it comes to the interior fit, both rings are similar: mostly smooth on the inside, without any intrusive bumps. But considering the overall shape and feel, the Oura Ring 5 is just more comfortable to wear throughout an entire day.

The Oura Ring 5 comes with a plug-in charger, which isn’t very convenient, but will get the job done. You can buy a slim, rounded charging case that easily fits in your pocket for $99. You need to match the size of the case to the size of your ring, and the charging case is not compatible with earlier versions of the device. It’s good for 30 days of charge, according to Oura.

The Ultrahuman Ring Pro comes with a charging case that is heavy and bulky with prominent corners, but good for an extra 45 days of battery life. The case fits any size of Ultrahuman Ring Pro, but is not compatible with previous versions. You can have the case play sounds if you’ve misplaced it.

The Ultrahuman ring lasts slightly longer on a charge: up to 15 days, according to the company, versus six to nine for the Oura Ring 5. The Ultrahuman ring also has several different battery modes, with “chill mode” lasting me about two weeks when I tested it. The company says some users are finding the latest software update extends battery a bit further.

To sum up: the Ultrahuman ring lasts longer on a charge and has more capacity in its charging case. You also get the charging case for free. But the Oura Ring 5’s charging case is smaller and much easier to carry around. Once again, we’re looking at two decent options: The Oura case is more expensive for what you get, but it’s also nicer to use.

Oura is the most expensive smart ring out there, and it requires a subscription. That makes it the priciest option, giving Ultrahuman an opening to beat it simply by virtue of being cheaper. But this one is closer to a wash, depending on the choices you make. If you’re looking for the cheapest possible smart ring, well, you’d probably end up with something else entirely, like a RingConn Air. But between the Oura Ring 5 and the Ultrahuman Ring Pro, the latter is cheaper than the Oura Ring 5...but only if you’re saying no to all the extras. Let me break it down.

The Oura Ring 5 costs $399 for the shiny black and silver models, and $499 for gold, rose, and the matte versions of the black and silver. The subscription costs $5.99/month (or $69.99/year, which is only a $2 savings), and the Oura is basically useless without the subscription.

Here's how the cost works out on an annual basis:

Oura Ring 5 in black or silver: $399 + $5.99/month subscription = $470.88 for one year, $542.76 for two years

Oura Ring 5 in other colors: $499 + $5.99/month subscription = $570.88 for one year, $642.76 for two years.

The Ultrahuman Ring Pro is $479 for all colors, and there is no subscription for basic use of the ring. But you can't necessarily stop there, because the Ultrahuman app includes “PowerPlugs” that will give you extra features or analysis screens. Some are totally free, including the caffeine window,  smart alarms, a new parent mode, and a limited version of the cycle and ovulation tracker, but others carry a monthly fee. And if you consider all the optional subscription fees for different PowerPlugs, they can quickly add up:

HealthEx, to connect medical records: $4.99/month

Most people probably wouldn't choose all of them, but even if you just wanted, say, respiratory health and cycle & ovulation pro, you’d quickly outstrip the price of an Oura Ring’s subscription. On the other hand, Ultrahuman also offers an Ultrahuman Max plan for $9.99/month or $99.99/year that includes all the PowerPlugs mentioned above, plus the Les Mills workouts that normally run $11.99/month. That's cheaper than subscribing to all of the options individually, but it will also make the Ultrahuman Ring Pro more expensive than the Oura Ring 5: $578.99 total for one year, or $678.98 for two years. In short, if you want everything that each ring has to offer, the Ultrahuman will cost you more.

Here's the big caveat: I wouldn't recommend bothering with most of the PowerPlugs. For example, "UltraSync for Tesla" recommends settings for your car based on how rested you are, which will be useless if you don't have a Tesla, and probably even if you do. "Cardio adaptability" measures a metric that Ultrahuman says is subtly different from HRV; Oura doesn't measure this adaptability metric, but it's not clear to me whether it's even worth measuring at all (I'd argue probably not).

Ultrahuman's respiratory health PowerPlug ($3.99/month) records sounds while you sleep, which Oura doesn't do; but Oura reports breathing disturbances based on the ring's data, which Ultrahuman doesn't do. Ultrahuman's feature is more expensive.

Ultrahuman offers a premium version of its cycle tracker for $3.99/month, while Oura has a partnership with Natural Cycles that cost $149.99/year. Either will provide more detailed (and, each company says, more accurate) cycle tracking than the basic tracking each app provides without the extras. Oura's option is more expensive.

Ultrahuman's HealthEx Powerplug ($4.99/month) displays information from your medical records throughout the app; Oura lets you import your medical records for free, but uses them mainly in the Advisor (chatbot) and dedicated areas of the app. Ultrahuman's option is more expensive.

Oura's app gives you scores for your readiness, sleep, and recent activity, and it tracks how stressed you seem to be throughout the day. A message at the top of the main screen gives you advice for what to do that day—for example, scaling back your workouts if you seem to be tired or stressed. Ultrahuman does pretty much the same thing, giving you a "next best action" that changes throughout the day, but tends to stick to predictable themes: get more activity if you've been sitting, and that sort of thing.

Both give detailed breakdowns of the factors that contribute to your scores, and both likely overstate how useful their scores are (you don't actually need to change your workout plans just because you had a less-than-perfect night of sleep). But the apps handle the basics pretty similarly: Both have partners and integrations, and you can book blood tests through either app, if you want to do that for some reason.

Ultrahuman gives you a bit more guidance on circadian rhythms, urging you to get in extra steps during certain times of day, and offering to micromanage your caffeine intake. It has a "longevity" tab that puts your long-term habits in terms of how many years they are supposedly subtracting from (or adding to) your lifespan, including measurable metrics like VO2max and a few things that are more inscrutable, like arterial stiffness.

Oura has a whole tab of "vitals" that it calculates from your day-to-day data, which I find more useful than Ultrahuman's data views. The items here include "resilience," which compares your stress to your recovery; a "symptom radar" that can sometimes flag when you're sick; and metrics of sleep regularity and how you're breathing. And, of course, you can check your "cardiovascular age" to see how much younger (or older) you should feel.

Overall, I prefer Oura's approach because the metrics make more sense, are easier to find, and are less likely to feel like they're going way out on a limb relative to the underlying science. Ultrahuman wants you to feel like a cutting-edge biohacker; Oura does a bit more to keep things down to earth. It is a bit funny to remember that both apps, and their wealth of data, are basically just pulling from heart rate readings throughout the day and night. Neither app gives you any truly important information the other doesn't, but Oura's makes more sense to me.

Updated 11/10/2026 to note that the Ultrahuman Ring Pro's stated battery life is up to 15 days, not 8-10 days.

#3479. ‘Elsbeth’ Is Ready to Play a ‘Ted Lasso’ Star’s Game in First Look at This Week’s New Episode

After venturing into country club society and solving a murder on the green involving Nat Faxon, it's time for Elsbeth to head somewhere a little more fun. Season 4 has already been a busy one for the pink-clad sleuth, between not just solving murders but helping plan her son Teddy's (Ben Levi Ross) wedding. What better area in all of New York City, then, for a day of fun than the legendary amusement district that is Coney Island? Episode 5 of CBS' hit murder mystery procedural will take Carrie Preston to the park where business once again awaits her in the world of competitive eating with a Ted Lasso star.

Titled "All About Eats," the episode unfolds in the aftermath of a deadly donut-eating competition after which a Coney Island champion dies under mysterious circumstances. Enter Elsbeth to follow the crumbs and find out who's responsible for the gastronomical crime. She soon finds a suspect in Cody Baxter, an up-and-coming eating star and superfan of the sport played by Tim Robinson's Detroiters partner, Sam Richardson. It appears he may have gotten a little too hungry for the crown and bit off a little more than he could chew to knock off his top opponent, but to expose him, Elsbeth will have to play at his game.

Ahead of the premiere this Thursday, Collider can exclusively share a new sneak peek that sees Elsbeth running into Cody on the famed Coney Island boardwalk, where he works as an "independent contractor." He doesn't like being called a "carnie" because it gives the impression he's "weird," but he doesn't exactly do a great job of breaking the negative connotation in their awkward conversation.

After they exchange pleasantries, his demeanor immediately changes when Elsbeth mentions visiting his grandmother for a "very informative" chat. She assures Mimi only told them the nicest things about how helpful he was, including purchasing donuts for her, a line that Cody immediately tries to get away from by activating the carnival booth they're at. Elsbeth is definitely down to show off her skills with a water gun, though when she mentions her accuracy, it comes off more as a challenge to Cody that she will outfox him and expose his crimes.

Britain makes more detective television than any country has any business making, and somehow almost all of it is good. Here is the one you belong in, what it says about you, and the case for it being the best of the four.

You want the tea, the gossip and the vicar behaving oddly. Midsomer is a county where the scenery is beautiful, the fete is on Saturday and the murder rate is roughly that of a small war, and absolutely nobody involved thinks this is strange.

You feel other people's grief as if it were handed to you personally. Broadchurch is less a whodunnit than a study of what a small town does to itself when it finds out that the answer was always going to be somebody everybody already knew.

You go through things rather than around them. John Luther is the best detective in London and a liability to everybody who works with him, and the show is completely honest that those two facts are the same fact.

You say the thing and you do not dress it up. Vera Stanhope turns up in a hat and a mac, is rude to almost everybody, and is the only person in the room prepared to ask the question that the family has been waiting years for somebody to ask.

Season 4 of Elsbeth has been just as star-studded as ever, with Richardson adding to a lineup that has thus far included Nicole Scherzinger, Nicholas Braun, the aforementioned Faxon, and even an appearance from New York Knicks star OG Anunoby. However, while the series still has more guests from its first round to get through, even more big names have recently signed on to join Robert and Michelle King's procedural. The Big Bang Theory star Simon Helberg will be one of the new suspects, playing a Revolutionary War reenactor whose spot is threatened by an up-and-comer. He'll be followed by SNL alum Molly Shannon, who plays a rising star creator of a female superhero, and Manchester by the Sea star Lucas Hedges as the founder of a prediction market. With them helping to fill out the rest of the season, Elsbeth is showing no signs of slowing down as the fall season winds into winter.

#3478. Five Creative Ways to Spend Your FSA Funds Before the End of the Year

If you have a flexible spending account (FSA), you know the drill: Use the funds before the end of the year, or lose them. Unfortunately, chances are slim you can pack the rest of the year with doctor's appointments. Does that mean your hard-earned funds go to waste? Definitely not. You can spend your remaining FSA funds on other qualifying healthcare costs. And what counts as "qualifying" might surprise you—for instance, you can use your FSA or HSA funds to get yourself a sweet new fitness tracker or smartwatch.

As the end of the year approaches, here are all the ways you can spend any leftover money in your FSA balance.

Many over-the-counter medications and health items are FSA-eligible, including pain relievers, cold medicine, bandages, dental care products, menstrual products, and more. Scan your medicine cabinet and make a list of anything you need to stock up on.

FSA/HSA eligibility for smartwatches and other fitness wearables is real, but the main “catch" (as I’ve previously explained) is proving the device is in fact necessary, which requires you to obtain a Letter of Medical Necessity (LMN).

Screenless recovery trackers like Whoop, Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Oura Ring can usually be justified as HSA/FSA eligible around sleep quality, HRV-based stress monitoring, or recovery tracking tied to a chronic condition. Similarly, smartwatches can qualify the same way a basic tracker does, as long as you can link a relevant documented health concern. For instance, Coros offers FSA/HSA eligibility for all its watches and heart rate monitors through its partnership with Truemed. Amazfit similarly lets you filter by HSA/FSA eligibility for its smartwatches.

If you want to get creative with it, the official FSA store lets you filter by "surprisingly eligible." Similar to the section above, for some of these items, you'll want to brush up on how exactly to get an LMN to justify certain tech as FSA-eligible for you personally. In the meantime, go crazy and snag yourself Epsom salt for $8.99, Supergoop! sunscreen for $38.00, or perhaps a snazzy massage gun for $349.99.

Knee braces, wrist splints, compression socks, and other orthopedic items can help relieve chronic pain issues. Rather than wait for these issues to rear their heads down the line, use FSA money to offset the costs of these fixes now. If you use eyeglasses or contacts, consider using your FSA dollars to update or refresh your prescriptions. Don't forget to stock up on eye drops and lens solution, too.

If you have medical procedures scheduled for early next year, many healthcare providers will allow you to pre-pay the estimated costs this calendar year using FSA funds. This includes dental work, physical therapy, chiropractic visits, Lasik eye surgery, and more.

However you choose to spend your FSA funds, don’t let that money go to waste. After all, it came out of your paycheck. Check in with your employer’s rules for any balance remaining on Dec. 31 this year, so you aren’t left forfeiting your hard-earned funds. You can find a complete list at the FSA store here.
