#3477. Casey Bloys to Receive the Milestone Award at 2027 PGAs

The Producers Guild of America (PGA) has announced that Casey Bloys, the newly instated co-chair and chief content officer of Skydance Direct-To-Consumer, will be honored with the Milestone Award at the 38th annual Producers Guild Awards on Saturday, February 27, 2027, at the Fairmont Century Plaza in Los Angeles.

The PGA’s Milestone Award is meant to honor individuals or teams who have made historic contributions to the entertainment industry. Past recipients include Louis B. Mayer, Walt Disney, Alfred Hitchcock, Steven Spielberg, Sherry Lansing, James Cameron, Bob Iger, Donna Langley, Ted Sarandos, George Lucas and Kathleen Kennedy, Charles D. King, Dana Walden, and Jason Blum. Related Stories Best Actress Frontrunner Julianne Moore Nailed ‘The Debut’ by Singing, Styling Her Hair Like Liza Minnelli, and Avoiding Playing ‘Some Suffering Mom’ How John Malkovich Nailed the Role of His Career with ‘Wild Horse Nine’

“Considering Hollywood’s recent history, no one is more deserving of the Milestone Award than Casey Bloys. Over the last decade, Casey has had a front row seat to all the disruption and consolidation facing our industry. All the while he has remained a true and steadfast champion of the creative process,” said recently elected PGA presidents Donna Gigliotti and Mike Farah in an official statement. “He is a friend to producers, writers, actors and everyone who has dedicated their lives and careers to entertainment. Casey and his talented team help shepherd television that shapes our culture, stands the test of time, and protects the originality of storytellers. While Casey is never one to seek the spotlight, the Producers Guild of America is proud to recognize the breadth and depth of his exceptional career with the Milestone Award.”

“Receiving the Milestone Award is an incredible honor, particularly from an organization that represents so many of the people I’ve had the privilege of working alongside throughout my career,” said Bloys in his own statement. “I’ve always believed our job is to create an environment where talented people can take risks, tell ambitious stories and do their best work. I’m enormously grateful to the Producers Guild for this recognition and to all of the producers, storytellers and colleagues who have been part of that journey.”

In his new role at Skydance, Bloys oversees all original programming for HBO Max and Paramount+ in addition to strategy, operations, communications, and performance across the company’s streaming platforms.

Since becoming President of HBO in 2016, Bloys has led the development and production of award-winning and critically acclaimed series like “Succession,” “Euphoria,” “Barry,” “Girls,” “Veep,” “Insecure,” “Mare of Easttown,” “Big Little Lies,” “The Pitt,” “The White Lotus,” and many more. That has resulted in HBO and HBO Max’s original television programs receiving 21 Emmys across eight original programs this past year, as well as several other industry awards. Seven of Bloys’ current original series also saw cross-platform audiences averaging a milestone number of more than 15 million U.S. viewers per episode.

#3476. 6 R-Rated Superhero Shows Better Than The Boys

The superhero landscape looked very different back in 2019 before The Boys came around, as despite there being a fair few R-rated projects on the market, none were as crude or graphic as Prime Video's mega hit. Alongside putting a completely different spin on the genre by having mainly evil superheroes, The Boys also parodied Marvel, DC, and various other franchises.

However, with The Boys ending earlier in 2026, it left a big gap in the world of R-rated superhero shows, and while spinoffs such as Vought Rising and The Boys: Mexico will continue this universe, things simply won't be the same without the main series. Fortunately, there is already an abundance of great competitors out there.

Originally, it looked like Gen V would be The Boys' replacement before being canceled, but if you are looking for R-rated hits that are even better than anything this violent franchise produced, these six projects are definitely worth checking out.

Despite lasting just two seasons, The Punisher feels like a complete series that extends Frank Castle's story after first appearing in Daredevil. Getting to learn about the tragic events that turned him from a loving husband and father to a merciless killing machine is fascinating, and The Punisher certainly doesn't pull any punches with its violence.

As we've seen in the 2004 movie, characterizing Frank isn't always easy, as without the right nuance, he can feel empty and hard to connect with. However, Jon Bernthal delivers an outstanding performance that shows the humanity behind this vigilante, making it easier to root for him, despite not always agreeing with his actions.

The first season comes across as more personal, with Frank getting vengeance on those who were responsible for the death of his family, and the supporting cast is a key part of his journey. Ebon Moss-Bachrach, Amber Rose Revah, and Ben Barnes all do a great job with their respective characters, and while it can be an uncomfortable watch at times, The Punisher's story is ultimately very satisfying.

Season 2 presents a different vibe, with Giorgia Whigham's Amy Bendix bringing out the more fatherly side of Frank. Not only does he risk his own life to protect Amy, but he stands up for injustice outside his own personal grievances, with the final scene showing him fully embracing his Punisher persona.

Considering the character has been brought back as part of the MCU and even had his own special, it's clear Bernthal made a big impact as the Punisher, and the show successfully delivers exactly the type of brutal action needed to make it an all-time great that eclipses The Boys.

With James Gunn and Peter Safran stepping down from their leadership positions at DC Studios, the future of Lanterns is uncertain, but after just one season, it has already made a huge impression. Culturally, the show was massive, as it rejuvenated interest in the Green Lantern mythos and had people constantly bringing new theories and memes every week.

Sure, it definitely proved divisive as comic readers had major issues with the character and story direction, but as a whole, Lanterns was incredibly popular. The season 1 finale pulled in over 10 million viewers in just three days, and even those who hate the show can't deny how exceptional Kyle Chandler is as Hal Jordan, with Aaron Pierre shining opposite him.

Even though the series leans more into the mystery and detective genre than classic superhero elements, there are still several fun action sequences that definitely qualify it as a superhero project over something like The Penguin. Additionally, Lanterns sets up John Stewart to be more powerful in Man of Tomorrow, which should make up for the lack of major fight scenes.

It's rare that a modern show makes such a seismic impact in just nine episodes, but in terms of quality and consistency, Lanterns trumps The Boys, despite the latter having higher highs. The desire for a second season and Hal's return highlights how good the HBO series really is, and hopefully there's still a future for this surprise hit.

Much like Lanterns, Peacemaker's future is uncertain, even more so since James Gunn directed it, but it seems like season 2 was always planned to be the last anyway. Still, in just 16 episodes, Peacemaker manages to turn a bunch of obscure and original characters into fan favorites who audiences became 100% invested in.

John Cena's Peacemaker first appeared in 2021's The Suicide Squad, and while he was originally portrayed as arrogant and overconfident, viewers came around to him until he betrayed Rick Flag. That made centering a show around him extremely risky, yet Cena delivers a career-high performance full of emotion and vulnerability, adding so much depth to this anti-hero.

With an absolutely phenomenal cast for support, the series really thrives in its character work, making it almost essential that they return in future DCU projects. Both seasons feel incredibly different as they take place under completely different hierarchies, yet Gunn's vision allowed them to connect and achieve a similar quality.

Once again, it's a show that had people talking every week, predicting what would happen next, and somehow, people managed to guess season 2's most outlandish twist. At its core, Peacemaker is fun, hilarious, brutal, and surprisingly deep, cementing it as one of the greatest live-action superhero shows of the 21st century.

Its killer soundtrack only gives it more personality, and it has two of the best superhero show opening credits ever made, showing how much care was put into crafting this legendary series.

After the highly underrated 2009 movie, it wasn't clear how much legs the Watchmen franchise had in the highly competitive superhero market, but the TV show that premiered a decade later didn't disappoint. The series follows mostly different characters than the film, creating a unique spectacle, but one that is every bit entertaining.

Even though it's an original story, the tone and visuals capture what made the comics so great, and it isn't afraid to dive into culturally relevant topics. It tackles issues like racism in a mature manner, while having a compelling direction that isn't easy to predict, keeping viewers on their toes throughout all nine episodes.

Like the other entries on this list, the acting is top drawer, with Jeremy Irons standing out as the unhinged Ozymandias. The score is also worth mentioning, since it helps create the moody tone that makes Watchmen so gritty. That said, the show isn't afraid to get a little goofy at times either, with the humor separating it from DC's usual brand of comedy.

The story ties together nicely, and while the ending is packed, Watchmen still sticks the landing, making it no surprise it's so widely celebrated. It won 11 Emmys and was nominated for 26 in total, emphasizing the quality of this limited series, which didn't overstay its welcome.

Over 10 years ago, Daredevil debuted on Netflix, and to this day, many still see it as the greatest superhero show ever made. As a blind lawyer by day and a ruthless vigilante at night, Matt Murdock is the perfect protagonist for a dark, bloody show, and the three-season masterpiece couldn't have portrayed him any better.

Matt possesses all the charm and charisma needed to make him instantly likable, yet his disability and tragic origins cement him as a true underdog. Luckily, Foggy Nelson and Karen Page act as the optimal allies for him, which makes it all the more heartbreaking when he pushes them away, even if it's supposed to be for selfless reasons.

The drama is ever-present, and the choreography is perhaps still the gold standard for superhero projects, with that iconic one-shot hallway brawl remaining relevant all these years later. That's not to overlook Frank Castle's prison fight or the office brawl between Daredevil and Bullseye in season 3.

Speaking of Bullseye, he and Kingpin were so good that they both returned for Daredevil: Born Again with the same actors, confirming these villains were irreplaceable. Daredevil also has fantastic cinematography, with vibrant colors and shots helping forge an identity that the Disney+ show couldn't replicate, despite trying its best.

Between the fantastic cast, gripping storylines, flawless editing, and all the other qualities Daredevil possesses, it's no surprise it has such a stellar reputation. It is a superhero show that changed the genre forever, and while The Boys did the same, it simply doesn't measure up to Netflix's Daredevil.

While The Boys deserves a lot of credit for breaking the traditional Marvel and DC dominance by becoming one of the biggest superhero shows of the past decade, its Prime Video competitor did the same and is even better. Invincible arrived two years after The Boys, but the animated hit is far more consistent, and still has a healthy future ahead of it.

As a faithful comic adaptation, Invincible retells the story of Robert Kirkman's original series, albeit with some tweaks and additions. Its vast roster of characters is among its biggest strengths, as alongside having a fleshed-out, complex protagonist, there are so many wonderful heroes, villains, and other supporting allies that make the universe feel alive.

There is no holding back when it comes to fights either, as the gory injuries make even The Boys look tame at times. Invincible also does a great job of adding genuinely hilarious gags and jokes into its otherwise serious narrative, which is far less shocking or in your face than its Prime Video counterpart.

Some of its very best episodes have near-perfect ratings on IMDb, putting them among the greatest in TV history, and mixed with a fantastic soundtrack, A-list cast, and constant drama, there is no denying that Invincible is a better superhero series than The Boys.

The fact that the show managed to overcome its biggest weakness by shortening the gap between seasons to release regularly means it is bound to keep getting better, and with several seasons still to come for Invincible, it deserves to be recognized as one of the best in the genre.

#3475. These 10 New Features Are Coming to iOS 27.3

Apple dropped the first developer beta for iOS 27.3 on Tuesday. While this update isn't as large as iOS 27 proper, it's surprisingly feature-filled for a 0.3 update. This is only a beta, so anything could (and likely will) change before Apple officially launches the update. But, as it stands, iOS 27.3 tests 10 new features—including one feature the company trialed in the previous beta.

Technically, anyone with a compatible iPhone can try out iOS 27.3 right now—assuming you enroll your Apple Account in the developer program. But a word of warning: Betas can be temperamental, and could be risky. As such, I'd recommend avoiding the beta until Apple releases the public beta, which comes after a bit more testing to iron out larger issues. Either way, make sure to make a full backup of your iPhone to a Mac or PC first, as issues with the beta could result in permanent data loss.

With watchOS 27, Apple released "Audio Intelligence," a new set of features for Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Audio Intelligence uses the watches' new S11 chip, along with on-device AI and cloud-based AI, to run new features, like Sound Recognition and Shazam (music recognition).

With iOS 27.3, however, the company is now officially testing the other two Audio Intelligence features it originally announced with watchOS 27. First, there's Live Rewind: By double-clicking the watch crown, you can pull up a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation. Siri Recap, on the other hand, displays summaries of conversations you had that day, in case you need a refresher on any chats you might have otherwise forgotten about,

The company generated some controversy when it first announced these two Audio Intelligence features, since, on the surface, it sounds like these new Apple Watches are essentially spying on people all day long. According to Apple, however, that isn't really the case. The company says Audio Intelligence is private, and never records or stores any audio. No speakers are ever identified, and text results (both transcripts and summaries) are deleted automatically after a set period of time unless the user saves them to the Siri app. You can read more about how Audio Intelligence works here.

Despite their claims, I'm sure there will still be strong feelings surrounding these Audio Intelligence features. We'll have to see whether Apple can prove Live Rewind and Siri Recap aren't all that creepy throughout the iOS 27.3 beta process.

iOS 27.3 also introduces app actions for Siri AI. Apple is testing new abilities for Siri AI, including organizing files, planning events, or adding photos to albums. You could ask Siri to organize your Downloads folder, or delete files that haven't been opened in more than a year. You could ask Siri to find a coffee shop you went to last week, or to save an article to your Reading List in Safari. You could ask Siri to check your calendar and set up a time for an event based on when you're free. You can even ask the assistant to schedule, edit, or unsend messages.

For example, you could ask Siri AI to help you plan a trip with your friends. You could ask the AI to put together a themed playlist in Apple Music, schedule a message to a group about an upcoming trip, organize the websites you've been visiting in Safari into a tab group, and, after the trip, ask Siri to move your best photos to your favorites album. These new actions work in the following apps: Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. Developers can also add Siri AI app actions support to their own apps.

Apple started testing its new Health app with the iOS 27.2 beta, but pulled the redesign before the official release. Now, with iOS 27.3, the new app is back. The new Health app has a health dashboard for the first time, as well as new features like Health Age and movement assessments. It seems to be pulling from some popular competitor services, hopefully, for the better. For more on the new Health app, check out Lifehacker health editor Beth Skwarecki's explainer.

Continuing on the Health track, iOS 27.3 also introduces "Gym Strength." This is a new Fitness+ feature that offers a personalized four-week strength-training plan. You can customize these plans to meet your goals, experience level, and schedule, and they adapt as you progress. You'll get recommendations based on your experience with exercises, reps, and sets, including video demos for exercises. You can access Gym Strength on both iPhone and iPad, and Apple Watches are optional—though you can log your progress with the wearable if you have it.

Vertical tabs have been a favorite among browser aficionados, as they give you more screen real estate in your browser while keeping your tabs off the side. Apple hasn't made the jump—until now. This feature works with iPads running iPadOS 27.3 as well as Macs running macOS 27.3.

Another new Safari feature in testing is "Adaptive Dark Mode." This feature forces websites into a dark theme, if they don't have a native theme of their own. There are third-party apps that can do this, but this is the first time Apple has offered this feature built into Safari.

Apple is also testing new StandBy experiences with iOS 27.3, which were previously only available on the iPhone Duo. When you turn your iPhone sideways while plugged in, you'll find new Analog and Digital Clock faces with new customization options. There's also a new Photos face, with the option to pull images from Shared Albums.

"Reachability" pulls your iPhone's display down towards the bottom of the screen, so you can access items towards the top of the display with one hand. It's a useful feature for those of us with big iPhones, and now, there's no iPhone bigger than the Duo. With iOS 27.3, Apple is testing Reachability for its first foldable phone. It's a bit like the inverse of how Reachability currently works: You can swipe on the left or right side of your Duo's display to shift the other side of the screen towards your current position. If you're holding your Duo in your left hand, a swipe of the left side will pull the right side over to the left, and vice versa.

Apple is also rolling out new languages for Siri AI in iOS 27.3. Now, Apple's smart assistant supports Traditional Chinese, Vietnamese, Turkish, and Norwegian.

If you have an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPad running iPadOS 27.3, you now have access to Siri Mode in Camera. As with iOS, you can open the Camera app on iPadOS to access Siri Mode, and ask Siri about your surroundings.

#3474. Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey Officially Sets Home Release Date

After a $1.8 billion run at the global box office, Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey is coming home. Universal Pictures Home Entertainment confirmed that Nolan's adaptation of Homer's epic will get a digital and physical release in November, letting viewers relive The Odyssey at home — now with "exclusive content never-before-seen by audiences."

Universal says that The Odyssey's home video release will arrive "months" before the film comes to streaming services (likely NBCUniversal's Peacock), confirming a 2027 debut on streaming.

The Odyssey will officially be released on digital platforms, 4K Ultra HD, Blu-ray, and DVD on Nov. 17.

The home release will include more than 90 minutes of special features, which were "personally overseen by Christopher Nolan," Universal said in a news release. The collection of bonus features includes behind-the-scenes footage, interviews with the cast and crew, and the film's IMAX-exclusive prologue. Some of the film's special features will be exclusive to The Odyssey's physical releases.

* Denotes features only available on physical formats

The Odyssey was written and directed by Christopher Nolan. The movie stars Matt Damon, Tom Holland, Anne Hathaway, Robert Pattinson, Lupita Nyong’o, and Samantha Morton, with Zendaya and Charlize Theron. They are joined by John Leguizamo, Jon Bernthal, Himesh Patel, Bill Irwin, Elliot Page, and Benny Safdie.

Nolan's adaptation of Homer's epic was both a box office success — it's the second-highest-grossing film of 2026, behind Spider-Man: Brand New Day — and a critical darling. In Polygon's review of The Odyssey, entertainment editor Jake Kleinman called it "one of the most epic and beautiful films of all time."

The Odyssey, Kleinman wrote, is Nolan "at the height of his power, using every skill, trick, technique, and ounce of Hollywood cred at his disposal to tell a story that's both awe-inspiring and shockingly unambiguous. With a sprawling cast of stars, jaw-dropping special effects, inexplicable visuals, and a masterful score from Ludwig Göransson, The Odyssey is Nolan's purest picture ever. It's his Lord of the Rings trilogy boiled down to one three-hour saga, a meticulous tribute to a beloved story told with just the right mix of fealty and creative liberty to forge something timely and timeless all at once."

#3473. ‘The Rings of Power’ Season 3 Review: Amazon’s ‘Lord of the Rings’ Series Is Just Going Through the Motions

The charges against Amazon’s epic (and epically priced) “Lord of the Rings” series, “The Rings of Power,” stacked up quickly. The first two seasons were pretty good by blockbuster standards — and I wasn’t alone in saying so — but the record-breaking costs, as well as the franchise’s lofty pedigree, set expectations higher than Great Eagles can soar. When the most expensive TV series ever made struggled to yield the requisite viewership spikes and comparable cultural impact, the claws came out.

Showrunners J.D. Payne and Patrick McKay’s series was, among other prominent complaints, a lackluster imitation of Peter Jackson’s films and an all-too-obvious ploy to become TV’s next “Game of Thrones.” Even when the visuals wowed, the characters weren’t memorable enough (save for the dwarves), the stories weren’t fun enough (again, except for the dwarves), and the twists weren’t smart enough. (The dwarves, in their infinite wisdom, did not partake.) Perhaps most damning for a show paid and made for an audience of one, Jeff Bezos’ pet project didn’t get J.R.R. Tolkien’s text — at least, not on at any depth. Related Stories Casey Bloys to Receive the Milestone Award at 2027 PGAs ‘Victorian Psycho’ Review: Maika Monroe Scares Up a Very Different Kind of Final Girl

On the whole, these criticisms weren’t enough to spoil a flawed but ambitious saga. Sure, “The Rings of Power” was made with too much deference to the past and too little innovation for the present — repeating itself (and other “Lord of the Rings” adaptations) while lacking the deft touch and sweeping imagination viewers crave from their greatest fantasy series. But it was still thrilling in its spectacle, from sets to sound design, costumes to vivid colors. (“House of the Dragon” it was not.) Episodes easily conveyed the filmmakers’ giddy excitement for the next big battle scene, the next big twist, and the next big moment in their Tolkien translation. All that money was on the screen, where it belonged, and dreams of spending it elsewhere — like, say, on many shows instead of just one — were set aside when Mount Doom erupted and the Siege of Eregion was underway.

I say all this, dear reader, not just as a handy recap of where things stand for yet another series with lengthy breaks between seasons, but to establish my position on a franchise that’s reached its sudden, somewhat unexpected nadir (for now, at least). While flaws were evident before, “The Rings of Power” Season 3 is undone by them. The listless episodes aren’t just hamstrung by additional exposition and a dearth of deadly combat; there’s a lingering wariness to it all, as if the filmmakers have run out of surprises and settled for treating their adaptation like the supplementary material it’s based on.

The third season begins with a recap of its own: Five years have passed since the Elven city of Eregion fell, and Sauron (Charlie Vickers) controls more of Middle Earth than ever. His army of orcs are tracking down the rest of the titular rings, which are safe(ish) with the elves in the luxe strongholds of Lindon and Rivendell, as well as my beloved dwarves in the sonorous mines of Khazad-dûm. But the Dark Lord himself is right where we left him, trying to forge the one ring to rule them all. Celembrimbor (Charles Edwards) was the only Elf who knew how to forge it, and now that he’s dead, Sauron grows more desperate by the day.

Not that you could tell from Vickers’ affectless portrayal. In “The Rings of Power,” the Australian actor is saddled with an arguably impossible task: Take the very presence of evil — which Tolkien so profoundly established in readers’ limitless imaginations as “an image of malice and hatred,” before Jackson sagely (and cinematically) channeled that energy into a giant, all-seeing eye — and embody that transcendent menace within a guy who looks like the guitarist next door. Vickers was able to hide his Sauron in plain sight during Season 1, when no one knew who Halbrand really was, but the big reveal didn’t lead to a bigger (or more sinister) performance, and attempts to lend human dimensions to evil incarnate similarly suffered.

What Sauron means to the series is more powerful than what he does on a scene-by-scene basis, and Season 3 throws that balance way out of whack. Absent significant conflict elsewhere, the story keeps returning to Sauron and his schemes, but none of his scenes have enough juice to elevate him to adequate levels of intimidation. A lengthy climactic sequence near the end of the season deploys shifting aspect ratios, operatic music cues, and dead-eyes stares aplenty, but they don’t add up to the riveting spectacle its creators intended. Instead, they only remind audiences how little Season 3 has to show off, not to mention how misguided some of those showcases can get.

Númenor, with its warring cousins Míriel (Cynthia Addai-Robinson) and Pharazôn (Trystan Gravelle), remains a bland, human-centered snooze-fest. (My god, these people are boring.) The desert empire of Rhûn fares slightly better with Ciarán Hinds’ Dark Wizard (those eyebrows!), but the man long known and now confirmed as Gandalf (Daniel Weyman) is still little more than a mysterious symbol. (Just wait ’til you see him… put on his hat?)

And what’s become of Prince Durin (Owain Arthur), Princess Disa (Sophia Nomvete), and my rambunctious, sunless dwarves? You’d think lifelong cave dwellers would thrive in a season that’s lost a considerable amount of its light (times are tough in Middle Earth, and “The Rings of Power” has never been subtle), but my feisty friends are stuck in a plot so predictable it’s all but spelled out in the very first episode by accident! (When the wisest dwarf speaks, we all know to listen.)

New additions feel slotted in, as if emotional attachments are expected to emerge from name recognition alone (sorry to Celeborn, Galadriel’s long-lost hubby), while old favorites are nowhere to be found. (Nori and Poppy are entirely absent through seven episodes.) Others that do show up aren’t developed thoroughly enough to support their dramatic turns, like the Southlands boy turned tree-chopping, Mordor-enslaved man Theo (Tyroe Muhafidin), or get wasted in order to prop up other, less compelling characters, like Arondir (Ismael Cruz Córdova).

Perhaps “The Rings of Power” Season 3 is just a temporary dip — the midway point of a five-season plan that needs to set the table so we can feast for the two final seasons. Even if that’s the case, it’s no excuse. “The Lord of the Rings” may engender enough goodwill to give “The Rings of Power” a little leeway, but a full season lacking in evident ingenuity and attentive investment is enough to strip away the nostalgic sheen.

The biggest slight against the series has always been its status as a prequel: Based on appendices to “The Lord of the Rings,” this is the story the movies ran through as an epilogue, so it’s going to take a little extra sumthin’ sumthin’ to prove expanding into a five-season series is warranted. Instead, we’re given the same ol’, same ol’. Not everything needs to be realized onscreen just for the sake of seeing it happen, step by step, beat by beat, ring by ring. Yet bearing witness to the inevitable is Season 3’s greatest ambition.

“The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power” premieres Wednesday, November 11 on Amazon Prime Video with four episodes. Two episodes will be released November 18 and 25 to complete the season.

#3472. ‘John Wick’ Mastermind Unleashes Brutal Samurai Action in New Thriller Trailer

“[Arlo’s] not just cool, he’s empathetic and wise; there’s a lot of stuff about that kid that was on the page that needed to be there,” said Firstman, who on this week’s episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, called the casting search the most “nerve-wracking” part of making “Club Kid.”

“Club Kid” had the right casting director for the job. Carmen Cuba has a legendary track record of finding child stars, including the original “Stranger Things” ensemble. But as Cuba pointed out while participating in IndieWire’s Craft Roundtable of Casting Directors, “Club Kid” was different from those previous assignments.

“I do six-month searches for kids,” said Cuba. “On ’Stranger Things,’ ‘Starfighter,’ you have time and money, and this was a small film.”

The $4 to $6 million production (reports on “Club Kid’s” budget have varied; A24 did not reply to IndieWire’s inquiry) could not afford a lengthy search. It didn’t even have the money for Cuba to fly to London with Firstman for auditions. She would be reliant on a UK casting team, working within a limited budget, to help her find a needle in a haystack.

“I was very nervous about just sort of the plan of attack, because I was going to have a UK team, and you need a British kid who looks like he’s half-Jordan,” said Cuba.

Right before jumping into “Club Kid,” Cuba went on her yearly vacation with a group of close casting director friends. As the holiday wound down, Cuba tried to work through her upcoming casting dilemma with some of her closest colleagues.

“I [said], ‘How am I going do this?’ just trying to map it out for myself before I left to go start it,” recalled Cuba of the conversation. “And one of those friends is Lucy Bevan, who had just finished her ‘Harry Potter’ search, so she so generously said, ‘Why don’t I share some of the names.’”

To cast the first season of the $200 million-plus upcoming HBO series — based on the first Harry Potter book, “The Philosopher’s Stone,” in which Harry turns 11 — Bevans had just finished her own six-month search. She had auditioned thousands of young British actors to play the next generation of Harry, Hermione, Ron, and their Hogwarts classmates.

“This is just a testament to our relationship because Lucy would not normally do UK casting on a tiny movie,” said Cuba of the prominent British casting director, whose credits include “Barbie,” “F1,” and “The Batman.”

“She had just seen 40,000 kids,” said Firstman of Beaven, who early on showed him a photo of Reggie Absolom. “I saw his face and I was like, ‘that is the face that I’ve seen in my head.’ Even in the script, he’s supposed to be a quarter Indian – “Innit Babes” [Peter and his friends’ nickname for Reggie’s mom based on her favorite expression] is supposed to be like half Indian — and Lucy [said], ‘Let’s not focus on that. That’s not going happen.’ And Reggie’s a quarter Indian. Every single thing that I had asked God for, this kid came to me in Reggie.”

In total, according to Cuba, Bevan showed Firstman 90 kids, with a wider range of ages — Cuba and Firstman went back and forth about how old Reggie should be, with the character originally skewing younger than 10 — but Firstman never wavered from Absalom, whose résumé included roles in “Silo” and “The Other Bennet Sister.”

“Lucy was so generous. They had no money to fly me to London to do the session in person, so she hosted the callback session there,” said Cuba. “Jordan is incredible with kids, he was like, ‘Let’s not do it in this casting office, let’s take it outside.’ So suddenly Lucy’s assistant is outside with the camera, and they’re walking and talking. I rewatched that audition recently, and it’s just amazing. Jordan’s brain, and how he connects to everyone that he casts. I think that’s what you feel in the movie; it’s so familial.”

On the podcast, Firstman talked about how beyond his decade of drug-fueled clubbing in Europe and New York City, one of the inspirations for “Club Kid” was the bond he formed with one of his close friend’s child, something he felt would be essential to replicate with Absolom.

“The reason kids like me is I don’t treat them as kids,” said Firstman. “They’re surprised at my candor, or the inappropriate things that most adults wouldn’t be willing to say in front of a kid. I know what Reggie sees on the internet. I’m not going to say something too much, but I can push it a little bit.  I think he always appreciated that in me, and once he understood that I liked to be made fun of too, everything shifted. Once he got permission to make fun of me, the whole dynamic shifted, and we just got so much more comfortable around each other.”

Much like his unorthodox, take-it-outside, walk-and-talk callback audition with Absolom, Firstman quickly realized, after casting the young actor, traditional preparation wouldn’t work.

“We tried doing traditional rehearsals, and it was awkward,” said Firstman. “I [said], ‘Let’s just keep hanging out, and keep having pizza together, and keep talking about music, and keep talking about TikTok clips we’ve seen, and send each other TikToks,’ and that’s how we bonded.”

An A24 release, “Club Kid” is now in New York City and Los Angeles theaters, and will expand on Friday, November 13.

#3465. Taika Waititi’s Sci-Fi Disaster Officially Removed From Cinemas After Earning Just $15 Per Theater

He has covered everything from Marvel to the Oscars, and Marvel at the Oscars. He also writes obsessively about the box office, charting the many hits and misses that are released weekly, and how their commercial performance shapes public perception. In his time at Collider, he has also helped drive diversity by writing stories about the multiple Indian film industries, with a goal of introducing audiences to a whole new world of cinema.

Director Taika Waititi was the toast of the town after resurrecting the stagnant Thor series with his trademark take on the po-faced superhero in Thor: Ragnarok. The movie is still considered among the finest achievements in Marvel Cinematic Universe history. It afforded him significant creative freedom not just on its immediate follow-up, Thor: Love and Thunder, but also on his prestige play, Jojo Rabbit. Waititi ended up winning a Best Adapted Screenplay Oscar for Jojo Rabbit, but his career curiously took a hit almost immediately afterward with two major critical and commercial underperformers.

Besides Thor: Love and Thunder, which fell short of its predecessor's box-office haul and is generally considered rather self-indulgent, Waititi directed two would-be awards contenders in the same vein as Jojo Rabbit. While that movie ended up grossing more than $90 million worldwide against a reported budget of $14 million, Waititi's two follow-ups suffered troubled productions and tanked commercially. First out of the gate was the sports drama Next Goal Wins, which languished on the shelf for over a year before grossing $18 million worldwide against a reported budget of $14 million.

Waititi's latest film, on the other hand, has delivered such a poor performance at the box office that its distributor, Sony, stopped reporting its grosses after two weeks. The movie in question is based on a sci-fi novel by the Nobel Prize-winning Kazuo Ishiguro. It features the six-time Oscar nominee Amy Adams and the ingénue Jenna Ortega, the star of Netflix's most-watched original series, Wednesday. Despite the talent involved, the film opened to poor reviews, which reportedly prompted Sony to cancel its wide release and global rollout. The movie eventually debuted in a little under 900 theaters on October 23.

We're talking, of course, about Klara and the Sun, which made $701,000 in its opening weekend and $157,000 in its second. By November 5, Sony stopped reporting the film's daily grosses. The movie's total global haul stands at less than $3 million against a budget that has been reported to be as high as $44 million. Its final daily haul was reported to be just over $13,000, which represents a per-theater average of just $15.

Klara and the Sun received poor reviews and is now sitting at a 26% score on the aggregator website Rotten Tomatoes. The site's consensus reads, "Flattening the nuanced ideas of its acclaimed source material with a tonally broad approach, Klara and the Sun aims to be endearing and inspiring but winds up cloying and twee." In a rare instance of a filmmaker publicly lashing out at critics, Waititi posted a note on Instagram slamming those who've disliked his movie.

You'll have to wait for Klara and the Sun to hit the PVOD market to check it out. Stay tuned to Collider for more updates.

#3463. Eight 'Winter Arc' Rules That Will Actually Deliver Results

There are a lot of terrible social media trends out there aimed at self-improvement, yet even though everybody has been making fun of the "Winter Arc" craze, I actually think it’s a good one. During your Winter Arc, you promise yourself you’ll stick to your fitness and self-care routines during (and despite) the end-of-year chaos. It's a good goal, with one caveat: Make sure you choose rules that will actually improve your life and deliver results.

Think of the “arc” in the sense of a “story arc.” The Winter Arc is a self-improvement journey that unfolds over the last few months of the calendar year. The most hardcore #gymtok-ers will tell you the Winter Arc officially begins on Oct. 1, but others start in early November, or whenever they get around to it. The "when" isn't critical, though—whenever you read this is a fine time to start. The close of the Winter Arc is fixed, however: It ends Jan. 1, just as everybody who is less dedicated than you is waking from their holiday food comas and resolving to get in shape.

You get to choose your own terms for your Winter Arc. The general vibe is one of locking in, committing to your goals, and actually doing the things you’re always saying you’ll do. TikToker @carlyupgraded has said that her own mental image of someone nailing their Winter Arc is “hood up, headphones on, getting ready to go for a run in the rain at 5 a.m.”

It turns out I’ve accidentally been Winter-Arc-ing for years; I just didn’t know it had a catchy name. Why save your gym routine for New Year’s when you’ll have the place to yourself all December? We’re even gifted with an extra hour in the mornings to fill with something productive.

I really love the mindset shift involved. Commonly, people are active in the summer (great time for outdoor fun), may or may not stick with their routines in the fall, and let everything fall apart as the holidays approach. Who has time to go to the gym when you’re planning Thanksgiving, attending holiday parties, studying for final exams, or whatever else the end of the year throws in front of you?

But that’s the exact reason why this time of year is the best to start (or restart) a fitness routine, or really any kind of routine. When you start a routine during a busy time of year, you’ll be forced to make it sustainable. The gym routine you can stick with amid the chaos isn’t going to be one you drop after a few months. You’re already training yourself to work around obstacles as they come up, which is a key component of self-efficacy. And when the chaos clears on Jan. 1, your routine will be even easier to stick to.

Of course, there are ways to lean in too hard: Choosing unsustainable habits, falling for bad diet advice, mistaking not masturbating for some kind of health hack, the usual suspects. There’s also the pitfall of focusing too much on the vibes and too little on what you’re actually going to do or how you’ll benefit.

And then there’s the framing: You were working on yourself all year, but you’re in danger of letting up on the gas, but you’re committed to locking in so that you’re a step ahead of everybody who takes this time to slack off. I really don’t love this tack. Self-improvement is not a competition. There’s a difference between being consistent in your training and healthy eating (good) and seeing the pursuit of health and fitness as something where you always have to work harder because you’re at risk of getting left behind.

I also don’t love how gendered the Winter Arc TikToks tend to be. When you search for Winter Arc content, the first few suggestions include “winter arc for women” and “winter arc for men.” When I first started looking at the Winter Arc trend a few years ago, the women’s versions were more likely to include restrictive dieting or to focus on how the Winter Arc will finally (sigh) snatch your waist. These days, the focus is more on personal goal setting: Lots of the girlies filming their Winter Arc rules are doing so in a notebook and talking about journaling exercises that will help you identify what you need to work on to get to your "best self." Sometimes this is all monetized; training plans and journaling prompts can, of course, be purchased at the link in bio.

I do like that many of the women’s versions emphasize sustainability and setting your own goals rather than copying somebody else's. I don't love the enormity of the mental burden you're supposed to shoulder before even beginning. Should I really have to file an in-depth written report with myself before revamping every area of my life with a 100% commitment to multiple goals?

The men’s versions tend to go off the rails in another direction, with rules like “no girls” or “go ghost.” No distractions! Here, I've seen a shift over the years as well: at first there was overly serious content, followed quickly by satire (yelling at the viewer to get divorced and go work out in the dark). Now the men's videos tend to be more vibes-based, featuring images of pre-dawn workouts and plates full of salad with motivational quotes playing in the background. When the men give their rules, they tend to be simpler than the women's—no journaling exercises—but they often boil down to the same overly strict routines. (And then, of course, they'll offer to sell you a 90-day or 60-day plan.)

If you’re going to do a Winter Arc (or if you’re already doing one), make sure to structure it in a way that benefits you. Choosing 10 overly ambitious goals and setting yourself up for failure is not a healthy way to approach self-improvement, OK? Pick goals that are meaningful, achievable without divine intervention, and trackable with tools you already have at hand (for example, tracking your steps with a Fitbit or your running mileage with a Garmin watch).

It’s also helpful to think of developing yourself over this arc, rather than taking it as a three-month (or two-month) challenge where you have to do everything right all the time. If you currently wake up at 8 a.m. and want to wake up at 5 a.m., you don’t have to set your alarm for 5 a.m. tomorrow. It’s OK to aim for 7:30 a.m., make that a habit, then try for 7:00 a.m., and so on.

With that in mind, here are some "rules" I've seen from creators that I'm actually on board with (so long as you don't overwhelm yourself with them):

Wake up earlier. A great goal, especially if you take advantage of the time change to make things easier on your body.

Get to bed on time. Never a bad idea. Cultivating good sleep habits in general is always worthwhile.

Get your steps in. Be thoughtful about what your target is: 10,000 is not for everybody. Better to choose a number that would be a modest improvement on what you already do.

Exercise X times per week. Pick a number that works for you, and get into it. Be realistic about your goal, and for the best results, be consistent even if you’re sore at first.

Eat healthy. This is a great goal, with the major caveat that there are a lot of ways to eat healthy. You don’t need to cut out sugar or pretend that there’s something evil about seed oils. Do get more protein and veggies.

Be more thoughtful about using social media. I’m not going to tell you to delete all your apps (“except TikTok,” as the TikTokers say). But it’s fair to consider whether you might want to delete a few apps, turn off some notifications, or put your phone on Do Not Disturb for more hours of the day.

Journal or read more. Journaling can be great for working through your feelings or cultivating a creative habit. Reading can be entertainment or a great way to learn. Choose whichever you need most.

Learn a new skill. I’ve mostly seen this one in the men’s TikToks, and I love it. They’re often thinking of “skills” that will help in some kind of entrepreneurship grift they’re about to sell you, but there are tons of skills that will come in handy in life, or that are at least fun to learn. Practice a language, get better at cooking, make some art. Skills are, as I’ve noted, a multi-layered exercise for your brain. And they may come in handy someday.

This year I've slacked off on my fitness routine as I've gotten more involved in other hobbies, but I'm actually looking forward to being more consistent. My winter goals include exercising early in the day when possible and reading 20 minutes each day. (I'm even tracking the second one with a sticker chart.)

#3462. ‘Ink’ Star Jack O’Connell on His ‘New Era’ as a Leading Man: ‘Thank F**k for Danny Boyle’

Jack O’Connell was feeling a little bashful. Seated outside for coffee, taking in the fresh fall air at the remote Salamander Resort in Middleburg, Virginia, the actor revealed that communication between him and Oscar-winning filmmaker Danny Boyle began long before he was cast as the lead in the director’s latest film, “Ink.”

“I used to write to Danny a lot. I wrote all the directors that I admire,” said the 36-year-old star from Derbyshire, England. “Not cap in hand, trying to get anything out of them, just letters of appreciation, lovely stuff that’s affected me and inspired me. ‘I hope we get to do it someday.’ And, in Danny’s case, we did.” Related Stories How Casting the New ‘Harry Potter’ Helped ‘Club Kid’ Find Its Adorable 10-Year-Old Star Casey Bloys to Receive the Milestone Award at 2027 PGAs

Technically “Ink,” in which O’Connell plays influential newspaper editor Larry Lamb after he’s recruited by outcast media magnate Rupert Murdoch to take over The Sun tabloid in 1969, is the second time the actor has worked with Boyle. The pair first officially met when he was brought in to play antagonist Jimmy Crystal in last year’s “28 Years Later,” directed by Boyle, and more prominently in January’s “28 Years Later: The Bone Temple,” directed by Nia DaCosta.

“It was right before I went and shot ‘Sinners,’” he said, referencing another major turn as a villain that loomed prominently over cinema this year. “The initial meeting wasn’t an audition. I just didn’t have the role. It was a meeting discussing the role with Danny and Nia.” It was the first time Boyle had acknowledged O’Connell, though he had a sneaking suspicion that he had been on the director’s radar for a while, having starred on the same iconic British teen drama “Skins” from which Boyle had found the star of his Best Picture winner “Slumdog Millionaire.”

“Listen, he cast Dev [Patel]. He knew about ‘Skins.’ I think his daughter put him onto ‘Skins’ in the first place. So whether or not he stuck it out for our generation, I don’t know,” said O’Connell.

It’s been almost two decades since he first played fan favorite Cook as part of the second generation of the trailblazing E4 series, which ran from 2007 to 2013. “Skins” still stands out as an experience that helped shape his ethos as an actor. “I certainly felt like we were on the coolest show around. It was so amazingly written. The directors we had were brilliant. The whole model of the way that you audition en masse and then they find their characters. I love that,” said O’Connell. “It’s really quite pure, isn’t it? People are just getting the roles because of ability.”

The “Ink” star first trained as an actor at a free program in Nottingham called the Television Workshop, which eventually helped lead to his first breakout film role in the coming-of-age drama “This Is England.” However, it was “Skins” that felt like a “crash course” continuing education. “You’re doing all the heavy stuff, the tough stuff, the really laborious side of doing a TV show like that. But also the fun and the joy that gets provoked by all the art, the amazing writing and everything else,” said O’Connell. He’s quick to remind that notable “Skins” alumni include not just Patel, but also writers like Emmy winner Jack Thorne and Tony-nominated playwright Lucy Kirkwood.

But free programs like the Television Workshop are increasingly hard to come by, meaning there are less and less egalitarian-type opportunities in the United Kingdom for an actor from a working-class background like O’Connell’s to find their own “Skins.” Asked what he would tell the next generation of artists, the “Ink” star said, “I wouldn’t know what advice I would give nowadays, which is a shocking indictment.”

What attracted O’Connell to playing Lamb in “Ink,” a role that has brought him to the Middleburg Film Festival to receive the Spotlight Actor Award, was the opportunity to address how the UK, and the world in general, reached this place of inequality. “We see this man just excavate his morals, and his soul, and his decisions, and this newspaper. Being the best-selling newspaper, he’s had to part with what makes people more human. To me, it’s a comment on capitalism,” said the star. “The beginning of hyper capitalism, post-war England, and individual opportunity versus looking after everyone else and your responsibility within society. That was all just getting ripped up.”

“Ink” is an adaptation of James Graham’s 2017 play of the same name, with Graham also serving as the screenwriter of Boyle’s film. Another major factor in O’Connell’s decision to play Larry Lamb was working with the playwright and the director, who had come from a similar background. With Boyle, “I came to his work as a fan first, before I knew I was going to try and be an actor,” he said. “I remember watching ‘The Beach,’ and that made me want to go and see the world. And watching ‘Trainspotting’ and that made me want to never take heroin. But also the amazing soundtrack that’s in there and the fucking unforgettable performances.”

With “Ink” they were preparing to tell what O’Connell sees as a quintessentially British story, and “what [Danny’s] films have meant for British cinema and British culture as a result is undeniable. Thank fuck for Danny Boyle. He is an artist by every stretch of the word. I would argue that his films have perhaps meant the most to us as a collective growing up. His work at the Olympics opening ceremony makes you tingle to watch it. It is fucking monumental.”

Boyle is why O’Connell, an outsider to the film and TV industry in the same way Lamb was to the publishing industry, could still envision himself becoming an actor one day. “His style has been able to make you feel part of the film. It takes you along. You feel like you’re in the movie somehow. You don’t feel like an observer, like a spectator. They give you a feeling and mood as well,” he said.

As for Graham, “We’re not too far from each other in a particular pocket of the UK. And although my town and his town famously don’t get on — that’s all to do with football and Brian Clough and whatever else — but he is a dramatist. He’s also interested in analyzing culture and the culture around him and examining it,” said O’Connell. “He’s a great spokesman for under-representation in the industry at home because eight percent of the entire industry are from our background.”

The actor added, “Once he knew that I was somebody that could be trusted with his words, not someone who was going to try and fucking destroy them, we really hit it off.”

Here the three were, as what some would call a band of outsiders, telling a story about these insurgents to the distinguished Fleet Street, where the most esteemed newspapers like The Daily Mirror were published. Playing Lamb was a bit of an exercise in what would happen if O’Connell’s comeuppance led him toward the dark side. “The intoxication of power is something that really interests me. And Larry, he began as a socialist, voted Labour, celebrated socialist politicians. He left Fleet Street having been knighted by Margaret Thatcher. … Talk about excavation, a whole U-turn politics there, colluded with Rupert Murdoch in tearing up the unions and workers’ rights. Sold his soul,” said O’Connell.

“There’s a great contradiction with Larry that he begins as an outsider. Even within the duration of our film, he’s trying to become an insider. He wants to be part of that gang. In fact, that’s where he ended up, Sir Larry. So there’s a great contradiction in the man. So I can’t afford to go all the way ‘outsider with a chip on his shoulder,’” said the actor.

With “Ink” following the successes of “Sinners” and “28 Years Later” so quickly, O’Connell has a newfound feeling of security and sense of becoming that sought-after leading man. “It probably is my most mature role to date,” he said. “I look back on my career and I just feel so fortunate. There’s not a single regret. So if this is a new era, yeah, brilliant, bring it on. A lot of my heroes, a lot of their work that I really celebrate, were around my age, so maybe that is inspiring and gives me cause to kick on.”

Netflix will release “Ink” in select theaters across the United States on Friday, December 11. The film will debut on the streaming service on January 8, 2027.

If you prefer wired connections for devices that need a more stable link, the main router has three 2.5GbE LAN ports and a 2.5GbE WAN port, while the satellite offers two 2.5GbE LAN ports. This gives you plenty of room to connect a gaming console, desktop PC, or smart TV, and you can also use wired backhaul if your home has Ethernet cabling.

Once everything is connected, you can handle setup and day-to-day management through Netgear's Orbi app, while a web dashboard offers additional settings (for anyone who wants more control over their network), including VPN access and port forwarding, notes this PCMag review. There's no USB connectivity or 10GbE support, and some of its more advanced security and parental control features require a separate subscription after a free 30-day trial. Its Smart Parental Controls, for instance, cost $7.99 per month or $69.99 annually.

#3460. Why Ari Aster and Lars Knudsen’s Square Peg Built a Therapy Circle for Hollywood’s Next Generation in Texas

Talent labs and mentorship programs are plentiful for aspiring filmmakers — but where do you turn when your career has already started, after your first movie or on the precipice of one, and especially when filmmaking can be such a lonely enterprise?

Enter Square Peg Social, the Austin, Texas-based filmmaking summit launched by Lars and Amy Knudsen and Ari Aster that offers four days of singular community-building: brutally honest advice, commiseration, and idea exchange shared among 35 participants, with the program now in its second year.

A weekend of panels, discussion, and camaraderie designed for filmmakers at the early stages of their career, this year’s talent-incubating event was even crashed by the likes of Zach Cregger and Richard Linklater — both of whom were down to get frank about their filmmaking highs and lows. (In fall 2025, IndieWire did a deep dive into Square Peg Social’s first year, just to show how much the event has already grown.) Related Stories ‘Ink’ Star Jack O’Connell on His ‘New Era’ as a Leading Man: ‘Thank F**k for Danny Boyle’ How Casting the New ‘Harry Potter’ Helped ‘Club Kid’ Find Its Adorable 10-Year-Old Star

But the program’s stable of 2026 mentors and panelists — i.e., filmmakers keen not only to open up to new filmmakers about their own struggles, but also to scout new talent — also counted “Primetime” and “You Can See Everything” director Lance Oppenheim, “Sing Sing” filmmaker Greg Kwedar, “The First Omen” director Arkasha Stevenson, and “Mother Mary” director David Lowery among them.

The closed-door, off-the-record, noncompetitive summit opened to applicants in May, later unfolding from September 17-21. Partners including the Austin Film Society, Belvedere, and Airbnb offset the cost, besides a modest application fee, for participants to hole up for four days and nights at Soho House that don’t promise job opportunities — but instead, the kind of lasting industry connections that can take years (and many starts and stops) to build. Also, no job opportunities isn’t entirely true. Take last year’s Square Peg Social mentee Yona Strauss, who’s now working for Knudsen and Aster’s Square Peg.

Just a sampling of this year’s participating producers and directors: producer Annie Huang, who worked on franchise IP like “Barbie” and “Wicked” at major studios; Jack Auen, co-founder of the filmmaking collective Cosmic Salon, which this year directed the New York critics’ favorite “Chronovisor”; Emmy-winning director of the Netflix short “The Turnaround,” Kyle Thrash; SXSW 2026 Neon Auteur Award winner Oliver Woolf; and many more who have their foot in the door, but are ready to cross the threshold.

IndieWire spoke to Lars Knudsen and Aster (who also co-founded the production company Square Peg, which this year backed “The Drama” and “Primetime”), plus Stevenson, Oppenheim, and Kwedar, along with three participants, to replay the on-the-ground experience in Austin. Late nights, early mornings, and vulnerabilities abounded across a long (but in some ways too short) weekend of intimate panels, small group sessions, and candid remarks from established filmmakers about the times they were trying to hold their own projects together with Scotch tape and paper clips. Think of it like a mini summer camp devoted to obsessive ambition.

“When you’ve been doing it for this long, sometimes it feels like you’re just a little bit going through the motions. You’re going from movie to movie to movie, and you sometimes forget why we do this thing that we do. We’re in this world working with these artists where they don’t have a plan B. Having now worked with 30, 40 filmmakers, I realized that when my wife brought up the idea of doing something because she has her own aversions to the industry, and that there isn’t really — it sounds cliché — but there just isn’t a lot of kindness or compassion or openness in our industry.

“There’s a lot of fear, there’s a lot of rejection. We wanted to create a space for filmmakers where there’s radical transparency and where it was truly, truly focused on a selfless thing: helping young filmmakers navigate the industry at a time in their career where things can either take off or not, and really demystifying the process of making movies, especially during the stage where they’re often in the back seat, which is financing or casting. Because for all these filmmakers that I work with and all the filmmakers that we’ve invited there, even the producers, it’s the first thing to think about when they wake up and the last thing to think about when they go to bed. Nothing is more important. I wanted to create an event where that is treated with the utmost importance, almost like it’s a life-or-death thing because it is all they want to do.”

“When Lars and Amy first broached the idea with me, I realized that it was something that I wish I had when I got out of school [at AFI], because I really did have to navigate that on my own. I was making a lot of shorts with whatever money I could raise and writing screenplays and trying to get one screenplay going. When that failed, writing something else and really looking for any sort of mentorship or guidance, It’s a very demoralizing process, and it was very, very hard for me to find traction, and it hasn’t gotten easier. It’s as bad as it’s ever been. There’s just so much uncertainty right now in the industry, not just for filmmakers. Even the lives of these studios are suddenly in danger and in question.

“There are a lot of filmmakers that Lars and I have been championing and films that we’ve been trying to get financing for that have proven almost impossible… It felt like a good thing to create a space where filmmakers can come together and commiserate and share experiences and connect. More important than even the connections that are made between the mentors and the mentees here are actually the relationships made among the people who are attending. A lot of them end up working together because we have producers and directors coming in. Last year proved really successful, and I would just say it was refreshing for us, too, that it galvanized us to keep doing this. Because last year it was almost an experiment: Will this work? How will we feel having done this? … Everybody walked away feeling good and feeling like it was a really useful and positive experience.”

“I’ve never really had the opportunity to just hang out with so many great filmmakers, not only just working filmmakers whose work I’ve loved, like David Lowery, who I’ve idolized for so long, but there’s so many filmmakers that were actually in the program as participants whose work I also have really admired. So having a space where we could all just kind of talk and vent and really nerd out on stuff that you never really get the opportunity to do.

“Because this was so filmmaker-driven and filmmaker-led, it encouraged the spirit of vulnerability [where] everyone really went there. I felt like maybe I should go back to therapy or something, but I felt like this was a great opportunity to therapize and also dump all of my feelings into a forum where you could just be open and honest about the process of making films… Most people had made features before, and were in the process of making features. It felt much more like we were at a film festival and everyone was able to connect with each other in a much deeper way, more than anything I’ve been to before.

“The first night I was there, I stayed up till like three in the morning, and I went on one of those electric scooters, the limes with Lars and Christian [Vasquez], my producer, and a producer from the event, too. We went to Whataburger and just kept talking. I think that was sort of the vibe. I don’t know. I guess everyone was encouraged to hang out for as long as they wanted to and to kick back and relax. There was another night we closed down the Soho House lounge bar, and Amy was like, ‘Let’s keep hanging out.’ So we were outside the bar, and everybody pulled together all of the drinks in their mini bar, and we created an ad hoc bar outside of the Soho House, and we kept drinking and hanging.”

“I don’t think you can really do film if you have a plan B because there’s always an escape hatch, and film requires every single atom of your body, mind and soul. It naturally becomes a very therapeutic place. I think because we’re all in this constant state of obsession, that can get really tiring, and it can get really lonely. … [The industry] attracts very sensitive souls. [With Square Peg Social] I didn’t even realize how badly I needed it until the first year. I’d known Amy and Lars before that, and Amy said that she wanted to start a Social. … I thought it would be much smaller, smaller. It ended up being this great big thing where, yeah, it does feel like a therapy circle, really.

“Everyone was really struck by the safety of the event. There was this unspoken agreement that everybody would be checking your egos at the door, and that this would be a very safe place to share your personal vulnerabilities, which is exceptionally rare in film because resources are so limited, and it’s just naturally a very competitive industry. Letting yourself be very, very vulnerable in front of your peers is something you were, in a sense, trained not to do but sometimes desperately need. At Square Peg, also, the line between mentee and mentor blurs quite a bit, which is why I think it’s so beneficial for everybody who goes there.

“It kind of reminds me of summer camp a little bit because you’re up until two or three in the morning talking to people, and then you’re up at eight again.”

“I always think of this term, like, whenever you take an elevator up, if you get to the top floor, send it back down for someone else to get on. [Square Peg] is one of the busiest production companies working today. To dedicate this weekend for emerging artists to have a forum where they can come and feel completely comfortable being very vulnerable with their ambitions, but also the things that they’re afraid of, and to hear that echoed from industry mentors who are being just as vulnerable about their ambitions and the things that they struggle with and the heartbreaks they’ve had, it’s an amazing table that’s set.

“I had ulterior motives in the, in the sense that Clint [Bentley] and I have started this new company, Ethos, and we have a deal at Netflix to finance films from emerging artists, and so I was also there … to look for talent. We’ll be following up with a lot of these artists to just hear more about the films they want to make. One thing that I appreciated about it was that it wasn’t like a pitch fest. You’re not there to pitch your project. You’re there to soak it in and learn.

“It had this healthy blend of these panels, and not the normal kind of panel. One was a panel of filmmakers led off by Ari and Lars, telling a very, very brutally honest story of how hard one of their films was to make. That kind of created a pathway for how the rest of the weekend would unfold.”

“I think the whole reason anyone works in film is that we were once kids making videos in the woods with our friends, making with a shitty camera. And there’s nothing else in this world, and I think I probably speak for everyone, where I can’t imagine film is the only thing that’s our main passion and hobby and something we can also make a career out of. So there was never a plan B at all. Whenever someone asked me, ‘What do you think you’d do if you couldn’t do anything film-adjacent?’ I have literally no idea, maybe a teacher or something. That’s super nice that Lars and the rest of Square Peg was saying that there is no plan B. There’s only: If it takes longer to get to Plan A, then it takes longer to get to Plan A.

“I remember on the very first day before we even properly began, Lars did a little speech with Ari, and Lars was like, ‘We’re going to be 100 percent transparent with you guys.’ And I remember thinking, ‘Oh, that’s cool, but I wonder how transparent.’ And by the end of it, I was like, ‘Fuck me, that was transparent.’ There really was nothing off the table.”

“It was definitely something that I’ve never experienced before in this industry, to experience that level of candor and to hear these traumatic experiences that they have gone through in not a sensationalistic way, but almost in a very personal and almost relatable way, despite me having never experienced that level of millions of dollars of movie budget making — but on a personal level of how the heartbreaks had felt for them individually and the hardships of filmmaking. Coming into this program, there are so many people within our cohort who are incredibly talented, who have accomplished so many things. And coming into it, oftentimes you’ll have a fear of: ‘OK, how do I compare in relation to their accomplishments?’ But in hearing Lars and Ari talk about their own hardships, I think that’s what influenced me to really share some of mine coming up in the industry and producing independently.

“Some of the traumatic experiences that I have also faced are ones that I feel like I have to not talk about or hide from people, for fear of them looking like mistakes or of me looking like I’m not good enough to be doing this. And we were able to share that, like Ollie [Woolf] and I, in our own little producer’s therapy session with the mentors, with Lars. That was really healing for me.”

“[Ari, Lars, and the mentors are] on, not a different level, but they’re all going through similar issues and this and that, whether it’s a low budget or a higher budget type of ordeal. Everyone’s going through the same thing in their own way, in a sense. Just to know the people that I’ve been looking up to for a very long time, the reason in large part why I got into making films, to know that they’re going through similar things and just keep going, and it’s fine. No matter what level we’re going to be at, there’s still something to navigate. So I thought it was very cool to see, over the course of five days, to hear these individual experiences and stuff and how you could relate it back to what we’re going through right now and where we are.

“It was information overload in the best way possible. At a certain point, I hope I’m retaining everything that was said over those five days because it was nonstop, all useful information. I wasn’t even taking notes at a certain point because I’m like, ‘I can’t write all this stuff down. I’m just going to try and soak it all in.'”

#3459. Disney+ Has Failed To Reverse Moana's $250 Million Disappointment

Disney+ has become a place for Disney's biggest movies to become even more popular or finally find a wide audience after initially releasing in theaters. The streaming service has propped up major blockbusters like Avatar: The Way of Water and Zootopia 2, while it gave a box office bomb like Tron: Ares some redemption.

The latter category is where Disney believed 2026's Moana would fall. The live-action remake of the beloved 2016 animated movie came out in theaters this summer, and brought significant box office expectations with it. The animated Moana movies were massive hits on the big screen, with Moana 2 making over $1 billion just two years ago.

The live-action remake could not go nearly as far. The $250 million production bombed with a $323 million worldwide gross. After the film's poor opening weekend, Moana was projected to lose over $100 million for Disney. Rather than immediately declaring the remake a misfire, Disney's new CEO Josh D'Amaro suggested that it brought in substantial revenue elsewhere and believed it would draw significant interest on Disney+.

Moana entered its streaming era on October 21, which is when it officially debuted on Disney's service worldwide. This should have been the start of a successful run for the movie as a global audience enjoyed the film at home, and despite finding some more fans, the reception on Disney+ has failed to reverse the movie's disappointing run.

At first glance, it's easy to think that the live-action remake has been a hit. Moana found streaming success on Disney+ immediately, as it climbed to #1 on the charts. Nearly three weeks later, it still holds this spot globally (via FlixPatrol). However, whereas it was the biggest movie in 71 countries then, it is down to only 14 now, one of them being the United States.

Moana's chart-topping performance is not as good as it seems thanks to its viewership numbers. Disney has not officially announced any details about how the remake has performed in its debut. The silence speaks volumes in a case like this. Disney loves to celebrate its biggest streaming hits and announce when new films do great on the streamer. Clearly, the Disney+ viewership is not worth bringing to light for Disney.

This isn't just an assumption, as Nieslen's data backs this up. The global service tracks viewership across all streamers every week, and from October 19–25 (the week Moana debuted on Disney+), the movie was watched for 579 million minutes. That is equivalent to just over 5 million views based on the film's 115-minute runtime. While that was enough for Moana to be the biggest movie on streaming that week, it was poor for Disney.

As reported by Netflix & Chiffres, the 5 million views in its first 5 days on Disney+ give Moana one of the lowest launches for a live-action Disney theatrical movie on the streamer. It just edged out The Fantastic Four: First Steps and was ahead of Freakier Friday and Tron: Ares, but that's where the list ends.

This makes Moana the worst Disney+ launch for a Disney live-action remake. The Little Mermaid doubled its viewership (10.2 million views). Lilo & Stitch performed well with 7.4 million views. Even Snow White debuted to 5.3 million views. This lack of interest at launch doesn't inspire confidence that Moana's additional time on the streamer will right the ship, putting the franchise in uncharted waters.

The animated sequel has also been a massive success during its time on streaming. Disney announced last year that Moana 2 launched to 27.5 million views in its first 5 days, which was the third-largest debut for a theatrical movie at the time. It went on to become Disney+'s most-watched movie in 2025, earning 80 million views (via What's On Disney Plus).

Both Moana movies charted on Disney+ ahead of the live-action remake's release, adding to their impressive viewership figures. It was anticipated that the 2026 feature would have a similar level of popularity once it came to streaming. Instead, the live-action Moana received less than 20% of the initial views that Moana 2 did less than two years ago.

As a result, Disney+ has not been the saving grace for Moana that everyone associated with it hoped for. It has simply been another opportunity for audiences to largely reject the remake. Now, the 2026 movie will go down as a critical, financial, and streaming disappointment.

The results are surprising for the Moana franchise, but there were questions about its viability as a remake from early on. Many of these were diminished due to the assumption that general audiences would still be eager to see Moana and Maui's adventure in this new format, which proved to not be the case.

The biggest hurdle the live-action remake faced was timing. Disney changed a Moana Disney+ show into Moana 2 to give the studio a major box office hit, even though the live-action remake was already announced and gearing up to release. While the remake was delayed a year to space out the releases a bit more, it's clear audiences weren't ready for this type of movie. Not only did they just enjoy an animated sequel, but the original hit was only a decade old, eliminating the nostalgic pull of remaking something like Lilo & Stitch.

It didn't help that 2026's Moana received largely negative reviews, which primarily revolved around its lack of imagination and being far too similar to the original. Dwayne Johnson's decline as a reliable box office star in recent years was also a knock on the movie, but this would've been a bigger hit for him and Disney if the final product was better and came out at a different point in time.

It's worth noting it came out a week before The Odyssey and three weeks before Spider-Man: Brand New Day. Those became the event films of the summer, and with families showing more favor to Minions & Monsters (which came out just 9 days before) and Toy Story 5 (released one month before), the stacked summer competition proved to be too much for Moana to combat.

Now, the question becomes what comes next for Moana. The IP is too valuable to Disney for them to let it die. Just as Moana was brought back to life in Moana 2's ending, the franchise will live on despite the disappointing outcome this year.

This will come with an extra focus on animation versus exploring more live-action avenues. Dwayne Johnson confirmed Moana 3 is in development ahead of the live-action remake's release. He revealed that Jared Bush and Dana Ledoux Miller are writing the script for Walt Disney Animation Studios, which has yet to formally announce plans or a release date for the third animated film.

What 2026 really means for Moana is that we won't be seeing any more live-action remakes. Disney isn't going to try and redo the animated sequel right now, with Moana 3 the priority. By the time that movie is ready to come out, and the studio even begins contemplating potential next steps in the live-action space, Catherine Laga'aia will have aged out of the teenager role. Something like a live-action Maui prequel could have happened in the interim if the 2026 movie was successful, but that's not getting a greenlight now.
