#3458. The 10 Most Intense Movie Scenes of All Time, Ranked

Looking over some of the most intense movie scenes of all time is also going to reveal a bunch of movies that themselves can be counted as the most intense of all time. Overlap’s inevitable, but the focus below will be on those individual scenes. Sure, a scene can be long, taking up 10 to 20 percent of a movie’s runtime in some cases, or if it’s suspenseful for a shorter amount of time, maybe it’s an especially harrowing two to three minutes.

Also, talking about specific scenes will mean spoilers can be found below, but not every scene here necessarily takes place near a film’s conclusion. And for one more “also,” these movies have all been out for at least a few years, and most are quite well-known, so you're unlikely to have too much genuinely spoiled here, if you're interested enough in movies overall to read (or skim) a ranking like this.

Since 2027 is less than two months away, at the time of writing, Children of Men might well be an even more stomach-churning watch nowadays than it might've been back in 2006. Most dystopian movies are intense in one way or another, for hopefully obvious reasons, but the bleak future (which isn't a future for much longer) of Children of Men feels especially so.

The first scene is shocking, as are two set pieces that involve a car (one of them in the car, and one involving a car that doesn’t start), yet the final sequence, which sees the surviving characters (not too many) caught up in an all-out war zone, is the most full-on in Children of Men. It contains the most elaborate of the movie’s long takes, and it does an uncomfortably good job at making you feel like you're caught up in all the horror and bloodshed yourself.

There was a time when the shower scene in Psycho might've been genuinely surprising, but nowadays, you know, it’s the shower scene from Psycho. It comes before the halfway point of the movie, and it features the only character who’s been in the entire movie, scene by scene, up until that point. And out of nowhere, she’s murdered in a way that was very shocking by the standards of the early 1960s.

It’s a real shock to the system, or would've been before it became legendary, and so for all that, this scene’s well and truly earned its reputation.

It’s about as famous as thriller movie scenes get, and it played a part in rewriting the rules of what you could and couldn’t do early on in a movie. It’d be shocking enough to have the shower scene happen at the end, but when it happens where it does here, it’s like, “Wow, there’s an hour left, and now literally anything can happen… and actually, what even can happen?” It’s a real shock to the system, or would've been before it became legendary, and so for all that, this scene’s well and truly earned its reputation as an all-time great moment in cinema history.

Alfred Hitchcock got a shout-out here by highlighting Psycho, and then David Fincher, who’s also got a knack for directing suspenseful and effortlessly intense movies, is going to be mentioned shortly. In similar territory is Brian De Palma, and it feels necessary to highlight at least one scene he’s done as being especially intense, so of all the candidates (often finales; see Carrie and Scarface), here’s the big shootout in The Untouchables.

Well, it’s kind of big. The gunfight itself doesn't technically last too long, but The Untouchables spends an agonizingly long time building it all up, and then the use of slow motion during the build-up and when the shooting itself starts also draws the scene out in the best of ways. It’s such an expertly done set piece, and even if De Palma might have some movies that are darker and more consistently tense than The Untouchables, it’s this single scene that best demonstrates his knack for crafting cinematic suspense.

Make no mistake: pretty much the entirety of Zodiac is tense, and then when it’s not tense, it’s more disquieting and despairing. The search for the Zodiac Killer is at the core of the story, unsurprisingly, and most of the tense parts play out when the killer himself is at large, with the more subtly uneasy parts being found in the back half, when the chances of actually finding the killer seem to dissipate further scene by scene.

The terror does come back in full force, though, with the infamous basement scene in Zodiac, which happens closer to the end and involves Robert Graysmith possibly encountering the killer, but the not knowing – and the darkness of the sequence visually – bring the film the closest it gets to outright horror territory. It’s far from the only memorable scene in Zodiac, of course, but it does leave the biggest impact.

The scene you probably remember as being the opening one, even if Saving Private Ryan does start decades after the end of World War II before flashing back, it’s that famous extended sequence depicting the D-Day Landing at Omaha Beach. Guess it is chronologically the first scene that takes place in Saving Private Ryan, and it does have such an impact that it sticking in one’s mind over the actual opening scene is understandable.

There is also a large-scale battle sequence near the end of Saving Private Ryan, and that’s no slouch in terms of showing some truly visceral combat either. However, it's this opening sequence that proves most startling, coming earlier in the film, and it’s also a depiction of an actual battle, so it has that extra sense of dread and terror to it (the final battle is fictionalized, though it does aim to convey World War II-era combat nonetheless).

There are pictures here. You need pictures in an article, apparently. There was an effort made with all the other movies to source relevant pictures (you know, not just showing any moment from Saving Private Ryan or Psycho, but screenshots that convey the scene in question and the relevant intensity). With The Silence of the Lambs, though, the notably tense sequence – or at least the most intense part of that sequence – is memorably very dark, and it’s harder to make things out when it’s not in motion.

It involves Clarice Starling finally confronting Buffalo Bill, and eventually thwarting him, but not until after he switches off all the lights and stalks her around his already creepy house/basement while wearing night-vision goggles. It’s perhaps the part when The Silence of the Lambs most feels like a horror movie, though any big scene with Hannibal Lecter is, quite naturally, also frightening (an honorable mention should go out to his big escape sequence).

You do know this one is coming at all points, and sure, there is even some relief when it happens, just because 127 Hours so perfectly captures – and makes you feel – the utterly nightmarish situation its central character is in throughout. He is hiking without sufficient company and safety equipment, and ends up trapped when a boulder falls on his arm, crushing it and then ultimately not being movable.

So, after several days, he makes the decision to amputate his arm with the very few pieces of equipment he has nearby, and it is what saves his life, sure, but it does also prove nauseating to watch because nothing is shied away from. It’s one of the most painful-to-watch scenes in relatively recent memory, yet it has to be, and there is an understandably great sense of relief alongside the absolute nausea you'll feel witnessing it all.

Jaws is another Steven Spielberg movie that, like Saving Private Ryan, technically begins near or on a beach, and also in a manner that proves surprising and famously intense. That first shark attack scene is monumental, as are a bunch of the sequences that follow throughout the first hour or so of Jaws, though the final act is where the movie obviously crescendos, and if you want to call it the “final showdown,” then that’s it. That’s what’s going here.

You’ve got a whole movie of things not really letting up, and it’s still all quite patiently done, not to mention in a manner that makes being truly invested in that climax inevitable. Jaws is – and forever will be – the best movie about three guys who have to go out to sea and kill a shark, and this extended climax is a big reason why.

Everything in Inglourious Basterds is pretty great, and it’s also a film that has a handful of standout scenes that all manage to feel incredibly tense, but usually in different ways, so there’s no real repetition here. It’s longer than a fair few Quentin Tarantino movies, albeit paced in a way that really makes it all fly by, and all the big scenes help immensely in that regard.

That does also make highlighting one over all the others tough, but here, the one that’s going to be singled out is the tavern sequence. All the other show-stopping scenes are perfect and 10/10-worthy, with this one, like, being an 11/10 scene. Movies don’t get much more nerve-wracking than this, and it’s a shame you can only ever see something for the first time just the once, since being able to experience a scene this perfectly surprising again would be wonderful.

There’s no shark here, but Whiplash does a similar thing to Jaws in terms of having suspense and unease pretty much right from the start, and then having those feelings become more intense as things progress. You're not given a lot of time to breathe, and the dynamic between a dedicated student and a tyrannical instructor gets impossibly uncomfortable, not to mention psychologically harrowing, continually reaching new heights… or lows?

Anyway, that does result in the climax being the biggest and most jaw-dropping sequence in the movie. Whiplash also twists the knife after it’s over, since the movie leaves you hanging in terms of the implications of the eventual moment of triumph, or tragedy. Or it could be a bit of both. It’s hard to know. You'll never know. So you're on the edge of your seat for the final 10 to 15 minutes of Whiplash, and then you continually feel queasy for the next 10 to 15 years after Whiplash came out, whenever you think about it and its ending. That is undoubtedly impressive stuff for a movie’s ending to do.

#3457. Your Android Can Get Hacked Without You Doing Anything at All

You probably know that clicking suspicious links online or opening attachments from strangers in an email or text is a recipe for hacking. It's a dangerous world out there online, so it's always important to be vigilant. However, the danger doesn't always involve something you do. There are ways to hack your devices without requiring any intervention on your part whatsoever—and one such example is likely plaguing your Android device right now.

As reported by The Hacker News, there is a critical Android security flaw that could enable remote code execution on your device. In other words, bad actors could use the flaw to run their own code on your phone, effectively taking over the device for their own gain. The flaw, identified as CVE-2026-58868, isn't universal, but it is widespread: It currently affects Android 14 through Android 17, the latest version of Google's OS. If your phone runs Android 12 or Android 13, it may be unaffected, as Google doesn't identify these versions in its security bulletin, but it doesn't explicitly rule them out, either.

There are two silver linings here, however. One, Google hasn't confirmed any active exploits for this security flaw. While that isn't a guarantee that bad actors have missed this exploit so far, it at least opens that possibility. As such, there may be time for users to patch their devices before hackers truly take advantage of the flaw. Second, Google does have a patch for the flaw. The patch may not be available to you right away, however, as it's up to both the manufacturer of your phone and your carrier to issue these updates. Still, a patch is, at the very least, on its way.

This flaw is perhaps the most important to fix, but it's not the only serious issue. In all, Google's latest bulletin highlights 216 vulnerabilities, and, of those, 23 are "critical." As The Hacker News explains, two other of those critical flaws could also allow remote code execution when exploited.

To see whether the patch is installed on your end, open the Settings app on your phone, tap "About phone" or "About tablet," then choose the Android version on-screen. Look for a date of "2026-11-01" or later. All security patches from Nov. 1 and on will fix this issue. If not, you'll ned to wait for the patch.

#3455. Anatomy Of A Fall Ending Explained: Was Daniel Lying?

At the end of Anatomy of a Fall, Sandra is acquitted, although the facts of the case still aren't entirely clear, making the true cause of Samuel's death ambiguous. The 2023 movie is a legal drama from French director Justine Triet, featuring performances from Sandra Hüller, Swann Arlaud, Samuel Theis, Milo Machado Graner, and more. Anatomy of a Fall received great reviews and enjoyed lots of awards success, winning the Palme d'Or at the Cannes Film Festival and picking up five Oscars 2024 nominations, winning for Best Original Screenplay.

After the mysterious death of her husband, Samuel (Samuel Theis), Sandra Voyter (Sandra Hüller) becomes the prime suspect. Sandra's best defense is to claim Samuel died by suicide, which even she tells her lawyer, Vincent (Swann Arlaud), is implausible at first. The only person who can back up her version of events is her blind son, Daniel (Milo Machado Graner). When an audio recording revealed in court proves she was also covering up evidence of domestic turmoil, Daniel appears to have doubts about her innocence but ultimately gives testimony that leads to her acquittal.

Initially, Daniel said he heard Sandra and Samuel having a casual conversation as he went past the shed to walk the dog, Snoop. He was positive he was standing next to the shed because of the texture of the tape Samuel put there for him to identify the location.

It's entirely possible recreating the moment jogged Daniel's memory, but it's also conspicuous that he changed his story to maintain a favorable outlook for Sandra at the end of Anatomy of a Fall.

When the investigators tried to recreate the scenario to determine how loud Sandra and Samuel had to be talking to match his story, Samuel suddenly changed his testimony to say he was inside the front door. It's entirely possible recreating the moment jogged Daniel's memory, but it's also conspicuous that he changed his story to maintain a favorable outlook for Sandra at the end of Anatomy of a Fall.

Daniel says his memories returned to him again at the last second, providing a new testimony about Snoop eating aspirin from Samuel's vomit to back up Sandra's claim of an alleged suicide attempt. Once again, Daniel's testimony is conveniently altered to favor Sandra's version of events, which supports a suicide theory Sandra didn't even initially agree with when strategizing with Vincent. Daniel's story is plausible, but his odd behavior, asking Sandra to leave the house, and having Snoop eat aspirin before changing his story invites skepticism, especially considering his story seemed to be the deciding factor.

The audio recording Samuel makes of his fight with Sandra is one of the most damning pieces of evidence against her, especially since she tried to cover up the fact that they fought at all, but its very existence calls other factors into question. As Sandra says, it's possible Samuel provoked the fight to get a recording. If true, the recording may have been intended for use as literary inspiration, but if he'd already begun contemplating suicide (as his alleged previous suicide attempt would indicate), then the recording may have been an attempt to implicate Sandra in his death.

If he was legitimately jealous and resentful of Sandra's success, particularly after she used one of his novel ideas in her own writing, the claims made in the recording tarnish her professionally, in addition to the hit her reputation would take from being indicted in the first place.

Considering he was aware of the recording and Sandra wasn't, his accusations against her, while containing legitimate frustrations, could also be performative, knowing the recording would be discovered and played in court after his death. If he was legitimately jealous and resentful of Sandra's success, particularly after she used one of his novel ideas in her own writing, the claims made in the recording tarnish her professionally, in addition to the hit her reputation would take from being indicted in the first place.

Granted, Sandra tells Vincent his depiction of Samuel's "final year" wasn't an accurate reflection, so she may not agree with that theory, although the existence of the recording makes it plausible.

The only flashbacks in the movie, Samuel's argument with Sandra and his conversation in the car with Daniel, are presented as possible versions of the story, through the audio recording and Daniel's recollection, rather than moments to be taken as fact.

After Sandra is acquitted, she goes to dinner with Vincent and says she feels weird because there's normally a reward for winning. While avoiding a conviction is certainly a form of reward for her, if she's innocent, then she's now left to process Samuel's suicide for the first time. Sandra initially disagreed with the idea that Samuel died by suicide and even disagreed with Vincent's depiction of "Samuel's final year" as presented in court.

She may never truly escape her guilt as Daniel will be a constant reminder.

For that to be the theory that exonerates her leaves Sandra to process complicated emotions associated with her husband's death for the first time or may even leave her wondering about some other cause. There is also the lingering awkwardness with Daniel. Despite the fact that his testimony saved her, they are both now aware that he at least considered for a time that his mother killed his father.

On the other hand, if Sandra truly did kill Samuel, she now has to live a lie for the rest of her life, including lying to Daniel. Additionally, if she was lying about Samuel's suicide to cover up her involvement, Daniel may have also been lying to back her up, in which case she knows Daniel is aware of her deception.

Unfortunately, there's no clear explanation for what truly happened to Samuel, and while Sandra may have certainty of her guilt or innocence, it may not be possible for anyone else, including Daniel, to ever truly trust her version of events. For example, the blood splatter and autopsy indicate he was likely struck with a weapon before he fell, but at the same time, it's improbable that Sandra was able to lift and push him over the edge in the way the prosecutor indicated. No single theory fully accounts for both the blood splatter and the body falling where it did.

The coroner determines that Samuel received a blow to the head before hitting the ground, but the autopsy proves inconclusive and offers no hard evidence. The prosecution brings in a blood spatter expert who testifies that Samuel's death must have come from an intentional blow to the head, delivered by another human, before his fall. He's clearly convinced of his interpretation and has video simulations to help prove it. A second expert says Samuel fell onto a shed, then bounced into the air, his body spinning, releasing blood in exactly the pattern discovered.

Looking closely at the shed after Samuel falls in the beginning of the movie, there appears to be a point of impact where his head could have hit, aligning with the defense's blood splatter theory, but it's still not enough to provide any decisive conclusion about the true nature of Samuel's death.

Daniel's testimony is equally shaky, especially considering his own conflict of interest. He knows his testimony could be the strongest factor in influencing his mother's verdict, but he doesn't know if he can fully trust his mom, which is why he seeks advice from Marge (Jehnny Beth), who unfortunately can't comment on the case to him.

Memory is fallible, so his multiple shifting testimonies are easy to explain, but the fact that his testimony always shifts in favor of Sandra and only in response to evidence that looks bad for her, makes it look like he's changing his story to protect her.

In his final testimony, Daniel recalls that while he and Samuel were driving Snoop to the veterinarian, his father spoke to him about the need to be prepared that those he loves will die. Samuel was specifically talking about Snoop's short lifespan, but Daniel concludes that it reflected his father's own suicidal thoughts. On the witness stand, he says that if his mother did this, he can't understand it, but if his father did it, he can. Knowing he can't be certain what happened, he admits it's easier to believe Samuel died by suicide than that Sandra was a murderer. Daniel's testimony works, and Sandra is acquitted.

As the audience, we know even more than the investigators and prosecution, making Sandra's position even more complicated. On one hand, she doubted the suicide theory from the start, but if she were guilty she should be more eager to support the strongest alibi. Looking closely at the shed after Samuel falls in the beginning of the movie, there appears to be a point of impact where his head could have hit, aligning with the defense's blood splatter theory, but it's still not enough to provide any decisive conclusion about the true nature of Samuel's death.

At the end of Anatomy of a Fall, there's still a lot of ambiguity around how Samuel died and how truthful Sandra and Daniel are. As Sandra tells Samuel's therapist:

"What you say is just a part of the whole situation. You know. I mean, sometimes a couple is kind of a chaos and everybody is lost."

Anatomy of a Fall ends not with Sandra alongside her son, but with their dog, Snoop. It's a moment that, aside from showcasing the unconditional love of a dog, highlights how alone Sandra still is. Her husband is dead, and while her son may or may not have lied to protect her, there's still a great distance between them. Having Snoop in there is an important reminder to Sandra there is still love for her, while simultaneously reflecting on her loss and grief.

Snoop was played by a border collie named Messi.

Justine Triet doesn't want to over-explain Anatomy of a Fall's ending, which is why the writer-director purposefully made things ambiguous. However, just like audiences, she has her own ideas and feelings about what the truth might actually be. In an interview with The Wrap, she explained that finding the "doubt" was the key to the ending, but when asked how she responds to questions of whether Sandra was guilty or not, she said:

Well, what can I say? It’s the same thing as in life. Who knows the real truth? To me, I think maybe that Sandra could be not guilty of murder but responsible for pushing him to commit suicide. Maybe? It’s a question of: What are we all responsible for in our lives? The film is opening so many other doors. And in a way, I think, well, she lied two times in the movie. So maybe we can cast doubt on her and say, “Hmm, is it possible she did do it?” But I don’t want to say that.

Sandra Hüller has described her own version of that uncertainty. She said that two days before filming started, she called Triet and thought, "What if she actually tricks me into something?" She had two days to decide what to do, and she realized it's really not so important whether Sandra is a murderer or not. As Hüller put it, it's really about what other people think of her.

While the Anatomy of a Fall ending leaves plenty of possibilities of Sandra being guilty, the real purpose behind the movie is the exploration of this marriage. Part of Sandra's frustration is having to defend aspects of her marriage from people who could not possibly know the truth as she does. From the prosecutors to Samuel's therapist to the spectators getting a glimpse inside her intimate world, they are deciding what her marriage was based on very little information.

Looking at the ending of the movie as if Sandra is innocent provides perhaps the most compelling arc. While her marriage to Samuel was not perfect, there were no issues that would drive her to murder him. Yet Anatomy of a Fall's courtroom scenes pick apart every aspect of their relationship, magnifying hard moments and blowing them out of proportion.

It's frustrating for Sandra that it's almost impossible to combat the assumptions that are made based on this "evidence". She cannot convince people that there is a difference between an argument between a couple and a conflict that leads to death. In that sense, Daniel is the only one who can save her. With no one else able to see what she sees, Daniel chooses to believe his mother in the Anatomy of a Fall ending, even if he might lie in his testimony. His testimony gives the court a believable suicide version of Samuel's death, but it doesn't prove what happened. Daniel chooses the version of his father's death that he can survive, and the movie never confirms that he invented his final testimony.

Anatomy of a Fall arrived to more-or-less universal praise when it premiered in 2023. Director Justin Triet's legal drama currently holds a 96% critical score and 90% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes. These high numbers represent both the quality of Anatomy of a Fall overall, and the strength of its ending, since movies based on complex legal mysteries are rarely (if ever) well received if the story is betrayed by a sub-par ending. The main praise for Anatomy of a Fall was in two areas - the performance of Sandra Hüller, and the emotional impact of the story. As far as the latter is concerned, the ending is incredibly important.

For many critics and audiences alike, the key strength of the ending of Anatomy of a Fall was the way it decompresses the immense tension building throughout the rest of the film, while also leaving things on an ambiguous note. It was incredibly risky for Justin Triet to end the story without fully clarifying if Sandra was guilty or not, but walking this narrative tightrope ultimately became the key strength of the final moments.

By refusing to elaborate on Sandra's guilt or innocence, the Anatomy of a Fall ending helped ensure the movie was an intimate psychological character study. Had a definitive answer been given, it would have shifted the tone entirely, especially during second or third viewings. By keeping the possibility that Sandra could be a victim of a terrible situation or the perpetrator of a murder, none of the thematic character-driven depth of Anatomy of a Fall is lost during the final moments.

Ultimately, the ending of Anatomy of a Fall was the perfect way to wrap up the story, ending the narrative on an ambiguous yet satisfying note that few dramas, modern or classic, can match. Yes, there were a few plausibility issues, such as with Daniel's testimony, and there are still some viewers out there who would have preferred the movie clarified if Sandra was guilty or innocent (depending on their interpretation). However, these camps are in the minority, and overall the end of Anatomy of a Fall was incredibly well received as a complex ending to an equally complex story.

While ambiguous endings can be a tricky thing to pull off, some movies, like Anatomy of a Fall, can leave lingering questions because the answer is not the point of the story. This is reminiscent of the ending of Inception, which leaves the audience with the iconic final shot of the top spinning, cutting to black before the audience knows for sure if Dom (Leonardo DiCaprio) is dreaming or awake. While the answer has been debated for years, the point is that Dom doesn't care anymore if this is real or not.

Anatomy of a Fall pulls off a similar ending. In fact, the movie is more effective with that fact left as a mystery. That is not to say audiences are meant to continue digging for clues, but rather they are being left with the same uncertainty the characters now have to live with.

Without having the answers as well, the audience is put in the same position as these characters in the final moments.

Anatomy of a Fall is not about the outcome of a murder trial, it is about these characters and what these accusations have done to their lives. If Sandra is guilty, she and Daniel have to live with knowing he lied to protect her. If she is innocent, she has to live with the knowledge that he might not believe she is innocent.

Without having the answers as well, the audience is put in the same position as these characters in the final moments. The ending of Anatomy of a Fall achieves a brilliant sensation of relief followed by the unnerving and sad reality of what comes next.

Anatomy of a Fall (2023) is a French courtroom drama about a writer accused of murdering her husband after he is found dead outside their isolated Alpine home. As the trial dissects their troubled marriage and forces their blind son to testify, the mystery becomes less about proving exactly what happened than about how imperfectly people can ever know one another. The film won the Palme d’Or at Cannes and the Academy Award for Best Original Screenplay.

#3454. 'Ocarina of Time' for Switch 2 Might Already Have a Weird Glitch

Thursday is a big day for Zelda fans. That's when the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time officially launches on Switch 2, marking the first major linear (i.e., non-open-world) 3D Zelda game since the 2016 Twilight Princess remake on Wii U. I, for one, have been waiting for this day for years. I loved the N64 original and the 3DS remake, so to have the chance to play a modern take on the definitive Zelda is so exciting—that is, if it actually runs as it should.

I stumbled upon this interesting post on X from Austin John Plays, a YouTuber with a host of Zelda coverage. According to Austin John Plays, Ocarina of Time already ships with a weird glitch that won't necessarily break your experience, but which may slow it down for a while, and perhaps even confuse players into thinking something is wrong with their game or their console.

As his post explains, if you're playing the physical copy of Ocarina of Time, and it's the first game you've ever played on your Switch 2—maybe you got one of those fancy new Zelda anniversary consoles and want to break it in properly?—you may run into glaring performance issues: The game may freeze, your controller may stop working, and the FPS may drop to single digits.

Luckily, Austin John Plays says the fix is easy: just wait. Eventually, your game will boot back to the title screen. When it does, don't try to play right away. Instead, close the game, restart your Switch 2, then try relaunching Ocarina of Time. Austin John Plays advises you may need to repeat this process two or three times, but after that, you shouldn't continue to run into issues. I wouldn't be surprised if Nintendo releases a patch right away for this glitch if it turns out to be as widespread as this post implies.

However, seeing as the game doesn't come out until tomorrow, there's something you can do to prevent it. Austin John Plays thinks the bug only impacts Switch 2 consoles that haven't run other games before. If you've had your console a while, you're likely set. But if you just bought the 40th anniversary Zelda edition of the Switch 2, you might not have had a chance to run a game on it yet. As such, download a game from the e-shop—even a free demo—just to get the system running. Hopefully, that will be enough to circumvent the glitch, and prevent issues when Ocarina of Time launches tomorrow.

This week’s selection of new movies across the best streaming services is set, and there’s a little something for everybody, from seasonal flicks to twisting thrillers. Netflix, HBO Max, Paramount+ and Apple TV will have new offerings, alongside arrivals on premium streaming. With so many movies to consider, I’m picking the highlights of this week’s fresh films.

Below, you’ll find full details on my top picks this week, followed by a rundown of all the new movies heading to streaming this week. And be sure to check out our guide to the top new TV shows this week.

Not since 2018’s “A Star is Born” have I heard as much sobbing in a movie theater as I did when watching “Heart of the Beast” in a cinema back in September. This survival thriller is a real tearjerker. But it’s also an exhilarating ride that really focuses on the survival aspect of its genre. And while Brad Pitt's name is biggest on the poster, the real scene-stealer is Odin, a German Shepherd that you will absolutely fall in love with. So, “Heart of the Beast” is indeed very intense, but it's also very tender.

Pitt stars as James Belmont, a former military man, traveling through the Alaskan wilderness with his loyal companion, a former combat dog. After Belmont suffers a heart attack while flying his plane, the pair crash into the unforgiving landscape and face a grueling trek to return to civilization. Battling the harsh elements and naive animal predators, the conditions would likely kill any other man and dog, but Belmont and Odin are made of strong stuff.

Watch on Prime Video (buy/rent) starting November 10

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

In this Christmas movie with a faith-based twist, a struggling pastor (Tank) inherits his family’s church in a broken New York neighborhood. With the threat of foreclosure and personal temptations around every corner, this lapsed man of faith needs the local community to get by, and turns out they might just need him as well. With overflowing holiday spirit and some very soulful singing, “The Gospel of Christmas” shows the power of community, and that even the most wayward soul can be found.

Director Sian Heder, the filmmaker behind the Best Picture-winning “CODA,” follows up with a biographical drama adapted from the memoir of Judith Heumann, an inspirational disability rights activist. A little less saccharine than Heder’s previous movie, a good thing in my book, “Being Heumann” holds a strong 86% rating on Rotten Tomatoes, with praise dished out for the screenplay, cast, and most importantly for the movie’s focus on vital disability activism and representation.

After being ignored by bureaucrats, including Joseph A. Califano Jr., the United States Secretary of Health, Education and Welfare (Mark Ruffalo), in 1977, Judy Heumann (Ruth Madeley) and a scrappy group of outsiders stage the longest occupation of a federal building in American history, demanding that their voices be heard. “Being Heumann” assembles the largest cast of disabled actors in movie history, a key achievement, with disability representation one of the movie’s foundational pillars. This Apple original is a stirring biopic that chronicles how Judy and her allies led a revolution that changed the lives of millions.

“The End of Oak Street” feels like an ‘80s movie that got left on a shelf somewhere and then released in 2026. It’s got huge Amblin energy! Directed by David Robert Mitchell, it tips its cap and then some to the Steven Spielberg classics that dominated the decade. Its throwback charms are especially appropriate as its narrative is hooked on an ordinary street block being thrust back in time. Oh, and it stars Anne Hathaway and Ewan McGregor, two very capable leads; the former, in particular, is great as a strong-willed mother fighting to protect her kids.

Set in the 1980s (of course), it sees an unexplained cosmic event transport a Michigan suburb to prehistoric times, when fearsome dinosaurs roamed the land. Caught up in the chaos are the Platt family, led by a husband and wife (McGregor and Hathaway), who are also dealing with marital issues. To survive in this hostile environment, the family needs to pull together and try to avoid the dinosaurs stalking their once welcoming suburban streets.

Netflix’s original movie slate for November isn’t just holiday movies. Case in point, “Heartland.” This new mystery thriller combines the ever-popular thriller genre with country music, which is having a resurgence. On paper, it looks like a very appealing combination; throw in an Oscar winner to anchor the movie, and “Heartland” could be a candidate for the Netflix No. 1 spot this week. Of all my picks this week, “Heartland” is definitely the most intriguing.

Jessica Chastain plays Misty Jones, a former country music star now living in seclusion. When her niece (played by IRL country star Carter Faith) goes missing, Misty returns to Nashville to investigate. This forces her to grapple with her own past and also delve into Music City’s underbelly. Turns out the country music capital is a whole lot less glamorous behind the curtains. Fingers crossed this Netflix original doesn’t disappoint.

Romance gets a bad rep for being the guilty pleasure of TV. It's considered as the genre people binge in secret and never put on their "best shows" lists. That reputation is a little unfair, though. A truly great love story is one of the hardest things to pull off on screen. It takes chemistry that can't be faked, and a slow build that makes the audience desperate for two people to finally get it right. When a romance gets all of that right, it becomes something viewers return to again and again, long after they know exactly how it ends.

The shows on this list are the ones that understand romance is really about vulnerability rather than the boring, one-dimensional stereotypes people usually associate with the genre. They give viewers messy, complicated people who have to get out of their own way before they can fall in love. This is a list of romance shows that are 10/10 masterpieces because they do justice to the very act of falling in love.

One Day is a right person, wrong time story that is both heartwarming and unbearable to watch, and that is the mark of a true romance. The series, based on David Nicholls' bestselling novel, begins on July 15, 1988, when Emma Morley (Ambika Mod) and Dexter Mayhew (Leo Woodall) spend one night together after graduating from university in Edinburgh. Every episode then drops in on them on that same date, year after year. The two characters couldn't be any different. Emma is a sharp, working-class aspiring writer who never quite believes she’s good enough, while Dexter is a golden boy who survives on pure charm until his life starts to unravel.

The genius of the show is in its format. Since the audience only sees one day a year, entire relationships and careers happen off-screen, and every episode feels like catching up with an old friend who has changed as life has gone on. Both characters experience genuine growth over the years, and it's impossible not to root for their connection. Just be warned that the final episodes take a turn that hits like a gut punch, and the show ends with a twist that is guaranteed to stay with viewers for days. One Day is the perfect love story about missed chances, and is guaranteed to wreck anyone who makes it to the end.

Nobody expected a Canadian hockey romance to take over the internet, but Heated Rivalry did exactly that within a few weeks. The series, based on Rachel Reid's Game Changers novels and created by Letterkenny's Jacob Tierney, follows two of professional hockey’s biggest young stars. Shane Hollander (Hudson Williams) is a disciplined, focused Canadian, while Ilya Rozanov (Connor Storrie) is a cocky Russian who loves getting under his skin. The two have been rivals since their rookie days in 2008, and on the ice, they can't stand each other. Off the ice, though, they get secretly caught up in an affair that could end both of their careers if anyone found out.

Beneath all the steam, Heated Rivalry is really about two men who have been taught their entire lives that wanting each other could cost them everything. The six-episode season stretches across a decade, so the audience gets to watch a secret fling slowly turn into something neither of them is ready to name. The two are a perfect mismatch, and every stolen moment they get feels charged because things can fall apart at any time. On top of that, the show delivers a second great romance through hockey captain Scott Hunter (François Arnaud) and his boyfriend, Kip (Robbie G.K.), whose story nearly steals the spotlight. Heated Rivalry turned a niche book series into a global obsession, and it has more than earned its place among the great modern love stories.

There are slow burns, and then there's a love story that literally spans two centuries. Outlander, based on Diana Gabaldon's novels, follows World War II nurse Claire Randall (Caitríona Balfe), on her second honeymoon in Scotland who is suddenly thrown back to 1743 after touching an ancient standing stone. Suddenly, Claire finds herself in the middle of a brewing Jacobite rebellion. To protect herself, she is forced to marry Jamie Fraser (Sam Heughan), a young Highland warrior, even though she already has a husband waiting for her in the future.

Unlike most romances, Outlander gets its central couple married early and then asks what happens after they say "I do." Claire and Jamie face wars and impossible choices together, and their love grows deeper with every hardship instead of fading. It's hard not to melt every time Jamie calls her "Sassenach," the nickname that started as a jab and turned into a declaration of love. Claire is also a refreshingly modern heroine, a woman who refuses to stay quiet in a century that expects her to. After eight seasons, Outlander remains the gold standard for epic, sweeping romance on TV.

Bridgerton is Shonda Rhimes' version of Regency, and provides a refreshing take on London high society's ruthless marriage market. The series, based on Julia Quinn's novel series, follows the Bridgerton siblings and their individual love stories. Bridgerton Season 1 centers on Daphne Bridgerton (Phoebe Dynevor), who strikes a deal with the brooding Duke of Hastings (Regé-Jean Page) to fake a courtship, only for real feelings to get in the way. The following seasons follow a new Bridgerton sibling and cover a new romance trope with every season, from enemies-to-lovers to friends-to-lovers, and even a Cinderella-style love story. Of course, overseeing all this drama is the anonymous gossip columnist Lady Whistledown, voiced by Julie Andrews, whose scandal sheet keeps the entire ton on edge.

Bridgerton stands out from other period dramas because of how unapologetically modern it feels. The show reimagines Regency London with a diverse cast and swaps classical music for string-quartet covers of songs by artists including Ariana Grande and Taylor Swift to help the audience relate to the era. Not to mention the series tells its love stories from the women's point of view, which makes the fight for independence just as important as the search for a husband. Bridgerton took the stuffy period romance formula and turned it into a feel-good show that has made period romance cool for a whole new generation.

With The Life of a Showgirl getting an encore edition this week, the era argument is live all over again. Here is yours, what it says about you, and the case for it being the best one she has made.

You are the reinvention. 1989 is the record where she walked away from the thing that made her famous and rebuilt everything from scratch, and it worked so completely that people forgot there had ever been a risk.

You are the one who stopped explaining. Reputation arrived after a year of being written off, with almost no interviews and no attempt to be liked, and it turned out that saying nothing was the loudest available option.

You are the quiet one who was paying attention the whole time. Folklore appeared with less than a day of warning, made entirely indoors, and swapped autobiography for invented characters who somehow felt more personal than the real ones.

You feel everything at maximum volume and you have never apologised for it. Red is the messiest album she has made and the one most people love best, because it is the sound of somebody refusing to be reasonable about how much something hurt.

Heartstopper is proof that a love story doesn't need heartbreak or emotional trauma to make viewers cry. The series, based on Alice Oseman's graphic novels, follows Charlie Spring (Joe Locke), a shy, openly gay student at an all-boys British school. When he's seated next to rugby team star Nick Nelson (Kit Connor), Charlie develops a massive crush, which he knows will never go anywhere. As the two become close friends, though, Nick begins to realize that his feelings for Charlie run much deeper than he expected.

Heartstopper is a show about the small moments. Every awkward "hi" between Charlie and Nick perfectly captures the feeling of a young love and the hand-drawn visual elements in the show make the audience feel like Oseman's novels have come to life. The show is refreshingly kind to its characters, but doesn't shy away from harder topics like bullying and mental health. One of its most moving scenes comes when Nick comes out to his mother, played by Olivia Colman, and it's impossible to get through that without tearing up. Heartstopper is the comforting, joyful queer love story so many viewers wish they had growing up, and it deserves all the appreciation it gets for that.

A South Korean heiress falling for a North Korean soldier sounds like the setup for a joke, but Crash Landing on You makes it work without feeling gimmicky. Yoon Se-ri (Son Ye-jin) is a wealthy, fiercely independent businesswoman who gets swept off course during a paragliding accident and crash-lands on the wrong side of the border. Stern but honorable army officer, Captain Ri Jeong-hyeok (Hyun Bin), finds Se-ri and decides to hide her in his village until she figures out a way home. From there, the story works both as a sweeping romance and a tense thriller, while also being one of the funniest K-dramas out there. Crash Landing on You has something for everyone.

Even viewers who have never watched a K-drama will find Se-ri and Jeong-hyeok's dynamic endearing because of how well-written it is. The two have lived completely different lives, but they slowly realize they understand each other better than anyone else ever has. The border itself is what gives the romance its ache, since the two come from countries that can never truly let them be together. Every loving moment they share feels borrowed, and the audience spends the whole series dreading the day all this ends. Crash Landing on You is the perfect gateway into K-dramas, and it's easily one of the most beloved romances of the decade.

In Pride and Prejudice, Mary Bennet is mostly remembered for embarrassing herself at the piano while the rest of the room cringes. The Other Bennet Sister, based on Janice Hadlow's novel, finally gives her a story of her own. Mary (Ella Bruccoleri) is the bookish, awkward middle child who has spent her life being compared to her prettier and livelier sisters. When she gets the chance to start fresh in London with her kind aunt and uncle, the Gardiners (Indira Varma and Richard Coyle), Mary finally gets to discover who she is outside of her family's shadow. In London, she finds herself caught between two very different suitors, the reserved Mr. Hayward (Dónal Finn) and the charming Mr. Ryder (Laurie Davidson). Now, for a woman who has never been anyone's first choice, being noticed is thrilling and terrifying at once.

The love triangle isn't really about which man wins her over, though. It's about Mary learning what she actually wants, rather than settling for whoever will have her. The series turns one of Austen's punchlines into a heroine worth rooting for, and that's exactly why it's so satisfying. Mary is prickly and earnest, and she's funnier than anyone ever gave her credit for. Her love story doesn't arrive in one sweeping moment. Instead, it grows alongside her confidence, which makes every step toward happiness feel truly earned. Anyone who has ever felt like the overlooked one in their family will see a little of themselves in her. The Other Bennet Sister is a sweet, clever twist on Austen, and it's the kind of underdog romance that's impossible not to love.

#3451. 10 Shows Like 'Phony' You Should Watch Next

Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

What if you knew your mom wasn't really your mom, but no one believed you? That's the improbable but entertaining premise of Hulu's Phony, which stars Sam Nivola as a teenager who wakes up from a car accident and quickly comes to believe that his mother (Friday Night Lights' Connie Britton) is an imposter. Of course, no one believes him. I'm not sure I believe him, but it'll be pretty boring if it turns out that he just had a really bad concussion the whole time.

It's a coming-of-age drama and a surreal mystery with hints of comedy, and though it borrows elements from other shows, it stands apart for the skill with which it blends everything together. While you wait to see how the story plays out, here are 10 more twisted mysteries to stream now.

A twisty-turny (and well-reviewed) bit of fake identity folderol, Apple Cider Vinegar stars Kaitlyn Dever as Belle Gibson, a real-life Australian cancer survivor (except not really!) With a cheeky sense of humor and a willingness to distort reality, the show follows the wellness influencer as she fakes multiple cancer diagnoses in order to better market her alternative, MAHA-esque app and remedies to the unwitting. As her livelihood comes under threat, her lies grow more elaborate. Stream Apple Cider Vinegar on Netflix.

Alia Shawkat stars here as Dory Sief, an aimless millennial who decides, after seeing a missing-person poster for a college acquaintance, that she's going to make it her purpose to track her down—with the extremely begrudging support of her friends. But neither Chantal nor her disappearance are anything like what Dory expects. The show shifts focus from season to season. Initially a darkly comic take on a Nancy Drew-style mystery, it later finds the gang desperate to cover up a mostly unintentional murder, and getting in deeper each season. It's a funny, smart, and weird and shares talent with Phony in the form of writer/producer Anthony King, who serves as co-showrunner on the new series. Stream Search Party on Netflix.

This one's largely about adults, so it skips the coming-of-age angle central to Phony, but it has a quirky mystery, gaslighting, and a protagonist whose sanity is questioned by just about everyone all the same. This fun and very loose adaptation of the 1989 Tom Hanks film finds Keke Palmer's Samira and Jack Whitehall's Rob moving back to his impossibly safe and tidy hometown. Their house happens to be across the street from a dilapidated Victorian eyesore that may or may not have been the location of a murder a couple of decades before—a murder of a girl who made the mistake of trying to get away. As Samira adjusts to new motherhood and life on the cul-de-sac, she learns that even the nicest of her neighbors have secrets, and comes to suspect that her husband knows more about the missing girl than he's letting on. Stream The 'Burbs on Peacock.

When pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate, working her way into the missing girl's social circle, and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

Based on a Harlan Coben novel, Fool Me Once is a bit more of a political thriller than a coming-of-age thing, but we're still in "what the hell is up with my family?" territory: Michelle Keegan plays Maya Stern, a former special ops pilot dealing with the murder of her husband, whom she then impossibly catches playing with their daughter on a nanny cam. The resulting mystery ties into the earlier death of her sister and leads to a web of conspiracy involving her husband's family and a shady pharmaceutical company. Stream Fool Me Once on Netflix.

A vibe match more than anything else, this dark and twisty mystery with a slightly surreal sense of humor also features a single mom who is definitely not what she appears to be. Kim Mo-mi (Lee Han-byeol, initially), the Mask Girl of the title, is a uniquely complicated woman; she always wanted to be a K-Pop idol, but it was always made clear to her that she's not nearly pretty enough for that kind of stardom. So, in order to fill that void, she's got a side hustle. On top of her boring office job, she puts on a blonde wig and a mask to perform as a camgirl for anonymous men. It's a means to express herself creatively and sexually with a level of control—until a mistake causes her to lose that control, a co-worker discovers her secret life, and desperation leads to murder. The show shifts perspectives continually, feeling most like Phony when it focuses on Mo-mi's daughter. Stream Mask Girl on Netflix.

Flipping things around a bit, albeit in a similar "am I just being paranoid?" vein, The Girlfriend deals with a mom who may or may not be freaking out for no reason. Starring Robin Wright as Laura Sanderson, a wealthy art gallery owner in London whose son (Laurie Davidson) brings home a new, working-class girlfriend, Cherry Laine (Olivia Cooke)—immediately strikes Laura as not-our-kind. But is there more to it? Can someone with the name "Cherry Laine" truly be trusted? There's definitely something off, and we're kept guessing as to whether or not this is the story of a dangerous con artist or an overbearing mom—or maybe a little of each. Stream The Girlfriend on Prime Video.

Coming from Irish playwright and Derry Girls creator Lisa McGee, this show eschews the relatively subtle dark comedy of Phony for something much more gloriously surreal. Three high school friends from Belfast reunite after learning that an estranged bestie has died unexpectedly—except that maybe she didn't; a mixed blessing given that they all have secrets that they were hoping would be buried with the maybe departed. Now they're off to investigate the mystery of the murder(?), which turns into a hunt for the friend that they only thought they knew, while inadvertently revealing plenty of secrets of their own. The tone is all over the place in a way that somehow works, with flashes of sincerity balancing out the comedy. Stream How to Get to Heaven From Belfast on Netflix.

Shin Hye-sun offers up a phenomenal performance as Sarah Kim (well: sort of), a wealthy businesswoman who is discovered, at the series' opening, under a sewer grate. The police detective charged to investigate quickly finds inconsistencies in the woman's identity, and after interviewing Sarah's friend and business associate, comes to feel that neither woman is exactly (or anything, like she seems. Though it takes itself more seriously than Phony, it's still an addictively twisty mystery built around a constructed identity. Stream The Art of Sarah on Netflix.

There's a lot going on in this steamy, telenovela-esque drama. Camila Román (Carolina Miranda) finally meets Fernando Castell (Rodolfo Salas), a Tinder match, in Las Vegas, and things get very hot very quickly—he's everything he seemed to be and then some. If anything, she's the sketchy one: a dancer, not a nurse as she said, and with a possessive ex following her around. Still, it's all going great until she decides to surprise Fernando after he flies back to Colombia (which: never do that), and gets a totally different dude when she asks for him at his work. And that's just the beginning! Stream Fake Profile on Netflix.

Why installing Grand Theft Auto 6 isn’t as simple as hitting download

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

After years of waiting, GTA 6 is finally within reach. But with preloads opening and the game demanding up to 212 GB of storage, launch day is already exposing hardware bottlenecks for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S owners.

Since Rockstar has skipped physical game discs entirely, shipping boxed editions as digital download codes, every single player will be pulling this colossal install through a network connection.

To ensure you aren't stranded staring at error codes, download pauses, or an overheated machine, here are the five essential checks to run on your console right now.

A 212 GB install means most players will need to make some tough sacrifices. Before opening your wallet, start with a thorough clear-out: head into your console’s storage manager to purge games you haven't touched in months, lingering DLC add-ons, and video captures quietly eating up dozens of gigabytes.

If you already own an external USB drive, you can temporarily offload old titles there as a "cold storage" archive, but current-gen performance demands mean you cannot play GTA 6 directly from an external USB port.

If deleting your backlog still doesn't free up enough space, upgrading your high-speed storage is your only remaining option:

Xbox Series X|S: Slot an official storage card like the WD Expansion directly into the port on the back.

PlayStation 5: Install an approved internal M.2 NVMe SSD into the expansion bay beneath the faceplates.

Preload timing varies significantly between platforms, with release windows shaped by whether your console operates on a unified global rollout or a regional schedule:

Xbox Series X|S: Preloading unlocks simultaneously worldwide, going live first in the US on Monday, November 9 at 7 p.m. ET / 4 p.m. PT (which corresponds to midnight GMT on Tuesday, November 10 for UK players).

PlayStation 5: Downloads roll out on a strict regional basis, unlocking at midnight local time on Tuesday, November 10 across each player's respective time zone globally.

If you opted for a physical boxed edition, keep in mind that these packages rely entirely on an enclosed digital voucher rather than a physical disc. These boxed versions will not arrive on store shelves until Thursday, November 12.

While players with digital pre-orders get a two-day head start over physical buyers to clear that massive 212 GB download, physical buyers will still have a full week to download the files before servers officially open on launch day.

Nothing kills download momentum like an unexpected system lockout. If an essential operating system update is pending, your console will pause your queue and cut off background network services until it is installed.

Power up your console manually ahead of launch day, check for any pending firmware updates, and install them so your machine is clear to download uninterrupted:

Xbox Series X|S: Press the Xbox button on your controller to open the guide, then navigate to Profile & system, Settings, System, and Updates. If your console is fully up to date, you won't see an available update.

PlayStation 5: Head to Settings, System, System Software, System Software Update and Settings, and run any pending updates.

Both consoles can quietly pull down the entire 212 GB package overnight, but only if your standby settings actually allow it:

Xbox Series X|S: Check Settings, General, and Power options. While the default "Shutdown (energy saving)" mode allows basic auto-updates, switching your power mode to Sleep ensures an uninterrupted network connection so queued preloads won't stall overnight.

PlayStation 5: Head to Settings, System, Power Saving, and Features Available in Rest Mode. Ensure Stay Connected to the Internet and Enable Turning On PS5 from Network are toggled on, then check under Settings, Saved Data and Game/App Settings, and Automatic Updates to confirm auto-downloads are active. You can switch back to energy-saving mode once the install finishes.

GTA 6 will push the PS5 and Xbox Series X processors harder than almost any title this generation. If your console has accumulated a carpet of dust inside its vents over the past few years, extended play sessions will quickly trigger thermal throttling or abrupt emergency shutdowns.

Pop off your faceplates and vacuum the dedicated dust catchers on the PS5, or use a soft brush and compressed air around the Xbox vent grills.

And, as is standard practice, ensure your console sits in an open space with at least 4 to 6 inches of clearance on all sides, free from enclosed entertainment cabinets, deep carpets, or tight wall corners.

#3448. Ole Miss Racist Video: Student Apologizes, Claims She Didn't Know Who Lived There

One of the University of Mississippi students caught in the shocking video making monkey noises at the door of several Black students is apologizing profusely ... and insisting it was an honest mistake

Alaina Kunes -- an 18-year-old freshman at Ole Miss -- released a statement on Tuesday ... starting by apologizing to both the women who she offended and the university community.

She says, "Before the incident on November 6, I never met the women involved and was unaware of their race, however, I recognize my actions were insensitive, inappropriate, and deeply harmful."

Alaina insists she would never intentionally make noises or gestures like she did in the video toward a person of color ... and she says she's personally apologized to them for her actions.

She notes she can never understand the pain she's caused them ... and she says the women she's hurt "deserve to feel seen and understood" -- while adding it's not a reflection of who she's trying to become.

As we reported ... video of the incident went viral -- showing two women making the noises and gestures while a third walked behind the other two and simply glanced at the door.

Our sources say this was supposed to be harmless, silly fun ... claiming the girls were making animal noises at several different doors as they walked by.

The American Civil Liberties Union became involved after the incident ... noting it was looking into several complaints.

#3447. Firefox's New 'Mini Window' Feature Is a Game Changer for Productivity

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

For many of us, web browsing involves juggling dozens of tabs at once, and it's easy for important pages to get lost in the chaos. Now, Firefox has introduced something I think could help us multi-taskers: a "Mini Window." As highlighted by ZDNET's Jack Wallen, this new Firefox feature works like picture-in-picture overlays for videos—only here, that PiP displays a website.

"[Mini Window] lets you move a tab, or a selected section of a page, into a compact window that stays on top of your other windows while you browse," runs Mozilla's official blurb. "It's useful when you're multitasking and need to keep a few sources of information in view at once: Reference docs, a chat, a video call, a form you're filling out." As such, Mini Window doesn't necessarily replace running tabs side-by-side; rather, you can prioritize one tab in a full-size window, while keeping another page in view at all times.

This is a feature that's still in its early stages, and right now you can only get it in the "Nightly" version of Firefox, a very early beta version of the browser. Mozilla says it will push the feature to the full version of the browser later this month.

If you want to try this out as soon as possible, first install Firefox Nightly on your Mac or PC. Once up and running, you can launch Mini Window by right-clicking on a tab header and choosing Move Tab > Move to Mini Window. The tab shrinks and drops down to the lower right corner by default, staying on top of all other windows (not just Firefox). You can then scroll through the page and follow links as normal in the Mini Window—any links set to open in a new tab (manually or automatically) will launch in the main Firefox view, not the window overlay.

By dragging the title bar around, you can put your Mini Window anywhere you want on screen, and you can change its size by dragging the edges of the window too—so it doesn't necessarily have to be all that "mini." Firefox hides all buttons by default—including forward, backward, and refresh buttons, together with the address bar and buttons for closing the window or putting it back as a normal tab—though they appear when you hover over the Mini Window.

I'm finding the feature most useful when writing up articles where I need to refer to something else already on the web (so almost all of them), but there are a host of ways this can be used. It's particularly handy on a small laptop, where you don't necessarily have the screen space to put two tabs side by side, or when running a lower-priority window (like checking a social media site while reading an important document). No doubt, Firefox will continue to refine and improve the feature as it makes its way to the stable version of the browser, and it feels like something other browsers (looking at you, Google Chrome) might adopt as well in the near future. Eventually, using Mini Windows might become as common as opening up a long row of tabs.

#3446. Steven Spielberg’s 10-Part Sci-Fi Thriller Is Perfect for ‘Person of Interest’ Fans

15 years ago, CBS delivered one of its best procedurals with Person of Interest. The series, which focuses on a mysterious "Machine" and a former Special Forces operative tasked by the Machine's creator to protect the people it identifies, perfectly blends a high concept sci-fi pitch with the standard procedural formula. Like Lost before it, Person of Interest saw a wake of similar shows premiering after its debut, most notably Almost Human. One series boasts the pedigree of being a direct sequel to one of the best sci-fi movies of the 21st century.

That series is Minority Report, which picks up in the aftermath of Steven Spielberg's sci-fi thriller. The Minority Report series follows Dash (Stark Sands), a former precognitive whose visions were used by the "Precrime" police department to stop crimes before they happen. Haunted by visions of murders yet to happen, Dash contacts Detective Lara Vega (Meagan Good) to help stop those crimes before they happen. Though it only lasted a single season, Minority Report had similar vibes to Person of Interest, including deep questions about the nature of justice.

Part of the draw of Minority Report is the dynamic between Dash and Vega, especially as she gets used to the fact that he can see the future and transitions into a normal life while still using his abilities to help others. The episode "The Present" is perhaps the strongest example of this dynamic at work, as Dash gets a flash of Vega's death and works to solve it while she deals with the unresolved matter of her father's death. Another element that makes Minority Report stand out is its approach to the future, especially since the series takes place 11 years after the movie. Spielberg was ahead of the curve by asking scientists what technology would look like in the 2050's, and showrunner Max Borenstein said he took a similar approach when envisioning his take on Minority Report.

"One of the refreshing things about the film is that it didn't posit a single catastrophic event that led to the future. It said, "50 years from now, what is the world going to look like?" And the answer was that the world is going to be good and bad in equal measure to today. We have horrible thing that happen in our world, so I don't think we need to conjure up an apocalypse on our show to have real stakes."

Minority Report would also continue to incorporate elements from the movie, including Dash's siblings Arthur (Nick Zano) and Agatha (Laura Reagan). Both of them have wildly different visions; while Arthur gains knowledge of people who are about to be murdered, Agatha ends up psychically stepping in their shoes, which is just as horrifying as it sounds. The duo ends up helping Dash and Vega, but they have to be careful, as mysterious forces are hunting all three precogs to use their abilities. If Person of Interest is a story about the dangers of unchecked technology, then Minority Report asks what the law will do to keep people safe.

Despite being based on one of Steven Spielberg's most iconic movies, and even boasting Spielberg as an executive producer, Minority Report only lasted a single season. The deck was stacked against it from the start, as Fox cut the first season's episode order from thirteen episodes to ten and had it airing in the same time slot as NBC's The Voice, which was at the height of its popularity. Bad reviews didn't help, either, as many critics felt that Minority Report lacked the spark of the movie that inspired it.

The cast and crew of Minority Report has managed to find success with other sci-fi projects. Max Borenstein helped kick off the MonsterVerse movies, Nick Zano would become an integral part of Legends of Tomorrow, and Li Jun Li would go on to headline buzzy projects like Sinners and Spider-Noir. Still, for a series that was about predicting the future, Minority Report never saw its own end coming.

#3445. 31 Years Later, The Line That Changed The X-Files Is Still A Work Of Genius

Faith Roswell is a Senior Writer on Screen Rant's Classic TV team. Since earning her degree in Creative Writing over a decade ago, Faith has written articles on film and TV from a variety of different angles. Faith now combines her knowledge of psychology with her love of monster movies to give more insight into what makes the best ones.  You may have read her Screen Rant lists and features covering horror, sci-fi, and fantasy, or read her Amazon Top 10 book, "Movie Monsters of the Deep." Faith has had an extensive career as a writer, appearing on BBC live radio, researching true crime for Rotten Mango podcast, and writing for publications including Mental Floss, Atlas Obscura, and The Daily Jaws before beginning here at Screen Rant.

The X-Files' impact on both the sci-fi genre and culture is arguably second only to that of Star Trek. Through Dana Scully, "The Scully Effect" encouraged more women to pursue careers in the sciences, while the iconic 90s sci-fi series popularized the monster-of-the-week format, which inspired later TV shows like Warehouse 13 and Supernatural. The X-Files' classic episodes were never predictable, but viewers knew to expect a lineup of monsters, mutants, out-of-control computers, and other paranormal phenomena with every season, until one season 3 episode expanded The X-Files' scope with two words.

The fourth episode of The X-Files' season 3 sees Mulder and Scully investigating a string of gory murders targeting psychics, when they come across the tormented Clyde Bruckman, who claims that he can see how everyone he ever meets will die. The premise initially sounded fairly standard for The X-Files, but the episode, "Clyde Bruckman's Final Repose," contained a shocking twist. After Scully spends the episode trying to debunk Clyde's psychic powers, curiosity gets the better of her, and she asks him how she will die. Clyde responds, "you don't."

The line turned the series into an existential and spiritual mystery that had viewers discussing its implications for years afterward, even after The X-Files continued with its monster-of-the-week format for some time afterward. This moment, and the standout acting and directing kept "Clyde Bruckman's Final Repose" among the best X-Files episodes of all time, and the line's eventual payoff completed a four-year masterclass in suspense.

According to IMDb, "Clyde Bruckman's Final Repose" is The X-Files' top-rated episode, earning a 9.2/10 mark, and it attracted an audience of 15.38 million viewers. A few episodes of the show have not aged well, but "Clyde Bruckman's Final Repose" is still among the X-Files episodes that are considered masterpieces today. Written by Darin Morgan and directed by David Nutter, who would later go on to win an Emmy Award for Game of Thrones, the episode is extremely dark, verging into film noir territory, and many of the references are hidden tributes to cinema's silent film era.

The genius of the episode is not just in the plot, but the way Mulder and Scully are developed further as characters in ways that are not easy to achieve within a monster-of-the-week format. While remaining the show's skeptic, Scully has previously been sensitive to influence by psychics, with "Beyond the Sea" flipping her and Mulder's roles in the show. Now, she remains unconvinced by the psychic aspect but sees Clyde as a tragic and human figure, which allows her to set aside the cold and scientific demeanor she sometimes puts on, while Mulder treats him as a case study.

"Clyde Bruckman's Final Repose" won The X-Files two Emmy Awards. Darin Morgan won Outstanding Writing in a Drama Series, while Peter Boyle (Clyde) won Outstanding Guest Actor in a Drama Series.

The episode is full of tiny unpredictable scenes and surprises for viewers, introducing a dark comedy moment when Clyde heavily implies that Mulder will die during a sexual mishap, but it was Clyde's line to Scully that reportedly sent fans into a frenzy, with the "Immortal Dana Scully" theory being the inevitable result. It is a testament to the quality of the episode that it is remembered for so many factors, from the acting to the heartbreaking ending, despite delivering the line that changed The X-Files, even though this line was later revealed to be a misunderstanding.

Four years after Clyde Bruckman appeared to confirm Scully's immortality, the season 6 episode "Tithonus" reinforced this by having her survive against impossible odds. While investigating Alfred Fellig, a seemingly-immortal photographer on a mission to photograph Death, Scully is shot, yet Fellig takes her place. By this time, The X-Files had already begun making references to events in earlier seasons, tying its mythology together as the show moved away from the monster-of-the-week approach, and expanding its universe. However, this reference may not have been made had it not been for Clyde's line originally being misinterpreted.

Found an error? Send it info@screenrant.com so it can be corrected.

Chris Carter's Reddit AMA thread sees a fan ask him if Scully really is immortal, getting the reply, "Yes, it said so right in the show," but Darin Morgan has repeatedly explained that he had meant this line as a way for Clyde to be kind to Scully, knowing how she died, yet denying that she would. He told TVLine, "that was not my intention. That was something fans went crazy with — and they're free to go as crazy as they want." Immortal Scully or not, "Clyde Bruckman's Final Repose" remains one of The X-Files' must-watch episodes.

To enable Siri Recap on your Apple Watch, first download and install iOS 27.3 beta on your iPhone. Then install watchOS 27.3 beta on your Apple Watch. Note: Only the latest Apple Watch models support this Apple Audio Intelligence feature, including the Ultra 4 and Series 12.

The last step is to setup and listening schedule for Apple's Siri Recap feature (or not). To set one, tap on "Times" and select and confirmed your desired listening hours. Or, tap Not now” to set one up later. On the following screen, enable notifications for Siri Recaps or don't by tapping "Not now."

#3442. These Signature Sony Headphones Are Under $200 Ahead of Black Friday

The Sony WH-1000XM6 headphones are the most recent entry in Sony's 1000X series, which has been around since 2016. They're the best over-ear headphones in terms of audio quality currently on the market—but not everyone can (or needs to) drop nearly half a grand on headphones.

The WH-1000XM5 are a generation older and were at the top of their class until they were supplanted by the XM6. I have been a loyal customer of the 1000X line for many years; they're my go-to headphones for most activities. The WH-1000XM5 received an "outstanding" review from PCMag for their top-notch audio quality and exceptional audio when using the best-in-class active noise cancellation. The headphones are also well-designed to be comfortable for long listening sessions. The ear controls use tapping and swiping, which isn't my favorite, but it's what all modern headphones are moving toward. There's a companion app that lets you adjust your EQ settings to your liking, including what the swiping and tapping functions do.

These headphones also have a stereo 3.5mm connection, which is perfect for those who want to use a cable and not worry about battery life. And speaking of battery life, Sony says you can expect about 30 hours, but it will vary depending on your use of ANC. They are compatible with AAC, LDAC, and SBC codecs and have multipoint connection, meaning you can pair them with more than one device at the same time.

Personally, I think the value for the money you get with the XM5 for $198 is better than paying full price for the XM6. If you're looking to get ahead of the Black Friday chaos and secure an amazing deal on great headphones, this is it.
