Using AI as your assistant shopper before you take the plunge

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It seems like in recent years, Black Friday sales happen a whole lot sooner than the actual day we all expect them to hit our timelines.

Instead of rushing out of the house as soon as it hits midnight while my Thanksgiving dinner is still digesting, I just have to keep an eye out for all the early online deals in the weeks leading up to that cost-effective holiday. The likes of Best Buy, Amazon, Walmart and Target are already posting up their biggest discounts, which have compelled me to set up an alert with Meta Muse whenever any ones geared toward video games go live.

But before I decide to go all-in on any Black Friday purchase, I’ve promised myself to tag in ChatGPT as my online shopping assistant to do a few things first. And with the following methods, fitting prompts and a bit of outside research, you’ll have a much easier time navigating the bargain-filled waters of Black Friday.

From choosing what’s actually worth purchasing to doing a final audit of everything you’re planning to buy, these are the best ways to use ChatGPT before you spend a single dime on Black Friday.

For the past couple of years, my Black Friday wishlist has been dominated by OLED TVs, gaming headsets, kitchen appliances (I’ve been in the market for a soda maker for far too long…) and anything else that requires it to be plugged in.

But once I actually look over that list and consider what’s worth adding to my already crowded bedroom that’s ruled by every piece of consumer tech you can think of, I start to wonder if I really need all of the items I’m hoping get a major Black Friday sale. ChatGPT can come in to help during this sort of conundrum by helping you decide what items on your wishlist are worth a purchase and which ones should be skipped entirely.

This prompt should make your final Black Friday purchasing decisions a lot easier to deal with:

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

Here’s my Black Friday wishlist: [list of items]. My total budget is [dollar amount], and I already own [list of items]. Ask me [number] questions about what I actually need, then rank my list into buy, consider, and skip. Explain your reasoning.

Coming across a major price drop for something you’ve been eyeing for a good while hits all the right happiness sensors in my brain. But it’s always good to snap out of that optimistic mode and be more of a realist to see if that price is really that good of a deal.

ChatGPT can step in to check whether the advertised Black Friday sale price you’ve come across is really a steal or if that newly discounted price isn’t as great as it’s being marketed. Doing some price-drop digging with this prompt could propel you to look for a better deal on your most wanted Black Friday item:

This exact model [number or product link] is advertised at [dollar amount], supposedly down from [dollar amount]. Search for documented price history and previous sale prices. Is this unusually cheap or a routine discount? Cite dated sources and say what you couldn’t verify.

I’m prone to balling out on Black Friday, which is a bad habit I’m trying to leave in the past this year. To the point where I’m going to try to stay under $200 while I pick up the discounted items I really need. So, for the types of items that have the best practical uses in my kitchen and mancave, I’ll look up specific products I’ve been keeping a close eye on while also considering cheaper options that may fulfill the same uses as my wish-listed goods.

The following prompt is worth using if you’re approaching your future Black Friday sales from the same viewpoint:

I’m buying a [product name] for [list of specific uses], with a maximum budget of [dollar amount]. Identify my must-have specifications, then compare three suitable options. Include a cheaper or previous-generation alternative and explain what I would actually sacrifice.

For those items that require spending a whole lot more than just the initial entry price, it’s good to know what else you might be putting money toward when that item comes into your possession. Printers, coffee makers, video game consoles and mobile phones immediately come to mind as the products that reach into your pocket for additional charges. Subscriptions, required accessories, replacement parts, delivery and possible installation of said devices spring up as the type of charges I’m alluding to.

Putting the following ChatGPT prompt to good use during Black Friday should give you a clearer picture of everything you’ll possibly be paying for beyond the entry fee for whatever you’re considering buying:

Compare the first-year and three-year costs of these products: [links]. Include required accessories, subscriptions, replacement supplies, shipping, and installation where relevant. Separate optional extras from necessities and label estimates.

I love to go digging for product reviews on Reddit since I feel like the takes on there are usually pretty reliable. Anyone who takes the time out of their day to pen a 2000+-word review of their new SteelSeries Arctis Nova Pro gaming headset for free in a dedicated headphone subreddit has to be reliable, right? The same goes for folks who list out all the pros, cons and accompanying pics of whatever product they chose to say a few words about in the Amazon reviews section.

The following prompt should do you a lot of good when it’s time to see if the Black Friday item you’re planning to buy is highly rated or a total bust that comes with a serious cause of buyer’s remorse:

Research independent reviews and owner feedback for [exact model name or product link]. Identify recurring complaints, long-term reliability concerns, and the strongest positives. Distinguish measured test results from anecdotes, cite sources, and explain who should avoid this product.

There are those instances where you come across a price that may be a bit too good to be true once Black Friday sales start taking over your timeline. That highly discounted price may carry some factors that you may have never considered before, such as its actual seller (even if it’s being sold through a major online retailer), its condition (new or refurbished) and everything that comes with its return policy.

Putting the next prompt into ChatGPT should help you get a better understanding of what you’re planning to pick up and what catches (if any) may be attached to it:

Review this listing and its policies: [links or text]. Identify who sells and ships it, its condition, warranty coverage, return deadline, return shipping costs, restocking fees, and exclusions. Flag anything unclear that I should confirm before paying.

Before hitting that checkout button, it might be worth taking one last look at your digital cart full of Black Friday goodies and seeing if you need everything or could do without a few of them. Presenting your cart to ChatGPT and asking it to consider the biggest arguments against actually getting anything inside it is worth a shot. Sometimes you just need a second opinion to talk you out of buying yet another set of kitchen utensils or a blender just because it’s heavily discounted (and because you probably have one already and just want a new one).

Take this final prompt to ChatGPT and let it help you take a closer look at your Black Friday cart to reconsider what you’re buying:

Audit this cart: [items and prices]. My budget is [dollar amount], and my priorities are [priorities]. Make the strongest practical case against each purchase. Flag duplicate functions, compatibility issues, and unnecessary extras. Recommend a final cart within budget, allowing me to buy nothing.

We’re nowhere near Black Friday, but a whole slew of sales have begun littering everyone’s inboxes and timelines in the weeks ahead of that consumer-friendly holiday. With ChatGPT in your corner as a digital shopping assistant, you can use any of the aforementioned prompts to let it help you shop smarter.

Gather the evidence the chatbot has presented to you, do a bit of research of your own to check if its claims are factual and make your Black Friday purchasing decisions from there. Going the extra mile to use AI to help you comprehend what you’re considering buying on Black Friday is certainly worth doing this year and beyond, once you recognize how helpful it can be.

#3438. Five Hacks Every Una Watch User Should Know

The Una watch is pretty much made to be hackable, with its interchangeable parts and open development environment. But it’s also pretty barebones at launch, without many features available yet. However, here are five things I’ve discovered I can do with it—and I hope to expand this list quite a bit as the device and its community mature.

Because the Una watch has a regular USB-C port, you don’t need to remember any specific cable, dongle, or adapter to charge it. I knew that, but it didn’t occur to me until recently that I didn’t need a computer or a wall outlet to plug into the other end. I was able to take a USB-C to USB-C cable—the same kind I might carry around to charge my phone—and plug one end into my watch and the other into my phone. It charged!

(You can also charge some other devices from a phone, including an Apple Watch, but you’d need to carry around that specific adapter, which is why nobody bothers.)

The Una watch doesn’t have any built-in sleep tracking, but a few community-built apps aim to provide it. The Slumber app, for example, will let you know how long you slept and compare your most recent bedtime with when you usually get to bed. There are no sleep stages (honestly: refreshing, since watches are rarely good at this anyway), and the analysis is done on the watch itself.

But if what you’re really hoping for is a recovery score or an overnight HRV reading, the HabitLab app combines that with habit tracking. Every evening, the watch will buzz and ask you to check off which habits or factors played into your day: Alcohol and late meals are among the options, and the watch will automatically detect morning or evening workouts to add them to the list. In the morning, the watch asks you how you slept, and then it gives you a score based on your resting heart rate, HRV, and your subjective rating.

The app is supposed to be able to put together trends and insights from this data, but I haven’t managed to get it to do this. Maybe it’s waiting for more data (I’ve been using it a little over a week), or maybe it’s just buggy.

By contrast, the barcode app worked even better than I expected it to. It’s meant for a parkrun barcode; each participant in the free weekly 5K has a number that you can use to check your results online. But it works just as well for other barcodes.

I installed the Barcode app and entered the number for my library card. Perhaps because of the watch’s MIP screen, I found this barcode scanned more reliably than any barcodes I’ve previously tried to use on a watch. The library scanner picked it up just fine on the first try, and a phone-based scanner also had no problem with it. You can store up to six barcodes, so I’ve also entered a few others, like my grocery discount card.

The app supports QR codes as well as regular barcodes, and to enter a QR code, you just type in a shortened URL. (It needs to be 22 characters or less.) This means that the Barcode app is also a QR code creator, a nifty feature indeed.

Seeing how soon the sun sets is a bit of a downer as we leave daylight saving time and get into the dark winter months, but it’s also helpful in planning. The Sun & Moon Face puts a graphic on your wrist that shows how far along the sun is in its trajectory across the sky for the day. When evening is approaching, you’ll see just how little time you have left.

The app grabs your GPS location once a day, which means that for the first few hours I wore it, the sunrise and sunset times were incorrectly listed as 6 a.m. and 6 p.m. But as long as you aren’t flying to a drastically new location every day, the app does the job just fine. As a bonus, it changes the color of the screen’s sky to show daylight, nighttime, or sunrise/sunset colors.

If you want to hack this hackable watch, you might as well take the plunge and try to build something yourself. Instructions are here to download the development tools for Windows, Mac, or Linux, and there are tutorials for different features you might want to use and implement. There are also about a dozen example apps you can build on, including activity trackers, watch faces, and glances. I'm not much of a coder myself, but this is the friendliest setup I've seen for someone to get into building their own apps for a watch.

#3437. The Best Ongoing Science Fiction Franchise Is A Secret To 99% Of Fans

Science fiction comics have no shortage of sprawling universes, but one of the most ambitious currently being built has taken an unusual route to reach readers. Three Worlds / Three Moons, or 3W/3M, is a shared science-fiction setting created by Jonathan Hickman, Mike del Mundo, Mike Huddleston, and Nick Spencer. It began online in 2021, inviting readers to follow the worldbuilding process as it happened rather than simply receiving a finished comic.

That approach has helped 3W/3M grow into something bigger than a conventional comic-book series. Its creators have developed thousands of pages of stories and lore, experimented with digital reading platforms, and built a community around the universe. Dark Horse's 2026 publishing partnership is bringing the project to a much wider comic-shop and bookstore audience, but the printed books are only one part of its appeal.

Hickman introduced the project on August 9, 2021, describing it as a "concept universe" rather than a single storyline. Individual characters, locations, histories, and comics would contribute to a larger whole. Its foundational conflict moves through recurring eras in which science and magic rise and fall, giving the setting room to support stories across vastly different periods.

The premise is deliberately wider than a single space-faring adventure. The worldbuilding ranges across Akva, Therra, and Heir, alongside three moons, with societies, belief systems, economies, and political structures that give each corner of the universe its own identity. The creators wanted those details established before individual plots needed them, so the world could feel as if it existed beyond any protagonist.

The original creative group brought together Hickman with artists del Mundo and Huddleston, whose visual and design work helped shape the setting from the ground up. Nick Spencer later joined the core team, while other writers and artists contributed individual systems and stories. The project was conceived as a place where different creative voices could build connected material, not simply as one writer's long-running serial.

That approach also explains why the series can feel different from a traditional monthly comic. Hickman wanted stories of varying lengths and formats, with releases appearing when the work was ready rather than being forced into a standard issue count. He was also interested in restoring surprise to comics publishing, letting readers encounter new stories and artwork without every release being mapped out through conventional previews.

Jonathan Hickman and Mike del Mundo's 64-page graphic novel

Jonathan Hickman's introduction to the universe

Further exploration of the setting's lore

Geography and locations across the three worlds and three moons

Historical events, stories, and additional lore

The audience was part of the plan from the beginning. In his launch essay, Hickman said the team wanted readers to have a front-row seat during the creation process, with meaningful input at certain stages. That did not mean turning every plot point into a vote or handing over authorship. Instead, the creators made the development of characters, environments, lore, and creative decisions unusually visible.

That transparency became a key part of 3W/3M's identity. Through online posts, the team shared comics alongside process material and conversations about how the universe was designed. Readers could see how visual ideas connected to cultural details, why a place appeared where it did, or how a society's rules influenced the stories set inside it. Worldbuilding became part of the entertainment, not disposable bonus material.

The move into wider print distribution began with Dark Horse's announcement in February 2026. The publisher brought the universe to the direct market with Foundations, a 32-page, magazine-sized one-shot released on July 8 for $6.99. Written by Hickman and Spencer, with art by del Mundo and Huddleston, it follows astronaut and explorer Tajo Vallar on a doomed expedition to a dormant moon, where he uncovers mysteries that reignite an ancient conflict. Foundations builds on earlier digital material, including Fable and Ruin, which introduced Tajo, but gives new readers a clear entry point that does not require navigating years of online posts.

Dark Horse followed that launch with three oversized hardcover sourcebooks announced on July 17, 2026: [SYSTEMS], [MAPS], and [HISTORIES]. Each is planned as a 200-page, 8.5-by-11-inch volume combining comics with reference material and lore. The first, [SYSTEMS], is scheduled for February 2, 2027, at $39.99. Its twelve stories and data pages examine Therran birth assessments, royal duels on Heir, pirate searches for the treasure Khor, and the lore surrounding the gods.

Astarion, Karlach, and other fan-favorite heroes are officially returning in 2027 with new adventures that expand the world of Baldur’s Gate 3.

[MAPS], due April 6, 2027, functions as an atlas, charting locations from Akva's Khor-rich waters to Therra's labyrinths and Heir's rougher districts. It also includes twelve stories, with contributors such as James Stokoe and Juni Ba. [HISTORIES] follows on June 1, 2027, collecting six comics with lore and data that establish the worlds' timeline. Together, the three books offer newcomers a structured introduction to the setting while giving longtime readers more context for its cultures, geography, and past.

#3436. 10 Greatest Disney Movies That Are 10/10 Masterpieces

In 1923, brothers Walt and Roy O. Disney founded the Walt Disney Company to create their own run of animated shorts. From such humble beginnings, Disney has now grown to become perhaps the largest media conglomerate in the world, having absorbed the likes of Lucasfilm, Marvel, and 20th Century Fox. Though they now have their hands in everything from live action movies to theme parks, they still put effort into their animated movies, though recent years have seen them eclipsed by studios like DreamWorks and Sony when it comes to creativity and effort.

Still, there's no denying Disney has created some of the most well-known and beloved movies of all time. Regardless of when they first released, these movies continue to delight new and old viewers thanks to their strong writing, iconic characters, catchy songs, and the sense of fun and classic "Disney Magic" that ties them all together.

Aladdin (Scott Weinger) is a street rat living in the city of Agrabah with his monkey Abu (Frank Welker), who longs for a life of wealth and luxury so that nobody will ever look down on him again. After he is arrested following a chance meeting with the rebellious Princess Jasmine (Linda Larkin), Aladdin is recruited by the Royal Vizier, Jafar (Jonathan Freeman), to go inside the Cave of Wonders (Frank Welker) and retrieve a magic lamp. Aladdin discovers that the lamp contains a genie (Robin Williams) who is bound to grant three wishes to whomever holds the lamp, which he plans to use to become a prince and woo Jasmine.

Aladdin is one of the best examples of Disney's ability to combine comedy with heartfelt storytelling. Williams' performance as the Genie is so iconic that it changed how animated films handle celebrity voice actors, but when not throwing out rapid-fire jokes, he has a very sincere relationship with Aladdin that plays into the movie's themes about self-acceptance and integrity. The rest of the film is also great too: Jaffar stands tall as one of Disney's best villains thanks to his charisma, the animation is colorful and stylistic, and the songs catchy and all key to the story and characters.

While sailing from England to Port Royal, Elizabeth Turner (Lucinda Dryzek and Kiera Knightly) helps to rescue a young boy named William Turner (Dylan Smith and Orlando Bloom) from a shipwreck, and takes his golden medallion so he wouldn't be mistaken for a pirate. Years later, Elizabeth is kidnapped by the dreaded pirate ship The Black Pearl, and learns that the medallion is the key to freeing them from their curse of undeath. To save her, Will recruits the help of Captain Jack Sparrow (Johnny Depp), an eccentric pirate who has a history with the Pearl and its captain, Hector Barbossa (Geoffrey Rush).

Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl is the most successful live-action adaptation of Disney’s theme park rides, and spawned an entire franchise of swashbuckling adventure stories. The movie is the perfect combination of memorable characters, fast-paced sword fights, high-seas action, and creative storytelling that weaves mythology and real history. Of all the characters, Jack Sparrow easily stands out the most thanks to Depp's phenomenal performance, and has cemented himself as one of the most iconic pirates in pop-culture history.

Ariel (Jodi Benson) is the youngest daughter of the Sea King, Triton (Kenneth Mars), but, much to his frustration, she has a fascination with the surface world and regularly goes looking for human artifacts. One night, she rescues Prince Eric (Christopher Daniel Barnes) after his ship is caught in a storm, and falls deeply in love with him. The whole affair is overseen by the sea witch Ursula (Pat Carroll), who plans to use Ariel's emotional vulnerability in her plan to usurp control of the sea from Triton.

The Little Mermaid is the movie that kick-started Disney's Renaissance, an era where Disney became the undisputed king of pop-culture. Even today, the movie still captivates audiences with its Broadway-style musical numbers by Alan Menken and Howard Ashman, and the underwater world is so lavishly animated. Character wise, Ariel and Eric have a pretty solid romance thanks to the film giving them time to develop as a couple, Triton is a solid father who goes through an arch regarding letting his daughter live her own life, and Urusla is so deliciously evil with her showmanship and Carroll's bombastic voice.

When an evil queen (Lucille La Verne) learns that her stepdaughter, Snow White (Adriana Caselotti), is more beautiful than her, she tasks her huntsman (Stuart Buchanan) with killing her. The huntsman can't bring himself to do it and instead tells the princess to run into the woods and never return. With the help of woodland animals, Snow White arrives at a cottage inhabited by seven dwarfs, who agree to let her stay with them.

Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs is not just the first Disney film, but also the first animated feature film in North America, and the first cell-shaded animated feature film. The movie set the bar for how to do fairy tale adaptations, with a story that plays on the audience's emotions to pull them into the character's struggles, hopes, and ambitions. The queen also set a very high bar for Disney villains thanks to her majestic and commanding presence in her normal form, and the cackling, bombastic villainy she exews upon transforming into her grotesque hag form.

Deep in the woods on a spring's day, the son of a stag called the Great Prince of the Forest (Fred Shields) is born. Named Bambi (Bobby Stewart, Hardie Albright, John Sutherland, and Donnie Duunagan), he grows up in the care of his mother (Paula Winslowe) and makes friends with a rabbit named Thumper (Peter Behn, Tim Davis, and Sam Edwards) and a skunk nicknamed Flower (Stan Alexander, Tim Davis, and Sterling Holloway). However, things become more difficult as the seasons change, and a mysterious creature called Man comes to the forest.

Bambi has gone from being a financial failure on release to one of the most beloved and respected animated animal films. It avoids excessive anthropomorphization of its characters, which, combined with the more realistic animal designs, presents the movie more as a snapshot of the natural world than a proper narrative. Its backgrounds by Tyrus Wong are also some of the most stylistic in any Disney film, using watercolor patterns to create a forest that feels all the more realistic and mysterious.

Four of the largest communities on the planet, and four completely different reasons to belong to one. Here is yours, what it would give you, and the argument you would be having within a week.

You belong to the fandom that is really about comfort. Hogwarts works on people because it is a place rather than a plot, and the pull is not the wizard war so much as the corridors, the food, the weather and the sense that somebody is expecting you.

You belong to the deepest fandom on this list, the one where somebody has always read further than you and is quietly delighted to say so. Middle-earth rewards patience more than any other world in popular culture.

You belong to the loudest and largest tent of the four, the one where three generations are all watching the same thing and none of them agree about any of it. That disagreement is not a flaw in this fandom, it is the main activity.

You belong to the thinking fandom, the one that turns up for the argument rather than the explosion. Trek has always been a series of ethical problems in space, and the people who love it love being asked what they would have done.

In an alternate 1940s where humans live alongside living cartoon characters, Eddie Valiant (Bob Hoskins) is a private detective who has fallen onto hard times after the death of his brother at the hands of a toon. The day after he photographs Jessica Rabbit (Kathleen Turner) playing patty cake with the owner of Toontown, Marvin Acme (Stubby Kaye), he learns that Jessica's husband, Roger (Charles Fleischer), apparently murdered Acme in a jealous rage. Roger, however, seeks out Eddie to prove his innocence and protect him from the psychotic judge of Toontown, Judge Doom (Christopher Lloyd).

Who Framed Roger Rabbit is a revolutionary movie that has some of the best examples of mixing animated characters into live-action footage. This is thanks to the incredible level of detail that went into their creation, from using strings to move items the toon characters would hold to actively changing the shading on the characters to reflect changes in lighting. Beyond its technical achievements, it's also a very solid mystery with a strong film noir aesthetic, and some terrific performances from Hoskins and Lloyd.

To repair Mickey Mouse's declining popularity, Walt conceived an animated short based on Paul Dukas' symphonic poem The Sorcerer's Apprentice. As the budget grew too big to justify, Walt decided to turn the project into a feature film that would combine multiple shorts based on classical music. Leopold Stokowski was brought on as conductor, and Deems Taylor served as Master of Ceremonies.

The result was Fantasia, an ambitious film that combined music and animation like never before or since. The Disney animators put their all into each segment, matching the music with everything from proper narratives to simple abstract shapes that might come to one's mind as they hear the music. Disney would try to make similar films, but none of them ever matched the artistic creativity of the original movie.

Frustrated that his children Jane (Karen Dotrice) and Michael (Matthew Garber) have driven off another nanny, George Banks (David Tomlinson) places an ad in the paper for a strict nanny who will set them right. The next day, a wind blows away all the women who came to apply, and George instead hires Mary Poppins (Dame Julie Andrews), a woman who flew in on an umbrella, and meets the requirements of a separate ad made by the kids. Mary is indeed stern with the kids as needed, but also takes them on fantastical adventures with the help of her handyman friend, Bert (Dick Van Dyke).

Mary Poppins was famously despised by the author of the original books, P. L. Travers, but to general audience, it is one of Disney's biggest successes. This is thanks to its ability to blend the fun, whimsical adventures that Mary Poppins takes the children through with the hard-hitting but relatable reality of a father trying to rebuild a relationship with his kids. The songs by The Sherman Brothers help to convey this wide spectrum of emotions, with one song in particular, "Feed the Birds," having the honor of being Walt Disney's favourite from any of his movies.

All the animals of the Pride Lands travel to Pride Rock to celebrate the birth of the lion cub Simba (Johnathan Taylor Thomas and Matthew Broderick), son of King Mufasa (James Earl Jones). As he grows, Simba is educated by his father about the importance of maintaining the circle of life, but the young cub is too focused on how exciting it will be when he has the throne. Unfortunately, his uncle Scar (Jeremy Irons) lusts after the throne himself, and makes an alliance with a clan of hyenas to eliminate both Simba and Mufasa so he can take it.

The Lion King began life as a side-project to fill a 1994 release slot while Disney's best talent worked on Pocahontas, but it has since gone down in history as one of the most beloved animated films, and the highest grossing traditionally-animated one. The movie uses bold colors, wide shots, and foreground tricks to make the African Savannah feel massive and epic in scale, which pairs well with the story's themes about duty, responsibility, and learning from the mistakes of the past. Scar is also widely regarded as one of the best Disney villains thanks to how seamlessly the animation by Andreas Deja mixes with Irons' performance, creating a cunning, vicious villain who actually gets further in his plans than most Disney antagonists.

After refusing to shelter an old woman during a storm, a spoiled prince (Robby Benson) is turned into a beast and told to find love and be loved in return before the last petal of an enchanted rose falls, or he and his staff shall be cursed forever. Ten years later, he imprisons an inventor named Maurice (Rex Everhart) who trespassed during a storm, and meets Maurice's daughter, Belle (Paige O'Hara), when she comes looking for him. Belle offers to take her father's place as the Beast's prisoner, and, though things don't start off the best, the two do eventually come to see that there is more to the other than first appears.

Beauty and the Beast overcame a brutal production to not only receive near-universal acclaim, but also become the first animated film to be nominated for the Academy Award for Best Picture—and remains the only 2D animated film and the only one from when the Oscars had five nominees instead of ten. The reason for this success is how seamlessly the movie weaves the classic themes of the original fairy tale with an updated story that gives all the characters more developed personalities, resulting in a believable romance and both Belle and Beast ranking among Disney's best characters. The animation is also beautiful, the songs by Menken and Ashman iconic, and its message about change and seeing what lies beneath the surface is timeless.

Thomas Markle cut off his ankle monitor in the early morning hours Tuesday ... the Department of Justice says.

#3434. Everything You Should Know About This Year's Black Friday Sales

As is often the case with major sales these days, retailers are increasingly blurring the lines between early deals and the official start of a sale. Black Friday sales appear to be becoming a month-long event, with early deals appearing in the first week of the month. If you haven't been paying attention, major retailers have already put out their plans and even started churning out deals. But you're still in time to make this upcoming Black Friday sale a great one. Here is everything you need to know to prepare you for the big sale.

Black Friday is always the day after Thanksgiving. This year, Black Friday starts at midnight on Nov. 27. Cyber Monday is the Monday following Black Friday, which starts at midnight on Nov. 30.

The major retailers doing sales are the usual: Amazon, Best Buy, Target, Walmart, Home Depot, and many others. Currently, Walmart has publicized its plans already and has early deals available. Best Buy is offering one of the largest Black Friday and Cyber Week sales, with multiple events and early deals. Target has a three-day event. Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Cyber Monday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026.

Black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, use price trackers or refer to guides like our live blog that use price trackers for you, and don’t stress over finding the perfect timing. The “best” deal will always depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers that can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot.

Unlike Spring or Summer sales, Black Friday doesn't focus on specific categories, which means everything is fair game for discounts. In previous years, we've seen tech, tools, fitness equipment, outdoor supplies and furniture, bedding, video games, kitchen appliances, and more. This is one of the best times to make a list of what you need and start tracking prices. You're likely to find what you're looking for discounted, and probably at its lowest price it has ever been. If you'd like to avoid having to do all that work, we always do it for you. Just follow our Black Friday coverage.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Use price tracking tools to determine if the deals you're keeping tabs on are actually a deal. If you feel like that's too much work, we already do that for you, so follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products makes you focus and make smarter decisions.

Yes. Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and Home Depot will all have in-store deals, some of which you might not find online, so if you're able to take a trip to your local retailer, keep your eyes open for different deals.

Prime Day and Black Friday are the two best times of the year to get the best deals on most purchases. Of course, depending on what you're shopping for, you might find other opportunities throughout the year, but in general, Prime Day and Black Friday have the best sales.

I’ve been pretty vocal about what I don’t like about the iPhone Duo so far, from the lack of a telephoto zoom and missing Face ID to the unoptimized apps and hefty weight. (Why can’t this thing be as light as the Galaxy Fold 8?)

But now that I’ve been living with and testing the iPhone Duo for about a month, there’s some things that I really like about this device that I think puts it at the top of our best foldable phone list. Here are 7 reasons why I think it’s worth the $2,000 price tag.

To say that I’m a Slack power user would be an understatement. As editor in chief of Tom’s Guide, I’m constantly jumping between multiple threads, weighing in on everything from photos and production, to collaborating with other departments. And it’s really nice to be able to quickly scroll through rooms and contacts, while still seeing message content on the right.

The iPhone Duo is even smart enough to adapt the layout as you fold the device. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 app isn’t even two columns.

Slack looks pretty slick on the front screen, too, even though the menu items take up a lot of real estate on the right side. You can quickly respond with the wide keyboard without a problem.

Yup, it’s overdue, but I really appreciate being able to run two apps side by side on the iPhone Duo. For example, I can look up what to order in DoorDash while having a chat with the family in Messages.

I also like being able to easily drag and drop images from the Photos app into Google Drive without having to start all over again each time by looking up the folder name. It’s a huge time saver. To be fair, the Galaxy Fold 8 can do three apps at once, plus floating windows on top. But I’m fine with two apps for now.

You might not be able to run four apps at once, but the Multiview feature in YouTube TV on the iPhone Duo lets you watch four of your favorite shows at the same time in a grid — just like Android foldables. You can tune into the audio on any of the four windows just by taping your finger on the live video thumbnail. And you tap again to watch the show in full-screen mode. It’s one of those things you just can’t do on a regular iPhone.

For me, I like being able to toggle between multiple NFL or NCAA football games on the weekend or ESPN’s First Take and CNN during the week.

Part of the reason why I don’t make many FaceTime calls is that I don’t really feel like holding up my phone the whole time. That complaint goes away with the iPhone Duo, which lets you fold the phone in half and prop it up like a laptop. When you’re in this view, you can make FaceTime calls hands free, which is nice because I like to talk with my hands anyway.

The 4MP FaceTime camera isn’t the sharpest, but it gets the job done.

If there’s one app that I would show people if I had 30 seconds to explain why the iPhone Duo is cool, it would be Netflix. The app has been developed from the ground up for this foldable, and it shows.

For example, on the cover display you can skim through mobile-friendly shorts that fill the screen, like Instagram or TikTok. As you’d expect, shows and movies look great on the large 7.6-inch display, as I discovered when watching “The Diplomat” on a long flight. But if you want to snack while you’re watching, you can put the Duo in tabletop mode so your video is up top and controls down below. Or, if you prefer, you can watch in tent mode.

Standby is one of my favorite iPhone features from the past few years, because you can turn your device into an alarm clock when you’re ready to go to bed. But the iPhone Duo takes that to the next level. You get a clock when you put the Duo in tent mode, and when it’s time to get up a soft glow emanates from the inside of the foldable to help wake you up.

Plus, there’s another Standby mode. When you put the Duo in portrait mode and fold it half-way standing up on a table or desk, you’ll see a clock and calendar on the left and some of your favorite photos on the right. It’s like a digital photo frame. Plus, you can still easily access Spotify in this mode via the Dynamic Island.

Because the iPhone Duo weighs down my front pocket when walking around, I’ve mostly defaulted to carrying it in my back pocket. And lots of times I’ve sat on this foldable phone — forgetting to take it out first, whether I’m sitting at my desk at the office or just plopping down to watch TV at night.

At least so far, the iPhone Duo has survived my daily use without a scratch or crack. The titanium frame feels super durable to me, and even after a few weeks the crease is not prominent at all when using this device.

Back pain doesn't always originate from your back. For example, tight or weak hips, core muscles, or glutes can cause lower back pain or stiffness, and your back muscles may under- or overfire if you don't focus on proper posture.

That's why exercises that strengthen the muscles around your spine and pelvis, like your core, hips and back, are crucial — it's not just about stretching. There's a specific two-step exercise tucked neatly away that I like to bring out for this exact moment.

It's technically two moves — one for your posterior chain (your back, glutes and hamstrings) and one for your deep core; together, they can strengthen your postural muscles and reduce pain and stiffness.

It gets met with a groan every time I introduce it to my clients' sessions, but if you suffer from a tight lower body or symptoms of sciatica, this could help.

If you struggle with the intensity, reduce the time spent in each position by 10 seconds and try again. Focus on squeezing through your core as you face upward (known as the hollow hold exercise), then squeeze your back and glutes when you are in the prone position (face down, known as the Superman exercise).

You can softly bend your knees if you need to, but otherwise, try to keep your legs straight and toes pointed in both positions. Once you feel comfortable, try adding a gentle rocking motion, a bit like a rocking horse, to the hollow hold.

It's crucial to breathe during exercise, which might sound obvious, but a surprising number of us hold our breath when the body is under stress or strain.

It's crucial to breathe during exercise, which might sound obvious, but a surprising number of us hold our breath when the body is under stress or strain. During workouts, breathing helps regulate blood pressure; did you know your diaphragm also counts as a core muscle? Expansive breathing helps keep your core engaged and posture in check, while diaphragmatic breathing in general is known to help reduce stress.

Focus on generating most of the movement in your Superman position from your mid to upper back rather than excessively arching your lower back, creating a soft banana shape with your body. Switching on your glutes will also help protect your spine as you lift your legs into the air.

It can feel mentally and physically challenging, but done regularly, the two exercises combined can counteract weak postural muscles, which are a negative result of sedentary lifestyles.

Take long, deep breaths and use your exhale to deepen the pose and lift higher.

A novel solution for connecting to the internet on the go, the TP-Link Roam 7 travel router is now down to $87.99 from $119.99 in an early Black Friday deal—marking its lowest price to date, according to price trackers. This is not a full-size home router but, as the name suggests, a compact travel companion that measures roughly the size of a paperback book, with foldable antennas so it slips easily into a bag.

More about convenience than chasing top speeds, you can use the Roam 7 as a standard router, connect it to public wifi to create a private network, or share your phone's internet through USB tethering. It also supports Ethernet input and USB modems, along with range extender and wireless client modes. That flexibility is particularly useful when you’re juggling a laptop, phone, and maybe a tablet and would prefer not to sign each one into a shaky network separately. Setup is straightforward through the TP-Link Tether app: scan a QR code, choose your connection type, and you’re online in a few minutes.

Once it’s running, the hardware covers the basics, with a 2.5 Gbps port for a wired connection like a hotel’s Ethernet jack, a 1 Gbps port for a wired device, and a USB 3.0 port for a storage drive or phone tethering. And since it draws power over USB-C (5V/3A), a basic power bank can keep it going through a long layover or a camping trip. As handy as it is on the road, though, it’s not meant to replace a full-size home router—even with its 5 GHz band and Wi-Fi 7 support—which will generally offer better coverage and more consistent speeds. Real-world performance also depends heavily on your connection and setup. USB tethering, for example, can feel slower than using your phone directly. It also leaves out features like automatic band steering, so you may end up managing networks yourself. Still, if you travel often or need a portable network hub for multiple devices, you’ll find it holds up pretty well.

#3427. There's a New Way to Automatically Back Up Your Android Photos for Free

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you're an Android user looking for a way to save your photos and videos without maxing out your cloud storage space, your device may soon be able to back up automatically to your PC. As spotted by Android Authority, Google included automatic backups from Android to Windows via Quick Share in its release notes for Google Play services v26.43.

Quick Share is a wireless file-sharing feature for Android that allows users to send photos, videos, and documents to nearby devices, including Windows computers and iPhones with AirDrop. The new automatic backup feature, which is likely to roll out gradually, uses Quick Share's functionality to transfer copies of photos and videos on your phone to your PC when nearby.

Since these backups happen locally, you don't need to rely solely on cloud storage in your Google account, nor do you need to remember to initiate transfers of photos and videos between devices. Plus, this is all free and doesn't require a separate cloud service subscription. While you can back up your media to Google Photos, as of earlier this year, more data from your Android backups count toward your Google Account storage cap unless you exclude specific types. Alternatively, you can also cobble together a decent amount of cloud storage from other providers at no extra cost, but automatic backups between Android and Windows minimize the likelihood that you'll forget to save data, and your PC provides plenty of space for free.

Once the feature is available on your device, you'll be able to initiate backups in the Quick Share for Windows app. Your Android and Windows devices must be in close proximity and signed into the same Google Account. You can toggle Automatic backups on and change the settings for what gets backed up and to where. The transfers will then occur wirelessly in the background.

As Android Authority reports, early hints at this feature suggested that Samsung phones and PCs would be excluded from automatic backups, but the release notes don't specify any further details.

If you're clued into social media, or terminally online like I am, you may have noticed posts of people realizing that photos shot on iPhone look different if they stick their hand in the frame. Instead of the drab, washed out browns and greens, you end up with a photo with warmer and more vivid colors than before. The only trade-off is that you need to have your hand in frame to get the effect.

Obviously, I was curious about whether this was actually true, and how much of an impact sticking your hand in shot actually makes to the final photo. As it turns out, yes, I could mimic the same effect by putting my own hand between the camera and the foliage.

And there's a very good reason for it, and that reason means iPhone 18 Pro owners can avoid going to these same extremes.

iphone can’t handle anything colorful unless there’s a hand in the frame https://t.co/C8FVp17gkoOctober 31, 2026

The above pictures were taken on the iPhone 18 Pro Max, and the final pair which were shot with the iPhone 17 Pro Max. As you can see, the coloring in all of the images is pretty washed out with a dreary gray sheen that seems pretty typical of the Old English Autumn. Unlike New England, the leaves aren't nearly as vivid here — but they certainly don't look like that.

Once my hand is in frame (with some help of my white sleeve) the coloring changes for the better. The various shades of red and yellow seem to pop a bit more, and even the greens, which are usually rather unremarkable, seem to look a lot more vibrant.

The effect is more prominent in some photos compared to others. The change is most noticeable with the blackberry bush, to the point that you wouldn't even realize that those photos were taken seconds apart.

You can actually see the change happen in real time with the above video. This screen recording was taken on the iPhone 17 Pro Max, and when my hand pops into frame you can see the color of the preview change. The overall color gets warmer, and the colors start to pop a little more than they had before.

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

In other words, if you're having trouble with the color of your fall foliage not looking as nice as you thought, it's possible that sticking your hand (or something in a very light color) might help things along.

There's a very good reason why this happens, and it all comes down to the fact that most iPhones rely on automatic white balance. In fact, only the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max give users the chance to adjust white balance, a feature that is more common (and more robust) on other cameras — including non-Apple smartphones.

Auto-white balance is common enough, and is used by the camera app to compensate for the ambient light in a specific scene or location. However, utilizing it over manual controls does leave you at the mercy of computational photography algorithms. And in the case of some phones, like older iPhones, you don't have any choice in the matter.

PetaPixel speculates that the iPhone camera could be confusing warmer Fall lighting with an unwanted color cast. To compensate, the camera cools down the image temperature and dulls the natural coloring in the process.

But if you stick something white, or close enough to it, the iPhone camera app will automatically adjust the color temperature across the photo to compensate. That also means that the foliage in the background takes on a warmer hue, and the fall colors appear to be a lot more vivid than the original washed-put image.

Obviously this technique is only going to work for people with lighter skin tones. While we haven't done any testing to see what happens when someone with darker skin puts their own hand in frame, logically the effect would be totally different compared to my own pasty-white hands.

But in those cases you could experiment with using white objects to help trick the software into tweaking the color temperature.

That said, anyone with an iPhone 18 Pro or Pro Max has better control over white balance by tapping the camera menu button on the bottom right of the screen, tapping white balance and then picking one of the five preset options.
